en: The Lamp of Rituals (*Karmapradīpa*). First Chapter, First Section. Homage to the Sāmaveda. Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Table of Contents for the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. May that Lord Hari protect the world—He who is half of the speech of the Four-faced One (Brahmā); whose command, consisting of the Śrutis and Smṛtis, is victorious; whose dust from his feet is worshiped by certain virtuous ones as Dharma, having attained the name "Ganges"; and whom the wise place before them to destroy the darkness arising within the body of knowledge. 1.

In this world, how many kings have there not been whose feet were ever worshipped, who were of pure birth, who were enjoyers of the earth’s nectar, and who were melted by their own splendor? (2) In their great lineage was born one who was the very embodiment of all poetic meters; for he received instruction from a Brahmin, and because of him, Rāḍhā here attains supreme honor. (3) From him issued the fourth section, the Piśāca-khaṇḍa, and likewise another, the Ūlāja; from that came another, the stainless Aṅgulasthāna, beginning with the twice-born caste. (4)
In some manuscripts, the reading is "bāpā. [He was] a lamp of knowledge;

he was born as the sole cause for purifying the circle of the earth, one whose expansion of intellect was constantly clarified through the Vedic ritual, the son of Paritras, named Dhanamjaya, whose conduct was in accordance with his name, and who was previously honored in the assembly of the learned. (5) From him was born Madrekharī, an abode of virtues, worthy of salutation by all the wise, the foremost among the virtuous who stand in the midst of the good, and one whose heart was consecrated by service to the feet of Murāri. (6) From him was born Adadhara, a sovereign of the twice-born... [1.9.1]

His mind was turned away from accepting gifts from kings; he spent his days and nights solely in performing meritorious deeds and for a long time maintained a state of tranquility. From him arose Umāpati, the preeminent leader of the Prabhākara school, who adorned the circle of the earth with his disciples and grand-disciples, and whose crest-jewel was the *Viṃda* [treatise]. That virtuous man, his heart burning with compassion for the petitions of the multitude of supplicants, accepted from King Jayapāla a great gift of many excellent horses.

His younger brother, the virtuous Gna, who had given away his entire fortune as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), rose up like a guru in the *tantra* tradition, being a knower of the Purāṇas. [He was] beneficial to the whole world, possessing stainless qualities, and a Bhūmideva-Vācaspati (a lord of speech among the gods on earth), whose face caused the quarters of the sky to be washed by the mass of flowing currents of the celestial river (the Ganges) poured forth by his grace.
(In the manuscript of the Mahāśrāda, the reading is *hartika*.)

In some manuscripts the reading is *tasā*; in the manuscript of the *Kāmadīpa*, it is *viprajanīna*. In whose heart, which is solely absorbed in the feet of Kṛṣṇa and which bears the locus of authority over Dharma, the abodes of the twice-born dwell, and his glories have shaken off all faults. [1.1] From him was born one who is a worshipper of those learned in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas, who has attained proficiency in the system of the Prabhākara school, and who is bowed to by the virtuous in the assembly and by his circle of friends. Śrī...

Nārāyaṇa, whose soul is eternally devoted to Kṛṣṇa, [composed this]. For the sake of making all matters clear in the *Chandaḥpariśiṣṭa*, that wise man composed this supplement (*pariśiṣṭa*) called the *Akāmā*. [He also composed] the *Prabhā* and the *Anukramaṇikā*. We worship that Great Light (*mahas*), from which everything arises, in whom everything is dissolved, and which is the all-pervading All. I bow to Lord Ṭuṇḍira for the destruction of the array of obstacles; I salute Viśveśa, who is full and complete, for the increase of my wisdom.

I bow with great effort to the great seer Garga, to the sage Kātyāyana, and likewise to the author of the *Pariśiṣṭas*. And I bow again and again to my ancestral teachers, by whose mere touch of grace my intellect has become firm. This commentary named *Prabhā* is being composed by me for the *Chandaḥpariśiṣṭa* created by Kātyāyana, which is like a lamp illuminating the path.

"By that very [author]," so reads the manuscript *ka*. **Karmapradīpa** [Chapter 1, Section 1] Now, I shall clearly demonstrate, like a lamp, the procedure for those rites prescribed by Āśvalāyana, as well as for other rites, which are not clearly defined—such as the rites of the householder’s stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) for the young student (*māṇavaka*) who has completed his Vedic studies, beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), and other rites enjoined by Manu and others. **Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa** Now, following the study of the Veda, for the sake of the young student entering the householder’s stage of life, I shall explain the procedure for the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarman*) such as the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) and others prescribed by Āśvalāyana, as well as for other rites not clearly stated, such as those mentioned by Manu and others, according to the rule: "Whether sitting, standing, or moving forward, wherever there is no such specific injunction."

I shall demonstrate the correct performance of these [rites] and others, like a lamp. Just as a lamp makes objects that are unclear clear, so too am I like a lamp because I clarify what was unclear; this is the "lamp-like nature" attributed to the author or the work. Therefore, the word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetvarthe*). Since the rites prescribed in the scriptures are unclear, I therefore make them manifest. Otherwise, from the performance of household duties in a deficient manner, the young student (*māṇavaka*) would incur sin (*pratyavāya*).

The word *atha* (now/then) also signifies auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). As it has been said: "In ancient times, the two sounds *m* and *tha* emerged from the throat of Brahmā; therefore, both are auspicious. [Commentary: Here, indeed, the venerable Kātyāyana composed this work titled *Karmapradīpa*, also known by the name *Chandaḥpariśiṣṭa*, for the purpose of clarifying those domestic rites (*gṛhyakarman*) prescribed in the *Ṛgveda* as well as other rites that were unclear. This is its brief commentary (*vṛtti*).
[The reading in the manuscript is *anuṣṇavāt*. *L.* (Line number)

[1.1] *Karmapradīpa* begins: "Now, therefore," and so forth. This is the first section (*kāṇḍa*) of the *Karmapradīpa*, which is intended to be explained. Therein, the word *atha* (now/then) is employed at the beginning of a work by a Ṛṣi; according to the Vedic tradition (*śruti*), it serves the purpose of an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*). Alternatively, it signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*), meaning "after the study of the Veda"—this is its sense. The word *ataḥ* (therefore) signifies the reason (*hetu*).

Because some domestic rites (*gṛhyakarmāṇi*) have been taught by Gṛhyasūtras and not all rites to be performed according to the Vedic meters (*chandoga*) have been taught by Gṛhya authors—for this reason, after the study of the Vedas, one who is a *chandogabrahmacārin* and desires to enter the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) must study the Gṛhyasūtras and related texts in order to fully understand the domestic rites and so forth.

In that regard, due to the absence of a correct understanding of the procedures for other rites that are unclear or whose performance is prescribed by Śaunaka, there may arise a deficiency in the ritual or an error in its execution. Therefore, I shall clearly demonstrate, like a lamp, the procedure for those rites stated by Śaunaka and for other rites to be performed according to the Śaunaka tradition that are not explicitly clear. Just as a lamp clearly reveals objects that are indistinct in dim darkness, such is the purpose [of this work].

And since there is no dispute regarding the fact that the rites mentioned here are to be performed by the *chandoga*s (singers of the Sāman), it is understood that other rites as well must likewise be performed by the *chandoga*s. According to the maxim: "When a well-known meaning is present in proximity to one that is not well known, the latter is understood to belong to the same class due to the force of that association. Furthermore, they say: "Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*viprayoga*), association (*sāhacarya*), qualification (*virodhita*), purpose (*artha*), context (*prakaraṇa*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and the proximity (*saṃnidhi*) of another word—these are the means [of determining meaning]. This is like a lamp.

The sacred thread (*upavīta*) should be stretched upwards, woven with threads, and not twisted; it should be spread out, and for it, a single knot is prescribed. [1.1] "Competence, propriety, place, time, gender, and accent—these are the causes for the recollection of specific meanings when there is no restriction regarding the meaning of a word. Thus [it is said]. This very point is confirmed by the established tradition of the middle region (*madhyadeśa*). For students nowadays call this work the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*, and the author of the treatise likewise [intends it so].

Just as one might see something written among mostly insignificant items and think, "This must be significant," so too, when something is recited among what is mostly to be performed by the *chandoga* (sāmavedic priests), the thought arises: "This is to be performed by the *chandoga*. If such a thought arises, it is not proper to discard it without a reason. And thus there is the maxim: "Because of the statement regarding the majority. Therefore, whatever else is prescribed among the flow of duties to be performed by the *chandoga*, that too is determined to be a duty to be performed by the *chandoga*.

Therefore, when a sequence of ritual acts (*karmavāha*) is to be performed both before and after [the *chandoga* section], whatever is recited in their midst—whether it be a ritual act or not—will, according to the maxim of the "worn-out third" (*ajaratṛtīya*), not belong to the *chandogas*, but rather to those other than the *chandogas*. Why then is this improper application [of the term] made? Indeed, I do not understand this. And thus ends the *Parishishtaprakasha*.

Gobhila stated that the ritual must be performed by one wearing the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread) and holding water in the palm of the hand; he further stated: "One makes the *yajñopavīta* from a thread, or from cloth, or even from *kuśa* grass. By this, it is merely stated that the *yajñopavīta* is a thread. That very point is clarified by the mention of its specific qualities. [15.1b] *Karmapradīpa*: Having wound three threads counter-clockwise (*vāmāvarta*), they should be made into a triple-strand (*triguṇa*) by winding them clockwise (*dakṣiṇāvarta*). In this way, there are nine strands.

That same thread, when spread out, constitutes the *upavīta*. Sages prescribe that it should have three strands (*trisara*) and a single knot (*granthi*). As for the material of that thread: for a Brāhmaṇa, it should be made of cotton (*kārpāsa*) or silk (*kauśeya*). Thus says Manu: "The *upavīta* should be made of cotton, consisting of three threads (*trivṛt*), and twisted to the right; for a Kṣatriya, it should be made of hempen fibers (*śaṇa*), and for a Vaiśya, it should be made of wool. Baudhāyana states: "The *yajñopavīta* may be made of *kauśa*, gold, or *visti* [wool], reaching down to the navel. Here, *kauśa* refers to what is produced from the *kosi* plant, such as flax and the like; *sauva* refers to cotton (*kārpāsa*).

*Visvitam* means that which has been spun ninefold; this is the meaning, according to the Vedic revelation: "The *vivarta*s are indeed nine. And as for the statement of Devala: "Cotton, linen, wool, hemp, silk, and bark—these are always available for the sacred thread (*upavīta*) to be worn by the twice-born," that is intended to prescribe the subsequent materials in the absence of each preceding one. Likewise: "One should make the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*); the threads should consist of nine strands, joined with a single knot, or doubled, or tripled."

The term *dviguṇa* (twofold) means that when a *visara* (strand) is not possible, it refers to a *disara* (pair of strands). As for the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "The sacrificial thread (*upavīta*) of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton with six strands and be triple-stranded (*trivṛt*); that of a Kṣatriya should be of linen; and that of a Vaiśya should be of wool"—this also prescribes six strands in the absence of nine strands. According to the *Karmapradīpa*: "Triple-stranded" means *visara*. Alternatively, "ninefold" means six strands by way of two *visaras*. *Kṣauma* is that which is produced from *atasī* (flax).

By this, the statement in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*, "The *upavīta* consists of an odd number of strands and has an uneven number of threads," is also clarified. Furthermore, this wearing of the thread as an *upavīta* applies in the absence of a cloth. Thus says the *Nigamapariśiṣṭa*: "One should make the sacrificial *upavītas* out of cloth; in its absence, with a triple-strand cord (*trivṛt*), or with cords made of *kuśa* grass, *muñja* grass, *bāla* grass, or *śara* reeds. Here, "grass" (*bāla*) refers to *darbha* grass, according to the statement of Devala. And in the case of *kuśa*, *śara*, *bāla*, and so forth, there is no requirement for the rule regarding the number of strands (*guṇa*) and the like, because that rule is prescribed specifically for the [woolen] thread (*sūtra*).

However, threshing and other such acts, being characteristics of the rice (*vrīhi*), must be performed even when [the rice] is used for the purpose of that [sacrificial cake], because they serve its function. But the wearing of the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth is not like that; it does not belong to the sacrificial cake and the like. For the sacrificial cake and such items are not included within the meaning of the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*), but are merely the material substance (*dravya*). Otherwise, since there would be no extension (*atideśa*) of the primary [element], the consequence would be a failure of extension. Others, however, say: the term "wearing of the sacrificial cord" is used figuratively with respect to the upper garment (*uttarīya*) in order to indicate the manner of its placement. *Prabhā* (Commentary): [The commentary explains that while the ritual details of the model sacrifice are extended to the modified sacrifice, certain physical attributes of the materials do not follow suit unless they serve the specific function of those materials.]

Regarding the statement, "He makes the *yajñopavīta* [sacrificial thread], whether it be a cord, a cloth, or even a rope of *kuśa* grass," the *Gṛhyasūtra* of Āśvalāyana merely says, "He makes the *yajñopavīta* a cord. That very point is clarified by specifying its qualities: "triple-stranded" (*trivṛt*). Having made it threefold, it should be twisted; that is, the three strands should be woven together. Thus, by the tripling of the strands, nine threads are produced.

And so indeed says the *Karmapradīpa*: "One should make the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) with a thread consisting of nine strands. The author of the *Saṃgraha* states its definition: "Twisted three times by the right hand and folded by men according to their own scripture, it is remembered as the *yajñopavīta*. Even if the reading were *ūrdhvantu vitataṃ kāryam*, the meaning would be the same.

The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* states that the thread, having been wound three times counter-clockwise, should be wound clockwise. Thus, it becomes a *visara* (spreading) sacred thread (*upavīta*). Because of its connection with sacrifice (*yajña*), the *upavīta* itself is called the *yajñopavīta*. Regarding this, a single knot is desired by the teachers of the Vedas (*chandogācārya*). It is said that some indeed make a knot according to the number of their ancestral lineages (*pravara*); however, by the mention of "a single knot," disapproval of that [practice] is indicated.

As for that which has been stated by others as being doubled and consisting of six threads for the sacred thread (*upavīta*), that refers to those other than the *Chāndogas*. This is because they are the authors of Sūtras belonging to different Vedic branches (*śākhā*). Thus, by the employment of the specific term "its own" (*sva-śabda*) and because cotton is well-known [as the material] for that, the cotton sacred thread belongs to the *Chāndogas*. Likewise, since the Teacher (Āpastamba) mentions "thread or cloth," and from this it is understood that cloth is prescribed in the absence of a thread, it should be understood that the prescription of a thread in the absence of cloth also refers to those other than the *Chāndogas*.

In this regard, although threshing and other such acts are performed even upon barley—which possesses the form of rice according to the injunction "one threshes rice"—nevertheless, there is no rule regarding wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth with respect to clothing and the like that merely perform the function of the *yajñopavīta*. This is because, since the act of wearing the sacred thread is not included within the essential meaning (*padārtha*) of the term *yajñopavīta*, it lacks the status of a duty (*dharma*) pertaining to the *yajñopavīta*; consequently, such a rule does not apply elsewhere.

Since threshing and other such acts do not reside within the referent of the word *vrīhi* (rice), and because in the injunction for threshing and so forth, the word *vrīhi* indicates by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) that which is the means to the intermediate apūrva of the rice-sacrifice, it is indeed proper to perform those acts upon barley. 9. The Lamp of Rituals (*Karmapradīpa*). [1.1] That which, when held at the spine and at the navel, reaches the hips—that shall be the *upavīta* (sacred thread); it should be neither too long nor too short.

*Parīśiṣṭaprakāśa*: 10. Now he states the length of the *upavīta*. One should wear that *upavīta* which, being suspended from the spine and the navel, reaches down to the waist; it should not hang longer than that, nor should it be too short—meaning it should not fall below the knees. This is the rule for the followers of Gṛhyasūtra Ṛgvedin Āśvalāyana. For others, however, the authority is what was stated by Devala: "It must never be worn above the breasts or below the navel."

This same rule applies even to Baudhāyana’s statement, "The *yajñopavīta* [should reach] the navel. A *snātaka* should wear two *yajñopavītas*. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "For those who have completed their studies (*snātaka*), there should always be an inner garment (*antarvāsa*) and another [upper garment]; two *yajñopavītas*, a staff, water, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). (3) [Commentary: He states the measurement of the *upavīta*: "And on the backbone," etc.

That which, when placed over the back and held at the navel, reaches the waist—that is, it hangs down as far as the waist—is the *upavīta* that should be worn; it should not be too long, nor too high, meaning it should not be short. Regarding another measurement, Gṛhyāsaṃgraha states: "It must never be made above the breasts or below the navel; for [if] above the breasts, it destroys prosperity, and [if] below the navel, it causes the loss of austerity."

The reading in the manuscripts *ka*, *kha*, and *ga* is "nātibamyaṃ. [1st Praśna, 1st Khaṇḍa] *Kampradīpa*: "One should always wear the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and always have the top-knot (*śikhā*) tied. Whatever is performed by one who is without the top-knot or without the sacred thread, that has not been performed at all" (4). According to the maxim that "whatever is recited in connection with a specific subject belongs as an auxiliary to that very subject," the prohibition by Kātyāyana stating "it is not elevated" applies only to the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) mentioned therein, and certainly not to a ritual procedure not included in the *Kalpasūtra*.

Thus, it should be understood that the prohibition of making [the mark] below the navel applies specifically to the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) stated by him [Āpastamba], and not to the procedure stated by Kātyāyana. Therefore, this is an alternative regarding the measurement. Why? Because these [specific measurements] are stated in one's own scripture (*sva-śāstra*). As for the statement of Gārgīputra cited by the ignorant Nārāyaṇopādhyāya—"In no way should [the mark] be made above the breasts or below the navel"—that measurement given by Devala is to be disregarded. (3)

It has been stated that [the rule] refers to objects other than those mentioned in the *gobhila* [sūtra]. The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* states: The sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is an auxiliary to ritual action (*karmāṅga*), based on the sūtra: "The rite must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread and having sipped water. Thus, when it might follow that the thread is to be worn only during the time of ritual and not otherwise, he says: "One must be equipped with the sacred thread and have the top-knot tied. By this, the wearing of the top-knot and the sacred thread is established as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). There is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in not wearing them.

Since [the wearing of the sacred thread] is always maintained for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), it follows that it should be worn even at the time of performing a ritual action; therefore, he asks: "Is it not the case that it has no status as a subsidiary part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*)? To this he replies with the words beginning "one who is without the topknot" (*viśikha*). The intention is that whatever rite is performed by one devoid of the topknot and the sacred thread is as if not performed at all, because, being deficient in its constituent qualities (*viguṇatva*), it cannot produce the intended fruit. This refers merely to the performance of the ritual act itself. [1.1.12] For if it were for the sake of the person, then even if by chance the thread were not worn at the time of the ritual, the ritual would simply be deficient, while the person would incur sin (*pratyavāyin*). But if it were a subsidiary part of the ritual, this would not be the case.

And at that time, the expiation required for the failure to maintain the proper season must be performed; this is the purpose of the instruction regarding its status as a subsidiary element of the ritual (*karmāṅga*). By this, it is stated that the wearing of the sacred thread (*upavīta*) serves both purposes—pertaining to the ritual and pertaining to the person—just like curd, the *khadira* wood, and so forth. For this very reason, its wearing is clearly stated elsewhere as well: "If one drinks, urinates, or eats while not wearing the sacred thread, one should perform nine, twelve, and twenty-one breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) respectively."

Therefore, since the rule regarding the acquisition of wealth is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), the performance of a sacrifice with wealth acquired through agriculture—even by transgressing that rule—is indeed flawless; however, the person must perform penance due to the transgression of the rule. Furthermore, by the word "without a tuft" (*viśikha*), it is stated that even in the absence of a tuft or the failure to bind one, there is no flaw in the ritual itself, provided the tuft exists [at some point]. *Prabhā*: The status of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) as an auxiliary to the ritual is stated in the *Gṛhyasūtra* of Gṛmya: "The rite must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread and having sipped water."

And thus, its retention [of the sacred thread] at times other than the time for ritual action would not be established; therefore, he says: "by one with the sacred thread" (*sopavītinā*). A person must always be one who wears the sacred thread and always one who has bound his topknot (*śikhā*). By this, the wearing of the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) and the binding of the topknot are shown to be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Consequently, there would be a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in the case of their omission. Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the binding of the topknot and the wearing of the sacred thread are for the sake of the person, why do they continue even at times other than [ritual] action? Are these not for the purpose of ritual action? It is in response to such a doubt that [the author] states: "by one with the sacred thread. This means that a person must always be one who wears the sacred thread and always one who has bound his topknot. By this, the wearing of the sacrificial thread and the binding of the topknot are shown to be for the sake of the person. Therefore, there would be a transgression in the case of their reversal. In the *Karmapradīpa*, manuscript *ga* reads "naktaṃ likayutam. [1.1] It says: "viśikha" and so forth. Whatever rite one performs without a bound top-knot (*śikhā*) or without wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*), that is as if not performed at all. Because of its deficiency, it fails to produce the proper fruit; thus, the statement "it is not performed" is a deprecatory declaration (*nindārthavāda*). Since the binding of the top-knot and the wearing of the sacred thread have been previously stated for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), the latter half [of the verse]—by means of this deprecatory declaration regarding their omission—establishes their purpose for ritual action (*karmārtha*). Consequently, the term "viśikha" is interpreted to mean "one whose top-knot is not bound."

Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency between the preceding and following passages. In the phrase "with the bound crest" (*baddhaśikhena*), because the bound crest is present [in the context], it is the very bound crest that is referred to by the word "crest" (*śikhā*) as "crestless" (*viśikha*). By this, the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*—which claims that even in the absence of a crest, or in the absence of the binding of the crest, there is merely a deficiency in the ritual (*karmavaiguṇya*) rather than a failure of the rite only when a crest actually exists—is shown to be irrelevant and inconsistent.

If that were the case, then the wearing of the *śikhā* (topknot) would have to be prescribed as a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action—just like the tying of the topknot—and this would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, since the tying of the topknot and the wearing of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), their status as ritual subsidiaries is established through the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva-nyāya*), and not because there is another sacred thread to be worn for the sake of the ritual. However, regarding those who have completed their Vedic studies (*snātaka*), Vaśiṣṭha states that two sacred threads should be worn: "For those who have taken the final bath (*snātaka*), there should always be an inner garment (*antarvāsa*) and likewise an upper garment; [they should wear] two sacred threads and a staff."

"And water, as well as a water-pot. Thus, since the wearing of the *yajñopavīta* is prescribed for the sake of ritual action (*karman*) as a means to achieve the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), this same principle applies there as well. And they record in the Smṛtis: "The *yajñopavīta* is to be worn during the rites of the Śruti and Smṛti; a third is intended for the purpose of the upper garment (*uttarīya*), and it is desired when a cloth is lacking. [Karmapradīpa 1.14] Having sipped water and wiped the mouth twice, one should touch these [parts].

[One should touch] the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, chest, and head. (5) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Regarding the statement by Gṛhyasūtrakāra Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa that "the rite is to be performed with water already sipped" (*ācāntodakena kṛtyam*), this clarifies the indistinct nature of *ācamana*. Water should be taken up repeatedly; and the excellence of the act of consumption results from the excellence of the action and the agent. In that regard, the excellence of the object consists in its being free from foam and bubbles, and in its reaching the heart, and so forth. The excellence of the agent consists in the purification of hands and feet, sitting [in a proper posture], facing eastward, and so forth.

In this context, the excellence of the instrument (*karaṇaprakarṣa*) consists in its being a *brāhma-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to Brahmā) and so forth. Having thus sipped water twice, one should wipe the mouth at the base of the thumb; however, not on the tip. This is because, regarding the subsequent sipping of water (*punarācamana*), it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Accordingly, the *Pariśiṣṭa* states: "Having sipped water, one should sip again; having put on another garment, one should touch the two ears and the base of the thumb. And the wiping (*mārjana*) is performed with the base of the thumb, as will be stated by the author of the *Dakṣasmṛti*.

By this, that which was stated by Gobbila—"Having risen from the fire, having washed his hands and feet, and having sat down, he should sip water three times, wipe his mouth twice, and after sprinkling his feet, he should sprinkle his head"—is clarified: namely, that there are two occasions for wiping the mouth and three occasions for consuming water.

Regarding the statement, "Having released [the water] with the northward-pointed [grass-blades]," some maintain that the sipping (ācamana) which is an auxiliary part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*) occurs three times; however, this is refuted by the fact that the sipping prescribed for the four times in the verse, "Or let the wise man sip water four times," is established as having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). This is because the specific rule beginning with "Facing north... and so forth applies specifically to the sipping that is an auxiliary of the ritual, stating that it must be performed by one who has already sipped water. Consequently, there is a distinction based on the number of mouthfuls: if the three sips reach the heart, then the rule is "four times" for those who eat much.

The *Bhāvakamapradīpa* states that this is the established rule according to the *Kalpataru*. Gṛhyasūtrakāra Āśvalāyana has said: "One should touch the sense organs with water—the two nostrils and the two ears—if they are not to be examined. This clarifies what was previously obscure. One should touch these [organs] about to be mentioned in their vicinity, but not at each specific location, because they would become defiled.

The mention of the mouth (*āsya*) and so forth together in a compound is for the purpose of connecting them with the term "touching" (*spṛśati*); whereas the separate mention of the navel (*nābhi*) and so forth in a compound is for the purpose of connecting them with the mere act of "touching. And since this sequence beginning with the mouth has been declared by Dakṣa, that very same order should be adopted even when there is a restriction regarding the fingers. For Dakṣa says: "By this very procedure, one who has sipped water attains purity; having washed his hands and feet, he should drink three times the water that has been sprinkled. By "this," he means what is about to be described.

15. “Having closed the mouth with the base of the thumb, one should wipe it twice; having first joined three fingers together, one should thus touch the mouth. The meaning is that one should close the mouth and then wipe it. “Thus” means having joined [the fingers]. “Then, with the thumb and the index finger (pradeśinī), one should touch the nose; immediately thereafter, with the thumb and the ring finger (anāmikā), the eyes; again and again, the ears; with the little finger (kaniṣṭhā) and the thumb, the navel; and with the palm, the heart.”

With all [the fingers], he should then touch the head; with the tip [of the hand], he should touch [the body]. First, he should touch the mouth with three [fingers]; then the nose with the thumb and the index finger; immediately after, the eyes; and the ears again and again—this is the meaning. 5. The *Prabhā* commentary states: "The ritual must be performed by one who has sipped water (*ācāntodaka*). To clarify this prescribed sipping of water (*ācamana*), the *Karmapradīpa* (1.1) says: "He approaches... [and so on].

Having sipped water three times and wiped the mouth twice, one should touch the aforementioned parts—the mouth, eyes, nostrils, ears, navel, chest, and head. By this, it is clarified that the *Gṛhyasūtra* of Āśvalāyana—"One should touch the sense organs: the two eyes, the two nostrils, and the two ears"—is intended merely as a general enumeration and not as a prescription for a specific order. Thus, the meaning intended by the word "iti" has been demonstrated. Although [the text says], "One should sip water twice and wipe [the mouth] twice, having washed the feet..."

Regarding the statement "one should sprinkle [water] on the head," the *Gobhila-sūtra* prescribes the sprinkling of the feet and the head first, following the two-fold wiping (*parimārjana*) of the hands; nevertheless, that has been stated here for the sake of clarity. Alternatively, it may be for the purpose of completing the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) in certain circumstances even without that [sprinkling]. Regarding the rule for the fingers during the sipping, the right hand is shown by Dākṣa as follows: "By this very procedure, one attains internal purity; having washed both hands and feet, one should drink the prescribed water three times."

Conventionally, one should wipe the face twice with the base of the thumb; having first joined the three fingers together, one should thus touch the mouth. Immediately after, one should touch the nose with the thumb and the index finger; then the eyes repeatedly with the thumb and the ring finger. One should touch the navel with the little finger and the elbow, the heart with the palm, and finally the head with all the fingers, touching it from front to back. Thus it is said.

In certain instances, these words are employed in this very context as a lamp for ritual action (*karmapradīpa*). By the term "having gathered," one should touch the place where there is impurity (*almaraka*) after having covered the mouth with the hand. Otherwise, it would contradict the *Karmapradīpa*, which states: "Having sipped water (*ācānta*), one should sip again here, and having changed one's clothes, likewise touching both ears, one should stand where there is impurity. For if one were to touch the impure spot without the rule of sipping water prescribed by Vasiṣṭha, that [impurity] would not be removed.

Nor should it be said that this [practice] is not to be followed because it belongs to another; for it is untenable that what is stated in the *Smṛti* belongs to another. Even that which is stated in the *Smṛti* must certainly not be practiced if it contradicts one's own scripture (*svaśāstra*). Furthermore, there is no such contradiction here; moreover, since Datta is indeed considered by the authors of the *Smṛtis* to be like a supplementary author (*pariśiṣṭakāra*), no suspicion whatsoever need be entertained. Thus it has been stated by Dakṣa himself: "The sequence of rites has been declared, but the time [for them] was not recorded by the sages in the *Smṛtis*."

"For the benefit of the twice-born, Dakṣa himself declared thus. There is an alternative reading for the second quarter of the verse: "na kālastata eva hi" (time is not [an obstacle] because of that). Regarding the specific details of *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water), they should be understood from the *Gṛhyasūtras* and other *Smṛtis* as appropriate; they are not written here for fear of excessive length. Furthermore, since the drinking of water three times is prescribed in this very *Sūtra*, the rule of Gautama—"one should sip water three or four times"—applies to cases other than those specified by Gobhila.

As for what was stated by Nārāyaṇopādhyāya—that because of the injunction "one should touch [the water]," one should touch the sense organs themselves and not the openings, since those are full of impurity—that is inconsistent. For it contradicts the Gṛhyasūtra of Gobhila, which says, "One should touch the sense organs with the waters. Furthermore, even if there were impurity, it is illogical to assume a fault based on the mere act of touching when there is an explicit scriptural injunction; for a general rule can be understood as referring to a specific instance. As it is said: "The impurities have indeed fallen away from the body..."

—Thus, because impurity belongs only to those who have fallen from the body as recorded in the Smṛti, there is an absence of impurity for those remaining in the body. The mention of the mouth and other parts together in a single compound word is for the sake of their creation. The *Pradīpa* states: "When an action is prescribed but it is not stated which limb of the agent is to be used, the right hand is to be understood there as that which brings the actions to completion. In connection with the discussion on sipping water (*ācamana*) and other such matters, he states another common subsidiary rule (*aṅga*): "Wherever in the *Smṛtis* and other texts an action is prescribed to be performed, and the left or right limb of the performer is specified, there the right hand is to be understood as the instrument of the action. By this, [the rule applies] to offerings of food (*vali*), oblations (*homa*), and so forth, as well as to other unspecified acts mentioned by Śrī Bhṛgu.

The performance [of the ritual] according to the specific rule regarding particular limbs among those limbs ordained by destiny has been made clear. [Commentary: The separate mention of *nābhi* (navel) and so forth for the purpose of connecting them with *smṛti* (tradition/memory) is merely a conceptual construction; it is not to be accepted because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, such a view would result in an unavoidable contradiction of the scriptural injunction (*vacana-virodha*).

Therefore, the prefix follows the meaning of the verbal root. For this very reason, this specific distinction was not mentioned by any sage or by the author of the *Saṃgraha*. Where it is prescribed that "this must be done," and the specific hand of the performer—whether the left or the right—is not specified, there the right hand is to be understood as the one that carries actions to completion (*pāraga*) and is capable of performing all tasks, such as in the case of taking up a firebrand (*ulmuka*). Alternatively, the meaning is that the right hand is to be known as that which brings actions to their conclusion. In that case where there is no such rule as "one should perform [the rite] while seated with the upper body bent forward," that action must be performed by one who is seated. Standing like a staff, with the upper body slightly bent; by one standing thus like a staff. When worshipped, they gratify the worshipper by bringing about his prosperity. (8) He states the places of worship and their necessary implements: "In images made of silver, crystal, and so forth, which are bright... If the reading is *śahākhi*, it means "splendor. (11) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: This very point [has been explained]. This is the primary ritual procedure (*mukhyakalpa*). And with various kinds of offerings—such as perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cakes, and sweetmeats—he performed worship with a combination of devotion and faith. Because the *vasā* (the vessel) is a cause of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) by virtue of initiating all festivals, worship is appropriate during auspicious occasions such as marriage and the birth of a son. Or else, [it refers to] *vasa* and *agni*. [Commentary: It follows that the Mothers (*mātaraḥ*) are to be worshipped in images fashioned from silver and other materials. The Mothers are to be worshipped with various and manifold offerings, such as fragrances, flowers, incense, and diverse kinds of edible foods. (10) He states what is to be done after the worship of the Mothers: "One should draw a line... etc. One should draw a line—either seven or five streams—that touches the wall, which is neither too low, nor too short, nor too high, nor too long, for the fire situated on the sacrificial altar. Then, for the sake of longevity and peace, your grandson, being composed in mind, should commence the offering of the *śrāddha* for the six ancestors. *Parīśiṣṭaprakāśa*: "Beneficial for life" means for the destruction of inauspiciousness. Regarding that, at the beginning of the rite—after the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛpūjā*), the *vasudhārā*, and the recitation for longevity (*āyuṣyajapa*)—one should begin the offering of the *śrāddha* for the ancestors starting with the father, and for the maternal ancestors starting with the maternal grandfather. This [rite] is to be performed at the beginning of Vedic rituals as a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and it is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of that.

And so says Śātātapa: "One should not undertake a Vedic rite without having first offered [oblations] to the ancestors. And the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa states: "It should be known that [the offering to the ancestors] at the time of conception, during the *sīmantonnayana*, and likewise during the *puṃsavana*—indeed, whenever it is an ancillary part of a rite. This is an elliptical expression for all Vedic rites; for when there is a rite with a fruit, that which lacks a fruit [its subsidiary] is understood as being connected to it because it has been introduced [into the context]. Therefore, one should cause the stream [of water] to be poured—that is, one should perform it. The suffix *ṇic* is used here in a reflexive sense (*svārthika*). || 11 ||

Regarding the rite to be performed immediately after the pouring of the *vasordhārā*, he says: "The *āyuṣyāṇi*. These are those [mantras] beneficial for life (*āyuṣe hitāni*), which increase longevity; according to the *Madanapārijāta*, they are the hymns beginning with "ā no bhadraḥ kratavo" and so forth. And these are recited in the Taittirīya Śākhā.

For the sake of peace and for the destruction of inauspiciousness, one whose mind is either concentrated or distracted should first perform the *kāma* offerings; immediately thereafter, one should commence the offering of the *śrāddha* to the six paternal ancestors—beginning with the father—and to the three maternal ancestors, beginning with the maternal grandfather. This is according to the *Kamapradīpa* and the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. This is because the principle that "it is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of that" applies without distinction. However, in worldly rituals, the Vedic *śrāddha* is not a subsidiary part; rather, it is merely the occasion (*nimitta*) for that [worldly rite].

The effect follows immediately after the cause; therefore, it is established that the *śrāddha* occasioned by an eclipse of the sun and so forth—namely, the *abhyudaya-śrāddha*—must indeed take place at a time subsequent to the birth of a son. For this very reason, the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states: "I shall now describe the occasional *śrāddha* consisting of prosperity (*abhyudayātmaka*); on the birth of a son, that rite should be performed by men simultaneously with the *jātakarman*. This [mention of the *jātakarman*] is also intended as an illustration for the seeing of the son's face and other such events, because there is no difference between them in terms of being non-essential (*anupādeya*) and secondary (*apradhāna*).

By this, it has been clearly established that all other [terms] have meaning, and that the term *anvāhārya*—because it is brought forward (*anvāhriyamāṇa*) from the honoring of the mother and so forth—is synonymous with *dvitīya*. For this very reason, another *Gṛhya* text states: "That which is the *śrāddha* at the beginning of rites, and that which is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at the end, and that which is the second [offering] on the new moon day—that is called *anvāhārya*. Furthermore, because it consists of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, it is the second *śrāddha*. The phrase "having offered, then after that" (*juhvā tadanu*) is a stylistic convention of the manuscript.

Nor should a redundancy be suspected here, or rather, it is for the sake of a specific sequence. How so? It means that only one who has performed the *āyuṣyajapa* is entitled to the offering of food (*śrāddha*), and not one who has not performed the *āyuṣyajapa*. Because of the mention of "to six," there is no separate offering to the mothers and others of those who have chosen [the Vedic path]. And he will say: "Women should not give separately, except on the day of conclusion. (Kampradīpa; Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa; this is the meaning). And thus says Gṛhyabhila:

"The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is explained by the Anvaṣṭakya sthālīpāka. On the new moon day, that śrāddha is performed; the other [śrāddha] is on the Anvāhārya month. And at a rite for prosperity (vṛddhi) or a wedding, the ancestors (pitṛs) are the deities, characterized by the specific qualification of having their faces turned toward the east. Thus says the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "At the marriage of a daughter or a son, at the entry into a new house, at the naming ceremony of children, as well as at the tonsure ceremony and others, at the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), and at the first sight of the face of a son and so forth..."

"A diligent householder should worship the group of ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas. The *Brahmapurāṇa* states: "In rites pertaining to prosperity (*abhyudayika*), which are auspicious and beneficial—such as at birth, tonsure, and the marriage of a son—one should satisfy the ancestors, beginning with the Nāndīmukhas, according to the prescribed ritual. Śaunaka also says: "Having caused [the officiant] to recite for the deity, 'May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased,' [one offers to] the Nāndīmukha ancestors, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, [with the formula]: 'To the Nāndīmukha ancestors... etc.

In the phrase "to the fathers" (*pitṛbhyaḥ*), because the word *pitṛ* is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*), it includes the father and other ancestors of the sacrificer according to the principle of the foot (*padinyāya*). Therefore, it refers to the father and other ancestors of the sacrificer, and not [only] those described as: "The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—these are proclaimed to be the mouth-born (*vayasyamukha*) fathers."

In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, the reading in manuscript *kha* is: *iti*. In manuscript *va*, the reading is: *pitāmahaprapitāmahebhyaḥ*. [Regarding] "to the maternal grandfather, the great-grandfather, and the great-great-grandfather," although this is so, the *Kāmadīpa* and the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* state: "Let them be gratified"—thus it is said. "The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—these are proclaimed as the 'faceless' (*amukha*) ancestors. And those who are even earlier than them, who possess progeny and have flourished in happiness [are also included]."

"But it is not said that *nāndīmukha* means a joyful face (*nāndī-samṛddhi*). From the statement in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "Those who are after the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) are called *nāndīmukha*; they are known as 'those with joyful faces' (*prasannamukha*) because they are auspicious," the state of being *nāndīmukha*—in the form of having a joyful face—is indeed applicable only to the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), the father, and so forth. Furthermore, in the phrase "those who are after the grandfather," the term "grandfather" refers to the great-grandfather; and those who are even earlier than them are the ancestors (*pūrve*).

Those who are even earlier than them, who possess progeny and have thrived in happiness, are called *nāndīmukha*; "nāndī" signifies prosperity. Regarding the *kābhyudayika* (rites for prosperity) performed at auspicious occasions—namely, birth, the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), marriage, and the birth of a son—one should satisfy the *pitṛ-nāndīmukhas* according to the prescribed injunctions. This is because of the statement in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One should satisfy the *pitṛ-nāndīmukhas* according to the rule," which indicates that the offering is made to the great-grandfather’s father and the others. The *Karmapradīpa* will state this, and the *Parīśiṣṭaprakāśa* observes as follows.

Consequently, it would be logical for those very [ancestors] to hold the status of deity in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*; nevertheless, because of the rule "six [oblations] for the ancestors" (*ṣaḍ āhutayaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ*), it is logical that the status of deity is understood to belong specifically to the ancestors of the sacrificer. And thus it is clearly stated: "The father should give to his own ancestors during the sacramental rites of his son. This is because the word "own" (*sva*) is meaningful precisely as a qualifier that excludes the great-grandfather, the father of the father, and so forth.

Likewise, in the statement of Kātyāyana—"May the *nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased; may the grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and maternal grandfathers be pleased"—and in the *Gṛhyasūtra* of Gobbila—"May [the offerings] be for the pleasure of the *nāndīmukha* fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers"—it is understood that these refer to the ancestors of the sacrificer himself, because they are relative terms and because of their association with the term "maternal grandfather" (*mātāmaha*).

And their state of being *nāndīmukha* is their very splendor: "The father should offer to his own ancestors during the rites of consecrating a son. In this context, the word "own" (*sva*) is meaningful precisely as an exclusion of the great-grandfather’s father and others; otherwise, it would result in redundancy. However, the status of being a deity here belongs only to the ancestors—father and so on—as qualified by the specific attribute of being *nāndīmukha*. This is because of the designation in the *Śrāddhakalpa*: "The *nāndīmukha* ancestors," and so forth.

Thus, in that very context, there is the specific instruction: "To the Nāndīmukha ancestors, to the paternal grandfathers," and so forth. Furthermore, the formulation of the statement as prescribed by Bṛhad-Vasiṣṭha—"In the Nāndīmukha rite and at a wedding, one should utter the formula beginning with the great-grandfather (prapitāmaha); elsewhere, it begins with the father"—does not apply to the Ṛgvedins. [This is stated in] the Karmapradīpa and the Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa. [The fire] belongs to the boy just as its nature is that of fire.

Furthermore, in auspicious occasions such as weddings and the birth of a son, it is appropriate—even according to the *āryas*—to refer to those with tearful faces and inauspicious conditions by the auspicious term "nāndīmukha" during the performance of the *śrāddha*. For this very reason, even when referring to inauspicious objects like skulls (*kapāla*) and so forth, sages employ terms such as "bhagāla" instead of "kapāla," and use the word "bhaga"—which signifies the venerable [Bhagavat] and the knowledge of desire (*kāma-jñāna*)—in order to avoid inauspiciousness. In the same way, the recitation of long-life mantras (*āyuṣya-mantra*) will also be justified for the purpose of pacification (*śānti*).

Therefore, even in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, the instruction to recite the *Sūktas* for the sake of *svastyayana* (auspicious benediction)—namely, "One should recite the *Chandas*, the *Svastyaya*, and likewise the auspicious [hymns]"—will thus be appropriately established. Furthermore, in some places, the actual state of being *nāndīmukha* is shown in the *Brahma Purāṇa* as being based on the *Ṛṣi* (the seer) of a particular hymn, or for the sake of the *Ṛṣi* himself. Some, however, say that this position from the *Brahma Purāṇa* is restricted to a specific Vedic branch (*śākhā*). [Prabhā: 1st Praśna, 1st Khaṇḍa]

All of this has been analyzed by us in the *Śrāddhakalpa-bhāṣya* and other works; it should be investigated there. For fear of excessive length, it is not set forth here. As stated by Nārāyaṇa Pāṭhyāya: "Since one's own father and others are understood to be deities (*devatā*), they possess the status of being 'Nāndīmukhas' by virtue of their archetypal nature (*ārpeṇa*), just as the student possesses the nature of fire (*agnitva*). In auspicious rites such as marriage, it is appropriate to designate those who are inauspicious—the ancestors—by the auspicious term 'Nāndīmukha,' even through their archetypal nature."

For this very reason, sages employ words such as *bhagāla* (the forehead) instead of inauspicious terms like *kapāla* (skull), even though they are etymologically derived from the same root (*ārpāt*), in order to avoid inauspiciousness; rather, they use terms associated with the word *bhaga*, which signifies prosperity, desire, knowledge, and so forth. In some cases, the true meaning of the Vedic revelation (*ārpārtha*) itself is shown in the *Brahma Purāṇa* to be the actual reality, even when it appears otherwise due to a lack of understanding. This interpretation is indeed charming. [1st Adhyāya, 1st Section] The lamp of the Krama: "The injunction of Vasiṣṭha is to be seen here in its entirety, free from worldly desires."

Henceforth, I shall explain the specific details that may arise. First Section. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Others maintain that [the rule] is established for one whose father and the other three [ancestors] are living. That is incorrect; because in the statement "The father should give to his own ancestors," the performance of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* by the son is prescribed only in the absence of the father. Furthermore, Viṣṇu prohibits [the rite] when all three are living, stating "not at all when the three are living. Moreover, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is a modification (*vikṛti*) of that [general śrāddha].

Precisely because the state of being *nāndīmukha* has been attributed [to them], for that very reason, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states: "And likewise to the maternal grandfathers who are *nāndīmukhas*. Thus, the status of the maternal grandfathers as *nāndīmukhas* is declared. Similarly, by Kātyāyana through the formula "May the *nāndīmukha* ancestors be gratified," and by Āśvalāyana through "To the *nāndīmukha* ancestors," the status of the maternal grandfathers as *nāndīmukhas* is likewise declared. || 12 ||

He states the sequence in which the *śrāddha* should be performed: "The rule for the *pāṇi* [offering] which was declared by Vasiṣṭha in the *Bāndhava-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa* is its own authority. However, the meaning of the statement is not as such. Why? Because in the *Brahma-purāṇa*, after designating the great-grandfather (*vṛhat-prapitāmaha*) and the others with the name *nāndīmukha*, and then stating "in rites pertaining to prosperity" (*karmasv athābhyudayike*) and so forth, those very same ancestors are subsequently instructed regarding the *śrāddha*; therefore, such an interpretation is untenable. (12)

—Vasiṣṭha begins to state the procedure for the *anvāhārya-śrāddha*. [This work] is the *Pradīpa* (The Lamp), known as the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. It should be understood as setting aside all other conflicting views. Immediately following this, I shall correctly explain whatever specific details may exist regarding the injunctions of Vasiṣṭha. Honey must indeed be offered: "Rice of the *śāli* variety, mixed with curd and honey, along with jujubes (*badara*) and barley—these four, combined and shaped into balls (*piṇḍa*), should be the size of bilva fruits."

Thus, from the statement in the *Brahmapurāṇa*. [End of] the first section. *Prabhā*: The procedure (*vidhi*) which was declared by Vasiṣṭha for the *Pālacatru* sacrifice in the *Vāika-kalpa* is to be understood as the rule for the ritual action (*kṛtyavidhi*) in this sacrifice through the offering of a goat (*āmiṣapaśu*). Whatever specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) there may be in this sacrifice compared to that [other] procedure, I shall hereafter explain that distinction in detail. It appears to be the opinion of the venerable Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa that the *Vāika-kalpa* was indeed composed by Vasiṣṭha.

"Any other specific details, such as those beginning with 'those who have been invited,' are to be understood from the *Śrāddhakalpa* of Vasiṣṭha. This is because it is stated thus in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) of Gṛhyasūtra. Here, by the exclusion of meat (*āmiṣa*), there is an extended application (*atideśa*) of the entire rule prescribed by Vasiṣṭha; therefore, honey (*madhu*) is also understood to be an item to be offered. However, in the Kali age, it does not occur: "Unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), meat, and likewise honey... [is prohibited].

"One should avoid the five [kinds of marriage] in the Kali age; the birth from a brother-in-law [is one of them]," according to the scriptural statement found in the *Mayūkha* and other works. Thus ends the first section. The Second Section: Having seated the invited Brāhmaṇas in the morning, in pairs on both sides, he should give them *kuśa* grass with his right hand alone. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: He states a specific detail regarding those Brāhmaṇas who have been invited in the first hour.

Having seated those invited for the gods facing east and those for the ancestors facing north, just as in the *pārvaṇa* rite, he should place the *kuśa* grass on the seats with his hand held straight (without being bent). Prabhā: He states the specific detail that was promised, beginning with "in the morning": having seated the even number of Brahmins invited in the morning—both for the side of the gods and the side of the ancestors—just as in the *pārvaṇa*, with those for the gods facing east and those for the ancestors facing north; he should give the *kuśa* grass with a hand that is straight and not crooked.

In the *pārvaṇa* rite, it is stated that the invitation of the Brahmins occurs on the day before; however, here the invitation does not take place on the previous day, but rather this very morning. Likewise, while in the *pārvaṇa* an odd number of Brahmins is prescribed for the ancestors (*pitṛs*), here even an even number is required. Furthermore, in the *pārvaṇa*, the offering is said to be made with the *pitṛ-tīrtha*; here, however, it means with the straight hand using the *deva-tīrtha*. [Karmapradīpa, 1.2] Green *darbha* grasses are sacrificial, while yellow ones are...

Those used for *pākayajña* [domestic sacrifices] are green; those for the ancestral rites (*piṭadaivatyāḥ*) have roots; those for the *vaiśvadeva* [rites] are variegated. *Parīśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Since it is stated that "one should give *kuśa* grass," he describes what kind of *kuśa* grass is appropriate for which ritual limb: those for sacrifices such as the *darśa* are green; those for the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) are yellow; those for the ancestral rites are with roots; and those for the *vaiśvadeva* śrāddha are variegated. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "the *kuśa* grass is to be plucked. The reading in the *Kalpataru* is "those for the divine rites are indeed brownish-yellow (*kāṣāya*)."

And in that case, the meaning is indeed explicit. Furthermore, in this context, as a secondary point (*prasaṅga*), those [types of *kuśa* grass] intended for sacrifices and other rites are also mentioned. [Commentary on the verse]: Regarding the statement "one should give *kuśas*," he explains by way of this secondary discussion what kind of *kuśas* are used in which ritual acts: "green" means the *darbha* grasses used in sacrifices such as the *darśa*. Yellow-colored *darbhas* are suitable for *pākayajñas*. For rites dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛdevatya*), the *darbhas* should have roots—that is, they must be accompanied by their roots; the meaning is that in ancestral rites (*piṭakarma*) they must be with their roots.

The *darbha* grass intended for the Viśvedevas is "kalyāpa," meaning spotted or black-and-white; Samdhara recites that they are also "kalmāṣa," which means the same thing. Thus, the meaning remains unambiguous. Now, what indeed are these so-called *pākayajñas*? Regarding this, commentators disagree. Some say they are sacrifices that have cooking (*pāka*) as their constituent part. Others say they are the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*). Still others say they are commendable sacrifices (*praśastayajña*). Others again say they are sacrifices performed without a sacrificial post (*avyayaja*). Some say they are the sacrifices to the gods and so forth (*devayajñādi*). We, however, say:

Those sacrifices which involve a single fire are *pākayajñas*. Why? Because of the statement of the author of the Sūtras: "They call the sacrifices involving a single fire *pākayajñas*" (Śrautasūtra 1.2). *Karmapradīpa*: "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) should indeed be green, with its tips intact, dry yet glossy, well-laid out, measured by the span of the arms, and consecrated according to the rite for the ancestors. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

He states the measurement and other details for those intended for the ancestors (*pitṛ*): "The *sapillāḥ* (mounds) are one span (*prādeśa*) in measure, accompanied by fresh or dried flower clusters, having large leaves, being lotus-like, well-compacted with leaves not scattered here and there, and measuring the size of a closed fist; they are consecrated by contact with the *pitṛ-tīrtha* [of the hand]. The remainder is that these *piṭakas* (baskets/mounds) are to be accepted. Furthermore, the measurement of one cubit (*ratni*) applies specifically to those intended for spreading out the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).

Regarding the dimensions for the *āsana* (seat) and other items such as the sacrificial grass (*sarga*), they should be measured by the span of the ear (*karṇa*). Thus, the *Vāyu Purāṇa* states: "Kuśa grasses measuring one cubit (*ratni*) are recommended when consecrated with the *pitṛ-tīrtha*; likewise, those cut near the base are considered suitable for the purpose of a sacrificial mat (*prastara*). The *Brahma Purāṇa* says: "The *kuśas* should be green, with their tips intact, glossy, thick, and well-proportioned; they should be long enough to reach the ears, cut at the joints, and possess their roots. So too should the *dūrvā*, *śyāmāka*, and *kāśa* grasses be used with the *pitṛ-tīrtha*."

"Kuśas, avajas, and likewise others with sharp points; maujas and śādalas—these are proclaimed as the six types of darbha grass. [Commentary: Regarding the term *haritāḥ* (green): they are green in color, possessed of tufts (*sapicuḷāḥ*), accompanied by flower-clusters (*mañjarī-sahitāḥ*), or having tips (*sāgrāḥ*). *Puṣṭāḥ* means having thick leaves. *Siddhāḥ*, *kamalāḥ*, and *prakarkaśāḥ* [are also mentioned]. In the Kha manuscript, the reading is *kuśottamāḥ* (the best of kuśas). [The *Karmapradīpa*, 1.2, states: "Those darbhas which are spread for the sake of the *piṇḍa* offerings, and likewise for the sake of libations (*tarpaṇa*)."

Once the excrement and urine have been held [in the hand] and performed, their discarding is prescribed. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: The term *trṇavajjānām* (of those born from grass) is a qualifier for [the types of grass]. Therefore, in the absence of these, one must understand that there is a prohibition against all other grasses—excluding *śūkātṛṇa*, *śara*, *śaurya*, *vadbaja*, *mutava*, *nalasa*, and *uṇṭhava*—according to the rule of Gṛhyasūtra 1.34. Furthermore, the measurement of a *gokarṇa* has been explained in the *Abhidhānakṣepa* as being the size of a *prādeśa* or a *tāla*. In the absence of primary *kuśa* grass, one should take *dūrvā* and so forth.

In the absence of those [specific grasses], one should use *sarvataṇāni* (all kinds of grass), because of the statement by Gbhila: "Because of their being all-inclusive. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "In the absence of *kuśa*, one should offer *kāśa* or *dūrvā* in the place of *kuśa*. Regarding other *kuśas* that must be discarded: those *kuśas* used for spreading the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*), those used for the purpose of strewing, and those with which the root of the *vigama* was made—their abandonment must be performed. The meaning is that they are not to be used in further rites. Laghu-Hārīta also mentions others that are to be discarded: "As many as have been used, having been properly prepared... [The text continues: "...they are to be discarded."

Or [those] whose leaves have been scattered here and there; "ravi" refers to the span of the hand with the fist closed, and they are of that measure. These *darbha* grasses, consecrated by the *pitṛtīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors), are to be used for the *piṇḍa* offerings. Regarding other *darbha* grasses, he says "for the sake of the *piṇḍas*" (*piṇḍārtham*). Those *darbhas* which were spread out for the purpose of offering the *piṇḍas*, and those which were offered for the purpose of satiating the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*). The instrumental case in "by those held" (*bhṛtaiḥ*) is used in a figurative sense (*upalakṣaṇe*).

When a person has performed *vismūtra* (urination) using *darbha* grass held in the hand, there is a prohibition regarding all those *darbhas*. The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* states: "One should avoid six types of *kuśa* grass: those on the funeral pyre (*citā*), those on a path, those on sacrificial grounds, and those used for spreading, as seats, or for *piṇḍas*. Furthermore, it says: "One should know that those *darbhas* which are worn around the waist (*nīvī*) and those placed upon the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) are pure; as is the body, so are the *kuśas*. This [latter statement] is an exception (*apavādaka*) to the former rule. [1st Praśna, 2nd Khaṇḍa]

"The Darbha grasses that were spread for the sake of the *piṇḍas*, those with which the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) was performed, and those worn in the remains of the sacred thread (*sūtracchiṣṭa*)—their discarding is prescribed. Because Laghu-Hārīta states immediately after this, "in the middle of the *nīvī*," [the meaning is as follows]: "Discarding is prescribed" means that they are not to be employed in ritual acts (*karma*). If the Darbha grasses spread for the *piṇḍas* and those taken for the *pitṛtarpaṇa* were to be discarded, then the offering of the *piṇḍas* upon them and the libation to the ancestors by means of them would not be possible.

This is not the case. For if that were so, it would be impossible for the *darbha* grasses to serve the purpose of the *piṇḍas* when they have been spread out, and for them to serve the purpose of the libation (*tarpaṇa*) when they have been taken up. Therefore, what is being stated is that those *darbha* blades upon which the offering of the *piṇḍas* was made and with which the libation to the ancestors was performed must be discarded at other rites; it is not said that they must be discarded even during those very rites themselves. If that were the case, the instruction regarding the offering of the *piṇḍas* on *darbha* grass and the libation to the ancestors with *darbha* grass would be a mere idle utterance.

From this it is understood that even *darbha* grasses employed for one purpose may be employed for another. Thus says the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "Darbha grass, the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the mantras, Brāhmaṇas, sacrificial food, and fires—these are not exhausted by use and may be employed again and again. [The *Karmapradīpa* and *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* state: "But those things which are empty (or devoid of specific ritual function), though already employed, may be employed again. And thus says the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "Darbha grass, the black antelope skin, the mantras, Brāhmaṇas, sacrificial food, and fires..."

"These sacrificial grasses (darbhas) do not become exhausted; they may be used again and again. Here, "exhausted" (*yātayāma*) means worn out; that which is not so is "unexhausted" (*ayātayāma*), meaning fresh and fit for its purpose. In this regard, there is a specific rule stated by Marīci: "On the new moon day of the month of Nabhasya, the gathering of darbhas is prescribed; those darbhas are unexhausted and may be used again and again. Thus says Marīci [1.2]: "In the month of Nabhasya, on the new moon day, the gathering of darbhas is prescribed."

"Those *darbha* grasses do not become exhausted (*ayātayāma*) when they are used again and again. From this statement, the generally accepted rule is that *darbha* grasses gathered on the new moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa remain unexhausted and may be used repeatedly. However, some hold that based on the *Gṛhapariśiṣṭa*, *darbhas* are generally unexhausted. As for the statement of Marīci: "If a learned man ever cuts *kuśa* grasses while his hair is disheveled, he should, in the absence [of other grasses], twist them together and discard them on the following day."

Thus ends the section on exceptions. Laghu-Hārīta, however, mentions the avoidance of certain other acts as well, as follows: [1.2] "One should always lower the right knee while attending upon the gods; one should likewise lower the other knee while attending upon the ancestors. (Viśiṣṭa-pariśiṣṭa-prakāśa): He states another specific rule: "In the offering intended for the gods, while attending upon the gods, one should perform the lowering of the right knee."

While attending to the ancestors during the performance of the explanatory recitation (*arthavāda*) for that purpose, one should cause the left knee to touch the ground. (5) — *Prabhā*. "One should avoid these six types of *darbha* grass: *darbha* on a funeral pyre, *darbha* on a path, *darbha* on sacrificial grounds, and *darbha* used for spreading, sitting, or *piṇḍas*. Likewise, from that same source: "The *darbha* grass that has been spread for the sake of the *piṇḍas*, those by which the libation to the ancestors was performed, and those held in urine or food remnants—their disposal is prescribed."

"One should know that those *darbha* blades which are held in the middle of the *nīvī* (the waist-knot) and those held in the *brahmasūtra* are pure; as is the body, so too are the *kuśas*. Because of the statement, "by whom the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) has been performed," there is a fault in performing the ancestral libation with those same blades by which the libation to the deities (*devatātarpaṇa*) was performed. The phrase "and in the middle of the *nīvī*" is an exception (*apavādaka*) to the rule "and those held [in contact] with urine or impurities. In the verse "and those held with urine or impurities," some manuscripts read "and those smeared with urine or impurities" (*mūtracchiṣṭapralepe*). || 4 ||

Regarding "the right": while performing rites for the gods (*daiva-karma*), one should cause the right knee to fall—that is, place it upon the ground. While performing rites for the ancestors (*pitṛ-karma*), one should cause the left knee to fall. [The *Karmapradīpa*, 1.2.1–2, states: "Indeed, there is no instance where the left knee is used; one should never serve the ancestors as one would the gods. [1.2.3–4: "Having seated them upon *kuśa* grass after offering [the invitation] with 'To the ancestors' (*pitṛbhyaḥ*), and having addressed the ancestors by their names, one should cause the *arghya* water to be offered."

*Parīśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Here, there is no mention whatsoever of placing the left knee on the ground. What then? The meaning is that one should always serve the ancestors as one does the gods, until the arrival of the guest (*yāvāgama*). [Verse 6] Regarding the offering of *kuśa* grass on the seat, it should be given with reference to the ancestors and not to the Brahmins; thus he says: "With the hand indeed straight"—according to the manner stated, when [the offerings] have been given to the ancestors, light shines forth. By the word "always" (*sadā*), he teaches that even in the rites for the gods (*daivakaṇya*) included within the ancestral rites (*pitṛkarman*), the right knee must be placed on the ground. [Verse 5]

Having stated this as a digression, he speaks of the subject at hand with the words "the prostration" (*nipāta*). Here, the term "herein" (*atra*) is understood to apply both to what follows and to what precedes. Thus, in the *pārvaṇa* or *ābhyudayika* śrāddha, even when performing rites for the ancestors, one should not act with the left knee on the ground; rather, the meaning is that here, even in ancestral rites, one should serve the ancestors with devotion as if they were gods, and perform the ancestral ritual with the right knee on the ground. By saying "always" (*sadā*), he instructs that it should be done in this manner until the completion of the rite. || 6 ||

Having seated the Brāhmaṇas, one should give them *kuśa* grass with the right hand alone; thus it is stated in the *Karmapradīpa* and the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. Regarding the phrase "upon the *kuśa* grass": having seated those Brāhmaṇas and addressed them by their own names, one should cause the water and other substances contained in the vessels for the ancestors and the gods to be given—that is, one should give them. By this, it is meant that one should utter the names preceded by the appropriate honorifics (*sambodhana*). [1st Adhyāya, 2nd Khaṇḍa] *Prabhā*: He describes the manner of giving the *kuśa* grass with the words "to the ancestors," etc.

Having seated those Brahmins upon the *kuśa* grass offered here with the words "Svadhā to the Pitṛs, O Pārśva," and having addressed and connected them to the Pitṛs by their respective names, one should cause the *arghya* to be given—that is, one should give it. The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in the sense of the agent's own purpose. The plural form "by their respective names" (*gtranāmabhiḥ*) is used because there are many ancestors, or else for the sake of including the mention of the specific relationship to the father and others.

Since it is clearly stated [in the scriptures] that [the offering] is given with the words "tadava pitṛbhyaḥ" (this for the ancestors), and because the instruction regarding the addressing by individual names occurs after passing over the giving of the *kuśa* grass, the *kuśas* should be offered using the formula "to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ*) alone; there is no addressing by individual names at this point. Thus says Vyāsa: "The dative case is always prescribed for the seat and the water-offering (*salpa*), while the nominative is prescribed for the libation (*tarpaṇa*); others have declared that the vocative case should be used."

Thus, regarding the constant offering of a seat, he states the dative case; this statement is to be respected even by the followers of the *Chāndogya*. For among them, the nominative case is prescribed for the libation (*tarpaṇa*), while others prescribe the vocative. As for what was explained by Nārāyaṇa Pañcānana—namely, that "in the manner stated as 'with a straight hand,' [the offering is made] upon the *kuśa* grass offered to the ancestors"—that is inconsistent. It results in the word "iti" becoming meaningless, and it renders the phrase "to the ancestors" (pitṛbhyaḥ) redundant.

For it is indeed to the ancestors that the *bali* offering is given. This is the essential meaning of the formula of renunciation (*tyāga-vākya*). Regarding the abandonment of the object according to its actual purpose: if this were merely intended to designate a location, there would be no lack of purpose whatsoever, as there is no evidence to the contrary. Those who know the intent of the scriptures declare that when a word is heard, whatever meaning is understood from it is indeed understood. And that meaning cannot be abandoned without a reason, because the Veda is authoritative.

By this [statement], namely *iti* (thus), the explanation provided by the authors of the *Tattva*—that one should address the ancestors by their names in the manner being described, and that the *kuśa* grass is offered to the ancestors—is to be understood as inconsistent. This is because it has never been observed before for the word *iti* to function as a reference to what is being described. Likewise, the *Khādira-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa* states: "In all cases, the name ends in a vowel; 'sva' is used in rites for inexhaustible merit (*akṣayya-karma*), and 'svaḥ' is employed in the act of satiation (*tarpaṇa*). When used thus, the performer does not become confused."

"In all cases, O Father, one should use the name 'Pitṛ' during the rite of libation (tarpaṇa) and at the time of the ancestral offering (śrāddha); by acting thus, the performer does not become deluded. In the case of Śarmā, Ṛṣi, and so forth, one should use 'Śarmā' during the rite of libation and at the time of the ancestral offering; by acting thus, the performer does not become deluded."

Thus, because it is concluded with the words "in rites such as the offering of *arghya*," it follows that since the purpose of all the preceding statements culminates in the purpose of rites such as the offering of *arghya*, there is no mention of the drawing of lines (*ullekhana*) for the seat of grass (*kuśāsana*) prior to the giving of the *arghya*; this is what is being stated. Furthermore, the principle that a general rule is subordinate to a specific one remains established.

Thus, when the phrase "given to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ*) occurs, there is not only a lack of evidence for abandoning its literal meaning in favor of imagining another unintended meaning; rather, it is contradicted by evidence—this should be well understood. (7) *The Lamp of the Ritual Manual:* "In this case, the use of the *apasavya* (left-hand) position is not required, nor is the *paitra-tīrtha* (thumb-root) finger-tip intended. Indeed, one should have the filling of the vessels and other such acts performed with the *daiva* (right-hand) position alone. (8) *The Commentary on the Pariśiṣṭa:* [1st Adhyāya, 2nd Khaṇḍa]

41. He states another distinction: as in the *Pārvaṇa* [śrāddha], the making of the *prācīnāvīta* [sacred thread over the right shoulder] is not performed here, nor is the *pitrya* [ancestral] *tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) desired by the sages for the offering of water, fragrance, and so forth. What then? One should fill the *ardhya* vessels with water; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the offering of fragrance and other items at that very spot is included; and by the plural number, all rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pivarya karma*), such as the scattering of food (*annasarga*) and the rest, one should perform with the *daiva* *tīrtha* alone. The particle "eva" (only/alone) is used because: "A wise man should perform the *piṇḍadāna* rite for those who are *nāndīmukha*."

The phrase "whatever belongs to Prajāpati by means of the *prājāpatya* *tīrtha*" is intended to exclude the *prājāpatya-tīrtha* mentioned in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*. Furthermore, the state of being an *upavītī* (wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder) must also be observed here.
