As stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "In that rite, scattering sesame seeds is recommended, as well as barley; one who is performing a sacrifice should do everything while wearing the *yajñopavīta*, and not with the *apasavya* (thread over the right shoulder). The mandatory instruction using the verb "kārayet" (should cause to be done) implies that, according to the view regarding the assembly (*parṣad*), it may be performed through another person's hands as well. This is the conclusion.

In this *abhyudayika* (auspicious rite), the sages do not accept the practice of wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*) as in the *pārvaṇa* (ancestral rites), nor the use of the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors). The filling of the *arghya* vessels with water, scents, and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) implying that all other ancestral rites should likewise be performed by the *deva-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods) alone. Because of the prohibition against wearing the thread over the right shoulder, it follows by implication that everything must be performed while wearing the thread over the left shoulder (*upavītin*). Thus says the *Brahma-purāṇa*: [1.42] The lamp. (Note: The text fragment ends abruptly with "kapradīpaḥ", which appears to be a corruption or a specific reference; the translation reflects the preceding prose.)

5kha] Having formed pairs of hands with the thumbs joined and the tips of the fingers serving as sacred grass (*darbha*), the water for sipping (*arghya*) should be offered; it is not given to each individual separately. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: This means that the *vṛddhiśrāddha* (prosperity rite) must be performed, not like the *ekoddiṣṭa* (single-offering rite), and there is a rule that it must be performed by oneself. Likewise, it is not the *savya-pacāra* (left-hand procedure), but rather the *dakṣiṇa-pacāra* (right-hand procedure). As Śātātapa says: "The rite for the gods (*daivika*) and the rite for the sake of prosperity (*abhyudayārthaka*) should be performed in the forenoon."

"With the left hand, with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavīta*), and with straight *darbha* grass, by the wise one"—that is, with the left hand moving toward the right. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "Now, in the *abhyudayika* (prosperity) rite, the procedure is clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*). And Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa states: "Now, in the *abhyudayika* śrāddha, one should invite an even number [of Brahmins]; the procedure is clockwise. || 8 || Regarding the specific rule for the offering of the *arghya* water from the side, he says: "An even number of Brahmins representing the ancestors, with their hands placed one above the other (*jyeṣṭhottaraka*)"; that is, the hand of the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*), who was seated first, is on top.

"One should scatter sesame seeds there, as well as excellent barley; however, in all rites performed for the ancestors (pitr), one must not perform the circumambulation in a counter-clockwise direction (apasavya). And: "In this rite, one should serve the ancestors just as one serves the gods. From this it is understood that here the counter-clockwise procedure (vāmapacāra) is not to be performed, but rather the clockwise procedure (dakṣiṇapacāra). Accordingly, the *Śrāddhakalpa* states: "In the *ābhyudayika* śrāddha, one should cause the water-pots to be poured out while performing the circumambulation in a clockwise direction. He states the specific rule regarding the offering of the *arghya* water: "With the hands held such that the right is uppermost," and so forth.

The *Paṃtikarmapradīpa* by Jyeṣṭha; the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. Those whose hands are [raised] above are "tathā"; those who have the tip of the sacred grass (*pavitra*) at the tips of their hands are "karāgrāgrapavitrakāḥ. Having made them such, water, flowers, and so forth contained in the vessel for the *arghya* offering should be given into their hands. But it is not as in the *pārvaṇa* rite, where the offering is given into the hand of one Brahmin representing the father, and likewise to the grandfather, and likewise to another representing the great-grandfather; it is not done in that manner here. 8. [1 Pra. 2 Kha.]

43. *Prabhā*. "Of those whose hands are above the hand of the most excellent" (*śreṣṭhasya uttaraḥ upari sthitaḥ karaḥ yeṣām*), or "of those whose hands are upon the head of the eldest" (*jyeṣṭhasya karpare karaḥ yeṣām*); in both cases, the meaning is the same: the hand of the eldest is to be placed upon the hands of the other Brahmins—this is the intended sense. Having made their sacrificial grass-blades (*pavitraka*) such that the tip of the blade is at the tip of the hand (*karāgrāgrapavitrakān*)—that is, having made them such that the foremost part of the purifier is at the tip of the hand—the instruction should be given.

In the *āvābhyudayika* rite, the offering is not given into the hand of each individual Brāhmaṇa. For in the *Śrāddhakalpa*, regarding the *pārvaṇa* rite, it is stated: "He gives to each one with one [offering]," thus describing the giving of the *argha* into the hands of the individual Brāhmaṇas representing the father and the others. Here, however, it should not be done in that manner; rather, this is the specific distinction here: having joined together the hands of the Brāhmaṇas representing the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, the giving of the *argha* should be performed upon them.

This is because it is understood from the opening statement, "the pairs with the right hand uppermost," and from the concluding statement, "here [only] one [of each] is given. Otherwise, since the phrase "the pairs with the right hand uppermost" would imply that many pairs have their right hands uppermost, the statement "here only one is given" would be redundant. Therefore, this alone is the distinction here; however, the condition of having the tips of the blades of the *pavitra* facing the tips of the fingers is not a distinction, as it remains unchanged even in the *parvan* [rites].

Although the state of having the *pavitraka* at the tips of the hands is not explicitly prescribed for the *Pārvaṇa* rite, nevertheless, by this indicative mark (*liṅga*), its injunction there must be inferred. As they say in the *Karmapradīpa* (1.2.88): "A *pavitraka* made of *kuśa* grass, containing an endless [inner] core, consisting of two blades, and measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length—this is to be known as the *pavitraka* wherever it may be used. [From the] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

The *pavitra* made from *kuśa* grass is known everywhere as being three-finger-breadths (*prādeśa*) in length, with its interior hollowed out; however, this does not apply in the present case to the vessel for the half-offering (*ardhapātra*). [Verse 10] The rule is understood even from an indicative mark (*liṅga*), just as in the case of scattering (*vikira*) upon the *darbha* grass. Furthermore, it is impossible to infer there that the hand used must be the larger one, because of the injunction: "He gives with each [hand] to each [person]."

Furthermore, in the *Pārvaṇa* rite, the state of having the tips of the *pavitra* blades pointing southward (*dakṣiṇāgratva*) is not explicitly prescribed; however, since the offering of *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south is observed there, it is your established conclusion that the same should be inferred for the *pavitra*s as well. And thus, because of its internal proximity (*antaraṅgatva*), let only the state of having the tips of the *pavitra*s at the fingertips (*karāgrāgra-pavitrakatva*), which is seen in the *Ābhyudayika* rite, be inferred. For even when there is an observation in a modified rite (*vikṛti*), an inference is made regarding the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*) provided there is a need (*ākāṅkṣā*).

Since the distribution of the one hundred and twelve-fold sacrificial fee (*śatadakṣiṇā*) among the sixteen officiating priests (*ṣoḍaśartvig*) is specified for the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it is appropriate to determine the distribution of the one hundred and twelve-fold fee among the sixteen priests here as well—even though it was not explicitly stated in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), namely the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—just as it is determined there; so let it be, what is the use of further elaboration? (8) The *karāyāyapavitraka* has been described. In response to the inquiry as to what exactly constitutes a "purifier" (*pavitra*) therein, he says: "one that is not hollow within" (*anantargarbhiṇam*). In the term *anantargarbhiṇam*, the suffix *-in* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).

A lamp-wick (*kapradīpa*) is one that has its end [trimmed] with *kuśa* grass, is free from impurities, and measures ten fingers in length. This indeed is declared to be the definition of a wick (*picūlī*). That which is used for the purpose of clarifying clarified butter (*ājya*) is also exactly this much. (11) — *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

Regarding the rule "He makes the venerable one look upward with 'bhūḥ' using *darbha*-picūla-bunches" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.17.5), and elsewhere in the context of the *cūḍākaraṇa* (tonsure ceremony), the Sūtra states, "twenty-one *darbha*-picūlyas. The teacher has thus stated that even these *darbha*-bunches possess this very same characteristic. Furthermore, regarding the *pavitra* (strainer) made from sacrificial grass (*barhis*) of the measure of a span for the purpose of purifying the clarified butter—as stated in the Sūtra "From that very *barhis*, he makes two *pavitras* of the measure of a span"—that *pavitra* also consists of exactly that same number [of blades]. It does not, however, consist of two blades simply because of the use of the dual number.

The dual number [is used] because the word *pavitra*, which denotes a species of *kuśa* grass, is employed in reference to two blades. *Prabhā*: Two blades of *kuśa* grass are to be understood as the *pavitra* in all instances. By the phrase "wherever," the meaning of the commentary is understood; that is to say, wherever the word *pavitra* is employed, this meaning is to be recognized there. (10) He states this very point: "This same definition has been proclaimed by the sages even for the *picūlī*."

The meaning is that one should perform the purification (*pavitra*) with twenty-one blades. By this, the meaning of the word *picūlī* as used in the *Gṛhyasūtra*—specifically in the section on the *Sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) in the passage beginning "Then he parts the hair upwards with the mantra 'Bhūḥ' using *darbha*-blades," and likewise in the *Cūḍākaraṇa* (tonsure) section in the sūtra "twenty-one *darbha*-blades"—is clarified. Furthermore, the *pavitra* used for the purpose of purifying the clarified butter (*ājya*) is also of this same measurement and not more than that.

By this [statement], even though there is a dual-number designation in the Āśvalāyana Sūtra—"from that very *barhis* he makes two strainers (*pavitre*) of the measure of a span"—one should not understand there a duality of the strainer consisting of two specific leaves. If that were the case, the phrase "of the measure of a span" would be redundant. [The *Karmapradīpa* states: "Some say these [strainers] should be made of Kuśa grass, moistened with cow-dung or water; or they may be dry, made of withered flowers, and are called *picūla*. (1.2.12)

In the recitation of mantras for the ancestors (*pitr-mantra-anudravaṇe*), in touching oneself (*ātmālambhe*), in looking [at the sacrificial fire] (*avekṣaṇe*), in walking on a path (*adhvā*), in the expiration of life (*āyusamutsarge*), in laughing (*prahāse*), and in speaking untruth (*anṛtabhāṣaṇe*). The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* states: Some authorities say that the objects of worship (*pūjyāḥ*) are blades of *kuśa* grass, either fresh sprouts of the measure of a span (*prādeśapramāṇā*) or dried, or a cluster of withered flowers (*bhraṣṭapuṣpapicūlī*). This [type of blade] is to be used in the context of "two green blades with tips" (*haritāve sapilā*); elsewhere, however, it is only in the form of a *pavitra* [strainer]. [This applies to] the recitation of mantras for the ancestors, the touching of the heart prescribed at sacrifices and the like, and the looking [at the fire], which is its manifestation.

Because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of meaninglessness (*anarthakatva*). In the Sūtra, however, it is stated that there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *pavitra* toward the two blades (*dala*) that constitute the *pavitra*. As for the indication of the blades, it is because such is seen in mantras such as "The two *pavitras* belong to Viṣṇu" (*pavitre stho vaiṣṇavyau*). As for the singular number in the word *pavitra*, the intention is that it is used in a collective sense (*eka-vacana*), as seen in mantras such as "with the flawless *pavitra*" (*acchidreṇa pavitreṇa*). Alternatively, the word *pavitra* in the Sūtra may denote the genus (*jāti*) of Kuśa grass itself. Regarding the phrase "of this measure": other teachers [hold this view].

They say that a *pilī* is a mango blossom (*cūtakuṣumā*) that is the size of a region, whether fresh and moist or dried; and according to Nārāyaṇa Pāṭhyāya, this green variety with its stalk (*sapilā*) is what should be taken here. Regarding "the father" (*pitaram*) and "the crocodile" (*mākara*): in the recitation of the *pitṛ-mantra*, there is a reading in some manuscripts as *samu iti*, while in other manuscripts the reading is as follows: [1.2] *Kampradīpa*: upon touching a cat or a mouse, when one is reviled, or when a cry of distress occurs.

In all these instances, while performing ritual acts, one should touch water; this is the second section. [From] the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: When there is a prescribed act such as a sacrifice, upon the emission of wind (flatus), upon eructation, during loud laughter—but not a smile—when reviled or when harsh speech is uttered, and upon the arising of anger even without speaking but through the mind alone—in all these circumstances, at the time of performing a rite, one should touch water, but one should not perform the formal sipping of water (*ācamana*). The rest is explained by the literal meaning of the words.

The phrase “in the recitation of the Pitṛ-mantras” is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication). For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says: “Having uttered the Raudra, Paitṛka, Āsura, and likewise the Abhicārika mantras, and having touched himself and released water, he should perform another [rite]. (13–14) [End of] Second Section. [Commentary: Regarding the reading “in the carrying away of the Pitṛ-mantras,” the meaning is the same. In the case of “touching oneself” (*ātmālambhe*), it refers to touching the heart. Because the Self (*ātman*) is formless, the location is indicated by that which occupies the location.

[The following apply] when seeing a *caṇḍāla* or similar [outcaste] while holding the *mekṣaṇa* ladle; or, according to the reading "in looking" (*avekṣaṇe*), "looking" refers specifically to the touching and looking at the heart during a sacrifice or similar rite, as stated in the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: "when that which is beneficial for the heart occurs therein. [Also when there is] a collision with a cart, a horse, or a camel; [when there is] loud laughter (not a mere smile); [when there is] a struggle between a cat and a mouse; [when there is] "having been reviled" (*ākruṣṭe*)—here the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) denotes the state [of being reviled], according to the *Kampradīpa*. [Also when there is] harsh speech; or, according to the *Kṛdasaṃbhava*, even in the absence of harsh speech.

Regarding these occasions—by the use of the word "all," this includes other similar occasions—when such circumstances have arisen, one performing the rite should touch water but shall not sip it (ācamana). As Yājñavalkya says: "Having recited the mantras dedicated to Rudra, the Pitṛs, or the Asuras, as well as those for malevolent rites (abhicārika), and having touched oneself, one should perform the other [acts] after touching water. (1.2.48) Thus ends the second section. The Third Section.

Various types of non-performance have been declared for those who perform ritual acts: non-performance, performance contrary [to the rule], and thirdly, improper performance. (1) That fool who, abandoning what is prescribed in his own branch [of the Veda], desires to perform what is found in another branch, his effort is indeed futile. (2) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Non-performance is the failure to act; performance contrary [to the rule] is acting in a manner other than that which is prescribed, such as by means of a different sequence and so forth. These are the various forms of non-performance of rituals, because they result in fruitlessness. (1)

Regarding this, he states a specific distinction: "He who, having abandoned the *śrāddha* and other rites prescribed in his own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*), desires to perform those belonging to another branch (*pāraśākhika*) which are contrary to his own, is one whose knowledge is contrary to scriptural knowledge. Whatever is performed by him is fruitless. (Verse 2). *Prabhā*: In matters such as the offering of half a seat of *kuśa* grass and the like, regarding the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*), various methods have generally been taught by different teachers. And that [procedure] must be performed by those belonging to that same [branch], not by others.

But for another, performing something other than what is prescribed is as good as non-performance; thus he says, "non-performance" (*akriyā*). The sages have declared that there are three kinds of non-performance regarding the duties pertaining to the *karman*, the *karaṇa*, and the *gaṇa*—namely, non-performance (*akaraṇa*), performance of what is other than prescribed (*anyat-karaṇa*), and improper performance (*ayathā-karaṇa*). Improper performance is the execution of the rites through a reversal of the proper sequence. Regarding the phrase "based on one's own branch" (*svaśākhāśrayam*): this refers to the performance of the ritual belonging to one's own Vedic school (*śākhā*) without interruption. *Karmapradīpa* [1.3]

Whatever rite is not prescribed in one's own branch (*sva-śākhā*) but is prescribed in another branch (*para-śākhā*), such as the *Pārka-sava* sacrifice for the followers of the *Chāndogya*, that should be performed by those [of the former branch], just like the *Agnihotra* and other rites. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: That which is prescribed in another branch is, for example, the *Yājurvedika Agnihotra* for the followers of the *Chāndogya*. Or, it is a rite not prescribed in one's own branch that serves to fulfill a deficiency (*ākāṅkṣā-pūraka*) or constitutes its essential nature (*svarūpa*). For instance, regarding Manu: "The girdle, the deerskin, the staff, the sacred thread, and the water-pot..."

Regarding the statement, "Having cast out the vital breaths, these [offerings] are destroyed and struck down," those who know the ritual rules (*dharma*) must certainly provide the internal recitation of mantras that fulfills the requirement for such mantras. As for the Puranic and other [recitations], because they are common to all, they are not alien; thus, one performs them as well, following what has been previously explained.

It has already been stated that for such a person, there is no performance [of the rite]. However, as for the one of poor intellect who, having abandoned the procedure (*prayoga*) belonging to his own branch (*svaśākhā*), desires to perform a procedure belonging to another branch by means of borrowing (*yathājāpya*) and so forth—whatever he performs is fruitless. The word "tasya" (for him) takes the genitive case in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣa*). By the word "tu" (however), the author indicates the distinction of this case from the previous one. Regarding the phrase "that which is not recited here": whatever is not recited in one's own branch, even if it is mentioned elsewhere, it must be performed in detail provided it does not contradict one's own branch.

In this regard, there is an illustration: "like the *agnihotra* and so forth. It is said that the *agnihotra* is indeed mentioned in the *Chāndogya* recensional branch (*śākhā*), yet it is performed according to what is recited in other branches. There is something to be said here: in the first section, there are two readings, namely *paryukṣaṇavidhi-vat* and *paryukṣaṇavidhiḥ*. [This is] the *Āpastaṃba-kalpaprakāśa*. That which is more extensive than one's own branch must indeed be performed.

This refers to practices such as the recitation of mantras like *yathā devatābhyaḥ*. As for what is stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "Whatever rite is proclaimed in one's own *gṛhya* [text], even if it contains many details—if that much of the scriptural purpose is performed, the entire rite becomes accomplished"—this is intended to mean that the performance of common or optional rites is not mandatory; it does not mean that only what is stated in one's own *gṛhya* must be performed. For otherwise, the instruction regarding common rites not mentioned in one's own *gṛhya* would result in logical inconsistency (futility).

And because of the rule regarding other Vedic branches (Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa). [1.3] Commentary: In that regard, it was stated that this is the procedure. By the second verse, performing a rite according to another school's scripture while disregarding the rite prescribed by one's own school is prohibited. By the third, however, it is taught that whatever is not contradicted by what is prescribed in one's own school should be performed even if it is mentioned in another.

By the phrase "based on one's own branch" (*svaśākhāśrayam*), it is indicated that performing the practices prescribed in another school while abandoning those stated in one's own is censured. Furthermore, by the word "intermediate" (*parktā*), it is stated that at the time of performing the practice prescribed in one's own school, there should be no performance of an intermediate [practice]. Thus, its meaning is that one must not perform an intermediate practice intermittently within the practice prescribed in one's own school; otherwise, it would result in the practice being rendered meaningless.

Furthermore, it is impossible to exclude the occasional mention of the thumb from other treatises within the practical application prescribed by one's own scripture regarding the Śrauta rituals. This is because specific duties are assigned to each individual priest—such as the Hotṛ and others—within their respective branches (śākhās). Moreover, the sacrifice is accomplished by various priests belonging to different branches, such as the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, and Udgātṛ; accordingly, it is ordained in various places that "the Hotṛ utters the vaṣaṭ-call," "the Adhvaryu offers the oblation," "the Udgātṛ sings," and so forth.

Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣya*), it must be stated that the performance of the ritual as prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* is the light illuminating the path; otherwise, the performance of rites interspersed with those from other sources would be improper. Thus, the *Gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa* cited by Nīlāmbara in the *Śrāddha-bhāṣya* states: "The *prayoga-śāstra*, such as the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, is not to be combined with others, because its status as a *prayoga-śāstra* would be lost due to the rule against undertaking [multiple authorities]. Or rather, for whomsoever a rite is proclaimed in abundance according to his own *Gṛhya-sūtra,"* [that alone should be followed].

"When the purpose of the scripture has been accomplished to that extent, everything becomes accomplished. Regarding the Śrauta rites, whatever is intended by all the branches [of the Veda] applies to everyone; however, among those Śrauta rites, the common Smārta rules should be adopted. Likewise, the Gṛhyāsaṃgraha states: "In matters concerning one's own ritual system (tantra), one should perform what is prescribed in the systems of others. Indeed, the specific and general rules declared by the exponents of the Vedas—whether less or more than those—should be practiced according to what is stated in one's own scripture."

"Therefore, one should continue the sacrifice; one should not perform that which is dependent on another. He who, having abandoned his own branch (śākhā), practices the branch of another, and having rendered the seer (ṛṣi) [of his own tradition] invalid, sinks into blind darkness. These three statements of the venerable Gābhiḷaputra are identical in meaning to those of Kātyāyana.

In this regard, the first statement has the same meaning as "yathāmnātam" (as handed down in the tradition); the second statement has the same meaning as "parktā ca" (and that which is cooked); and the third statement has the same meaning as "svaśākhāśrayam utsṛjya" (having set aside what is based on one's own *śākhā*). Furthermore, they say: "The *prayoga* (practical application) does not admit of a combination (*samuccaya*) with its own *kṛtya* (prescribed duty). For if there were a combination, there would be neither its accomplishment nor a sequence. —Thus ends the *Kramapradīpa*, 5.3, *Prabhā*.

Nor should it be argued that the failure to incorporate the specific qualities [of one rite into another] contradicts the principle established in the section concerning different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*). For that principle concerns what is heard in the Vedic text (*śruta*), and because this case is based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*), the [general] principle does not apply. Furthermore, even if the rites are not distinct, since each is a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*) due to differences in form and so forth as far as possible, where could there be an incorporation of qualities? Indeed, the incorporation of the qualities of one ritual action into another ritual action is not sanctioned by the scriptures.

Therefore, by the statement: "Since another rite is not performed while one rite is already extended," he himself will later declare that the Vaiśvadeva and Bali rites are distinct rites by virtue of their general and specific characteristics. And as for that which is common to the end of the sacrifice, although it is not foreign [to the ritual], nevertheless, there is no inclusion of its subsidiary elements (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) in the performance prescribed by one's own scripture. This is because it constitutes a different rite, and in one rite, the inclusion of the subsidiary elements of another rite is improper.

Because the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* previously mentioned prescribes non-commencement [of other rites], and because other texts prohibit the combination (*samuccaya*) of the *Gṛhya* and similar rituals, one might think otherwise. However, he himself will state later regarding the Vaiśvadeva and Bali offerings that, after performing the practice prescribed by one's own school (*svaśāstra*), one may perform those [other rites] as well out of a desire for greater fruitfulness. This same principle applies even to the case of combination with those [rites] prescribed as "not to be commenced" (*anārambha*).

In the performance of those [optional rites], there is an abundance of fruit; however, even if they are not performed, the accomplishment of the fruit occurs through the performance of the domestic (*gṛhya*) rites alone. Thus it has been said: "Whether much or little, that which is prescribed in one's own *gṛhya*," and so forth. It is also stated in the *Madanapārijāta*: "If one is incapable, one should perform only what is prescribed in one's own *gṛhya*, for by that alone the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled. Therefore, among the Śrauta rites, that which belongs to another branch (*pāraśākhika*) should be performed, but among the Gṛhya rites, that [foreign branch practice] should not be performed.

However, that which is prescribed as independent (*anārabhya-vihita*) must be performed even in the domestic (*gṛhya*) ritual; for this is the *Karmapradīpa*: "If one should somehow perform an action that has already commenced otherwise than it was intended, then because it has become otherwise, one should conclude it from that very point. [1.3] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Regarding what must be done when an action is performed by chance due to a god or other cause, he says: "If one performs a rite that has been commenced—that is, already begun—otherwise, meaning with a different sequence, even while the performance is still in progress..."

In this regard, from whichever constituent element one has begun when it was performed otherwise, from that very point one should perform it again according to the stated method. For example, when the *gandharva* sacrifice is performed with a different sequence of the *gandha-dāna* offerings, at the time of performing it otherwise, once it is recognized, one should begin the performance again from that point. [Sūtra 4] Commentary: Success in the result comes from performing the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarma*); however, if those rites prescribed as independent (*anārabhyavidhi*) are performed, there is an excellence of the result.

The general rule of application, however, should be performed according to one's own desire following the application prescribed in one's own scripture; even so, a greater abundance of fruit must be sought. That which is to be done when an commenced rite is altered due to fate is now described as "the procedure for what has been set in motion" (*pravṛtta*).

If one should perform an action commenced in a different manner than it was begun, then, provided that he becomes aware of this while the rite is still incomplete—since awareness occurs after the commencement—he should complete that action starting from the very point where it went astray, rather than starting from the original beginning. Here, "performing otherwise" (anyathākaraṇa) refers to performing in a sequence contrary to the intended order; it is not a case of non-performance.

Furthermore, in cases such as the offering of a seat or *kuśa* grass, if any of these acts is omitted or performed out of sequence, then prior to the completion of the principal rite (*pradhāna*), one must begin again from that very point where the performance was altered; this is the rule. Thus it is said: "It must be performed again."

Or, for example, if among the sixteen-year rites (*ṣoḍaśāha*), the rite for anyone has not been performed prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, then starting from that point where it was omitted, it must be performed again. Just as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are accomplished over a month, or as the thousand-year sacrificial session (*sahasrasaṃvatsarasattra*) and others are accomplished over a year, so too the sixteen-year rite is a single ritual action accomplished over a year. This very rite is commenced in the first year and is completed by the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.

Just as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites, although the performance is accomplished over many days, it constitutes a single ritual act. As for what has been stated by the proponents of the *tattva*: "Because the principal recitations (*vāk*) are joined with repetitions (*āvṛtti*) in accordance with the sequence of their subordinate parts (*aṅga*), only that which has fallen [out of place] should be performed"—this is to be reconsidered. For there is a scriptural statement (*vacana*) that allows no other recourse; and since a logical principle (*nyāya*) does not apply to a matter that is established by direct scriptural injunction, it has been said: "What indeed could a scriptural statement not effect? There is no burden too heavy for a scriptural statement."

Furthermore, as for the statement that "one should perform [the rite] otherwise once it has commenced," and that this instruction is easily understood precisely within the context of the performance (*prayoga*), that too is a mere conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*), because there is no specific authority (*pramāṇa*) for it and because ease of performance is irrelevant. Nor can one find deliverance even by that much; for since the sixteen *vahās* are a single unit, the performance of that which is to be accomplished over a year is also a single unit. Thus, due to the non-duality of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) that produces the fruit, there is non-duality even in the ritual action (*karman*).

Among the sixteen sacrifices of equal status, one is the principal, as they themselves have stated: "The first [sacrifice] is like the Siddheśa. Furthermore, because the singular number in the phrase "during the autumn season, at the Great Sacrifice" (*śaratkāle mahāpūjāyām*) indicates that it is to be accomplished through a single performance, there is a unity of the *niyoga* (the mandate) which constitutes the meaning of the sentence produced by the entire complex of ritual acts. Thus, each individual act generates its own small portion of the *apūrva* (unseen potency), just as in the case of the various sacrifices involving curd and other offerings for Indra. This is explained in the section concerning the *Durgotsava*.

Therefore, even according to that view, there is only one performance and one commencement for the sixteen-fold sacrifice. [1st Praśna, 3rd Khaṇḍa] "If, while it is not yet completed, one should realize, 'This has been performed by me incorrectly,' he should perform only that much again; there is no repetition of the entire rite. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa:*

If one realizes that what was to be done has been performed otherwise—meaning, when there is the knowledge that an alteration has occurred regarding the performance of a ritual item—one should perform that very same item again in its proper sequence, but not the entire section of rituals (*karmakāṇḍa*) starting from the beginning. Furthermore, this re-performance should be carried out without delay and as easily as possible. However, where there would be delay or difficulty, one should simply remember Viṣṇu; there is no repetition of the rite.

Just as in the case of the *yathākṛt-sarga* (the creation according to what was done), when there is a subsequent performance (*bhajana*) by Brāhmaṇas, it is performed again within the interval of the creation; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*bādhā*) of subverting the greatness of the Brāhmaṇas. Thus [ends the section]. [Commentary: Regarding the phrase "of that one" (*tasyaika*), since there is no traditional injunction (*smaraṇa*) for the non-performance of anything prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, it cannot be prevented that the offerings (*vāḍāna*) beginning with that must be performed again. Let this suffice for the detailed discussion. Regarding the word "completed" (*samāpte*):

After the completion of a rite, if one realizes it was performed otherwise than prescribed, only that which was done incorrectly needs to be redone; however, from that point forward, the entire rite need not be repeated. But if the realization of the error occurs while the rite is still incomplete, the repetition of even what has already been performed is indicated by this rule as well. Furthermore, "performing otherwise" (anyathākaraṇa) means simply not performing [the act] at all, and not merely performing it with a reversal of the sequence. According to the reading in the Ka and Ga manuscripts, "this should be understood to apply when the principal part [of the rite] has been accomplished, in the case of a reversal of sequence. — *Karmapradīpa*.

Where there is a non-performance of the primary rite, that [rite] together with its auxiliary parts is performed again. But in the case of a non-performance of an auxiliary part, there is neither a repetition of the whole nor the performance of that [specific auxiliary]. (6) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Now, he states what must be done when there is a failure in the rite for the deities: if there is a non-performance—meaning the omission—of the primary action such as the offering of perfumes (*gandha*) and so forth, up until the *utsarga* (concluding dismissal), then that rite must be performed again along with the performance of its auxiliary parts.

If that subsidiary [rite] is not performed, there is neither a repetition of the primary rite already performed nor the performance of the subsidiary; rather, for the sake of rectifying it, one should perform the *yajñiyājñavalkya* [mantra]: "Whatever has been omitted or done incorrectly in the great sacrifices through ignorance, by the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu, that becomes complete"—so says the Śruti. Thus, when the ritual is concluded, otherwise there would be no result, as [the omission] would be ineffective.

The phrase "one should perform again" (*punaḥ kuryāt*) follows the style of expression seen in such examples as "at the end of ten days, one should perform [the rite] again" (*daśāhānte punaḥ kriyā*). Alternatively, it may be understood as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), as in the passage: "A woman who has miscarried before the *sīmanta* ceremony has been performed should place that hair upon her body and undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again. (5) Furthermore, he states a specific rule regarding the non-performance of the principal act (*pradhāna*): "In a case where only the subsidiary act (*aṅga*) has been performed but the principal act has not been performed, the principal act together with its subsidiaries must be performed again."

However, only the principal act (*pradhāna*) is performed; it is not the case that because of the repetition of the principal, there is a repetition of the principal together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*), nor is there the performance of only those subsidiaries. This is the meaning of this statement from the *Karmapradīpa* [1.3]: "For those who desire to recite 'Honey, honey' therein, after the *Gāyatrī*, one should recite [the verse] here, excluding the 'Honey-mantras'. The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* states: "Even regarding the knowledge of the performance (*karaṇa*), this very same resolution applies."

Others, however, maintain that if an auxiliary of a constituent part—such as wearing the sacred thread (*upavītitva*) and so forth—which is itself an auxiliary of the principal rite with its auxiliaries, is not performed, there is neither a repetition of the principal rite together with its auxiliaries nor the performance of the [omitted] auxiliary such as wearing the sacred thread; rather, they say that the mere recollection of it is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). || 6 ||

Vasiṣṭha states many other specific details: for those who wish to eat during the *pārvaṇa* rite prescribed by Vasiṣṭha, that which is connected with the *Śrāvaṇa* [month] should be recited after the *Gāyatrī*; one should recite "madhu-madhu-madhu" three times, and here the mantra "madhu vātā" should be recited either accompanied by its respective ritual formula (*tanmantra*) or without it. Thus, at the time of eating, the mantra must indeed be recited, because there was a prohibition [of it] at the earlier stage. [The commentary] *Prabhā* notes: from the previous statement, it is understood that performing the *pariṣecana* (sprinkling) otherwise results in its non-performance.

However, in that case, for the sake of the completeness of the ritual act (*karman*), one must perform the remembrance of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇusmaraṇa*). As stated by Yājñavalkya: "Whatever may fall away from the sacrifices through ignorance or negligence, by the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu, it becomes complete; such is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). Having thus mentioned this incidental matter, Vasiṣṭha states the specific rules regarding the *ābhyudayika* (prosperity rites) and others, beginning with the words "madhu-madhu" and so forth. The genitive case in the phrase "of those desiring [to attain]" (*abhilatumicchatām*) is used in the sense of a relationship (*saṃbandhalakṣaṇā*).

While the Brāhmaṇas are eating from the vessels prepared by Vasiṣṭha, they should listen [to the recitation]. However, one should never recite the *Pitṛ-saṃhitā* while eating; rather, another auspicious recitation, such as the *Smasāman*, should be performed. [This is] the end of the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. While they are eating, that recitation of the *Pitṛ-saṃhitā* which is prescribed there—beginning with "O Viśpati" (*yad vā u viśpatiḥ*)—must not be performed. Instead, in its place, another auspicious recitation, such as the *Smasāman*, should be carried out.

And so Kātyāyana says: "The recitation [of the *madhumatī* verses] is to be done by the father, excluding the mantra. [Commentary: Following the *gāyatrī*, after the recitation of the three verses beginning with "madhuvātā," it was prescribed that one should recite "madhu" three times; this [recitation] is to be performed excluding the *madhumatī* mantras. In the expression "madhu-madhu," the first word "madhu" refers to the substance honey (*madhudravya*). Therefore, they say that the threefold recitation there pertains to the word "madhu" which reveals that honey-substance.

In reality, however, the first word *madhu* refers to the triad of verses beginning with *madhuvātā*, because of the author of the Sūtras’ statement: “For Ṛg-verses, the rule applies by mentioning the first word when no specific instruction is given. The second word *madhu*, on the other hand, refers to the word-form itself, since in the *Śrāddhakalpa* it is stated that one should mutter the single word *madhu* three times (*virjapet*). Consequently, the muttering of the three verses beginning with *madhuvātā* is not to be performed at this point.

Because of the expression "desiring to eat" (*aśitum icchan*), the recitation of the *madhu-mantra* is prohibited only at the time prior to eating; however, it must indeed be performed at the beginning of the meal and so forth. "And not while they are eating": while the Brahmins are eating, the recitation of the *Pitṛ-saṃhitā* is prescribed. [1st Praśna, 3rd Khaṇḍa] That which is the method there for the food having sesame particles, that same method applies when they are near the leavings; but when they are satiated, it is the reverse. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: [The commentary on the above.]

In the *pārvaṇa* rite, that which follows immediately after the presence of the remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*)—namely, the scattering of sesame seeds—is here reversed; the meaning is that it occurs prior to the [guests'] satisfaction. Likewise, in that specific context, it should be performed with barley, so that it is accompanied by barley. [Commentary]: That which is prescribed for you must never be performed. However, something other than that—the recitation of the *Smasāna-mantra* and so forth—should be performed as an auspicious act.

The *Pitṛsaṃhitā* should be understood as that which is declared in the *Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa*: "When the Lord of the People (Viśpati) from of old has accepted the praise, and the ocean, roaring, has stepped across the three-backed [sacrifice]—this is the *Saṃhitā* named after the Father (*pitṛ*). Furthermore, the *Smṛtisāmans* are those sung over many Ṛgvedic verses recited in the *Chandasyā* and *Vike* [sections], such as "Flow forth, O Bull, with your stream" (*vṛṣā pavasva dhārayā*), and so on; they are read in the *Geyagāna*. [Regarding the verse beginning with] "He who... (*yastave*).

In the *pārvaṇa* rite, when the Brahmins have been fed, the scattering of barley is prescribed to be done in such a way that it remains near the leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*), just as with sesame seeds; here, however, it is the reverse: it must be performed in such a way that it is like the barley [scattered far away]. This reversal occurs because it is performed before the Brahmins have been fed, due to the use of the *devatīrtha*, the *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward, and so forth. The "scattering of food" (*annaprakara*) is what is called the "scattering" (*vikiraṇa*) and the offering of the *piṇḍas* to those not consumed by fire. (Kampradīpa, verse 8).

In the place where the question "Are you satisfied? (*tṛptāḥ stha*) is prescribed, one should say "It is well-prepared" (*sampannam*). After the question, when the Brahmins have replied "It is very well-prepared" (*susampannam*), one should inform the Brahmins that there is still food remaining. Thus ends the inquiry regarding satisfaction. (10) [1.3] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. Regarding the question "Are you satisfied? which occurs in the *Pārvaṇa* rite: in its place, one should say "It is well-prepared. Following the question, when the Brahmins have said "It is very well-prepared," one should announce to the Brahmins that there is also leftover food. Thus is the inquiry concerning satisfaction. (10) [1.3] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

—“It is accomplished,” says Kātyāyana. Regarding the phrase “it is accomplished”: in place of the question “Are you satisfied? which occurs at the Pārvaṇa [śrāddha], here the question “Is it accomplished? is prescribed—that is, it is to be performed. When the Brahmins have replied, “It is well accomplished,” one should inform them regarding the remaining food. How should one inform them? It is said: one should ask, “What shall be done with the remnants of the food? To that they should say, “Let it be eaten along with this sacrifice.”

And so says the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*: "Having asked permission regarding the remaining food, [saying] 'What shall be done with the remnants? Let them be eaten together with the sacrificial offering (*iṣṭi*)'. By this, the meaning is that one should ask for permission in this manner. As for the point that one should ask, "Where should the remaining food be given?", the reply is, "Let it be given to those who are dear (*iṣṭa*). This has been stated by the authors of the *Tattva* (the *Tattvaviveka*), citing the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "He said to them again: 'And where should the remaining food be given? They replied in unison: 'Let this be given to those who are dear.'"

That is incorrect; for the statement from the *Brahma Purāṇa* concerns the procedure for the *Śrāddha* performed by the Primordial Boar (Ādivarāha). [From the] *Chandogānāṃ Svaka-pradīpa*: [1st Praśna, 3rd Khaṇḍa] "Then, upon Darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, having first invoked [the ancestors] as before, one should pour water at the root-end [of the blades], saying 'May they drink,' omitting the sesame seeds. [From the] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

Having first designated the father by means of his name and gotra, as if in a formal address, one should pour water devoid of sesame seeds upon the roots of the kuśa grass spread out toward the east, saying "bhuvane niveti. In this matter, the specific distinction is that the tips [of the kuśa] should point eastward and be free of dew, according to Vasiṣṭha (11). This is because there are different instructions for different branches of the Veda; indeed, it is not appropriate to disregard those and instead rely on the statement from the *Brahma Purāṇa* concerning the ritual procedure performed by Ādivarāha.

In this way, there would be no remnant for the sacrificer, because the *Brahmapurāṇa* states that the remnant is to be given to those invited; likewise, there is the injunction in the *Gṛhyasūtras* and other texts: "One should announce the remaining food to the Brahmins. Furthermore, the explanation by Nārāyaṇopādhyāya is devoid of authority. For the ancestors are indeed those who have been invited. Since the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) becomes the enjoyment of the ancestors through that gift, he begins the section on the offering of the rice-balls with the words "on those [blades] with tips pointing eastward. The word "atha" (now/then) is intended to indicate the sequence immediately following [the previous rite].

The meaning is: after the Brahmins have replied and the extension of the *piṇḍa-pitṛ-yajña* has been obtained through the drawing of lines and so forth. Having addressed the first father with the words "O Father" (*pitara*) followed by the name ending in the vocative case, and having said "May there be [water] for you" (*astu te*), one should pour water without sesame seeds at the root-end of the *kuśa* grass previously placed on those eastern seats, for the purpose of offering the *piṇḍas*. From the statement "they are satisfied" (*nistitāḥ*), it is understood that the water contains barley; this is because of the rule stating "barley is for the sake of all purposes. (Kampradīpa 11)

The second [seat] is for the grandfather, and the third is for the great-grandfather; these, beginning with the maternal grandfather, are likewise to the left of these very [paternal ancestors]. Having taken up food from all [the portions], having sprinkled it with condiments, and having mixed it with barley, jujube fruits, and honey, he [the performer], facing eastward, [proceeds]. [Commentary on the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*]: The second is for the grandfather; the third is for the great-grandfather. As in the first case, having addressed them, one scatters [the offerings] among the blades of grass spread out, from the middle and the tips down to the roots.

In the same manner as the southern row was prepared, one should likewise scatter water, as before, upon the grass strewn with its tips pointing eastward in the northern direction for these same three [ancestors], at the root, middle, and tip sections for the maternal grandfathers and others. Immediately thereafter—taking a portion from all the primary food, mixing it with condiments, barley, jujube fruits, and curd, and adding clarified butter—the second [offering] is made.

Having addressed the second as the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) and the third as the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) as before, and having uttered the word "nivartasva" (return), one should pour water without sesame seeds in sequence into the middle and the front portions of the spread *kuśa* grass; this is to be supplied [to the previous injunction]. This is to the left of these same three, beginning with the father—that is, in the southern direction—because it is appropriate for the ancestors and others invoked for the offering of the *piṇḍas* to face westward. And this being so, the ritual procedure becomes performed in a clockwise direction (*pradakṣiṇa*).

The procedure for the maternal grandfathers and others—the maternal grandfather, the maternal great-grandfather, and the maternal great-great-grandfather—is to be understood as previously stated, following the same sequence of mantras and so forth. (12) He describes the method for offering the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) with the two verses beginning with "sarvasmāt": "Having offered rice-balls, each the size of a bilva fruit, according to the manner of the water-offering (*avanejana*), one should then perform the water-offering once more by moving those vessels. (14) This concludes the third section. [From] the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

Having prepared six rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) the size of a *bilva* fruit and facing east, he should offer them as in the ritual of sprinkling water (*avanejana*). Then, with the water used for washing the vessels that held the rice-balls, he should sprinkle water again. Here, because of the previously mentioned facing eastward, the rule from the *Āśvalāyana* regarding the *ābhyudayika* (prosperity) rite—stating that "an even number of Brahmins [are invited], the *darbha* grasses have their roots, and one should give to those facing east with [grass] pointing north"—is superseded by the facing northward. Thus ends the third section. *Prabhā*: The meaning here is "from the food intended for the *śrāddha*."

This is because it is understood in that very way from the statement, "one should offer the remaining food," and because of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the term "all" (*sarva*) refers to what is available; and also because it is seen in the *Pāraskara-gṛhyasūtra*: "From all the prepared food, [he should give] balls (*piṇḍa*) accompanied by honey and sesame."

Having removed [the food] from the original vessel, having placed it in another vessel, having moistened it with water poured out in three ways, and having mixed it with barley, jujube fruits (*karkandhu*), and curd, one should offer balls (*piṇḍa*) the size of a *bilva* fruit facing east, just as in the rite of washing (*avanejana*). One should then wash again with the water used for rinsing the vessel that held the balls. "Jujube and *vadarī*" [is mentioned]; the rest is well known. By the phrase "as in the rite of washing," the offering of the balls at the root, middle, and tip [of the grass-blades] is indicated. Because of the statement "one should wash," the practice of pouring water down is also understood. 13.

14 || Thus ends the third section. The fourth section begins: In the Śrāddha rite, by placing [the rice] higher and higher, the balls (piṇḍas) become successively higher; and by moving them lower, they become lower. Therefore, in all Śrāddhas—whether those performed on occasions of prosperity (vṛddhi) or others—one should offer the balls slightly smeared at the base, the middle, and the top parts [of the grass]. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa:*

He praises the offering of the *piṇḍas* according to the sequence beginning with the root: "By offering the *piṇḍas* one above the other in the sequence starting from the root, the giver becomes higher and higher, becoming a partaker of the world"—this is the praise. However, by offering them in the reverse order, one falls to a lower state; thus it is for the *śrāddha*. Therefore, in these and other rites such as the *pārvaṇa*, one should offer the *piṇḍas* slightly touching [one another] in the sequence beginning with the root. Prabhā.

He states the declaration of the fruit of offering the *piṇḍas* according to the sequence beginning from the root, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [in the verse] "He rises upward" (*uttarottarati*). By offering the *piṇḍas* in the Śrāddha rite in the sequence beginning from the root, that is, in progressively higher locations, the giver also attains an upward destiny. By offering the *piṇḍas* in the sequence beginning from the tip, that is, in progressively lower locations, the giver also attains a downward destiny. He concludes the offering of the *piṇḍas* according to the sequence beginning from the root with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since this is so, therefore, in all *pārvaṇa* rites and other *yātrās* involving those who possess prosperity, for the purpose of offering the *piṇḍas*, one should silently cast out the perfumes and other items; thereafter, one should cause the twice-born to rinse their mouths. This same procedure, excluding the use of barley and other grains, should apply elsewhere as well. (3) In a place sloping toward the south, while facing south, upon southward-pointing *darbha* grass—this is recorded as the rule for other occasions. (4) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa:*

Having offered scents, flowers, and other [substances] to the *piṇḍas* without mantras, one should cause the Brahmins to perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*). This is the procedure for the offering of the *piṇḍas*; in other rites as well, such as the *pārvaṇa*, it should likewise be devoid of barley, the [specific] deity, the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavīta*), and the movement toward the south. It is not only devoid of barley and so forth; it is also devoid of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Furthermore, unlike the *vr̥ddhi* rite, it is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), by a giver facing south rather than facing east, and upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south rather than pointing east.

"This is the procedure for the offering of the *piṇḍas*, as remembered by the sages for the *pārvaṇa* and other rites. [Prabhā: One should offer small *piṇḍas* suspended at the root, middle, and tip of the spread blades of grass. Hari is the one who pronounces the auspicious benediction (*maṅgalaka*). [Regarding "perfumes and so forth"]: one should place perfumes and the like upon the *piṇḍas* without reciting mantras. Then, one should cause the Brāhmaṇas who have partaken of the *śrāddha* to perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*); that is, one should cause them to cleanse their mouths and hands through the rubbing away of food residues and washing.

In other cases, even during the *pārvaṇa* rite, this same procedure shall apply, provided it is devoid of barley and the like. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*) in the phrase "barley and the like," there is the inclusion of [the use of] the *devatīrtha*, the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*apavīti*), facing the east, and the movement from left to right (*pradakṣiṇa*). Regarding the phrase "in the south-eastern part": in the southern region, for one facing south, there is the lamp. Then, one should sprinkle the ground with water, saying, "May it be well-swept," and "May the waters be auspicious," using an even number of vessels. Immediately thereafter, the offering of flowers is performed with the words, "May there be mental joy."

"May there be safety and freedom from misfortune; let him present the unbroken grains. (1.4) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: After the sipping of water (*ācamana*), he should ask, "Is the ground before the Brahmins well-swept? Then, with the words beginning "Auspicious are the waters," he should sprinkle water into the hands of an even number of Brahmins, not just one. (5) With the words "For a pleasant mind," he should place flowers in their hands. Immediately thereafter, with the words beginning "Unbroken," he should give barley grains. (6) *Prabhā*.

This is the rule for the offering of the *piṇḍas* by the performer upon *kuśa* grass with their tips pointing south; elsewhere, [the rites] beginning with the *pārvaṇa* have been prescribed by the sages. (4) Now, regarding the word "atha": immediately after the *ācamana* of the Brāhmaṇas, one should sprinkle the ground in front of them with water, using the formula "May it be well-sprinkled" (*susamprakṣitam astu*). The word "with water" (*udakena*) is to be supplied from what follows. With the formula "Auspicious waters" (*śivā āpaḥ*), one should sprinkle only the pairs of Brāhmaṇas, and not each one individually, with water; "in the hand" (*haste*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. (5) Regarding the word "saumanasyam": [one should offer flowers].

With the words beginning "saumanasyam" (for the sake of mental well-being), one should place flowers in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa. Immediately thereafter, with the words beginning "akṣatañca" (and unbroken rice), one should give barley-grains in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa. "Akṣatāḥ" refers to barley-grains; for it is said that "akṣatāḥ are barley-grains smeared [with ghee]. The term "dāpayet" (should cause to give) is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). Or, it may be intended as an instruction that the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* must be performed even through another person if one is unable to do it oneself. *Karmapradīpa*, [1st Praśna, 4th Khaṇḍa]: The offering of the *akṣayya-udaka* (imperishable water) is prescribed in the same manner as the offering of the *arghya*.

The sixth [case-ending] should always be used for the recipient of the honorific gift (*satkārya*), and never the fourth; such is the meaning. Just as when offering half a vessel of water, one should perform it for each of the two hands of the elder Brāhmaṇa individually. However, in that case, one should employ the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone after the name, and never the dative (*caturthī*). By stating "the sixth [case] always," the author prescribes the genitive in place of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) at the end of the name.

The phrase "never with the dative case" serves as a prohibition against using the dative in the expression "I offer this [oblation] to you" (*asmai te svadhā*); thus, there is no confusion. Abhilīya states: "The word *sva*, ending in a vowel, is used everywhere in the rite of offering water (*udaka-karman*). However, when *sva* is joined with a suffix (*prkta*), it refers to the agent; thus one does not become confused. Everywhere, the word *pitṛ*, when joined with a suffix, is used in the rite of offering water; however, in the offering of inexhaustible water (*akṣayya-dāna*) for the father, it is used by one desiring eternal satisfaction. Likewise, the form *śarma* is to be used in rites such as the invocation of the Ṛṣis, while *śarmā* is used in the rite of offering water."

"But that which is given to the ancestors at the *śarmannajyadāna* is inexhaustible. Prabhā: "It is *avayya*. Furthermore, the *ajyadāna* is prescribed as being like the offering of the *arghya*. By the phrase 'like the offering of the *arghya*,' an extension (*atideśa*) of the rule regarding the senior-most [brother] is established. The word *bhadrāpyatu* is supplied [from the previous context]; therefore, the formula used is *avayyam astu*. For this very reason, the subsequent requests such as *pratipṛcche* and so forth are appropriate for the *āvāsya* [rite]."

By the statement, "The gift of *sadācavya* should always be performed on the sixth [lunar day]," the *Karmapradīpa* expresses a connection with the *gṛha* (house). Through this, by means of the extension (*atideśa*) from the rule regarding the giving of food (*arvādāna*), there does not occur a connection with the *gṛha* via the genitive case-ending (*saṃbandhavibhakti*). This is because an original injunction (*upadeśa*) overrides an extended application (*atideśa*), just as sacrificial grass made of *śara* overrides sacrificial grass made of *kuśa*.

And so says the *Svāna-sūtra-pariśiṣṭa*: "In all cases, for the *ātayya* rite, one should use *gotra* ending in a vowel; *gotra* is used in the act of satiation (*tarpaṇa*), and thus the agent does not become confused. In every instance, for the *pitṛ* rite, one should use *pitṛ* ending in a vowel; *pitṛ* is used in the act of satiation, while for the *akṣayya* rite, it is used by one desiring inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors. For the *ārghya* and other rites, one should use *śarmān* ending in a vowel; *śarmā* is used in the act of satiation, while for the *akṣayya* rite of the ancestors, what is given becomes inexhaustible."

"Just as [in the texts] such as, 'Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for reaching this goal,' and 'The Great Lord, the Three-eyed One, alone [is the way], and not another,'" [the author here] shows that which is excluded by the particle *eva* in the phrase "only on the sixth," namely: "never on the fourth. This is a prohibition of what has been prescribed. For some, the offering of the *akṣayyodaka* (imperishable water) on the fourth day has been prescribed; and thus they recite: "May this [offering] go to the Nāndīmukha ancestors; may it be for them. (Gṛhyasūtra 1.4.68).

This is refuted by the following: as it has been stated, "because of the prohibition of what was prescribed. As for what the teacher Nārāyaṇa said—that by the rule "the sixth [case-ending] is obligatory," the sixth case is prescribed in place of the vocative at the end of a name, and never the fourth; thus, the phrase *svadhā te* is a prohibitor of the fourth case, and there is no redundancy—this is inconsistent.

Regarding the word *te* (them): since it denotes the object being addressed, when it is not indicated by the genitive case, there is no possibility of its meaning being non-integrated [with the ritual action], and thus a prohibition [of its use] would be untenable; for a lamp does not illuminate what is not present. [1.4] "In all prayers, the most excellent twice-born should pour water over the *piṇḍas* while they are covered with purifiers (*pavitra*), having placed the vessel face upwards. — *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

Immediately thereafter, among the five prayers beginning with "May it be well-prepared" (*susaṃskṛtam astu*), the [response] "May it be so, O Brahmin" (*astu saṃvit*) is prohibited by the Brahmins. This may be considered a perpetual restatement (*nityānuvāda*). Regarding the view that this constitutes a restrictive rule (*niyama*), by the prohibition of the mantra "ye cātra... in the offering of the *akṣayyodaka* (imperishable water) through the statement "never with the dative case," it is made known that the mantra "ye cātra... is to be recited everywhere except in the offering of the *akṣayyodaka*.

Otherwise, if the mantra for that [offering] were not applicable in the *akṣayyodaka* (water-offering for inexhaustibility), its prohibition would be impossible. As for the specific instruction of that mantra by Gṛhyasūtrakāra Āśvalāyana in those respective places, it is merely illustrative. That is incorrect, because it has already been shown that the mantra for that [offering] is not applicable in the *akṣayyodaka*. Furthermore, it has been stated that the fourth [section] consists of both prescriptions and prohibitions. Therefore, this is not a prohibition of the mantra "ye cātra tvā... (and those who are here with you).

However, since this is accepted by some as merely illustrative, how can it be understood that by this [rule] the mantra "ye cātra" applies to all cases? For if it were so, the specific instruction of Gbhila would be rendered redundant.

Regarding the phrase "prārthanāsu" (in the [verses of] entreaty): since the mantra "ye cātra tvā... is prescribed for the offering of *argha* (water-offering), and because of the extended application (*atideśa*) that it applies to the offering of *avayvya* (betel-leaves) just as it does to the *argha*, the prohibition of that mantra [in the context of the *avayvya*] is indeed appropriate. Therefore, I do not understand how this [prohibition] indicates the use of that mantra even in cases where it has not been specifically taught. This has been analyzed by us at length in the *Śrāddhakalpa-bhāṣya*, so we shall desist here. || 7 || [End of section on] the entreaties.

"May it be well-prepared," and so forth—these five prayers are from the *Karmapradīpa*. In the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*, it is stated that in the subsequent section, at the place where the *svadhā* recitation occurs, one should pour water over the *piṇḍas* covered with the strainers (*pavitra*) from the *arvāprapātrī* vessel, saying, "May they be offered to the Nāndīmukha ancestors. Immediately thereafter, having turned the inverted vessel face upwards, one should perform what is to be described beginning with "only pairs [of Brahmins]," and so forth.

The author of the *Gṛhyabhāṣya*, however, has explained that after performing the rites from "May it be well-prepared" (*susam̐sṛṣṭam astu*) up to the recitation of the *svadhā* formula, one should perform the *kṛtānnaprāśana*, place the *pavitra* strainers upon the *piṇḍas*, and then pour water over the *piṇḍas* with the mantra "vahantīr iṣaḥ" (*RV* 7.49.2). [Commentary: When the Brāhmaṇas have replied, "May it be as it should be" (*yathāyatham astu saṃvat*), one should turn the *nyunja* vessel upside down, place the *piṇḍas* separated by the *pavitra* strainers upon it, and pour water over them.

As for the explanation given by Nārāyaṇopādhyāya—that after offering the *piṇḍas*, one should turn the *nyūnapātra* (the vessel used for leftovers) face upwards and then perform what is about to be described—that is incorrect. For there is no authority for abandoning the literal meaning of the text; indeed, the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya* has stated that when a meaning is understood from the mere hearing of a word, it is understood as being true. And it is not proper to abandon what is directly heard in the scripture (*śruti*).

In the *Gṛhyabhāṣya*, Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa also explained "having turned the vessel upward" (*uttānapātrakṛt*) specifically as a qualification of the performer of the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*). As for what was stated by the author of the *Tattva*—that because it is seen in the text exactly as heard, Bhaṭṭa explained "having turned the vessel upward" as a qualification of the performer of the sprinkling—that is [refuted] by Āśvalāyana’s *Gṛhyasūtra*. For instance, after the sprinkling, Āśvalāyana says: "Having turned the vessel upward, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability. To this, we reply:

In the *Śrāddhakalpa*, however, the reading of the *Tattvakāra* is not seen; rather, the *Karmapradīpa* reads as follows: "One should pour a stream of water [saying] 'prabhā... svadhāniyanīye' and 'vahantīḥ'; having placed the vessel face upwards, one should cause [the officiant] to recite for the divine rite, 'May the Viśvedevas be pleased'; then, having moved the vessels containing the *piṇḍas*, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability. And this very sequence has been explained by the authors of the *Mādhavīya*.

In this regard, since there is no specific distinction for that which is recited in the middle—namely, "having placed the foot flat"—it is possible for it to be a representative indicator (*pratinidhi*) of what precedes it, as well as a representative indicator of what follows it; for both are seen in practice.

For example: "O Devadatta, when the sun has risen, eat your morning meal; having performed circumambulation (*caṅkramaṇa*), bathe at midday, put on two garments, and eat cakes. In this context, if Devadatta first performs circumambulation and then eats his morning meal, then the phrase "having performed circumambulation" is used as a reference (*pratīka*) to the preceding sentence; whereas in the opposite case, it is used as a reference to the subsequent [sentence]. And so it is with the sages regarding these instances of giving, receiving, and so forth.

In passages such as *nāmagrāha* and so forth, since it is observed that [the term] is used in both ways, the fact that *uttānaṃ pātraṃ kṛtvā* serves as a citation (*pratīka*) for a subsequent sūtra is not authoritative. Rather, according to the statement of Kātyāyana, who is [considered] inferior [in this context], it must be determined that it belongs to the preceding sūtra alone. Furthermore, it has already been stated at the outset that abandoning the literal meaning is improper; he indeed promised, "I shall correctly demonstrate the procedure for these low-caste rites. Therefore, enough with casting such side-glances upon those worthy of respect.

Because of the statement "always covered by the *pavitra*," a *pavitra* must be produced for the purpose of covering the *piṇḍas*. As for the description of the *viveta* (the separation), that is irrelevant; for there is no authority for the application of what has already been employed elsewhere. Otherwise, even the drawing of the lines for the offering of the *piṇḍas* would have to be done with that very same *pavitra*. [From the *Karmapradīpa*, Chapter 1, Section 4]: One should always address the blessings (*svasti*) to an even number of Brahmins and hold their thumbs.

Having done so, one should bow to the preeminent (*dhurya*) Brāhmaṇa and follow after him. [From] the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: One should give an even number [of gifts], not just one, and having performed the *svastivācana* with the offering of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should grasp the hand of the preeminent Brāhmaṇa—the one at the head of the row—excluding the thumb, bow down, and follow him. Here, the sacrificial fee consists of grapes, *āmalaka* fruits, and so forth. Likewise, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states regarding austerity: "One should offer grapes, *āmalaka* roots, and barley."

"One should always give those very same items as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) among these [recipients]. Regarding the offering of radish (*mūlaka*) and *ārdra* and so forth, it is said that this should be performed at the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, in the case of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, it should not be done for the mother; for it will be stated later that "one should not give separately to the women," and because this was not mentioned by Gṛhyapariśiṣṭakāra Āśvalāyana. However, in other cases, it must indeed be performed. Thus says the *Mātṛ-śrāddha-kalpa*: "The *śrāddha* for the mothers should come first, immediately after that the one for the fathers, and then for the maternal grandfathers; in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, this threefold *śrāddha* is prescribed."

In all three of these [rites], one who is pure should feed an even number of Brahmins. He should offer [the food] by circling to the right, beginning with the gods, using his left hand. The Commentary (*Prabhā*): "An even number only. This means that by giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should cause the *svasti* (benediction) to be recited; then, having grasped the thumb of the foremost Brahmin of the row and having bowed, this entire procedure for the *śrāddha* has been stated by me in brief. [1st Praśna, 4th Khaṇḍa] This is the complete rule for the *śrāddha*, as told by me in summary.

Those who know this are never deluded regarding the *śrāddha* rites. (10) 74 *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. By this statement, since it is declared that even the *mātṛvāsa* (the rite for the mothers) is accompanied by the deities (*sadaivata*), the claim made by some—that in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* the *mātṛvāsa* is without deities—is refuted. As for the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, which says: "Some men desire [the rite] devoid of the *Vaiśvadeva*," that is restricted to specific Vedic branches (*śākhā*). For this very reason, Laghu-Hārīta states: "But the *mātṛvāsa* with pairs..."

"It should always be thus with those facing east separately. (8) He concludes: "This aforementioned *śrāddha* procedure has been stated by me in its entirety with few words. Those who know this *śrāddha* procedure do not err regarding the matters of ritual action (*vāḍhakriyā*). (10) [Commentary: One should follow them. The giver of the *śrāddha* should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and the Brahmins should say "May there be well-being" (*svasti*); such is the meaning of the term *svastivāca*. (8) Regarding the word "this": [the aforementioned].

Thus, this very extensive ritual procedure for the *śrāddha* has been described by me in a brief text. Indeed, those who know this *śrāddha* ritual do not encounter any obstacle whatsoever in performing the *śrāddha*. (10) [Chapter 4, Section] *Karmapradīpa*: "He who knows this Śāstra, the Gṛhya-sūtra, and the Parisaṃkhyāna, as well as that which was spoken by Vasiṣṭha—he knows the *śrāddha*, and no other. (11) Thus ends the fourth section. *75. Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*

He praises his own work for the sake of those seeking excellence: "He who knows this treatise composed by Gṛhyāgmin, the work known as *Parisaṃkhyāna* famous by its own name, and the *Vasiṣṭhaka* named *Chāndogyagṛhya*, he truly knows; no one else. (11) Fourth Section. Commentary: Regarding the word "this" (*idam*).

One who knows this *Madula* treatise, the *Gṛhya* of Gṛhyaka, the *Parisaṃkhyāna*—well-known by its own name—which sets forth the *śrāddha* mantras, invocations, and so forth, and the *Śrāddhakalpa* composed by Vasiṣṭha, he alone knows the *Vāhe*; no one else who is unacquainted with these four texts [knows it]. Thus ends the fourth section. Fifth Section: The rites that are to be performed repeatedly by those engaged in ritual action do not require separate [invocations of] the Mothers for each instance, nor is there a separate *śrāddha*.

1 || *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: It has been stated that in all rites, such as those beginning with [domestic] rituals, there must be worship of the Mothers (*mātṛpūjā*) and the offering of the *yācñā* (supplication). Regarding this, he states a specific rule for certain rites: those rites which the performer of the ritual performs repeatedly—daily, monthly, or annually; such as the *Śrāvaṇī* and *Āgrahāyaṇī* festivals, the *Vaiśvadeva-bali* rites, the *Darśa-pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, and so forth—in these, the *Śrāddha* and the worship of the Mothers are performed only at the first performance, and not in the second performance and subsequent ones. || 1 ||

Prabhā: It is not stated that the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛpūjā*) and the *śrāddha* rite are required for all ritual acts (*karma*) and so forth. Regarding this, he states the distinction: "In those [acts] which... Those ritual acts such as the *vaiśvadeva*, the *balikarma*, the rites performed upon seeing or hearing the moon, and others, which are performed repeatedly by the performer every day, every month, and every year—in those, the worship of the Mothers and the *śrāddha* must be performed only at the first performance, not at every subsequent performance.

The same rule applies even to the recitation of mantras for longevity performed when a hair falls into the tongs or when a splinter of wood falls [into the fire]. However, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) serve as a fitting example of rites that must be performed every month; for it will be stated later that there is no separate mention of them.
The Vaiśvadeva and Bali offerings belong to the fire as well. — *Karmapradīpa* 1.1.

Regarding the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, as well as the *balikarma*, the new-moon day (*darśa*), and likewise the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsa*), and the *navayajña*—the wise who know the sacrifices declare that there should be only one *śrāddha* for these, not separate ones for each. [1st Praśna, 5th Khaṇḍa] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* (The Elucidation of the Supplements)

Regarding the performance of the *śrāddha* repeatedly during the intervals between the *āghāna*, the *agnyādhāna*, and the nine sacrifices such as the *sāyaṃprātaḥ-homa*, he states a specific rule: at the *āghāna* (the initial rite for establishing the fires), the *agnyādhāna* (the formal installation of the sacred fires), and during the rites ending with the nine sacrifices such as the morning and evening oblations (*sāyaṃprātaḥ-homa*), one should not perform a *śrāddha* for each individual rite. Rather, by performing the *śrāddha* once at the beginning of the *ādhāna* and so forth, it becomes as if performed for all of them. Thus, it is implied that for other occasions such as the *Śrāvaṇī* festival, a *śrāddha* must be performed for each respective rite. The *navayajña* refers to the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*. The rest is easy to understand.

In this same way, those who perform the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, animal sacrifices, and so forth every year, must also perform the Śrāddha at the beginning of each individual rite during their very first performance. This is because of the scriptural statement: "not repeatedly" (asakṛt). The *Prabhā* commentary states: Since it has been specified that there is no Śrāddha for each individual performance when rites are performed repeatedly, [the author] now states another distinction—that in certain cases there is no Śrāddha even for each individual rite—by means of the two verses beginning with "in the establishment of the fires" (*ādhāne*).

Regarding the Agnyādheya, the Vaiśvadeva offerings performed morning and evening, and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, those wise ones who know the sacrifice say this: what do they say? That is stated here: in these rites, there should be only one Śrāddha, not a separate one at the beginning of each individual rite. Thus, it is said that when a Śrāddha is performed once at the beginning of the Agnyādheya and so forth, the Śrāddha is considered performed for all of them, including the morning and evening Vaiśvadevas. 2 || 3 || 78 || 35 || *Karmapradīpa*, [Chapter 1]

5kha. ] One should perform a *śrāddha* at dramatic performances (*nāṭaka*), but a *śrāddha* is not desired during another *śrāddha*.
