Nor [is it performed] during the *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarman*, or rites for those who have arrived unexpectedly. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: He states an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding "rites and so forth" (*karmādiṣu*): "The *aṣṭakā*, the *viṣuvat*, and the *parvan*—these do not [occur] during a *pārvana* and other [rites]. Nor does it occur during the *sīmantonnayana* performed for the sake of an easy delivery, nor during the *tīrthayātrā* and other such [rites] involving the recitation of mantras such as the *tiras" and so on."

He should grind rice and barley with the same gesture by which he previously took hold of the child’s right hand—using the thumb and the little finger—and wipes the child’s tongue with the mantra, "This is honey" (*iyam ānedam*). Having wiped it, he should take hold of the eldest son with both hands and mutter, "From limb after limb you have descended. He should then smell the heads of the animals with the sound *hiṅ*, according to the purpose. In this very same way for the others.

Just as [the rule] "the smelling [of the food] by the women is done according to seniority" applies to the *mūḍenya* [offering], so too, the *śrāddha* consisting of the duties to be performed for the ancestors (*pitṛkarmaka*) brought by the remnants of the cooked food is not desired by the sages. [The commentary] says: "Not in the *aṣṭakās*"—he states another specific distinction.

In the case of all the *gṛhya* rites—namely, the various *aṣṭakā* sacrifices, the *anvaṣṭakya*, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the *anvāhārya*, and so forth; as well as the *sīmantonnayana* performed for a comfortable delivery as prescribed in the *gṛhya* texts; the *jātakarman* and *nāmakaraṇa*; and the single act consisting of the father’s smelling the head of his son and others upon returning from travel—the rule of silence (*vāgyama*) does not apply. By the sūtra stating that "all [these rites] possess the *anvāhārya*," the previously established requirement of silence is here prohibited. (This concludes the section) from the *Karmapradīpa*.

The group of rites beginning with marriage has been described; we have heard that the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) occurs at its conclusion. One should perform this very same rite at the beginning of marriage and so forth, and it should occur at the beginning of every subsequent rite. [1.5] 78. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Marriage is the beginning of which...

With his right hand he should touch the womb with this verse, "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb," and with the verse, "O Sinīvālī, bestow the embryo. Thus ends the Sūtra regarding the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*), which belongs to that group of rites beginning with the *caturthī-homa*, the eating of the *samaśanīya-caru*, the entering of the house, the honoring of the bridegroom, the four-footed [animal], the invitation, and the restoration from broken vows. We have heard from the tradition that within this group of rites, such as marriage and others, one should perform [the concluding rite] only once, not at the beginning of each individual rite.

"By performing [the rite] with just one [offering], all these become possessed of the *śrāddha*. (5) [Commentary: "Marriage and so forth" means: marriage is the beginning of a group of rites, and conception (*garbhādhāna*) is at the end of that group of rites; in this group of rites beginning with marriage, one should perform only a single *śrāddha* at the start—namely, for the marriage—and there should be no *śrāddha* for each individual rite.

Even by the phrasing "at the end of whose [group] there is an enemy," its status as being outside the group is understood. The intention is that the *garbhādhāna* is heard of as occurring at the end of the group, and not as being included within the group—just as one says "a mountain at the edge of the field. Furthermore, if the word "end" (*anta*) here were to mean a constituent part of the group, as in "the edge of a cloth" (*daśāntaḥ paṭaḥ*), then its inclusion would be merely figurative (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the doubt as to whether [the two rites] function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) or indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), the experts on reality have stated that it is logical to grasp them as qualifiers. This, however, is to be reconsidered, because they are mentioned in grammatical apposition (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). One may indeed accept that they occur at the end, since the word "end" (*anta*) is understood to mean "conclusion," as in such passages as "At its end, there is a *sāvitra* oblation of rice. For the Vaiśvadeva-bali and the Kāmya-bali are not constituent parts of the Nitya-Vaiśvadeva-bali; rather, they occur at its conclusion.

Just as the *sāvitrī* rite is not included within the *vrata* (vow), but is performed at the conclusion of the vow; so too here, the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) is not included within the group (*gaṇa*), but is heard of as occurring at the end of the group. Since it is accepted by both these [authorities] and others that when there is doubt regarding the meaning of a *smṛti*, the determination of that meaning must be made through corroboration with another *smṛti*, and since the *śrāddha* is mentioned in another *smṛti* in connection with the *garbhādhāna*: "At the time of *niṣeka* (impregnation), at the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair), and likewise at the *puṃsavana* (male-making rite)—the *śrāddha* should be known as an integral part of these rites."

Regarding the passage beginning with "siddhe" and so forth: as for what was stated—that this statement refers to something other than the Veda—that too must be considered. It lacks any supporting evidence (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, it would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): if that statement were intended to refer to something other than the Veda, then the word *anta* would have its constituent meaning [of "end"]; and if that were the case, the statement would refer to something other than the Veda. *Karmapradīpa*: On the day of the new moon (*darśa*), there should be a single Śrāddha; at the time of the fire-ritual (*agniṣṭoma*), one should enter.

It is not proper to perform the *śrāddha* at the first rite for prosperity (*puṣṭikarma*). [1st Adhyāya, 5th Khaṇḍa] 81. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: One should consecrate the cows being driven out with the mantra, "These [cows] of mine, possessing all-encompassing vigor" (*imā me viśvatas vīrya*); and when they have returned, with "These [cows], full of sweetness" (*imā madhumatīryam*). For the driving out and the entry, there are two specific mantras; however, regarding the entry and so forth, there may be a single performance by way of a common ritual procedure (*tantra*). Nor is there a separate [performance] even for the driving out. [This applies for one] desiring prosperity.

One should lick the forehead of a newborn calf that is sucking with one's own tongue and swallow it, saying, "Thou art the phlegm of cows. One desiring prosperity, when calves have been born, should kindle a fire in the cow-pen at night and offer melted butter as an oblation, saying, "For the sake of gathering, for the sake of gathering. One desiring prosperity, when calves have been born, should make a mark on a pair of oxen with a knife made of Udumbara wood. Since this is stated in the first section on rites for prosperity within the *Puṣṭika-karmāṇi*, it is not appropriate to perform a Śrāddha for the purpose of this first rite of prosperity.

"One who desires prosperity (puṣṭikāma) should perform a śrāddha at the time of [the cows'] exit. (6) [Commentary: Regarding the word "pradve" (at the time of exit): one should consecrate the cows as they are being driven out with the mantra, "These [cows] of mine, possessing all-encompassing power... and [consecrate them] upon their return with, "These honey-sweet ones have come back to me. Thus, according to Gṛhyasūtra, both the driving out and the entry of the cows are mentioned. Therefore, a śrāddha should be performed at the time of their entry (pradve), not at the time of their driving out. [This applies for] one desiring prosperity.

One should lick the forehead of a newborn calf that is sucking with the tongue and swallow it; this ensures there is no disease among the cows. One desiring prosperity, when the cows have recently calved, should kindle a fire in the cow-pen at night and offer a libation of melted butter (vilayana) while reciting: "O Gatherer, gather them! One desiring prosperity alone, when the cows have recently calved, should perform the rites separately for each of the six types of cattle—such as those born of Udumbara wood, etc.—as prescribed in the *Karmapradīpa*. However, for other types of cattle, one should perform the first rite once at the beginning of each group.

7 || 82 *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśaḥ*: Now, one who desires offspring, having cooked a mess of rice (*sthālīpāka*) under an auspicious lunar mansion, should offer oblations to these deities: to Indra, to the Maruts, to Parjanya, to Aśanī, and to Bhaga. He should also sacrifice to Sītā, Āśā, and Anamīvā. These indeed are the deities.

Regarding the six rites mentioned in the sūtra—"at the *sītāyajña*, *khalayajña*, sowing, reaping, and threshing"—one should perform the *śrāddha* separately for each individual rite and at every performance of each rite. For other rites, such as the *navayajña* and the *śravaṇākarma*, one should perform it only once at the beginning, but not at every performance. *Halābhiyoga* means driving the plough forward; that is, the commencement of agriculture.

The *sautāyajña* is performed when the grains have ripened in the middle of the ploughed field; the *khalayajña* is performed in the threshing floor (*khala*). *Pravapaṇa* is the sowing of seeds; *pralavana* is the reaping of the harvest; *paryayaṇa* is the bringing of the grains from the threshing floor to the house. [Commentary: Regarding the *sinīvālī-vatsa-dhenu-śrī-lakṣaṇa-karman*, [the text says] "thou art the world of the male first, then of the female, thou art the thousandfold. Thus, this rite for the nourishment of cattle was taught by Gārgya.

In that regard, first, as for this *puṣṭikarma* (rite for prosperity) consisting of the swallowing of the tongue after licking the forehead of a newborn calf with the mother’s milk—it is not proper to perform a *śrāddha* there. The sense is that the time appropriate for performing a *śrāddha* is not present. Regarding the phrase "in the *halābhiyoga* and so forth": now, therefore, at an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering), one should offer it to these deities: to Indra, to the Maruts... [1.5] ...as stated in the *Karmapradīpa*.

One who desires great leaves, small cattle, or well-being should offer oblations while reciting the *pariviśyamāna* verses; however, for those two [verses] dedicated to Sūrya and Indra, no *śrāddha* rite exists. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Regarding the phrase "the tree" (*vṛkṣa*) and "the five-fold" (*pañca-cam*), when the sun is being circumambulated during the second [rite], one desiring well-being should offer oblations of rice-grains (*akṣata-taṇḍula*) while reciting these [verses].

With the third [offering], one circumambulates the moon with sesame and rice grains for the sake of the well-being (*svastyayana*) of small livestock; with the two [other] threads, one circumambulates the sun for the sake of laughter, the celestial realm, great strength, and well-being, and one circumambulates the moon for the sake of the well-being of small livestock such as goats and rams—thus two rites named *homa* have been described. Regarding these, he praises them: "One should sacrifice to Parjanya, Aśani, Bhaga, Sītā, Āśā, Marutvatī, and Anaghā; these are the single deities. **Prabhā:** One should worship Parjanya, Aśani, Bhaga, Sītā, Āśā, Marutvatī, and Anaghā; these are the individual deities.

Regarding the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice, the threshing-floor sacrifice, sowing, reaping, and the carrying [of grain], according to Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa 2.10, one should perform a Śrāddha at the beginning of each of these six activities, such as plowing and so forth, individually. Not only should one perform them separately, but one should also perform a Śrāddha for the completion (pratiprayoga) of those six activities, such as plowing and so forth. However, for other rites such as the *Śravaṇākarma*, there is no Śrāddha at each completion; rather, there is only one Śrāddha at the first performance.

This is merely a restatement (anuvāda) of what has already been said, intended for the students so that they do not forget. Regarding the phrase "bṛhatpatra": "patra" and "vāhana" (vehicle/means of transport) are synonymous. A "large vehicle" (bṛhatpatra) refers to elephants, horses, and the like; a "small vehicle" (tuccha-patra) refers to goats, sheep, and the like. This is the meaning: with reference to the rule "vṛkṣa iva" and "pañcacaḥ," when the sun is being circumambulated, one desiring well-being (svastyayana) should offer unhusked rice grains with the second verse; when the moon is being circumambulated, one should offer sesame and rice grains with the third verse. [End of Kampradīpa, 1st Praśna]

5kha] It is not [permitted] for one who has not completed the ten knots, nor indeed in the case of an act performed by one bitten by a venomous creature; it is not [permitted] in the treatment of a wound inflicted by a worm, nor is it found in any of the remaining cases. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśaḥ*.

Another [instance of] apavāda is stated: "On a dangerous path, one should tie knots in the fringes of the garment of the wearer with the verses ending in *svāhā*," according to this sūtra. On a road where there is fear of thieves and the like, it is taught that one should tie three knots in the fringes using the three ṛks beginning with *anaṃ vā ekachandasya*, which are the ones under discussion and end in *svāhā*. Likewise, when one has been looked upon by someone possessed by poison, one should recite over water while muttering: "Do not fear; you shall not die."

"Atri says that one should recite the mantra 'krimiḥ' while sprinkling water upon a place infested with worms; thus, the treatment for poison is stated by himself. Therefore, in these rites, as well as in those following them—such as the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), the seat (*viṣṭara*), and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) to the worthy officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others—there is no *śrāddha*. 8. [Prabhā]

Regarding the phrase "desiring the welfare (*svastyayana*) of small livestock": when the sun and moon are surrounded by halos (*pariveśa*) formed by their own rays, there is no [auspicious] result from those rites prescribed for the welfare of large and small livestock, such as the *Bṛhat* and *Pavamāna* hymns. As for the halo (*pariveśa*), its definition is stated thus: "When the rays of the sun and moon form circles due to the wind and appear like garlands in the sky, that is called a halo. (8) Regarding the phrase "not when there are ten knots" (*daśāgranthika*).

On a dangerous road, one should tie knots in the fringes of one's garments; approaching those who possess clothing, one should perform a rite for the welfare of companions with mantras ending in *svāhā*. Regarding the *Karmapradīpa*: when rites are performed by groups (*gaṇaśas*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛbhyaḥ*) is done only once. The *Śrāddha* should occur only once at the beginning, not separately for each individual in the group. (From the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*): When rites are performed by groups as a collective, the worship of the Mothers is always performed only once.

For example, on a day when the obligatory *navayajña*, *vāstuśamana-yajña*, *soma-yajña*, and *akṣaya-yajña* are performed collectively, there is only one *śrāddha* at the beginning of that group; it is not the case that there are as many *śrāddhas* as there are rituals. || 10 || Prabhā.

The term *gbhilkta* refers to the tying of a knot in the fringes of a garment; likewise, it refers to the ritual for one bitten by a venomous creature, wherein one should recite [the mantra] while sprinkling water over the victim with the words "Do not fear, you shall not die. Furthermore, regarding a place infested with worms, one should recite while sprinkling water there with the words "A worm has entered your hand"; and if one wishes to drive away worms from cattle, one should strike a clod of earth in the afternoon and place it in the air, then recite while scattering its dust around with five verses. It is stated by that same [author].

Regarding the medical treatment for one bitten by worms, and likewise thereafter, there is no *śrāddha* ceremony in the offerings of water for the feet (*pādya*) and the respectful oblation (*arghya*) given to those worthy of honor (*arhaṇīya*). 1. Regarding the word "in groups" (*gaṇaśaḥ*): the word *gaṇa* denotes a collection or assembly.

When many rites are performed on a single day—for example, when the Navayajña, Vāstuyajña, Gṛhyayajña, and other such sacrifices are being performed on the day of the principal sacrifice, or likewise in the case of the Gaṇastha and similar rites—the worship of the Mothers (Mātṛpūjana) and the Śrāddha are performed only once; however, the worship of the Mothers and the Śrāddha need not be performed separately at the beginning of each individual rite contained within that group. [From the *Karmapradīpa*, Chapter 1, Verse 86]

5kha] Wherever there may be a *śrāddha*, there the Mothers [are to be worshipped]. This was mentioned incidentally; therefore, the primary subject is now stated. [End of] the Fifth Section. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: The word “are to be worshipped” (*pūjyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder. By the phrase “in rites and so forth” (*karmādiṣu*), it is indicated that the worship of the Mothers occurs at the beginning of Vedic rites and the like; alternatively, since the worship of the Mothers was already mentioned in the sequence of worship for you, the statement “wherever there may be a *śrāddha*” indicates that the worship of the Mothers applies even to those *śrāddhas* performed at the conclusion of events such as the birth of a son or the first sight of his face. Thus, there is no tautology.

"This was mentioned incidentally; therefore, the primary subject is now stated. This means that since the worship of the Mothers and the *ādhāna* (consecration) omitted from the Sūtra were established as incidental matters, what follows is the statement of the primary *ādhāna*. "Wherever, wherever": wherever a *śrāddha* occurs, there alone the Mothers are to be worshipped. By this, it is implied that where a *śrāddha* does not take place—such as at the *yavāṣṭaka* and other such occasions—the worship of the Mothers should also not be performed.

We have already established that even the recitation of mantras for longevity (*āyuṣya*) through the pouring of a continuous stream of water (*vasrghārāpātana*) is not to be performed by you. Furthermore, regarding the worship of the Mothers (*māṭṛpūjā*), the procedure for the *śrāddha*, its specific details, and the prohibition of performing *śrāddha* and other rites on certain occasions—all these are explained by Gṛhyasūtra authors in the context of clarifying their respective subjects. Herein, they conclude: "All of this is for the sake of others. From this point forward, the installation of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) is described. Thus ends the fifth section. The sixth section begins.

If the elder brother is not maintaining the sacred fires, one may establish the fires at the times prescribed for their installation and through the rites of begging and fire-consecration, provided he relies upon that [elder brother's] authority. (1) He who, being the foremost among elder brothers, performs the marriage and the installation of the sacred fires while the elder brother is still present, is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder); the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*. (2) [From the] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Having studied the Veda as a student (*brahmacārī*), he should place the final fuel-stick [upon the fire].

One should perform the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) in accordance with those times for the establishment of the fires which have been stated [in the texts] beginning with "desiring to seize the hand of his wife," and in accordance with those methods of obtaining the fire which have been stated beginning with "from the house of a Vaiśya" or "from a frying pan. This applies if the elder brother already possesses the sacred fires. But regarding the fault incurred when the elder brother lacks the sacred fires, he says: "He who performs the marriage and the establishment of the fires before his elder brother is known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder), and the elder brother is a *parivitti* (one whose younger brother marries before him). [Commentary: "The times for the establishment [of the fires]" refers to...

According to Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa: "A religious student (brahmacārī), having studied the Veda, should perform the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) based on those times for the primary rites mentioned in texts such as the *Citī* [section], and those fire-installations mentioned in texts such as 'one who has maintained the fires from a Vaiśya family,' 'during the rainy season,' and 'with a ladle' (*āmbarṣāhā*), provided that his elder brother is already possessed of the sacred fires. By this, it is stated that if the elder brother does not possess the fires, the younger brother need not perform the establishment of the fires. ||1||

What happens if the younger brother performs the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) while the elder brother still possesses his fires? The *Karmapradīpa* states: "The elder brother (*parivitti*) and the younger brother who marries before him (*parivettṛ*) both go certainly to hell; if they have not performed the penance (*prāyaścitta*), they partake of the fruit of sin. The *Parishishṭaprakāśa* explains: Thus, what is the fault? He says: if the two have not performed the penance, they partake of the fruit of that sin, which is a quarter of the fruit of the original offense. "Being the elder brother whose younger brother marries first, and the younger brother who marries before the elder..."

Thus, this [verse] was recited by Manu among the group of those who have married before their elder brothers. (3) The commentary (*Prabhā*) says: "Regarding the phrase *dārādhigamana*... *Dārādhigamana* means marriage. *Ādhāna* means the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*). When the elder brother has not yet performed his marriage or the establishment of the fires, the younger brother who performs the marriage and the establishment of the fires is a *parivettā*; the elder brother, however, is to be known as a *parivitti*. (2) Let that be; what fault lies therein? To this he replies: "*Parivitti*... The first half [of the verse] is for the purpose of providing instruction.

He states the certainty of their descent into hell: "Even if they have performed expiation" (*api kṛtaprāyaścittau*). The meaning is that even if those two have performed expiation, they still experience the fruit of hell; thus, their descent into hell is certain. Nor should it be argued: "Once expiation has been performed, since the sin is destroyed by that very act, how can they be subject to the fruit of the sin? For there is a scriptural statement regarding those who have no other recourse. As it has been said: "What indeed would a scriptural statement not accomplish? There exists the *parivitti* and the *parivettṛ*. (There is also a variant reading: *asti parivittiḥ parivettā ca*).

Furthermore, the reading in the Ka and Ga manuscripts is *api cīrtha-prāyaścittau*. The *Karmapradīpa* states: One does not incur blame by marrying (*parivindan*) those who are impotent, those with only one testicle, those lacking teeth, those who are aged; nor those who are excessively attached to Vaiśyas, outcasts, or those equal to Śūdras; nor those who have transgressed their duties; nor the dull-witted, the mute, the blind, the deaf, those born of a low family, the dwarf, or the hunchback; nor those who do not speak, those who do not study the Vedas, those devoted to agriculture, or those belonging to the king; nor those addicted to gambling, those addicted to the increase of wealth, or those who act out of mere lust; nor unchaste women, the intoxicated, or thieves. (1.6.4–6)

The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*, located in another region, states that there is no fault of superseding an elder brother (*parivedana*) in the case of a certain type of elder; he describes this as follows: "The *klība* is of six kinds. And so says Devala: "The *baṇḍaka*, the *vātaja*, the *ṣaṇḍa*, the *paṇḍa*, the *klība*, the *napuṃsaka*, and the *kaulaka*—thus this sixfold division of the *klība* has been declared. [88] *Prabhā*: "Because of the extreme harshness of the statement."

However, some read the text as *acīrṇaprāyaścittau* ("those who have not performed penance") and argue that those who have performed penance are entitled to only a quarter of the hellish fruit, in consideration of their [lesser] sin. They claim this is because Manu includes both "being superseded by a younger brother" and "the act of superseding" among the minor sins (*upapātaka*), and thus it is appropriate to describe the quarter-status in relation to those. Furthermore, since the reading *cīrṇaprāyaścittau* ("those who have performed penance") is seen in all the original manuscripts, we have explained the text according to that very reading.

3. Regarding the kind of elder brothers for whom a younger brother [is forbidden to marry]: when they have not performed their marriage (*vivāha*) nor established the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), it is a "lamp of the head" (*kapradīpa*) for the younger brother. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Among those [types of impotent men], one who has speech and gestures like a woman and possesses female characteristics is a *ṣaṇḍaka*. Furthermore, a man who first develops male organs and subsequently destroys them is likewise [a *ṣaṇḍaka*]. A woman who assumes the state of a man and possesses qualities like those of a man's conduct is called a *vāta-ṣaṇḍa* by name, or even a *strī-ṣaṇḍa* by name. Moreover, one with non-existent organs is a *ṣaṇḍa*, while a *paṇḍa* is one whose penis is flaccid.

"A man who has not had intercourse is a *klība*; one whose semen is lost is a *napuṃsaka*. A *sakṛtkṛt* is one who, having by nature made love to his own wife with another man, afterwards resorts to her alone. [1.6] The meaning of "a man who has made love" (*klītvā*) and so forth is as follows: the connection is that a man who, having performed other sexual acts, should break his own organ—that is the *ṣaṇḍa* named *vāta*. By this, the state of being unable to procreate, as well-known in the South, is described.

Likewise, a woman who, having taken on the male characteristics, approaches her own interior [for intercourse] is also a *ṣaṇḍa* born of wind (*vātaja*). Similarly, that same one who is a female *ṣaṇḍa* by name is also a *ṣaṇḍa* born of wind even though lacking the [male] organ; such is the connection. By this, it is stated that there are three types of *ṣaṇḍas* born of wind. [The others are: one who has the symptoms of impotence and urinary disorders but lacks [other] signs of change; one who eats filth and has the mouth for his vulva; and he who, out of passion, resorts to his own wife while she is being enjoyed by another is called a *klība*. This is the explanation.

Regarding the performance of marriage and the establishment of the sacred fire (*agnyādhāna*), he states that there is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] through three verses beginning with "deśāntarastha" (one residing in another land). The connection with the following verse is: "one does not incur sin by superseding elder brothers who are *deśāntarastha* and so forth. Regarding "another land," Bṛhan-Manu says: [text omitted]. [Commentary: *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: "Those having one wife" means those whose sexual pleasure and progeny are centered on a single woman. "Half-brothers" refers to sons of different mothers. Even those born of the same mother are not "half-brothers" if they have different fathers.

Therefore, the commentator on Manu states that there is no fault of *parivedana* (marrying before an elder brother) in the case of Bhīma’s marriage to Hiḍimbā. His livelihood was like that of a *śūdra*, such as servitude and so forth. For this very reason, Manu says [1.6]: "One should treat guards, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, and usurers like *śūdras," even if they are Brahmins. *Kuṇṭha* means one-eyed; others say it means lazy in all activities. They were without wives (*abhāryāḥ*).

The lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*), and mendicants (*bhikṣus*) are those who have no connection with activities forbidden by the scriptures. And the connection [of the term] is with "the lineage of the king. Those who act according to their own desire are those whose conduct is unrestrained. They are called *kulaṭās*—meaning those whose habit is to wander among other families (*parakulāṭana-śīlā*). In the reading *unmatta-paura-anit*, a *paura* is a city-dweller who lives as a servant and so forth. In the reading *kerān*, *kera* means one of dissolute character (*viṣama-śīla*).

The rest is easy to understand. Regarding these [cases], when one marries while [the other] is still alive, and among these instances of contact with a wife and the sacred fires (*agni*), he who enters into such contact with a wife and the fires does not incur sin. *Prabhā*: "Where there is an interval of a great river or a mountain acting as a barrier, or where they are separated by speech or effort—that is called 'another country' (*deśāntara*). That which exists even within the same district due to a difference in local names or rivers is also declared by Svayambhū himself to be 'another country. Or else, it is where news is not heard for ten nights."

82. *Kammapradīpa*: Light. [1st Section] Kātyāyana describes the eunuch (*klība*): "He whose urine is frothy and whose excrement sinks in water, and whose penis is not erect even when touched by the hands or feet—he is called a eunuch. Regarding this, Devala has stated six types of eunuchs, and Nārada has stated fourteen types; these are not shown here for fear of making the book too voluminous. One with a single testicle is *ekāṇḍa*.

The *Ratnākara* states that "one who is distinguished by learning" (*paṇḍaviśeṣa*) refers to a *vṛṣala* (low-born person) who has increased his knowledge of the *Ṛgveda*. The *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* says it is one who is capable of sexual pleasure with only a single woman. The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* explains that those who are not *sahodarāḥ* (uterine brothers) are those distinct from those born of the same womb; even those born of the same mother are not *sahodarāḥ* if they have different fathers. For this very reason, there is no fault of "supersession" (*parivedana-doṣa*) in Bhīma’s marriage to Hiḍimbā, according to the *Manuvṛtti*. One who is "excessively attached to a prostitute" (*veśyātisakta*) is one who is intensely addicted to a courtesan. One who is "degraded" (*patita*) is so due to a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) or similar offense. Regarding one who is equal to a *śūdra*, *Ṛtu* says:

In the *Vargacintāmaṇi*, Devala states: "Those who do not regularly perform the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), who always eat without having bathed, and whose purity is lost—these fall [from their status] and are equal to Śūdras according to Dharma. The term *ati* refers to one afflicted by an incurable disease. Regarding *jaḍa*, the *Mitākṣarā* explains it as one whose internal organ (mind) is impaired, meaning one incapable of discerning between what is beneficial and what is harmful. Mādhavācārya, however, defines a *jaḍa* as one who is incapable of engaging in necessary duties. Although there is no difference in the result even if the term were taken to mean "unwise," [the specific definitions are maintained]. A *mūka* is one incapable of articulating syllables. *Andha* and *badhira* are well known [as "blind" and "deaf"].

*Kula* refers to one whose body is extremely deformed due to specific defects such as flesh [growths] on the back; *vāmana* means short-statured. Hemādri states that *khaḍakī* refers to one whose two feet are broken. According to the reading *kuṇṭhaka*, Hemādri explains it as "one who possesses dull radiance" (*prabhā*). [The term] *kamaṇyaḥ* is used according to one's own preference, based on the statement in the *Medinī* lexicon: "The words *kuṇṭha*, *kamaṇya*, and *mūrkha* [are synonyms]. The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* explains *kāṇa* as "lazy in all activities," while Śūlapāṇi and Raghunandana agree with this.

"Kuṇṭha" means one who is slow in action; "mūḍha," "alyapaṭu," and "nirbhāgya" are synonyms according to Amara. Alternatively, the meaning is "one who is unskilled in actions. "Abhāryāḥ" refers to those whose connection with a wife is prohibited by the scriptures, namely those in the stages of life (āśramas) of lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin), forest-dwellers (vānaprastha), and renunciants (saṃnyāsin). In the phrase "nṛpasya," the genitive case is used in the sense of "belonging to" (śeṣa). By the word "ca" (and), it is understood that they are "saktān" (addicted); that is, excessively addicted to wealth.

Mādhavācārya states that those who do not perform marriage at all, acting according to their own whims, are "those who have abandoned marriage" (*vivāhābrihattāḥ*). Nārāyaṇopādhyāya, Śūlapāṇi, and Raghunandana, however, read the term as *kāmataḥ kāriṇaḥ*. Nārāyaṇopādhyāya explains *kāmataḥ kāriṇaḥ* as those whose character is to act according to their own desires. Śūlapāṇi and Raghunandana define them as those who conduct themselves according to their own will, regardless of the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti. Hemādri defines a *kuhaka* as one who is intent on deceiving others.

In the *Ācāramādhavīya* as well, the reading is exactly the same. However, Nārāyaṇopādhyāya reads it as *kulaṭa* and explains it as "one who glances at another's family. Raghunandana states that this refers to an adopted son (*dattaka*). Regarding the reading *caurān*, if one reads *paurān* instead, the meaning is "one who dwells in a city" or "one who serves in a city," acting as a servant and so forth. Regarding the reading *kerān*, *kera* means "the uneven-eyed one" (a leper). The rest is clear. In the word *parivindan*, because the prefix *pari-* has a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇārthatva*), the accusative case is used throughout.

And thus, having passed over these [elder brothers], if one marries and establishes the *agnihotra* while those elder brothers have not yet married or established the *agnihotra*, he does not incur sin; this is the meaning. || 6 || *Kampradīpa*: One who is burdened by wealth, a servant of the king, a farmer, as well as one who is afflicted—these one should wait for, even if one is in haste, for up to five years. || 7 || *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

The four elder brothers, such as the *vāṣika* and others, even if they are diligent and eager to take a wife and establish the sacred fires immediately after their return from studentship (*samāvartana*), must wait for the rainy season retreat (*varṣālaya*). Therefore, what was stated in the preceding verse—that "one who marries them [the younger brothers] becomes blameworthy"—should be understood to apply to the period of the rains. [Prabhā: Furthermore, he states a specific distinction regarding that very point: "one who is a debtor" (*dhanavārduṣika*) and so forth. [One should not marry] one who is a debtor, a servant of the king, or one engaged in agriculture.

Even one who has gone abroad, though he be harsh, should wait for three years for his elder brother who is engaged in marriage and the establishment of the sacred fires; the statement that "one who marries before these [brothers] does not incur sin" is qualified by the rule that this applies after three years. A *vārddhuṣika* is one who lives on usury; the genitive case here is used in the sense of a relationship. Regarding the *vārddhuṣika*, it is explained in the *Smṛti*: "He who, having taken up wealth at a moderate rate, gives it back at a high rate of interest—he is indeed called a *vārddhuṣika*, and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda."

"He who, while living, censures another and praises his own virtues, is indeed called a *vāīṣika*, and is condemned in the world. Because of this statement from the *Viṣṇu-smṛti*, it is said that for one who is wicked, the term *dhanavārṣika* is used to exclude others. By performing the *kharatri* rite even during the three-year period in the absence of a king, the implication of a longer duration is indicated; and that should be understood from other sources. [From the *Karmapradīpa*, 1.6]: "If one performs the *abdāt* rite toward one who does not listen [to the instruction], [the following applies]."

And when he has returned, one should perform a quarter of that [penance] for the sake of purification. (8) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: He states a specific detail regarding "one who has been sprinkled" (*prṣita*). The meaning is: "being resorted to," by means of a transposition of the suffixes, [referring to] one who has been superseded in marriage (*parivitta*). If one should marry after [the period] beyond one year, and then that [superseded brother] returns, then for the sake of his purification, one should perform a quarter of the penance for being superseded in marriage. However, if there is no return after one year, there is simply an absence of fault. But the waiting for one year applies specifically to the case where [the return] is expected.

"Even when he has returned, there is no fault" (8). 2.9 *Prabhā*: Regarding the case where [the younger brother] has already married, he states another distinction: "if he has married" (*prṣita*). By the transposition of suffixes, *amṛkhāna* means "one who has not married. The reading *akhāna* is favored by Ratnākara. If, in the absence of news regarding the elder brother who has departed, the younger brother performs the marriage and the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnihotra*) after one year, then upon the elder brother's return, he must perform a quarter of the penance for supersession (*parivedana*). However, if the elder brother does not return, there is indeed no fault.

And thus, for one who has been so requested, the observation of the word *brāhmaṇa* results in its application being restricted to the specific subject matter at hand. In this context, since the phrase "if he should perform [the rite] after the Āghāra-libation" functions as an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*), an injunction must be inferred from it—just as in the cases of "one offers either four-fold or five-fold portions," or "both the sacrificer and the Brahman priest [are required]," and so forth. As they say: "An injunction is to be known even from an indicative mark (*liṅga*), as in the case of scattering [grain] upon the Darbha grass.
And it is indeed observed: "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, having placed the offering dedicated to Bṛhaspati in the middle, [he should offer] after the Āghāra-libation"—this being another reading.

The Kāma-pradīpa: [1.6] Regarding the definition, the measurement of the line drawn toward the east is twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas). Attached to its base, the line toward the north is likewise nine finger-breadths longer. The Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa: Having leveled or smoothed out a place that is inclined toward the northeast or level, and having smeared it with cow-dung, one should draw a line from the center toward the east and another straight toward the north. Then, having drawn three lines toward the east in the middle [of the northern line], one should sprinkle water over them.

The definition of this [mandala] is stated in the Sūtra as being "like the [sacrificial] marks" (*lakṣaṇavat*); that definition is clarified here by the mention of the measurement of the lines. The first line, which runs from east to west, measures twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). The second line, attached to its base and running from south to north, has a measure of exactly twelve finger-breadths plus one; that is, twenty-one finger-breadths—so says the *Prabhā*.

Having offered the oblation, he should offer a supplementary offering (*abhivārayet*): if it is for a *rājanya*, an offering to Indra; if for a *vaiśya*, one to the Viśvedevas. Thus, even from this single statement, there is the injunction for the sacrifice (*kratu*). One should prepare a site sloping toward the northeast or level, having swept it clean and smeared it with cow-dung. Having drawn a line from the center toward the east, and a continuous line from west to east, one should then draw three lines from the center toward the east and sprinkle water over them. This definition is stated by Gṛhyasūtrakāra Āśvalāyana in connection with the laying of the fires (*adhāna*), as it applies to all [rituals].

That is squared by means of these two characteristics (lakṣaṇa). Regarding the characteristic: this first line extending eastward has a measurement of twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula). The line extending northward from its base is nine more—that is, nine finger-breadths greater—than that; thus the measurement is twenty-one finger-breadths. [1.6] This is the *Kampradīpa*. The remaining lines attached to the one extending northward are each the measure of a span (*prādeśa*).

"Having left a space of seven times seven finger-breadths, one should scratch [the lines] with a *kuśa* blade alone. (10) — thus says the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. Regarding the phrase "the remaining three which were mentioned": those three lines previously mentioned are to be connected to the northern line, separated by intervals of seven times seven finger-breadths, and measuring a *prādeśa* in length; these one should scratch with a *kuśa* blade alone. The word "with a *kuśa*" (*kuśena*) is connected with all [the actions]. (10) — thus says the *Prabhā*. Regarding the phrase "of that which goes northward": the remaining three lines, which were left over, are connected to that which goes northward and measure a *prādeśa*.

One should scratch [the lines] with a *kuśa* blade at intervals of seven times seven (*saptasaptāṅgula*) finger-breadths. The phrase "with a *kuśa*" and so forth applies to all the lines; the meaning is that the scratching of all the lines must be performed with a *kuśa* blade alone. This is one method. Another method has been stated by Gṛhyāsaṃgrahakāra:
"I shall explain its characteristics, its dimensions, and its deity.
Having said this, [he continues] not too far away:

"The lines drawn previously are to be known as belonging to the Earth (Pārthivī), while those facing north are remembered as belonging to Agni (Āgneyī). Those facing east are remembered as belonging to Prajāpati, Indra, and Soma. "The Pārthivī and Saumī [lines] are each twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) apart; the Āgneyī lines are twenty-one [finger-breadths apart]. Both are remembered as being one span (prādeśinī) wide. Those Āgneyī lines should be made with intervals of six finger-breadths. From the Pārthivī line, there are three [other] lines, each situated further to the north. [This concludes the section on the measurement of the lines. (1st Praśna, 6th Khaṇḍa)

When the act of measurement has been mentioned but the measurer has not been specified, the sacrificer (yajamāna) shall be the one who performs the measurement; this is the settled rule. He alone establishes the sacred fire, for he is praised by all; as for his status as the non-performer [of other rites], that is neutralized by the optional (kāmya) acts. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: The definition of measurement is stated here—it is explained by its very utterance. Consequently, it is established that measurements such as finger-breadths (aṅgula) and so forth are to be taken by the finger-breadth of the sacrificer. 11.

Many methods for leading the fire have been stated by the sūtra beginning with "vaiśyakulād vā ambarīṣād vā" (or from a Vaiśya's house, or from a frying pan). [The commentary] says: "Thus. And at the end: "This is the rule for drawing lines; indeed, in all cases, those lines should be made fine, straight, and well-proportioned. Having understood these principles, one should perform the domestic rites. Thus, there is an option between these two methods, because both are stated in one's own scripture. 10.

In response to the inquiry as to whose [measurement] should be adopted in the case of Aṅgulimāna and others, he states the definition of measurement: "In the act of measuring" (*mānakriyāyām*). The act of measuring itself is *mānakriyā*. Since that [act] belongs to the measurer, and the agent of measurement is the one who performs it, the conclusion of the learned is that the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should be the agent of measurement. (11) "Only merit," etc. According to Āpastamba, many [rules] regarding the fire-laying ceremony (*agnyādheya*) have been set forth for those born of the Vaiśya caste and others. [From the] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: "Or rather, having churned the fire-drill wood (*araṇi*), he should place [the fire] upon it."

By the rule, "The fire belongs only to the meritorious," it is stated that the *araṇeya* (fire produced from the churning sticks) is meritorious; therefore, one should kindle that very fire. For that *araṇeya* fire is praised by all because it is the cause of an excellence of merit (*puṇya*), and because once the fire has been established, even if it goes out, it is under one's own control through rekindling. Indeed, the fire used for the first kindling is the same as that used for the rekindling. However, for those such as the Vaiśya class, there is a different *Gṛhya* rule; since the fire is not under their own control during the act of kindling, they do not possess that excellence.

The fire is the same as the one previously maintained; for he himself will state later [in the first section]: "The fire is the very same as that which was previously brought at the rite of re-establishing the sacred fires (*punarādheya*). Now, it might be argued that even this [fire] is a means to prosperity, since it is said, "it becomes free from distress. However, the fire brought from the household of a Vaiśya and so forth is indeed a means to prosperity. Therefore, that alone is commendable, and not the other. And thus says another *Gṛhya-sūtra*:

"One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should establish the fire from a Brāhmaṇa family; one desiring freedom from disease from a Rājanya; one desiring sons and cattle from a Vaiśya; and one desiring rain, food, and grain [should take it] from a forest-born [fire], while one desiring merit should take from a virtuous person. Regarding this, he says: that which is the state of being a source of wealth for the forest-born fire is its establishment through those optional means that serve as instruments for spiritual luster and so forth. Peace is attained because the ritual action, along with its wife, is a means to prosperity. Furthermore, "establishment" (*ādhāna*) is the installation of the fire accompanied by the prescribed characteristics and rituals.

There is no requirement for haste or churning, because that is impossible in a Vaiśya household where there is no interruption [of the sacred fire], and because the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *bhāṅ* signifies "offering. (12) [In the case] of one whose daughter has been given away by some means through a verbal promise (*vācā satyena*), he should indeed offer the fuel-stick (*samidh*) when intending to perform the *sānti* rite, and not otherwise. (13) *Kampradīpa*: "When the fire has gone out" is the reading in manuscript *ka*; "by the fires established in the Bāraṇeya fire" is the reading in manuscripts *kha* and *ga*. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: [Commentary on the above].

By the text, "The student, having studied the Veda, being about to place the final fuel-stick," it is stated that by means of the fuel-stick placement prescribed for evening and morning, the student should place that fire into which the last, final fuel-stick is to be placed at the time of the completion of his studentship. Regarding this, he states a specific rule: "Or rather, having churned another [fire], he should place it; thus it becomes meritorious. Thus, the merit of the *āraṇeya* (churned) fire is stated. That is now explained.

One should establish the fire that is meritorious (*puṇya*), because it is praised by all for being the cause of an abundance of merit. Thus, another *Gṛhya* text states: "One who desires extensive merit [should perform] the Ārīya [fire-establishment]. Furthermore, it will be stated that when the re-establishment of the fire (*punarādheya*) is to be performed, the previous fires must be extinguished; in that context, this fire is praised because it is under one's own control (*svādhīna*). Other fires, such as those belonging to the families of Vaiśyas, are not praised because they are dependent on others (*parādhīna*).

As for the statement that by the word *anārbhuka* (not producing fire) it is meant that the *āraṇeya* fire does not produce prosperity (*ṛddhi*), that is refuted there by the words "by the oblations performed with a desire for prosperity, it is brought to rest. This is what is meant: it is true that the establishment (*ādhāna*) of the *āraṇeya* fire does not itself produce prosperity; however, when the *āraṇeya* fire has been established, prosperity indeed accrues to its establisher through the oblations performed with a desire for prosperity. [The text continues: "A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), having studied the Veda, having placed the final fuel-stick (*samit*)... etc. (1.6).

*Kampradīpa*: "But if that maiden, while still unmarried, passes away, the vow of the groom is not thereby [fulfilled]; he shall therefore marry another. (14) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: "If a maiden has been given by someone through a formal gift or a solemn verbal promise, he alone, when about to perform the final laying of the fires (*antyam agnidhānam*), shall establish the sacred fires, and not otherwise. (13)

If she should meet her death while still unmarried, then for him who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) but whose marriage rite was only verbally promised (*vāgdattā*), there is no sin in not cremating her with those fires. Rather, he should marry another woman using that very same fire. *Prabhā*: At the time of completing the period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) for the purpose of placing the final fuel-stick (*antya-samid*) has been declared by Gṛhyasūtras. Regarding this, he states the specific rule beginning with "of whom" (*yasya*). Here, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) indicates a relationship of connection.

If a girl has been given by someone with a truthful verbal promise (*satya-vāc*), he alone, intending to place the fuel on the fire, should establish the sacred fires (*agni*). Not otherwise—that is, not in the absence of such a verbal betrothal. The implication is that in such a case, if the girl is not obtained immediately after his return from studentship (*samāvartana*), he might remain without a prescribed life-stage (*anāśramin*) for some time. Regarding the phrase "as if unmarried": if that girl dies before the marriage is performed, then she does not become the wife (*patnī*) of one who has established the sacred fires.

With that very same fire, he should marry another girl. By this it is stated that with this consecrated fire (*āhita*), the cremation of a betrothed girl (*vāgdattā*) must not be performed; for if it were so done, his obligation as one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) would be violated, and the injunction "with that very same [fire] he should marry another" would become untenable. [1.6] Now, if he does not obtain another girl even while seeking her, he should incorporate that fire into himself and quickly enter the next stage of life (*uttarāśrama*). Sixth Section.

*Parīśiṣṭaprakāśa*: "And if, even though he seeks another girl, he does not obtain her"—by this it is stated that one must strive for the state of a householder (*gārhasthya*) even through an ignoble marriage preceded by begging, distinct from the *brāhma*, *daiva*, and other [approved] forms of marriage. Then, having performed the *prājāpatyeṣṭi* sacrifice, having consigned that fire into the *āvasathya* fire, he should quickly become an ascetic of the fourth stage (*caturthāśramī*). *Prabhā*: "And if" means: if, despite seeking, he does not obtain another girl.

Then, having internalized that consecrated fire and having offered it into his own self according to the procedure for the *Prājāpatya* sacrifice, he should without delay become a *Caturthāśramī* (one who has entered the fourth stage of life). By this statement regarding "begging," it is said that when excellent forms of marriage such as the *Brāhma* and others are not possible, one should strive to enter the householder’s stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) through a marriage preceded by a journey [to find a bride], even if it is not one of the most praiseworthy types. || 15 || Thus ends the sixth section. The seventh section: [The wood] from which the *Aśvattha* tree grows, which contains the *Śamī* within it and originates from a praiseworthy source...

The lower fire-drill (araṇi) made from that [wood] should have branches facing east, north, or even upward; the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇi) should likewise be made of that same wood. This [drill] is praised when it is made of solid heartwood, free from hollows, and well-crafted.

*Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: He describes the procedure for churning: the fire-drill (*araṇi*) and the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*) should be made from the branch—whether it be facing east, north, or upward—that belongs to a tree grown from the womb of *śamī* on a consecrated ground (*medhyabhūmi*). A churning-stick (*manthadaṇḍa*) made of wood such as *khadira* joined with a core (*sāra*), as well as a *vilī* (a wooden block) for the purpose of restraining the churning-stick, are prescribed as excellent. ||1||2|| *Prabhā*.

The method for churning the *araṇeya* (sacrificial fire) is first explained by means of two verses beginning with "ambaṣṭhyā," starting with the description of the components of the churning apparatus, such as the *araṇi*. The characteristics of the *śamī*-wood will be stated [later]. That *śamī*-wood which is born in a pure land—its branch that faces east, points north, or is directed upwards, serves as the lower *araṇi*; and the upper *araṇi* is made from that same material;
this is another reading (*pāṭhāntara*) for the *araṇi-maulī*. It is the same in the following case. 104.

The Fire-drill (Araṇi): [1.7] That which has its root joined with a *śamyā* is called "born of a *śamī*" (*śamīgarbha*). In the absence of such, one should fetch it from one not born of a *śamī* without delay. (3) Twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, six in width, and four in height—this is declared to be the measure of the fire-drill (*araṇi*). (4) *Commentary on the Pariśiṣṭa*: He explains "born of a *śamī*": that whose root is joined together with a *śamyā*, being firmly attached and unified with it, is designated as "born of a *śamī*" (*śamīgarbha*).

In the absence of that [wood], one should procure it from another *akhadira* tree, ensuring there is no delay. (3) He states the measurement of the *ara* (the churning stick): its width (*pārthava*), meaning its breadth or thickness (*prastāra*), is six finger-breadths (*aṅguṣṭha*). Its height (*ucchāya*) is said by the sages to be twelve finger-breadths. Furthermore, a churning vessel (*cātra*) made of wood such as *khadira* or other suitable materials is praised by the sages; the term *cātra* refers to the churning stick (*manthana-daṇḍa*), and the *cāvī* is a specific piece of wood for the purpose of restraining the lower part. (1, 2)

Now he describes the characteristics of the *śamgarbha* [fire-drill] with the words "having roots joined" (*saṃsaktamūla*). That *aśvattha* tree whose root is "joined"—that is, properly attached—to a *śamī* tree is called a *śamgarbha*. It is the intention here that, in the absence of an *aśvattha* tree containing a *śamī*, one should instead take the fire-drill (*araṇi*) from an *aśvattha* that does not contain a *śamī*, according to the maxim: "When the primary is unavailable, the secondary may be used. Furthermore, the term "not delayed" (*avilambita*) is stated in order to say that one should not allow a lapse of time while searching for a *śamgarbha*. || 3 ||

He states the dimensions of the *bharaṇī* and the other components with two verses beginning with "twenty-four": "Twenty-four thumb-breadths (*aṅguṣṭha*) in length above the *araṇi* constitute the measure of the *kāṣṭha* (the upper fire-drill). "The *pramantha* (the churning stick) should be eight thumb-breadths long, and the *āva* (the base block) should be twelve thumb-breadths. The *vilī* (the lower fire-drill) should also be twelve [thumb-breadths]; this is the apparatus for churning. The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* [comments]: The measurement of the *araṇi* has been stated; its height is four thumb-breadths.

The remainder is easy to understand. || 4 || Furthermore, a specific kind of wood for the purpose of churning while [the fire] is within the womb [of the araṇi] should be used; it should be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long. This quartet beginning with the araṇi is the "machine" (*yantraka*) for the purpose of churning; the meaning is "apparatus. The remainder is explained by its very utterance (*nigadavyākhyāta*). || 5 || "Radiance" (*prabhā*) means "dimension. Its width—that is, its breadth—is six finger-breadths; that is its dimension. The height of the araṇi—that is, the measure of its elevation—is four finger-breadths. This is the meaning.

Thus, the measurement of the *araṇi* has been described in its entirety. Regarding the phrase "eight finger-breadths" (*aṣṭāṅgula*): the specific piece of wood situated in the middle of the *cātra* for the purpose of churning is called the *pramantha*. It should be eight finger-breadths in measurement. The *cātra* and the *bila* together should be twelve finger-breadths in measurement. All of this, when assembled as arranged, is called the "churning apparatus" (*atyayantra*); the suffix *-ka* is used here in the sense of the base word itself, thus it is termed the "churning apparatus" (*manthana-yantraka*).

The *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* has stated this very same thing regarding the measurement of the fire-drill (*araṇi*). However, concerning the length of the forest-born wood, another pair of measurements has also been mentioned. Thus says the *Gṛhyasaṃgraha*: "One should make the lower fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*) from *Aśvattha* wood containing the *Śamī* within it; likewise, the upper fire-drill (*adharāraṇi*) should be twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long. As for the injunctions, "He binds it in a *Khādira* [wood], he binds it in a *Pālāśa* [wood], he binds it in a *Rohītaka* [wood]," these are to be understood as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*). Wherever the measurement of the thumb or finger is prescribed, there one should always measure using large knots made of *bṛhatparva* grass. A cord (*netra*) made of wool mixed with hemp, triple-stranded and circular, measuring one fathom (*vyāma*), should be used; by means of that, the fire is placed in the center. [1.7] (Parishishta-prakasha 1)

Wherever it is stated that "it should be made the size of a thumb" or "the size of a finger," one should always take the measurement from the joint situated in the middle of the thumb. || 6 || *Prabhā*: A cord for the fire-drill (*araṇi*) should be made of hemp fibers, three times the length [of the fire-drill], circular, free of knots, and with a width equal to two of one's own hands across; this shall be the cord. With that cord, the fire-drill should be rotated. || 7 || Regarding the word "thumb": [the measurement is taken from the middle joint].

[The text] with large-knotted joints and central lines; the rest is self-explanatory. (6) He states the cord (*netra*) which is the means for churning: "With fibers," etc. The connection is that it should be made of fibers mixed with hemp (*śaṇa*). "Cord" (*neva*) means a rope. He qualifies the cord with the words beginning with "threefold" (*triṣṭat*): threefold (*triṣṭat*) means triple-stranded; "round" (*vṛtta*) means circular; "without parts" (*anaṃśaka*) means devoid of [excessive] strands. "Parts" (*aṃśa*) refers to the minute subdivisions of the constituent threads.
A "vyāma" is defined as the horizontal distance between two outstretched arms; that is its measure. By means of that [measure], fire is to be produced through friction. || 7 ||

*sahastavāḍaiya*, thus is the reading in the manuscript. [1st Praśna, 7th Khaṇḍa] *Kampradīpa*: The ears, the cheeks, and the neck as the fifth—these are each the size of a thumb (*aṅguṣṭha-mātra*); the chest is said to be one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) wide. (8) The heart is a thumb’s breadth, and the belly is remembered as a thumb’s breadth; the hips are known to be one thumb-breadth, while the two groins (*vasti*) are the private parts (*guhya*). (9) The thighs, shanks, and feet constitute four [thumb-breadths] respectively; these are proclaimed by the ritualists (*yājñika*) to be the limbs of the fire-drill wood (*araṇi*). (10) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

Regarding the measurement of the forest-tree parts, he says: *kandharā* is the neck; *vaktrīvā* is the middle of the heart. And this measurement begins from the base, because for trees, wood, and so forth, such measurement is traditional (*śruti-lagikatvāt*). The rest is explained by the literal reading (*nigada-vyākhyātam*). || 8 || *Vasti* is the region below the navel; that is to say, the private parts (*guhya*, *upastha*). The rest is easy to understand. || 8 || The knee, the shank, and the foot are respectively four, one, and one *aṅguṣṭha*. These are the measurements of the forest-tree.

He states the measurement of its parts by means of three [verses], beginning with "sūkṣma" (fine). *Vak* means the mouth. *Kandharā* means the neck. *Vakṣas* is the space between the neck and the heart. The rest is easy to understand. And this measurement begins from the base (*mūla*), because for sacrificial wood (*havadāru*) and so forth, such a measurement is inherent; thus say the teachers headed by Nārāyaṇa. Regarding "of the size of two thumbs": two thumbs. The same applies hereafter. *Vasti* is the lower part of the belly. The rest is clear. Regarding "the thighs and the shanks": [the measurement continues as follows].

"Urū jaṅghe ca"—these [parts] are, in their respective order, the lamp of the head (*kapradīpa*). That which is called "the secret" (*guhya*) is known as the birthplace of the gods (*devayoni*); the fire that is produced therein is called "the doer of auspiciousness" (*kalyāṇakṛt*). [1.7] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Since these [parts] are to be used by those engaged in sacrificial practice, this is the division of the twenty-four thumb-units (*aṅguṣṭha*). The word "hi" is used for emphasis. That thumb-unit which was designated as "the secret" is the place of origin for the gods.

Therefore, the fire that is produced from that wood is said to be conducive to prosperity; for that reason, its churning must be performed. It is precisely for this purpose that the description of the division of the parts [of the fire-drill] is given. (11) Commentary: These measures consist of four, three, and one thumb-breadths (*aṅguṣṭha*). This is the division of twenty-four thumb-breadths. These constituent parts of the *araṇi* have been definitively stated by the ritualists (*yājika*) in their entirety. (10) He states the place for churning with the words "that which... (*yattat*).

By the two pronouns *yat* and *tat*, he indicates that [the subject] is well-known. That which is called "the secret" is said to be the place of origin for the fire of the deity. The use of the feminine pronoun *sā* is intended to emphasize its status as the grammatical predicate (*vidheya*). The fire produced by churning within it is described by the sages as the "doer of auspiciousness," the source of prosperity. Because he is the son of Gbhila, he says: "Having extended eight finger-breadths from the base, and three each on both sides..."

That is to be known as the *devayoni* (the womb of the gods); there, the fire is produced by friction. Having left eight finger-breadths from the base and twelve finger-breadths from the tip, that is to be known as the *devayoni*; there, the fire is produced by friction. (*Karmamadīpa*) In another case, that which is produced by friction elsewhere would incur both defects. For this rule applies to the first friction and to other subsequent instances. (12) The lower fire-drill (*pramanya*) should always be produced from the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*). Otherwise, through the confusion of lineages (*yoni-saṅkara*), one who performs the rite with a different [drill] becomes associated with a mixed lineage. (13) [1.1]

7kha] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Furthermore, regarding that which is churned elsewhere, from that [churning], they incur this same fault. This fault occurs at the first installation of the fires (*agnyādhāna*), but not again in the second and subsequent installations. (12) The *pramanyya* previously mentioned is produced by taking a small chip of wood from the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*) for the purpose of filling the cavity; it should exist at all times, even in the case of a second installation and so forth.

Regarding the fault in [holding] otherwise: for one who considers [the deity] to be different [from the mantra] becomes connected with the evil of the fault of confusion (*saṃkara*). 13. Thus, by the first statement, the divinity of the secret [mantra] is stated in another way; by the second statement, however, it is [the divinity] of its source—this is the distinction. This is the alternative (*vikalpa*). 11. Regarding "otherwise": *yat* is an adverbial modifier of the action of considering.

Furthermore, whatever is recited elsewhere by the divine sage, the churner incurs that same fear. And this rule applies only to the churning performed at the first establishment of the fires (*prathamādhāna*), and not to subsequent churnings when a re-establishment (*punarādhāna*) is to be performed. (12) Now he states the specific details regarding the construction of the churning sticks, beginning with "the upper churning stick" (*uttarāraṇi*). Regarding the phrase "those others who churn," there is an alternative reading: "they would incur the fear of *ṛg*. [Karmapradīpa 1.7]

One that is damp, full of holes, infested by woodworms, or cracked—such an upper fire-drill (*araṇi*) is not beneficial for sacrificers, nor is any other [defective] fire-drill. (14) The Seventh Section. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: "Full of holes" means having cavities; "infested by woodworms" means having its parts decayed by insects such as woodworms. The rest is explained by the literal reading. (14) The Seventh Section. *Prabhā*: Having extracted a small chip of wood from the chariot, one should produce fire by friction with it. This applies at all times, even in subsequent consecrations (*ādhāna*).

Regarding the production of the *pramantha* (churning stick) by means of another piece of wood, he states the reason: "The *pramantha*... Since the one who produces the *pramantha* from another piece of wood is joined with the fault of mixing the *yoni* (source), therefore the *pramantha* must always be produced from the upper and lower fire-drills (*araṇi*). Thus, the second half [of the verse] provides the reason for the meaning stated previously. He describes the specific quality of the *araṇi*: "With a hole... It has a cavity; it has a hole. A *ghuṇa* is a particular kind of insect. That which has such an insect on its limb is *ghuṇāṅgī*. The rest is clear.

Thus ends the seventh section. The eighth section begins: Having put on a new garment and having wrapped an upper cloth according to the rule, one should hold the *yantra* facing eastward, covered by that which is about to be described. *Parishishtaprakash*: Having put on a new garment and made it an upper cloth (*uttarīya*), one should squeeze the *yantra* facing eastward at night according to the sequence to be described, beginning with the *auli*. By the phrase "according to the rule," [it is meant]: "The side-loop tied outside the lower garment is indeed demonic (*āsuri*)."

"In ritual acts according to the Dharma, those who know [the law] should avoid [this garment] with great effort. Thus is the rule for wearing [the garment] stated by Yājñavalkya. "One whose cloth has slipped from the left shoulder and is worn around the waist—one should know him to be 'wearing only one garment' (ekavastra), and he should be excluded from rites for the gods and the ancestors. Thus is the rule for wearing the lower garment stated by Śātātapa. || 1 || [Commentary: Now, he describes the manner of churning [the fire-drill], beginning with the words "having put on. "Akrta" means that which is not prepared by a machine—that is to say, newly produced. "Vāsaḥ" (garment).

Having wrapped [the lower garment] and having put on the upper garment (*uttarīya*) as well; the phrase "according to rule" (*yathāvidhi*) is connected to both instances. Consequently, regarding the wearing of the lower garment and the putting on of the upper garment, the *Karmapradīpa* [1.8] states: "The side-loop (*kakṣā*) tied outside the lower garment is indeed demonic (*āsuri*); it should be diligently avoided by the learned in all ritual acts. And here: "The wise man, having firmly secured the end of the thread at the waist, should place the *araṇi* with its tip facing upward upon that [thread]."

The practitioner, being restrained and pure, should hold the fire-drill (cātrī) steady and motionless, having fixed its tip within the hole of the lower block (kīlaka) and pointing it toward the north. *Commentary (Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa):* Having made the tip of the upper friction-stick (pramanthā) motionless by filling the hole [of the lower block], one who is skilled in the churning should place the upper friction-stick with its tip pointing north upon the lower friction-stick which is situated above that [lower block].

Having placed the upper edge of the garment over the top of the left shoulder so that it hangs down across the chest, and having fastened it firmly, one should make it motionless by pressing it down and, with a single-minded focus and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and other preliminaries, one should recite [the mantra]. (3) Thus [ends the section on] radiance. Furthermore, it is said that the rule established in various *smṛtis*—such as: "One whose garment has slipped from the left shoulder and is wrapped around the waist should be known as 'one-clothed' (*ekavastra*); he is to be avoided in rites for the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*)"—is to be followed. This is what is intended.

Having become thus, facing the east, one should hold the churning apparatus (*manthayantra*) according to the procedure to be described. (1) Regarding the phrase "at the base of the churning-stick" (*cātrabudhne*): O wise one, having made the tip of the *pramantha* (the churner) immovable by filling the hole at the base of the churning-stick (*cātra*), and having placed the *araṇi* with its top pointing north, one should place the *cātra*—standing upright like a staff—upon the *araṇi*. (2) Regarding the phrase "the cavity of the *cātra*" (*cātroḍe*): that which is the hollow in the cavity of the *cātra* is where the enemy of the gods (Indra) resides. [1.8]

The Ghee-Lamp: Having thrice offered oblations with the *uḍeṭī* formula, he should then [offer] with the *neveṇa* formula; here, the wife should hold the hem of his garment. One should consider the eastern limit as far as the forest, just as there would be the displacement of the eastern fire. (4) The establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) must not be performed by the twice-born without even a single wife. One should know that it is unperformed if all [the wives] do not hold on to him. (5) *Parishiṣṭaprakāśa:*

Having wound the previously mentioned *bālarajju* (young rope) three times around the axle from top to bottom in successive order, the wife, wearing new garments, should stand facing the eastern direction at the front of the fire-enclosure, so that the fire may emerge toward the east. (4) If all the wives, being favorable through the drawing of their eyes during the *ādheya* rite, do not accomplish it, then it should be known as unaccomplished due to its deficiency (*viguṇatvāt*). The rest is explained by the literal reading (*nigadavyākhyātam*). (5) [Prabhā]

Having made the tip of the *mudga* bean [the lower part] smooth, having fixed it firmly, supported it, pressed it tightly, or having rendered the apparatus (*yantra*) motionless, one who is pure—having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and so forth, being restrained, that is to say, diligent and with a concentrated mind—should hold the apparatus. Regarding "three times around": immediately thereafter, having wrapped it three times with the thread characterized as previously described, moving from below upwards or from above downwards, the wife, wearing unwashed garments, should think of the *araṇi* fire-drills.

The churning of the fire-drills must be performed separately by these virtuous wives. (6) One should not employ a Śūdra woman for this task, nor one who harbors deep malice, nor one who is disobedient, nor one who has had sexual intercourse with another man. (7) [End of] the *Pariśiṣṭa*. *Prakāma*.

First by the Brāhmaṇī wife, and thereafter by the Kṣatriyā wife—in this manner, according to the seniority of caste (*varṇajyaiṣṭhya*) among wives of different castes and wives of the same caste, and according to the order of seniority of birth (*janmajyaiṣṭhyakrama*), as long as the emergence of the fire does not occur, so long must the churning be performed separately by those virtuous wives. (6) In this context of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*), one should not employ a Śūdra woman as a wife; even for a non-Śūdra [wife], [the rule regarding] life-breath...

Prabhā: Even with only one wife, the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) must not be performed; rather, it must be performed by all [the wives]. The meaning is that if all the wives do not perform the *anvārambhaṇa* (holding on from behind), then one should know that even though the *ādhāna* has been performed, it is as if unperformed. Therefore, the meaning is that the *ādhāna* must not be performed even in the absence of a single wife. *Anvārambhaṇa* refers to the act of holding on from behind to facilitate the churning [of the fire]. ||5||

Regarding this, he states the distinction: "by seniority of caste" (*varṇajyaiṣṭhena*). This means that when there are many wives of both the same and different castes, the churning must be performed by them according to the seniority of their caste; first by the Brāhmaṇī, then by the Kṣatriyā, and after that by the Vaiśyā. When there are many wives of the same caste, the churning should be performed according to the order of seniority by birth. According to the stated sequence, these virtuous women should perform the churning separately until the fire emerges. [End of verse 6: "Not here... (*nātra*).

One should not employ even a Śūdra woman who has been married for the churning of the fire. Therefore, whichever among those [wives] is most capable, or whichever other one is present, should churn the fire as desired. (8) [1.8] Having performed the rite of marking the newborn, having brought him forward and kindled the fire, and having placed the fuel-sticks, one should seat the Brahman priest. (8) 115 *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

A woman who acts perversely, who acts out of hatred, or who obstructs her husband's commands—even if she has associated with another man according to the rules of Niyoga—is not fit for the kindling of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*). Any other such woman, however, is indeed fallen. (7) Then, when the churning of the fire-wood (*marghana*) has been performed by all [the wives], afterwards, among those very women performing the churning, whichever one is most capable—be she even one of the initiated members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*)—should perform the churning of the fire-wood as desired until the production of the fire is achieved. (8)

Having performed the characteristic rites for the fire that has been produced—consisting of drawing lines and so forth—and having caused it to enter that place, one should offer fuel and perform the *brahmāvāhana* (invocation of Brahman). || 8 || [Commentary: Likewise, one should not employ a woman who is stubborn, who acts with malice, who does not carry out orders, or who has had sexual intercourse with another man. "Stubbornness" (*dr̥h*) means the desire to kill; "malice" (*dveṣa*) is well known. || 7 || [Commentary on] "Then":...

When the churning has been performed according to the stated sequence by all [the wives], afterwards, any one among those who have approached—that is, those who have been initiated—belonging to any of the three castes, whichever is most capable (śaktatama), meaning most powerful, whether she be of a different caste (asavarṇā) or of the same caste (savarṇā), she should churn the fire as desired. The meaning is that she should perform the churning until the emergence of the fire. Regarding the word "jātasya" (of the born): the genitive case here indicates a relationship of possession (saṃbandha-lakṣaṇā); it means "of the net" (jālasya). When the two are born, the lamp trembles. [1st Praśna]

8kha] Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* accompanied by all the ritual manuals (*tantra*), [the sacrificer] should give a cow and two garments to the *brahmā* priest at the conclusion of the *yajñavāstu* rite. *Parīśiṣṭaprakāśa*: After the seating of the *brahmā*, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* together with the entire procedure for the offerings, one should give a cow and two garments to the *brahmā* at the end of the *darbhajuṣṭikā* rite. *Prabhā*: This is the meaning when [the text] has been extracted.

Having performed the ritual acts designated as *lakṣaṇa*—consisting of drawing lines and so forth—and having brought that fire there, kindled it, and placed fuel upon it, one should cause the entry of the Brahman priest (*brahmopaveśana*).
