Having performed that taking possession of the ground (*bhūmigraha*), one should perform the sweeping (*parisamūhana*). Having mentally resolved upon Brahmā, [one should proceed] from the preparation of the *caru* offering onwards. (8) Regarding the word "then" (*tataḥ*): it refers to the ritual procedure (*tantra*). That is to say, immediately after the entry of Brahmā, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) together with all the ritual procedures for the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), at the conclusion of the rite named *Gṛhyasthālīpāka*, one should give a cow and two garments to Brahmā. (10) There is an alternative reading: "having done so" (*kṛtvā*). [This is from] the *Karmapradīpa*.

In the absence of a specific instruction regarding a liquid substance, the *sruva* ladle is prescribed by the sages; however, for any other [substance], the hand itself is used, and in this case, the *sruva* is not employed. (11) The *sruva* is known to be made of *khadira* wood, with a handle two *vitastis* long; the *sruk* ladle should be understood as being one cubit (*bāhu*) in length, and their handles are circular. (12) *Parishishtaprakashah*: For one who has performed the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), there are various types of oblations (*āhuti*). First, he states the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) concerning them: "In the absence of a specified vessel for receiving an oblation of a liquid substance, the *sruva* is prescribed by the sages."

In the case of an oblation other than a liquid, if no other vessel is prescribed, it should be offered with the hand alone. Since no specific vessel is prescribed for either type of oblation, there might arise a suspicion—based on the force of the technical name *juhū*—that even the *juhū* could optionally serve as the means of offering; therefore, it is stated that "the *sruva* is not used here. (11) This clarifies the *sruva* and the *sruk* as described by Baudhāyana: "Made of *khadira* wood, or of *palāśa*... [1.1]

8kha] 117. For the sacrificer who has performed the preparatory rites (*kṛtādhāna*), various kinds of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) offerings are prescribed by the Vedas. Regarding this, he first states the general rule (*paribhāṣā*): "The *brahma-pātra*. When no specific vessel is prescribed for the sacrificial implement, the sages have declared that for a liquid substance as an oblation (*havis*), the *sruva* ladle is the *brahma-pātra*. However, when the oblation is not a liquid substance, the hand itself is the *brahma-pātra*. In this context, since no vessel is prescribed, the offering is not made with the *sruva* ladle.

Because of the statement, "It is offered with the *sruk*," it is implied that this meaning has come down through the tradition of the practitioners (*yānika*). *Sruk* and *juhū* are not different things. (11) He defines the *sruva* and the *sruk*: "Made of *khadira* wood... *Parṇa* means *palāśa*. (118) *Karmapradīpa*, [1st Praśna, 8th Khaṇḍa]: "At the tip of the *sruva*, there is a hollow like a nostril, one thumb-span in circumference. The hollow of the *juhū* is like a shallow bowl, provided with a handle, and six finger-breadths deep. (13) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

Alternatively, the *sruva* ladle is traditionally said to measure two *vitastis*. The *juhū* ladle should be the measure of a forearm; its handle (*pragraha*) is so called by etymology, as it is that "by which it is grasped. Its bowl should be round like a *sruva*. || 12 || One should know that at the tip of the *sruva*, there is a circular cavity (*bila*) measuring four fingers (*aṅgulas*), situated in the middle with a boundary like a nostril. As for the hollow of the *juhū*, one should know it to be shaped like a shallow dish (*śarāva*), six fingers in length, provided with a channel (*praṇālī*)—so called because it carries out the offering (*nirvāha*) by serving as the means for pouring the oblation without remainder. || 13 ||

*Prabhā*: A *vitasti* consists of ten *aṅgulas*. A *sruva* ladle is prescribed to be measured at two *vitastis* and made of either *khadira* or *pālāśa* wood. It should be understood to have the measure of an outstretched arm. That by which one holds [the ladle]—the handle (*pragraha*)—is known to be circular (*vṛtta*). || 12 || Regarding "at the tip of the *sruva*": that hollow at the tip of the *sruva* should be made circular and round, measuring the width of two thumbs, like a nostril.

By the term *prāṇavat* (like the vital breath), he teaches that just as the two nostrils are situated in the middle with a boundary, so too the cavity situated at the tip of the *sruva* must be made to be situated in the middle with a boundary. The cavity of the *juhū* should be measured at six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and made like a shallow bowl (*śarāva*); moreover, it should have an outlet (*nirvāha*), meaning it is provided with a channel (*praṇālī*). For that [channel] is designated by the word *nirvāha* because it serves as the means for pouring out the oblation without remainder. [1ma. 8kha. *Karmapradīpa*: "Their [edges] should be fashioned with *kuśa* grass pointing eastward."

One should perform the wiping of those [utensils] that have been used for cooking with *kuśa* grass while facing east; however, for those that have been smeared [with food], one should first wash them with hot water and then heat them over the fire. One should place each item toward the east, and each toward the north of the fire, arranging each substance exactly as it is to be employed. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: For those [utensils] that are distinct and not used for cooking, the wiping with *kuśa* grass should be performed while facing east. But for those that have been smeared, after first washing them with hot water, they must be heated over the fire.

Or rather, the reading is *sampramārge* (14). One should place the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), the *tuṅga* vessel, and other implements in their respective order of use near themselves, starting from one side—first one, then another to its left—and so on in sequence, placing them to the north of the fire with their tips pointing northward (15). [The commentary says: "Of these. The plural number is used because there are distinct individual items, or to include other sacrificial vessels as well. For one who wishes to offer oblations (*juhuṣatā*), the wiping (*sampramārge*) of those [implements] should be performed with *kuśa* grass blades while facing eastward.

One should perform a thorough and complete wiping. The reading *sampramārja* is an archaic (Vedic) usage. Furthermore, those [vessels] smeared with clarified butter (*ājya*) and other substances should be heated over the fire; however, one should rinse them with warm water. (14) Regarding the phrase *prācaṃ prāñcam*: to the north of the fire, one should place the materials in the order of the *vasu* arrangement, placing each subsequent item to the east of the preceding one, with their tips pointing northward.

One should place first that for which the application occurs first; the lamp is that for which the application follows immediately after. [1st Khaṇḍa] Ghee is prescribed as the substance in oblations (*juhoti*) when no specific material is enjoined. Prajāpati is the established rule for both the mantra and the deity. (16) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: In the case of oblations (*homa*), when there is no instruction regarding the substance to be offered, it is prescribed that ghee (*ājya*) is the substance to be offered. "Ghee is from a cow" (*gavyam*) is an alternative reading.

Regarding the non-specification of the deity of the mantra, Prajāpati is the deity and the mantra itself is also Prajāpati; thus, the meaning is "Svāhā to Prajāpati. Others, however, say that the entire Vyāhṛti mantra belongs to Prajāpati. In that case, because the word *prajāpati* is employed in the mantra, it is evident that the deity consists of the mantra itself. Likewise, Yājñavalkya says: "For whichever mantra a particular deity is assigned, the form of that [deity] becomes his; such is declared to be the nature of the deity. (16) [Prabhā]

This means that one should proceed in this manner—reaching from one [point] to the next, and from that one to another, and so on in sequence. Just as in the case of the statement, "He scatters the husks with the potsherd of the cake," where the potsherd is designated by means of the future cake, so too here the eastern direction must be designated by means of the future fire-altar. Why? [Because it is said: "Having leveled the ground and having smeared it with earth..."

"Having placed the sacrificial materials (dravya) to the north, one should make the wife face the north. This is because the *Gṛhyasaṃgraha* states that the placing of the materials is to be done immediately after the smearing of the ground. [15] Regarding "clarified butter" (*ājyam*): when no specific oblation is prescribed for the *homa*s, clarified butter is the means of accomplishing the *homa*. [16] "A fuel-stick (*samidh*) should never be taken as thicker than a thumb; it must not be stripped of its bark, nor should it be split or cracked. [17] The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*:

Having placed the fuel stick (*samidh*), one should sprinkle water around it; this makes explicit the fuel stick by means of rules regarding its size and other characteristics. A fuel stick thicker than a thumb must never be taken for any ritual action; however, one that is thinner than that may indeed be taken. The rest is easy to understand. [17] *Prabhā*: The substance is provided by the teachers. When neither the mantra nor the deity is specified, he says that Prajāpati is the deity.

Although grammarians prescribe the rules for *śitap* suffixes when the meaning is the nature of the verbal root (*dhātusvarūpa*), nevertheless, because we observe the use of reflective pronouns such as "yajateḥ pūrvavat tvam," "mili īkṣate," and "naśabdaḥ" in the context of prescribing the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), its prescription must be understood to apply even to the abstract state (*bhāva*). For this very reason, the following is stated in the *Nyāyācārya*: "The wise proclaim the path to heaven and liberation; that which is the means [to these] is here defined as the Supreme Self. (16)

"Having placed the fuel-stick and having not yet applied the fire," according to the statement of Gābhiḷa, one should clearly define the fuel-stick by means of two [verses]: "In these [fires]" and "by one who knows. The phrase "in these [fires]" and "by one who knows" connects with the subsequent [verse]. A fuel-stick that is thick, exceeding the size of the thumb, stripped of its bark, and split—even if it is accompanied by wood-chips—should not be taken up in any of the fires by one who knows. However, one that is thinner than the thumb is not forbidden. [The *Kapradīpa* commentary on the first section: 17. 3. *** **Note on Terminology:** * *Samidham ādhāya*: Having placed the fuel-stick. * *Anupayucya*: Having not yet applied (the fire). * *Gābhiḷa-svktām*: As stated by Gābhiḷa. * *Vyaktam*: Clearly/Explicitly. * *Aṅguṣṭhāt*: Than the thumb. * *Hmeṣu*: In these [fires]. * *Vijānatā*: By one who knows. * *Uttara-kasyam*: With the subsequent [verse]. * *Avāpya*: Having reached/connecting with. * *Sthūlatayā*: By way of thickness. * *Tvacā vinirmuktā*: Stripped of its bark. * *Kṛtasahitā*: Accompanied by wood-chips. * *Vipāṭitā*: Split. * *Na grāhyā*: Should not be taken up. * *Aṅguṣṭhād ūna-sthūlā*: Thinner than the thumb. * *Na niṣiddhā*: Not forbidden. * *Kapradīpaḥ*: The *Kapradīpa* (a commentary). * *Pra.*: First [section].

8] A fuel-stick (*samidh*) should not be longer than a span (*prādeśa*), nor should it be branched, nor possessed of leaves, nor should it be discarded by one who knows these rules regarding the *ahomas*. The measure of a fuel-stick is proclaimed to be two spans; such indeed should be the fuel-sticks in all ritual acts here. 18–182. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

By the command of the Lord Indra, [the sacrificial post] should not be accepted by one who knows the Brahman, if it is longer or shorter than the prescribed measure, or if it possesses various branches, or if it has a companion, or if it is excessively decayed by being bored through by woodworms and the like. Others, however, say that "viśākhikā" refers to a post from which the branches have fallen off, or one originating from such a branch. (18) Now, regarding the rule in the Sūtra stating, "He prepares these [stakes], made of Khadira or Palāśa wood," the author clarifies them. The first half [of the verse] is explained by its own words (*nigadavyākhyāta*). Although the Sūtra says "up to a span (*prādeśāt*)," [the commentary] explains it as follows:

Fuel sticks (*samit*) that are longer than a span (*prādeśa*) or shorter than that, those with various branches, those with leaves, and those rendered powerless by being eaten by woodworms or being husky should not be accepted by the wise among us; this is the summary of what is to be accepted: "Fuel sticks that are not black, not thick, without branches, and not leafless—those that are not too long or too short grant all desires. Thus [ends the section]. 18.

Now, he prepares these [sacrificial implements], made of *khadira* or *palāśa* wood, as prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtra* of Gṛhyā; this is clarified by the two verses beginning with "two spans" (*prādeśadvayam*). The wise declare that eighteen fuel-sticks (*samidh*) are required for this [fire] at the New Moon (*darśa*) and Full Moon (*paurṇamāsa*) sacrifices, and twenty in other rites. (20) In the case of these fuel-sticks and similar items, they are devoid of both mantra and deity; they serve as fuel both before and after [the main offerings]. (21)

122. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Regarding the statement "aye mān," although this was said with reference to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, nevertheless, in all rites prescribed here in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, these [sticks] called *imā* should serve as the fuel (*samidh*). By the very sign of the name "fuel" (*samidh*), it is implied that even these *imā*s are intended for the purpose of kindling the fire. ||18|| He summarizes the characteristics of the fuel sticks. This is self-evident from the explanatory prose (*nigada*). ||20|| From the time a religious student (*brahmacārin*) brings fuel in the evening and morning, from then on, in all [rites], there is light.

The measure of these has been stated by the ancient teachers. Although these were mentioned by Āśvalāyana in the context of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, nevertheless, such kindling-wood (*samidh*) as these should indeed be used here in all the *Gṛhya* rites. Regarding the term "kindling-wood": the wise state that for this [Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa], the number of kindling-sticks is eighteen, while for other rituals it is twenty. Alternatively, the genitive case in the word *imasya* may be understood as indicating a relationship in general.

And at that time, the words "eighteen" and "twenty" denote numbers, and there [in that context] they are understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "fuel-sticks" (*samidhaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "in the case of fuel-sticks and so forth": the placing of fuel-sticks in the evening and morning that was prescribed for the religious student (*brahmacārin*) is what is grasped here by the term "fuel-stick" (*samit*). In all these sacrifices beginning with the fuel-sticks, there is a restriction of ritual action. Even the firewood (*idhma*) is traditionally held to be for the purpose of fuel for the fire during oblations of sacrificial food (*havis*); and where its cessation occurs, I shall clarify that.
In the rites known as *sisyanti* according to the *Aṅgirasamitta-tantra*, and in those for which this has been stated above, as well as in similar ones; || 23 ||

*Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Among these, the fuel-stick (*samid*) prescribed for the purpose of kindling the fire—which is devoid of both deity and mantra and is one span (*prādeśa*) in length—should indeed be used both before and after [the oblation]. (21) Even in the case of oblations consisting of sacrificial food (*caru*), cake-offerings (*purōḍāśa*), and so forth, the fuel-stick measuring two spans (*prādeśadvaya*) intended for kindling the fire is remembered by the sages. Since this too is for the purpose of kindling, it is to be offered there without reference to a deity; thus, in this case as well, there is an absence of both mantra and deity.

There is no room for the statement "of one's own mantra and deity" [in these cases]. Regarding the subsidiary rites (*aṅgakarmāṇi*) prescribed for the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), and so forth, [the mantra belongs] to another [deity] in those instances.

Prabhā: Therefore, both before and after [the main offerings], the aforementioned fuel-stick (*samid*), devoid of mantra and deity, should serve for the kindling of the fire; that is to say, it is to be cast into the fire. (21) Thus, since there is no distinction regarding the oblations of sacrificial food (*havis*), whether they be *caru*, clarified butter (*ājya*), and so forth, the previously described characteristics apply here as well. It is traditionally taught (*smṛta*) that these are indeed for the purpose of kindling the fire. Because of the statement "only for the purpose of the fire's fuel," in this case too, there is a mantra and a deity.

I shall clarify those matters in which there is a cessation of this [procedure]. Where and in what circumstances it is not to be performed—that very point is clarified by the *Aṅgahma* [1st Praśna, Khaṇḍa], the *Kampradīpa*: "In cases of misfortune such as the breaking of the axle, in rites such as the *jalahoma*, and in all *smārta* oblations—these [procedures] are not prescribed for these. The Eighth Section. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Because the leading forward of the fire (*agninayana*) and so forth constitute the primary acts.

Likewise, there are two kinds of *homa*: the *citra-homa* and the *tantra-homa*, as established in the ritual tradition (*yājñika*). Among these, the *citra-homa* refers to those such as the morning and evening *homas*, based on the etymological derivation that they are "performed quickly" (*citram hūyante*). The *tantra-homa*, however, consists of those accompanied by an expansion of auxiliary rites (*aṅga*), such as the sweeping around the fire and the spreading of sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

In this regard, those sacrifices which are performed with clarified butter (*sarpis*), those which are performed with milk (*payas*), and those for which this very substance is prescribed by the sūtra—"afterwards, he prepares these [substances] for the Vaiśvadeva, the Sāyamprātar, and so forth"—in these and similar sacrifices that are brief (*cipra*), the preparation (*nirvṛtti*) of the offering should take place. (23) The carrying away of the bride by the groom in a vehicle is prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras.

In that context, regarding the breaking of an axle, the loss of a draft animal, the overturning of a vehicle, or other such calamities, they should kindle the very same fire they were carrying, perform the *vyāhṛti* oblations, and having brought another substance, pour clarified butter over it with the verse beginning "Whatever [fault] has been committed" (*yad ṛtaṃ cid abhiśriyaḥ*). This sacrifice is prescribed with the *sruva* ladle for the purpose of remedying the failure of the axle or other vehicular misfortunes; and that which is performed at night on the full moon day when the two fires have not gone out.

Those mantras which indeed constitute the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the birth-rite, the naming ceremony, the tonsure, and so forth; those which are the constituent parts of the *sīmanta* (parting of the hair) ritual; and those which we recite for the sake of an easy delivery for a woman whose labor has begun—after these, including the *vaiśvadeva*, the evening and morning offerings (*sāyaṃprātaḥ*), and others, this substance called *etadima* is to be offered. Thus says the *Karmapradīpa-Parīśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

Having immersed oneself up to the navel, one should offer unbroken grains of rice with the mouth at the ends of the *ṛc*s, saying "Svāhā" into the water; by this sūtra, the immersion in water for one desiring land is prescribed using the first verse of the five verses beginning with "vṛkṣa" (tree), performed with the mouth. As for the phrase "yā ca smara-sāhuta," that is not a rule for the three [immersions]. Here, "aca" refers to a specific part of a chariot. By stating "ava isa vidhinivṛttiḥ" (the cessation of the rule is "ava isa"), he indicates that this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), and not a prohibitory injunction (*niṣedha-vidhi*).

One must raise the objection that there would be a conceptual distinction (vikalpa) regarding the injunctions and prohibitions concerning the *ācamana* and so forth; by the phrase "in water and so forth," the various substrates for the feet and other limbs are included. And thus says the Śruti: "He offers it on the path; he offers it on the track. And the Smṛti: "Whether in a worldly or a Vedic context, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice should be performed with the remnants of the oblation in water or on a fire-pile for the removal of the five slaughtering grounds (*pañcasūnā*). [1st Praśna, 8th Khaṇḍa] Eighth Section. Commentary.

Among those similar [acts], as well as other swift *brahmans*, there are indeed two kinds of *brahmans* well-known in ritual practice: the *tantra-brahmans* and the *kṣipra-brahmans*. Those *brahmans* which involve an extensive procedure, such as the sweeping around [the fire] and the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), are called *tantra-brahmans* because they consist of a collection of subsidiary rites (*itikartavyatā*) belonging to a *tantra*. And those which do not possess such an extensive set of subsidiaries are these *sāyaṃprātar-karmapradīpa* (Lamps for the Evening and Morning Rites). This is the light.

Likewise, by the etymological derivation "those which are quickly carried" (*cīrṇa-hiyante*), the *cīrabhras* (portable fires) are described. According to the *Gṛhyasūtra*: "In the event of the breaking of a vessel, the collapse of a mat, a reversal of the vehicle, or other calamities, having established that very fire which they carry, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should fetch another substance and anoint it with the remainder of the clarified butter using the mantra 'ṛte cidabhi śriyaḥ'. Thus, the *cīrabhra* is prescribed for the purpose of re-establishing the fire in times of misfortune such as the breaking of a vessel or the collapse of a mat; and also [that which is used] on the night of the full moon when the fire has not gone out.

Having immersed himself up to the navel, one should offer unhusked rice grains with the mouth at the end of each *ṛc*, saying "Svāhā" into the water; thus the *jalahoma* (water-oblation) is prescribed by the *Gṛhyasūtra* of Gṛhyābhila. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the *padahoma* (footstep-oblation) is also included. Likewise, regarding those oblations remembered as "smara-hutis," this [practice] is not performed by ritualists in any of these *homas*. If the reading is *avyāhutiṣu*, it means "in the case of malevolent (*abhicāra*) oblations. Thus ends the eighth section. The ninth section begins.

When the sun has reached twenty-six finger-breadths [below] the sunset mountain, the kindling of the fires (*prāduṣkaraṇa*) takes place; and in the morning, it occurs upon the appearance of the light. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Before sunset, having kindled the fire, one should offer the evening oblation once the sun has set. Having kindled it before sunrise, one should offer the morning oblation whether the sun has risen or not yet risen. Thus, in this *sūtra*, the kindling of the fire is prescribed. Therein, the upper limit for the time of kindling is clearly defined by the form of "sunset."

He clarifies what was previously stated: "In the sight of light" means in the eastern direction struck by the rays of the sun; the rest is easy to understand. || 1 || *Prabhā*: According to the *Gṛhyasūtra* of Āśvalāyana: "Before sunset, having kindled the fire, one should offer the evening oblation after sunset; before sunrise, having kindled [the fire], one should offer the morning oblation whether the sun has risen or not"—thus the time for kindling the fire is prescribed for both the evening and morning *homa* periods.

In this regard, the latter limits—consisting of sunset and sunrise—are clearly defined as the time for making manifest [the sacred fires]. Prior to these, the Sūtra clarifies the previously undefined limit: when the sun has reached thirty-six finger-breadths from the western mountain (astācala), it is the time for making manifest the fires that have been extinguished in the evening; when the rays of the sun (bhās) are seen, it is the time for making manifest those that have been extinguished in the morning. This is the former limit.

Because of the plural form "of the Blessed Ones" (*bhagavānām*), it should be understood that this very same time applies even for the kindling of the fire (*agniprāduṣkaraṇa*). [1 Pra. 8 Kha. *Kampradīpa*: "As long as the sun, having risen from the mountain, does not go beyond the hand, so long is the ritual procedure for those who follow the *Udita* [view] meritorious. [2] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Regarding the statement, "One should offer the morning oblation whether the sun has risen or not yet risen," the *Uditahomin* is mentioned in the Sūtra; [the author] clarifies the upper limit.

Having left the ground, as long as the sun does not go beyond a distance of one cubit (*hasta*), during that time the performance of the *brahmayañña* is recommended. For those for whom the sun has risen, no other time is recommended. By the inclusion of the prefix *abhi-* in the word *abhyudita*, which signifies "on all sides," it should be understood that even if the rising of the sun is not fully visible, it is still considered "risen" and not "not yet risen. By stating the excellence of this specific time, it is indicated that in the event of its impossibility, another time may be used. And so says the Sūtra:

"The evening oblation does not pass over the morning oblation; the morning oblation does not pass over the evening oblation. [Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.3.1.9] "...at dawn... one should offer the morning oblation whether the sun has risen or not yet risen. This clarifies the upper limit for the *abhyudita-homa* (oblation offered after sunrise) and *anudita-homa* (oblation offered before sunrise). From the moment the sun leaves the mountain of rising (*udayagiri*) until it reaches the height of the *hasta* constellation, this is the rule for the *abhyudita-homa* and *anudita-homa*; it is meritorious, but other times are not meritorious. There is an alternative reading: "having left the earth" (*bhuvaṃ hitvā*).

In the expression *abhyuditaḥ* (risen), the prefix *abhi-* follows the very meaning of the verbal root. This is the upper limit [of the time for performing the sacrifice]. Regarding the lower limit, the *Gṛhyasaṃgraha* states: "One should know that as the sun is seen even as a mere line, yet accompanied by its rays—that is sunrise; the wise man should perform [the rite] at that time. [From the *Karmapradīpa*, 1.8]: "As long as the stars are not clearly visible in all directions, and as long as the redness [of the sky] has not departed, so long is it considered evening."

130. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: "One should offer the evening oblation when the sun has set"—this [sūtra] clarifies the subsequent limit. As long as all the stars in the sky are not clearly perceived—neither subtle nor gross—and the twilight glow has not vanished, so long is the meritorious time for the evening *homa*. Even if this is impossible, the time indicated by the sūtra "until the morning oblation" is suggested. 3. *Prabhā*.

As for what Nārāyaṇa Pāṭhyāya stated—that because the prefix *abhi-* in the word *abhyudite* signifies "on all sides," the offering should be made only when the entire solar disc is visible, and not when it has merely risen—this is incorrect due to a lack of scriptural authority. Since the term "meritorious" (*puṇya*) is employed, this time is the primary one. However, in the event of a transgression, one should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and then offer it at another time. Thus says the Gṛhyasūtra of Gṛhyamāṇava: "The morning oblation does not lapse until the evening oblation; the evening oblation does not lapse until the morning oblation. || 2 ||

"One should offer the evening oblation when the sun has set"—this establishes the upper limit for the time of the evening oblation. "As long as" means: as long as the stars are not clearly perceived in all parts of the sky, and the twilight glow has not completely vanished, so long is the evening oblation offered by the ritualists. *Āpaiti* means "that which departs. *Karmapradīpa*: When the sun is obscured by mist, frost, smoke, clouds, or the tops of trees, one should offer the oblation directed toward the twilight; thus, his [duty] is not lost. (4)

A twice-born man should not perform the sweeping around the fire on the days of the new moon; he should not recite the Vairūpākṣa hymn, and he should avoid any calamity. [1.9] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Regarding what must be done when the rising or setting of the sun is not visible, it says: when the sun is covered by dust and the like, one should offer the oblation after determining the time of the twilight (*saṃdhyā*). Even so, this does not constitute a violation of the vow consisting of the obligatory rule for morning and evening rites. [4]

In rites performed quickly that do not involve Brahmins—such as the *syantī* and others performed morning and evening—one should not perform the ritual sweeping (*parisamūhana*) accompanied by mantras such as "O Brahmin, you are worthy of this sacrifice. One should also omit the recitation of the *virūpākṣa* and the *prapada* mantras. The *prapada* mantra begins with: "Austerity, splendor, faith, and strength... Accordingly, another *Gṛhya* text states: "In rites accomplished by a single person where there is no sacrificial grass (*barhis*), there shall be no ritual sweeping, nor the placing of the firebrand; for these are considered 'quick rites' (*kṣipra-brahman*)."

—Prabhā. Regarding what must be done when the rising and setting of the sun are not visible, he says: "By dust, frost, or clouds... When the sky is covered by dust, frost, or clouds, one should offer the oblation (juhuyāt) with reference to, that is, having determined, the *saṃdhyā*, i.e., the time of twilight. By offering in this manner, his daily observance (*niyama*) consisting of the morning and evening prayers is not violated. || 4 || Now, he states the specific rule regarding eclipses: "One should not [perform it]... [This is from] the *Tithipradīpa* and the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. Thus.

[Objection: But surely, for one who has performed the *citrahoma* (the fire-sacrifice) in the evening and morning, the sweeping (*parisamūhana*) is prescribed by the sūtra beginning with "having established the fire, having swept around... and so forth. [Response: True; however, that merely prescribes the gathering together of scattered ashes without a mantra. This, on the other hand, is clearly a prohibition of that [sweeping] when accompanied by a mantra. [Commentary: The term *citrahoma* refers to the evening and morning sacrifices and others of that kind.

Regarding those scattered fires, one should not perform the sweeping with the mantra "imaṃ stomaṃ... as stated by Gṛhyakāra Gbhila; for that sweeping accompanied by a mantra is not to be done. As for the sweeping mentioned by Gṛhyakāra Gbhila in the sūtra, "Having added fuel to the fire, having swept [around it]," which refers to the evening and morning homa—that is without a mantra and consists merely of collecting the scattered parts of the fire into one; thus there is no contradiction. And so says another Gṛhya text: "In rites accomplished by a single [fire], there shall be no sweeping when the sacrificial grass has been removed."

"And indeed, the *ndagāsādana* (the placing of the Brahman’s seat) is prescribed for you; for it is traditionally taught that [these rites] are performed by a single person. Because of the statement "in rites to be accomplished by one," the installation of the Brahman (*brahmasthāpana*) is not to be performed in the case of the *sāyam-prātar-homa* (morning and evening oblations) and other brief sacrifices (*kṣipra-homas*). Thus says the *Hautrāsaṃgraha*: "One should not appoint a Brahman in the *Rākā*, the *Piṭṛyajña*, the *sāyam-prātar-homas*, and likewise in the *balikarmans*. Similarly, in brief sacrifices, one should not recite the *Vairūpa* and *Vairāja* *prapadas*.

And regarding this, the Gṛhyasūtra of Āśvalāyana states: "In the *kāmya* rites, one should first recite the *virūpākṣa* mantra and then the *prapada*. In that context, the *virūpākṣa* is the mantra containing the word *virūpākṣa*: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, I take refuge in the Great Self, the Virūpākṣa-lamp. The sprinkling (*paryukṣaṇa*) should be performed everywhere with the mantra beginning "O Aditi," and at the end, there should be the singing of the *vāmadevya* chant, or alternatively, in three parts. This should also be done as prescribed even in the *ahīna* sacrifices upon seeing the moon.

The *Vāmadevya* [chant] is used in the *gaṇas*, O Agni, and in the *balis* and *vaiśvadeva* rites. (7) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: At the end of the *pakṣaṇa* rite, one should perform the singing of the *Vāmadevya* in all *cit* oblations as well. Alternatively, in the case of an inability to sing, one should recite "vidhā kayā na... and so forth. Or there is the reading "gānaṃ gurur hrasvas tridhā"; in that case, the meaning is quite clear. The remainder is self-evident. (6) The *Vāmadevya* should also be used in rituals even when devoid of mantras. For example, at the sight of the moon, [the mantra] "prabhā" [is used].

The mantra beginning with *pātsi* is the Vairūpāccha; the mantra beginning with *prapadye tapaśca tejaśca* is [the Vairāja]. Although the recitation (*japa*) of the Vairūpāccha and Vairāja is prescribed for optional rites (*kāmya*), since it is mentioned after beginning with the words "for those desiring [results] hereafter" (*kāmyeṣv ata ūrdhvam*), and these daily rites such as the morning and evening prayers (*sāyaṃprātaḥ*) are obligatory (*nitya*), one might object that their prohibition is untenable. However, because—as in the case of the *spayantha* and other such rites—an optional version of the *tripraśna* (three-fold inquiry) is possible, and because the rule "some [teachers] in the preceding cases" (*pūrveṣu caika*) allows for its application even to obligatory rites as a secondary alternative, its prohibition is not illogical. || 5 ||

"J paryucapanviti": In all cases, even in those rites devoid of *ṛks*, the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) must be performed with the mantra beginning "O Aditi, give your consent," and at the conclusion of the rite, the singing of the Vāmadevya hymn must be performed. Alternatively, for the sake of the singing, those *ṛcs* in which the Vāmadevya is sung should be recited three times. In the reading "one should perform the singing three times," this meaning is quite explicit. "In those devoid of *ṛks* as well": Even in those ritual acts lacking *ṛcs*, the Vāmadevya—[as explained in] the *Karmapradīpa*, 1.8].

In those cases where the spreading [of grass] is not prescribed as being beneath [the vessels], there should be no spreading; and because they serve the same purpose as a single body [of grass], one should also omit the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Regarding the departure [from the ritual ground], it has been stated: likewise, when rites are performed by a group, the *Vāmadevya* chant is for the group, but not at the end of each individual rite. Furthermore, regarding the *Vāmadevya* chant within the *Vaiśvadeva* oblation included among the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*), it is concluded [with that chant]; it should not occur immediately after the *Homa* alone. (7)

Having established the fire and strewn *kuśa* grass all around it, one should not perform the strewing for those rites—such as the evening and morning offerings—which have been prescribed by the *ṛc* verses from the section beginning with "yāni sāyaṃprātarādīni. Likewise, regarding the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), one should discard them even though they are mentioned as optional—"some also make enclosing sticks"—because they serve the same purpose. He states the reason: "because they serve a single purpose," and so forth. Just as the strewing has the purpose of forming a seat for the *brahmā*, which is to accomplish the encircling of the fire, so too is it for the enclosing sticks.

Therefore, because their function is identical, there is also the cessation of the *paridhi* (enclosing sticks). Alternatively, since it is accomplished by the mere agent who is the sole master of the house (*brahmārthaika-brahmakartṛ-mātra-sādhyatvena*), there should be a single performance of the *vāmadevya* chant. In this regard, there is an illustration: "as stated in the case of seeing the moon. This means that as it is stated regarding the departure upon seeing the moon, so too, when many rites are performed in groups, there should be one *vāmadevya* chant at the end of the group, not at the end of each individual rite.

Thus, the singing of the Vāmadevya [Sāman], which occurs at the end of the Bṛhaspati-sthāna within the five sacrifices (pañcayajña), should take place at the conclusion of the Bali-karma, and not specifically at the end of the Vaiśvadeva-Bṛhaspati-sthāna alone. || 7 || Regarding the phrase "yānyadha" (those below): according to the sūtra taught by Gṛhyāsaṃgrahakāra Āgniveśya, "Having established the fire, one should strew it all around with Kuśa grass," there is first the strewing (paristaraṇa) below; then, as stated in the *Karmapradīpa*: "The sacrificial grass (barhis), the sprinkling of water (paryukṣaṇa), and likewise the muttering of the Vāmadevya."

In all rites involving *kṛtyā* oblations, this triad does not exist. (8) Among sacrificial foods, barley is considered the foremost; after that, rice is prescribed. One should avoid black gram (*māṣa*), *kṛsara*, cow’s flesh, and so forth, even if they are available. [1.8] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Because of the absence of wind, there is a cessation of the spreading of grass and the encircling with water. The statement of Yājñavalkya, "Having first uttered the *praṇava*, then *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, and finally the *gāyatrī* and the *praṇava*—this is declared to be the recitation (*japa*)," refers to cases other than those of Gārgya and Bhāradvāja. This is because it was previously stated that "the *praṇava*, *bhūr bhuvaḥ svar*, and the *Sāvitrī* as the third," and since the "previous triad" is mentioned here as well, it is illogical to assume the addition of the *praṇava* at the end for the followers of Gārgya and Bhāradvāja.

Nor should it be argued that even the employment of the *praṇava* at the end is not contradictory to its being a single *praṇava*, as this is supported by the *Tattvakaumudī*. For, since the *praṇava* has not been mentioned previously, the phrase "the preceding triad" (*pūrvatrikam*) would be untenable. Furthermore, even with that much, the contradiction regarding the fourfold nature of the manifestations (*vyakti*) remains unresolved. Indeed, by the term "preceding triad," it should be understood that only three manifestations were mentioned previously. Moreover, in the *Sandhyāsūtra*, it is stated: "One should meditate upon and repeat the Gāyatrī in the morning. (14)

He summarizes this as follows: "In that [practice] where Brahminhood is established throughout the three junctions (sandhyā), those three junctions are said to be preeminent; he who has no devotion toward those three junctions is not called a Brāhmaṇa by the sages. (15) There is an alternative reading, *yadadhiṣṭhitam* ("that which is presided over"). [This is] the Lamp of Knowledge (Jñānadīpa).

(16) First Section. *Prabhā*: Regarding "from the one who performs the twilight prayers": *cakitaḥ* means "frightened" or "afraid. The rest has a different meaning. Thus ends the first section. "And being startled by the twilight" (*sandhyālpāñca cakitaḥ*) is an alternative reading. Second Section. Day after day, one should recite the Veda from the beginning according to one's ability; or one should worship Rudra before the Vedic recitation is completed. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

The necessity of performing the bath is indicated by the praise of bathing and by the statement that "as during the day, so in the morning. One should manifest Rudra by means of the Rudra-mantras; for the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *upa* has the sense of manifestation (*prakāśana*), as the Ātmanepada ending is prescribed by the rule *upānmantrakaraṇe*. Alternatively, one may perform the *upasthāna* (worship) of Rudra prior to the *japayajña*. Regarding the mantra for the worship of Rudra: "Obeisance, obeisance to the Supreme Brahman, the Truth, the Reality, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny, whose phallus is turned upward, the three-eyed one, the one of universal form. || 1 || [Commentary: Now he describes the *japayajña* with the words "the Veda," etc.

Starting from the very beginning, one should recite the Veda daily according to one's ability. After the recitation of the Veda, or alternatively, one should perform the *upasthāna* (homage) to Rudra. And for the *rudropasthāna*, the mantra handed down through tradition is: "Ṛta, Satya, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, dark and tawny, whose phallus is turned upward, the three-eyed one of diverse forms—to the one of universal form, salutations, salutations! Saying "I satiate" at the end of the name and "Om" at the beginning [of each name]. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Next, he describes the libation (*tarpaṇa*), which follows in due order. Therefore, Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa states that after reciting from "namo brahmaṇe" up to "ityevamantena," one should satisfy the gods with the mantra "agnistṛpyatu" using the hand with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya). Having described the libation for humans—beginning with "sanakādayaśca" and ending with "nivītam"—as a human duty, it further states that one should perform the *brahmayajña* daily according to one's ability, beginning with the recitation of the Gāyatrī eight hundred times or more, and so forth. This concludes the section on the libation.

By the passage ending with *gābhīlya*, the *brahmayajña* is stated to follow the libation (*tarpaṇa*). This is also indicated by the *Gābhīlya*: "When the time for the *āvasathya* [fire] has arrived, the libation follows immediately thereafter; afterwards, one should mutter the *Gāyatrī* and perform the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) according to the specific rules. [Commentary: Now he describes the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the words "with barley-water" (*yavādbhiḥ*). "Barley-water" (*yavāpa*) is a *madhyapadalopa* compound (meaning "water with barley"). One should satisfy the gods with water mixed with barley, and the ancestors (*pitṛs*) with water mixed with sesame seeds.

He states the formula for the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the words "at the end of the name" (*nāmānte*). Reciting "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*) at the end of the names of those to be satisfied, and saying "Om" at the beginning, one should perform the libation. In this way, the libation formula takes such forms as "Om, I satisfy Brahmā," and so forth. [Regarding the phrase] "also the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds," this is the reading in my own manuscript. [2nd Praśna, 2nd Khaṇḍa] According to the *Kampradīpa*: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Prajāpati, the Vedas, the meters, the gods, the seers (*ṛṣis*), the ancient teachers, and the year together with its parts."

"O divine Apsarases, gods, followers of the gods, Nāgas, oceans, mountains, trees, rivers, celestial beings, humans, others, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, Piśācas, the earth, medicinal herbs, animals, and the fourfold host of living beings"—thus he offers libations. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Thus, immediately after the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is prescribed. For this very reason, the libation is not [performed] by those belonging to the *Atharvaveda*. The libation for humans is performed with two handfuls of water using the middle part of the *kuśa* grass.

Likewise, the *Agnipurāṇa* states: "One should satisfy the gods with water whose flow is directed toward the east, humans in the middle, and the ancestors with water flowing toward the south—this is the single-day rite (*ekahavi-jala*). One should satisfy the ancestors with water containing barley and sesame seeds, saying 'I satisfy [Name]' at the end of the name, or saying 'Oṃ [Name]' at the beginning of the name. The word *cīn* (three times) indicates that the repetition should be performed three times for each individual, as they are present before one. || 5 || *Kavyavāḍ-anavam* is an alternative reading; *blapīcāna* is another alternative reading. 2 [2nd Praśna, 2nd Khaṇḍa] One should also offer libations to the eldest brother, the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, and the maternal uncle, as well as to the maternal grandfather and the paternal lineage. || 6 || "And those others who are worthy of water from me, I satisfy them"—this is the final *añjali* (handful of water). || 7 || Here are the verses:

This libation is the primary form of the *pitṛyajña* (ancestral sacrifice). That which is stated as the libation in the *Snānasūtra* is an ancillary part of the bath.

That [libation] is prior to the *brahmayajña*, while this [libation] is subsequent to the *japayajña*; thus it is not contradictory, as will be explained later in the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. The lamp of the Kapi; the mother of children, and the child—whether female or male—and the man [of the Kapi lineage]. *Prabhā* (light) and *chāyām*—the word *janitrīm* is a Vedic usage for *janayitrīm*, meaning "the progenitor. The rest is explained by the literal reading (*nigada-vyākhyātam*).
