The Second Section: *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. Since people desire water, therefore, out of fear of the sin (*pratyavāya*) produced by the failure [to offer libations], one must always perform the *tarpaṇa* (libation) as a rule. He states this very point explicitly: "A Brāhmaṇa, by failing to perform this, becomes tainted with great sin; for by performing it, he nourishes the entire universe. Therefore, there is sin in its non-performance. (10)

By the phrase "as by day, so in the morning," that which was stated regarding the morning bath being performed with the same elaboration as the midday bath applies only to one who maintains no sacred fires (*niragni*); however, one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgni*) should not elaborate the morning bath, but should perform it concisely. This concise form is as described by Yājñavalkya: consisting of the ritual assignment of the bathing place (*tīrtha-parikalpana*), the consecration of the water (*jalābhimantraṇa*), sipping water (*ācamana*), sprinkling (*mārjana*), muttering prayers while submerged in water (*antarjala-japa*), and the recitation of the *Aghamarṣaṇa-sūkta* three times. And thus, [the text says], "because it is so, therefore... [Prabhā].

Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa must always perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*). By failing to perform the libation, a Brāhmaṇa becomes joined with great sin. Furthermore, the statement regarding the fruit—"How indeed does he support this entire universe?"—is [explained] by the phrase "on account of its smallness. Because the time is short, and because of the [specific] nature of the bathing rite, [this is so]. From the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: "Bathing within the water, as well as sprinkling, sipping water (*ācamana*), the consecration of the water with mantras, and the visualization of the sacred site (*tīrtha*)."

"By means of the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn recited repeatedly and constantly—this is designated as 'various performance' by the great sages. [2nd Praśna, 2nd Khaṇḍa] He states the reason: because the time for the *brahma-yajña* is short and the ritual of bathing is extensive, there would be a transgression of the time for the *brahma-yajña* in case of expansion; since from that a loss of merit (*dharma*) arises and that is censurable, one should therefore perform it concisely in the morning for the sake of preserving merit.

Now, regarding the statement that "the morning rite should be performed immediately after the rising of the sun," even if the time is not extensive, there is no transgression of the *ahna* (day) period. Therefore, it is logical that this injunction refers specifically to the subject of the non-risen sun (*anudita-homa*). This is not so; for even for those who follow the risen sun (*udita-homa*), the offering of fire (*agni-pratipatti*) is prescribed prior to sunrise. Thus says Śāṅkhāyana: "Having kindled the fire before sunrise, one should offer the morning oblation either when the sun has risen or when it has not yet risen. Likewise, by the statement "as long as the sun is above the horizon," the *ahna* period itself is thus defined.

Furthermore, bathing in rivers and the like has been prescribed in detail. Therefore, because this entire [practice] would be lost through the elaboration of the bath and the journey from the river and so forth, there is no abridgment even for that. Likewise: "Having commenced the morning twilight [devotions] while the stars are still visible, one should practice the *Gāyatrī* according to the rule until the appearance of the sun. [The commentary on] *Prabhā* states: "Due to its lengthiness, one should not elaborate upon the morning bath. For if the bath is elaborated, the time for the *brahma-yajña* (Vedic study) would pass, and thus it would be deficient."

And that has been particularly censured. Thus ends the *Tadavakapradīpa* and the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. Regarding the statement from the *Narasiṃhapurāṇa*, "One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun is seen; but during the evening, one should remain seated until the stars clearly appear," and other similar passages cited by Gautama and others, it should be understood that they refer to those who do not maintain the sacred fires (*anagnis*). [End of] Second Section. [2nd Adhyāya, 2nd Khaṇḍa] 173. *Prabhā*.

Because the detailed procedure for the morning bath (*prātaḥ-snāna*) has been prohibited, it is stated that the bath should be performed in brief. The measure of this brevity is to be understood from another Smṛti text as follows: "Bathing within the water, the visualization of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the consecration of the water, as well as the sprinkling (*mārjana*) and sipping (*ācamana*), and always performing the ritual with the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn recited three times—this is declared by the great-souled ones to be the practice of bathing. Due to fear of prolixity, [the details of] the morning [bath are not given here].

Because of the prohibition of elaborate bathing, it is stated that the extension [of rules] such as "as during the day, so in the morning" pertains to those who do not maintain a sacred fire (*niragni*). Likewise, by the same logic, in the passage beginning with "one should stand before the sun's movement," it should be understood that this also refers to those who do not maintain a sacred fire. Thus ends the second section. The Third Section: Now, the rule for the five great sacrificial sessions (*satra*) is declared, by performing which a Brahmin shall eternally attain the eternal abode. *Parishishtaprakashah* (Commentary):

Immediately after the bath, he describes the five sacrifices that follow in due order: "Now, after the bath, the performance of the five great sacrifices (mahāyajñas) is declared. By constantly worshipping the gods and others through these, the Brahmin attains the stable state consisting of the nature of Brahman. Thus it is said in the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "The station of Prajāpati was established for those Brahmins who perform their duties. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* that there is an incidental fruit even in the obligatory rites.

"And likewise others [perform] the daily rites (*nityakriyā*) and the *śruti* which has incidental results (*anuṣaṅgaphala*). (1) **Commentary:** Regarding the phrase "of the five": now the rule for the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) is stated, by means of which sacrifices a Brāhmaṇa constantly attains his own traditional station (*bhāsvataḥ sthānam*). And they say: "The station of Prajāpati is ordained for Brāhmaṇas who are diligent in ritual action. (1) [2nd Adhyāya, Khaṇḍa] p. 175: "In due order, [the offerings] to the gods, beings, ancestors, Brahman, and men..."

One should know that these indeed are the great sacrifices (*mahāmakhāḥ*). Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*); the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*); the offering (*bali*) is the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*); and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men (*nṛyajña*). *Parīśiṣṭaprakāśa*: He states the five deities [of these sacrifices], which will be mentioned in due order. The phrase "these indeed are the great sacrifices" is intended as a rule for their technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*). The remainder is explained by the literal meaning of the words (*nigadavyākhyāta*). (2) Teaching is the sacrifice dedicated to Brahman; the same should be understood for the sacrifice to the ancestors and the others.

The suffix denoting the deity (*devatātaddhita*) is prescribed by the rule *devabhūta...* [Pāṇini 4.2.24], which states that "the deity of this [is such-and-such]. [Commentary: Regarding the term *devabhūta*: one should understand that the great sacrificial sessions (*mahāsattras*) to be shown in sequence belong to the deities (*deva*) and so forth. Those great sacrificial sessions are themselves the great sacrifices (*mahāmakhāḥ*), the great offerings (*mahāyajñāḥ*). The masculine designation is used with the intention of emphasizing the status of the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Thus, there are five sacrifices: the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), the sacrifice to the spirits (*bhūtayajña*), the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), and the sacrifice to men (*manuṣyayajña*). 2.

They explain those very five sacrifices as follows: "Teaching" (is the first). In the term *daiva-bhauma*, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is used in the sense of "for the sake of the deity. The rest is explained by the literal recitation of the words (*nigada-vyākhyātam*). As for the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛ-yajña*), it is "libation" (*tarpaṇa*); by the word *tarpaṇa*, the libation already mentioned in proximity is referred to. This is because, according to the established conclusion in the *Āgneyī-nyāya*, words denoting individuals refer to the individuals in immediate proximity; furthermore, it would be improper to disregard the previously mentioned libation and instead adopt a different, more remote libation. [End of section 3] Kamapradarśaḥ. [2nd Praśna]

3kha. Śrāddha, or the Pitṛyajña, or the bali offering established [on the ground], as well as the recitation of the Veda (*śrutijapa*)—that which is performed is called the Brahmayajña. (4) *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Śrāddha is obligatory. By this, since all three constitute the Pitṛyajña, even if they cannot be performed together, the transgression is avoided by the completion of the Pitṛyajña rite through the performance of even one of them. And so says Manu: "When the best of the twice-born, having bathed, satisfies the ancestors with water..."

"By that alone, they obtain the full fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña). However, when possible, the instruction regarding all three [the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahman] should be understood as a cumulative practice. Furthermore, that recitation of the *Ṛgveda* mentioned previously by the words "beginning with the Veda" is also called the *brahmayajña*. Previously, its designation was stated to be "brahmayajña"; that very same act is now being prescribed. By this, it is shown that there are two types of *brahmayajña*.

In this case as well, the alternatives (*vikalpa*) and the conjunctions (*samuccaya*) based on possibility and impossibility are to be understood as in the *pitṛyajña* (ancestral sacrifice). However, in the *Bhaṭṭabhāṣya*, it is stated that even study for the purpose of memorization is the *brahmayajña*, based on the following statement: "Whatever service and so forth one performs while studying under a teacher, all that shall be the *brahmayajña*; that is declared to be the highest austerity. [4] *Prabhā*: "Or the *śrāddha*" refers to the obligatory daily *śrāddha*. "The offering to the ancestors" (*pitrya bali*).

That which is this *balikarman* where an offering (*bali*) is given to the ancestors (*pitṛs*) may indeed be the *pitṛyajña*. Thus, for the followers of the *Chandoga* [Sāmaveda], the *pitṛyajña* prescribed by their own scripture is threefold: the *yācñā*, the *tarpaṇa*, and the *pitṛbali*. In this regard, at a certain stage, there is a prohibition against even one of these [at the time of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice] (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.5.3). And that [the *pitṛyajña*] should be performed either before the *tarpaṇa* or after the morning oblation (*prātarāhuti*). Or else, it is at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva*; it is not otherwise, because of the specific occasion (*nimitta*). — *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*.

The *brahmayajña* consisting of hearing and recitation (*śruti-japa*) should be performed prior to the *pitṛyajña*. For this very reason, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with barley and other materials is prescribed immediately after it. Alternatively, according to the rule "after the morning oblation," the *brahmayajña* known as teaching (*adhyāpana*) should be performed during the second division of the day divided into eight parts; thus says Dakṣa. Regarding the word "and" (*yaśca*): by performing [the former], the transgression [of the latter] is avoided; however, when possible, the performance of all [the rites] together through their combination should be understood. This is what is meant by "and."

By the phrase "beginning from the beginning of the Veda," that which was previously mentioned as *japa* is called the *brahmayajña*. Thus, for those who follow the *Chāndoga* [Sāmavedic] tradition, the *brahmayajña* is twofold according to the definitions of their own *śākhā*: namely, teaching (*adhyāpana*) and silent recitation (*japa*). However, in the *Bhaṭṭabhāṣya*, it is stated: "When one engaged in study under a teacher performs service and other duties, all of that constitutes the *brahmayajña*."

"that is said to be the supreme austerity. According to this statement, study under a guru, service to the guru at that time, and the other regulations for these [students] are established in the manner previously described; thus, this is called the *brahmayajña*. And that is easy (*alīka*). That *brahmayajña*, consisting of the study of the Vedas, is a lamp for the libation (*tarpaṇa*). From the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: "In the second part of the day, the practice of the Veda is prescribed. First, the acquisition of the Veda, then its reflection, its rehearsal, and its recitation (*japa*)."

"And that very [study] is the gift of the Vedas to disciples in five ways. Alternatively, at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* rite, the *brahmayajña* should be performed in the form of the recitation (*japa*) of the *vāmadevya* hymn. It should not be argued that because the recitation of the *vāmadevya* is a subsidiary part of a ritual (*karmāṅga*), it cannot possess the nature of the primary *brahmayajña*; for it is possible [for it to be both], just as in the case of the libations (*tarpaṇa*). For this very reason, even though curd, *khadira* wood, and so forth serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), they possess primacy by virtue of serving the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, Bhaṭṭa’s commentary states: "The recitation at the end of the *valī* offering, concluding with the singing of the *vāmadevya*, is the *brahmayajña*."

The particle *ca* (and) indicates an optional alternative (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). These [times] for the *brahmayajña* are optional, pertaining to distinct occasions: it should be performed at dawn, at midday, or at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. This was stated with emphasis so that it should not be performed on occasions other than these three specified times. However, the *brahmayajña* performed at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* must be done only after the *bali* offerings have been made, according to the injunction: "At the end of the *vaiśvadeva*, [one performs] the *bali*."

And this *brahmayajña* consists, according to some, in the singing of the *Vāmadevya* hymn; others say it consists in the recitation (*japa*) of the *Śruti*. These three times for the *brahmayajña* occur without fixed restriction. However, others—interpreting the word "or" (*vā*) as indicating a systematic arrangement—state that the recitation of the *Śruti* occurs before the libation (*tarpaṇa*), teaching occurs after the morning [libation], and the singing of the *Vāmadevya* occurs at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* offering.

They also cite the words of Dakṣa: "In the second [period], however, the study of the Vedas is prescribed as the *bhāga* (portion). This means that the Brahma-yajña must not be performed without these three conditions—time, place, and cause. Now, since the restriction is already established by the very mention of the time and place, the purpose of stating the further restriction "not elsewhere" (*nānyatra*) is as follows: *The Lamp of the Rituals* (*Karmapradīpa*). *The Elucidation of the Supplements* (*Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*). [End of] the meaning. Thus, without this triad of causes consisting of time, form, and occasion, the Brahma-yajña is not to be performed. And here, although the rule is established simply by the specification of the time and place, the intention behind the statement of the restriction "not elsewhere" is this:

Because the Brahmayajña is obligatory (*nitya*), and because time is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of it, and because an obligatory rite may be performed even by omitting some minor details, a doubt arises as to whether there is no fixed rule. However, since time functions as a specific qualification for the performer (*adhikāri-viśeṣaṇa*) by way of being a causal condition (*nimitta*), it differs from other subsidiary elements; and because one recognizes that there is no entitlement (*anadhikāra*) apart from that [time], it follows that the obligatory performance is necessitated. || 5 || [2.3] Commentary: "The composition of the Vedas, their prior investigation, their study, their recitation (*japa*), and their imparting to disciples—thus the study of the Veda is fivefold."

Thus [it is said]. Here, something remains to be stated. It was already stated at the very beginning that the *pitṛyajña* is indeed the *tarpaṇa*; therefore, it is the *tarpaṇa* itself that is understood here. Furthermore, regarding the rule that it should be performed prior to the *tarpaṇa*, there too, the inclusion is of that very *tarpaṇa* which constitutes the *pitṛyajña*. This is because of the statement of those who know the intent of the scriptures: "The reference to the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) is logical," and because of the maxim: "Cognition of what is proximate is internal (*antaraṅga*)," as well as the *āgneyī-nyāya*.

This should be understood in this way because of its consistency with the *brahmayajña* and other rites. Furthermore, that libation (*tarpaṇa*) which is of one kind—a primary rite in the form of a *pitṛyajña* to be performed immediately after the *brahmayajña*—has been described here; whereas in another text, a different kind of libation is stated to be a subsidiary part of the ritual bath (*snāna*), to be performed after the worship of the Sun (*sūryopasthāna*). Following that [in the latter], the recitation of the *gāyatrī* and the *brahmayajña* are prescribed.

In both cases, the primacy and the subsidiary status of the *tarpaṇa* (water libation) are to be understood from the context. Likewise, the *Khānasūtra-pariśiṣṭa* states: "The *tarpaṇa* should be performed immediately after the *āplavana* (immersion); thereafter, one should mutter the *Gāyatrī* and study the Veda according to one's ability. But if the *tarpaṇa* is performed before the *Gāyatrī* when the *āplavana* has been completed, the very act of bathing becomes futile. The *Prabhā*, a commentary on the *Karmapradīpa* [2.3], explains: "When the *āplavana* is finished, the *tarpaṇa* follows; then one should recite the *Gāyatrī* and perform Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) according to one's capacity. However, if one performs the *tarpaṇa* prior to the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* once the *āplavana* is complete, the bath itself is rendered useless."

Since it begins with "sadattra āplavane tu" and concludes with "snānameva vṛthā bhavet," it is established that the recitation of the Gāyatrī and the Brahma-yajña should follow immediately after the libation (tarpaṇa) which is an ancillary part of the bath. Therefore, the conclusion is that the libation as an ancillary of the bath is to be performed before the Brahma-yajña, whereas the primary libation in the form of the Pitṛ-yajña is to be performed after the Brahma-yajña.

Therefore, it should be understood that what was stated by the author of the *Tattva* (Nārāyaṇopādhyāya)—who failed to consider this distinction of subject matter—that for the Vājasaneyins, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) occurs after the Brahma-yajña, is inconsistent. Furthermore, it is improper to assume that the *Chandoga-pariśiṣṭa* refers to anything other than the Chāndogas. As for the other point stated by the author of the *Tattva*: "The libation as an ancillary to bathing (*snānāṅga-tarpaṇa*) is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the principal libation; therefore, even the latter must have the same time as the ancillary libation of bathing. [This is also incorrect.]

That too is incorrect; for it is untenable to conceive of a relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) between these [acts] as they have been described along with their accessories. Furthermore, since it is stated that "the [Brahmayajña] is to be performed after the libation (*tarpaṇa*)," it is untenable to postulate a different time by means of this injunction regarding time. We have examined all of this in detail in our commentary on the *Gṛhyasūtra*; it should be consulted there. For now, it has been stated that the Brahmayajña, consisting of the recitation of the Vedas (*śruti-japa*), is to be performed prior to the libation.

Furthermore, since the *brahmayajña*—consisting of the recitation of the Sāman hymns—is stated to occur after the *tarpaṇa* (libation) that is an ancillary part of the bath (*snāna*), one should also consider the relationship between which [act] and which [preceding rite]. *Karmapradīpa*: "Even if there is no other [guest], he should feed at least one Brahmin for the sake of accomplishing the *pitṛyajña*. This should be done without [invoking] the gods, whether [the food] has been cooked or even if it is uncooked. "Having set aside some food according to his ability and according to the rule, he should give it daily to the ancestors and to men, O twice-born! (6–7)

[2ma 3kha] 181 *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: He states what should be done when the three Brāhmaṇas are unavailable: "Even if only one Brāhmaṇa is available, in the absence of many, one should feed him without the *daiva* [portion], that is, devoid of the *vaiśvadeva* recitation, for the sake of accomplishing the satisfaction of the ancestors (*pitṛs*). However, one should not consider oneself to have fulfilled one's duty by merely performing the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and the offering of oblations (*bali*), thinking thus the *pitṛyajña* has been accomplished. And he (the guest) must be fed other than at the time of the *atithi* [reception]. Likewise, after the offering of the *bali*, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* says: 'Even if only one... [The text continues with *prabhā*].

If another Brāhmaṇa cannot be found, or if there is not enough food available to satisfy many Brāhmaṇas, then for the sake of the purpose of the Pitṛyajña—which is the satisfaction of the ancestors—one may feed even a single Brāhmaṇa. The meaning is that one should perform the obligatory rite (*nityavāha*) even with a single Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, that obligatory rite must be performed without the portion dedicated to the gods (*devapakṣarahita*).

By the phrase "for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the *pitṛyajña*," this is what is meant: one should not think that the *pitṛyajña* is accomplished solely by means of the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the ancestral offering (*pitṛ-bali*). Rather, when possible, one must certainly perform the *śrāddha* as well. The fulfillment of the *pitṛyajña* through those two [the libation and the offering] occurs only under certain circumstances. Regarding the term "having extracted" (*abhyuddhṛtya*): due to the non-availability of food or the insufficiency of clarified butter (*ājya*), if there is only a single lamp. *Pariśiṣṭa-prakāśa*.

"He should remain in the courtyard of his house for a period of exactly three *ghaṭikās* (twenty-four minutes) for the purpose of receiving a guest, or longer thereafter as he desires. A guest who has arrived there, the householder should honor with words of welcome and the like; he should regard that visitor with the thought that he is Hiraṇyagarbha. Following this, it is stated in the same work [2.3]: "O King, one should also invite another Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the *pitṛs*—one who is a fellow-countryman, whose conduct and birth are well-known, and who performs the five great sacrifices (*pāñcayajña*). The word "another" (*aparam*) refers to someone other than the guest.

Because the arrival and origin of a guest are unknown, and because there is no certainty regarding his purity (*śrāddhatva*) in the context of a *śrāddha* rite; for this very reason, Devala states in the section concerning guests: "One should not inquire about [the guest's] conduct, Vedic study, country, or birth; when a Brahmin has come as a beggar for food, one should give it without hesitation. Parāśara says: "One should indeed not inquire about conduct, Vedic study, or birth; one should simply cultivate a favorable disposition toward him when he has arrived of his own accord. Likewise, Yama says: "One should not announce one's country, self, family, learning, or wealth."

"He who has vomited [the food] among the duties pertaining to the sons of Vivasvat is called a *vāntāś*. *Prabhā*: Even with a friend who is a Brāhmaṇa, the performance of the *vājakaraṇa* rite is not possible; in that case, [the food] is like a lamp placed upon cooked food. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: However, if there is not even a single other person from that same region present as a recipient of the *śrāddha*, or if there is no food sufficient for the satisfaction of the Brāhmaṇas, then one should take a portion from the vessel and give it to a guest who is a twice-born man, such as Sanaka and others, for the sake of the ancestors and human beings.

The meaning is that one should use both hands. By this, the claim in the *Mahārṇava-prakāśa* that there is no daily offering (*nitya-vāī*) for humans is refuted. For this very reason, Kārṣṇājini [2.3] states: "One should offer food on a seat, but never in the hand; for in this way, the satisfaction of the ancestors, gods, and humans is scripturally established. And the *Brahma-purāṇa* says: "A daily offering to the ancestors is known to be performed by humans together with [the other classes]. Likewise, another *Gṛhya-sūtra* states:

One should feed the guest facing east, having dedicated him to one's beloved deity; this is for the sake of the human [guest]. Since it is a general rule that a Brāhmaṇa guest faces east while the sacrificer stands facing the Brāhmaṇas invited to the Śrāddha, his facing west is established by logic alone. Thus says the *Ṣaḍviṃśabrāhmaṇa* of the Sāmaveda: "This direction which is the west (pratīcī) belongs indeed to humans. Likewise, it is heard in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*: [text omitted].

The gods took the eastern quarter, the ancestors the southern, humans the western, and the Asuras the northern; according to others, humans took the northern. In the absence of [proper] sacrificial materials or when their procurement is impossible, one should give alms and so forth. By that also, the performance of the *pitṛyajña* (ancestral sacrifice) is accomplished. Thus says Śātātapa: "Having set aside even a little food according to one's ability, one should offer it to the ancestors, to humans, and to the divine beings such as Sanaka and others. [End of section].

Having said, "This for the ancestors," one should utter the word *svadhā*. For humans, one should utter *hantakāra*, and at the end of that, one should pour out water. *Parishṣṭaprakāśa*: "Whether it be alms (*bhikṣā*), or a *puṣkala*, or even a *hantakāra*, or if these are unavailable, one should always give a vessel of water. Alms consist of a single mouthful; a *puṣkala* is four times that. The wise know a *hantakāra* to be four *puṣkalas*."

And the Viṣṇu Purāṇa states: "One should give three portions of alms to a wandering mendicant (parivrāj) and a student (brahmacārin). And one may give according to one's desire, provided there is no obstacle. These are declared to be guests; and those who were previously mentioned as mendicants—one should honor these four, for by doing so one is released from the debt incurred by sacrifice. In the phrase "and one should give" (*dadyācca*), the particle *ca* serves to conjoin this with the feeding of the aforementioned guests. And that [giving] occurs when possible. However, in the case of impossibility, the mere giving of alms is sufficient, according to the statement of Śātātapa. (6)

7. Regarding the phrase "according to the rule," he states the rule previously mentioned: having said "This for the ancestors," one should give it daily to a Brāhmaṇa according to the rule, intending it for the ancestors. From this it is understood that there is also a daily offering (*nitya-vāda*) for Sanaka and others. And they record in the Smṛtis: "The daily offering should be divine; it is sung of together with [offerings to] humans. Thus ends the statement "according to the rule. He states that very rule: "For the ancestors," etc. At the end of that [is the *Karmapradīpa* / *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: ...].

When [the rite] concludes, one should utter the word *svadhā*. Having said, "This food for the humans," one should utter the word *hanta* at the end. At the conclusion of that, one should pour water for the purpose of disposal (*utsarga*). If it is a *brāhmaṇa* [rite], then because it is superseded by the specific requirements of the *pārvaṇa* [rite], the other [procedure] must be performed. Thus says the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "I shall now describe the daily [śrāddha], which is devoid of the invocation of the *arghya*; one should know that to be *adaiva* (without the gods); the *pārvaṇa* is remembered as being on the lunar festivals (*parvan*)."

Laghuhārīta states: "It should be perpetual, without [specific] deities, and devoid of the *argha* offering, the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), and so forth. This refers to the perpetual [Śrāddha] among the six types. For it is said in the statement: "A householder should feed even one Brahmin daily for all six; those six ancestors, being unsatisfied, consume him with their gaze. Likewise, regarding the daily Śrāddha subsequent to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, this same author has stated: "Accompanied by the *karpu* [rice-ball]," and so on. [Prabhā]: At the conclusion of the recitation of the mantra, one should offer water. This is the abandonment of the mantra.

*Nigada*: The rest has been explained. This very practice is generally considered a light, daily application (*nityāhāraprayoga*). *Kampradīpa* [2.3]: The sages have prescribed two meals for Brahmins dwelling in the mortal world as a constant rule: during the day and likewise at night, ending with the first watch (*prathamayāma*). *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Regarding that which was stated concerning the feeding of guests directed toward Sanaka and others—[it refers to] the sin incurred by men when a guest who has arrived during the day departs disappointed: [The verse continues: "Whatever sin belongs to men when a guest who has arrived during the day departs disappointed..."

"That same [food] becomes eightfold in merit when offered at sunset once the sun has turned away; for householders, a guest who arrives in the evening at the time of sunset must not stay in the house without eating, whether he arrived at the proper time or not. According to these two citations from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and the *Manusmṛti*, which prescribe that a guest should be fed even in the evening, [the offering] should be performed for the sake of humans such as Sanaka and others. But is it not so? "Morning and evening is the meal ordained by the gods for human beings. [Prabhā: No.

"In the rule for the Agnihotra, no meal should be taken in the interval. Since this statement by Bṛhan-Manu prescribes eating for humans both morning and evening, and since Sanaka and others are also human beings, they too must perform the *mānuṣa-vāha* (human offering) at night for the purpose of their meal. For this very reason, it is said: "A guest who has arrived at the proper time, or even at an improper time, should not remain in the house of householders without eating in the evening after sunset. There is an alternative reading: *sārdha-mahara-yāmāntaḥ*. Another reading is *muṃsām*.

The *Kampradīpa* and the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* state: "And in the fifth part of that [day], the distribution [of food] to the gods, ancestors, and men, as well as to those who have performed their duties, is prescribed"—according to this statement of Dakṣa, [the meal is taken] during only the fifth part of the day. Furthermore, from the statement of Bṛhan-Manu: "Eating in the evening and in the morning is the food ordained for humans by the gods; no eating should be done in between, for this is the rule equal to the *Agnihotra* sacrifice"—since the word "humans" (*manuṣya*) includes Sanaka and others, it is understood that the evening meal is indeed to be taken.

To dispel this doubt, he says: "That which was prescribed by the sages, such as Manu and others, for the twice-born to eat in the evening and morning... [2.3] ...the *Prabhā* commentary states: "Thus, Manu has also prescribed that guests should be fed in the evening; this implies that it should be performed with reference to Sanaka and the other [sages]. Anticipating this objection, he says, "by the sages. That which was prescribed as the daily meal for Brahmins by the sages, such as Manu and others, applies to those residing on earth (*bhūmivāsin*), and not to the celestial beings such as Sanaka and the rest.

By this it is stated that although the feeding of guests must necessarily be performed in the evening, it should not be performed with reference to Sanaka and the others. He states the time for eating: "In the night of *Tamaḥ-sandhyā*, within the first watch plus half a watch. This is one sentence. "In the night of *Tamaḥ-sandhyā*" means during the night. "The first watch together with the day" refers to the first *prahara* (watch) along with the day; "within that" means in the middle of that, and not even beyond it. And they [the authorities] remember: "When six *muhūrtas* have passed in the night, it is called *mahāniśā* (the great midnight)."

O Nārada, one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin by eating there; "sāīmaharayāmāntaram" means a period consisting of half a watch (prahara) plus a watch (yāma). [2nd Praśna, 3rd Khaṇḍa] The Vaiśvadeva rite and the offering of oblations (bali) must be performed both evening and morning; even if one is fasting, this must be done constantly, otherwise sin will arise. *Parīśiṣṭaprakāśa*: This refers to the Brahmins dwelling in the mortal world, not to the divine ones such as Sanaka and the rest.

By the second half of the verse, "and likewise during the day," it is stated that the words *sāyaṃ* (evening) and *prātaḥ* (morning) refer to night and day respectively. Furthermore, the fifth part of the day has already been declared as the time for eating. Regarding the night, however, he states the division of its parts: [it is] until the end of the first watch (*yāma*), not beyond that. This subsequent meaning is indeed explained by the words themselves; its essential purport, however, is this: because of the statement of Dakṣa, "and likewise in the fifth part," the meaning is exactly as follows. *Tathā*... *prabhā*. The meaning is precisely the same.

And in that context, since there is no reason to bypass the first [watch], the word *yāma* should be understood as referring to the first watch. Regarding the practice of eating by day (*divābhojana*), even though it is prescribed for the daytime in general, the specific time consisting of the latter half of the fifth watch is to be observed with particular care due to its excellence.

Although performing the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice at night is generally unpermitted, this was stated in order to dispel a further doubt: namely, that since it is directed toward Sanaka and others under the pretext of feeding guests (*atithi-bhojana*), and because the necessity of feeding guests at night has been mentioned, one might think it should be performed even for them. However, it remains established that [the *vaiśvadeva*] is not performed at night as a daily obligatory rite (*nitya*). "But in the evening and morning": even if one does not eat oneself, the *vaiśvadeva* and the *bali-offering* must be performed constantly in the evening and morning.

But if that is not performed, it occurs in the anus. As for the statement that cooking is possible only by means of firewood and so forth, it should be understood that this refers specifically to the evening [meal]. However, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is explained as follows; there is an alternative reading: *iti pāṭhāntaram*. *Karmapradīpa*, *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: "Having worshipped the gods, the sages, humans, the ancestors, and the deities of the quarters, the householder should then eat the remains. But that unwise man who eats before giving to these..."

"And while eating, he does not realize that his own food has been devoured by his household members" (Manu Smṛti 2.56). To dispel the doubt arising from this statement of Manu—that the Vaiśvadeva and Bali offerings must be performed only once by one who is eating—it is stated: "without fasting at morning and evening. Furthermore, the Viṣṇupurāṇa says: "O Lord of the Earth, having again prepared cooked food, even in the evening, one should offer the Bali for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva together with one's wife. Thus, [the offering] is repeated.

Because of the statement "having taken [the food] for cooking," it is designated as "evening. Therefore, when one's own eating is possible, [the offering is made] even without cooking; but when that is impossible, [it is made] only when cooking exists—namely at night for the Vaiśvadeva and Bali offerings, while during the day it is entirely forbidden. This has been stated by those who maintain its existence. That is inconsistent, because the meaning of "having taken" (*upādāya*) as "having prepared" (*kḷptvā*) must be described as something never heard before, and because there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for such a construction. Furthermore, in this construction where [one eats] without cooking when one's own eating is possible, again...

Regarding the phrase "having taken up cooking" (*pākam upādāya*): if one were to assume that even in the absence of one's own family members, cooking must still take place for the sake of guests and others, then the meaning of the word "constantly" (*satatam*) would not apply. Thus, under such an interpretation, both statements would be rendered meaningless. Therefore, the statement "having taken up cooking" should be explained as referring to the primary rule (*mukhyakalpa*), because this ensures consistency throughout. It is not intended for the purpose of excluding other alternatives, as that would result in the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

The *Karmapradīpa* on the Vaiśvadeva Bali offerings; the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. The distinction is that there is a twofold sin (*pratyavāya*) in its non-performance: one caused by the failure to produce the intended result, and one caused by the mere failure to perform the act itself. For this very reason, he says [in verse 10]: "Otherwise, indeed, there would be sin. [Prabhā, Pra. 3 Kha. Since cooking for that purpose is entirely justified as being for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*), when the primary method (*mukhyakalpa*) is impossible, the secondary method (*anukalpa*) certainly remains in force. And they say:

"One should offer the *bali* oblation for the evening meal at night. In reality, however, the meaning of the statement is that one should take the cooked food from the cooking and offer the *bali* again even in the evening; this is because the connection with the principal action (*pradhānakriyā*) is more significant. By this very logic, they [the grammarians] have also accepted the connection as "one should not look at the moon when it has risen on the fourth day" (*caturthyām udita-candre na īkṣitavyaḥ*), rather than "on the fourth day, the moon should not be looked at" (*caturthyām na īkṣitavyaḥ*). Or else:

The statement from the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, "Having prepared the cooked food even in the evening for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva," must be accepted even by one who desires its literal meaning; otherwise, since the phrase "for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva" could not be construed with anything else, it would result in meaninglessness. Therefore, the interpretation of those who claim to know the truth—that there is a clear injunction for cooking specifically for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva—is in every way untenable.

Because of the mention that "this is for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva," and because the offering of the *bali* is prescribed immediately after the Vaiśvadeva, it is implied that the Vaiśvadeva itself must also be performed in the evening. Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa-pādhyāya has stated that by not performing it, two types of transgressions arise—one caused by non-performance and one caused by eating; however, for one who does not eat, there is no transgression from non-performance. Let this suffice; what need is there for further detail? [From] the *Karmapradīpa*: "The offering of the *bali* is ordained with the words, 'Omniscience (Amogha), obeisance to you.'"

A salutation is performed for the purpose of offering the *bali* sacrifice. [25. śkhaḥ] *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: By the sūtra beginning with "That which he places first becomes the *bali* for Pṛthivī; then that which is offered in the intermediate space is for Vāyu; that which is third is for the Viśvedevas," etc., the offering of the *bali* to each respective deity has been stated. He states the mantra for this: by the word "amuṣmai" (to such-and-such), there is the inclusion of Pṛthivī and the others. Therefore, [the formula is]: "Salutation to Pṛthivī. *Prabhā*.

By the statement beginning with "That which he places first becomes the *bali* for the Earth," the deities of the *bali* offerings are declared by Āpastamba, and the substances for the *bali* are specified; therefore, he says "to such-and-such" and so forth. The offering of the *bali* is performed in the manner of "Salutation to such-and-such. He states the reason for performing the *bali* offering with a salutation in the words "because of the offering of the *bali*. The term "offering" (*dāna*) here refers to that which is being given, as it denotes the state of being presented.

And thus, since a salutation was performed for the purpose of offering the oblation (*bali*) being given, the collective meaning is that the offering of the oblation is made in this manner: "Salutation to such-and-such. The authors of the *Tattva* explain that "offering" (*pradāna*) means that by which [the oblation] is given, namely, the mantra. Regarding the reading "for the sake of the authoritative source" (*pramāṇārtham*), the teacher Nārāyaṇa holds that the word "authoritative source" (*pramāṇa*) refers to the mantra. In that context, "to such-and-such" (*amuṣmai*) is the designation of the deity; and so they record in their tradition.

"For whatever form that word is seen in a mantra, one should fix that form—the name of the object to be accomplished (sādhya)—in that place. — *Karmapradīpa*. *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*: Thus, the application of the mantra consisting of two words beginning with "namo brahmaṇe" is stated. [2nd Praśna, Khaṇḍa]. Here, in the phrase "ity evam," the word *iti* refers back to the two previously mentioned words; *evam* indicates the sequence.

And thus, the offering-mantras (balimantra) such as "Obeisance to Earth" (*namaḥ pṛthivyai*) are established; for words expressing the purpose of the offering, such as *svadhākāra* and others, are seen to occur generally at the end [of the mantra]. This is how it should be understood, because [the author] will later state: "One should offer with the *svadhākāra*," and so forth. Furthermore, in this context, there are mantras of salutation such as "Obeisance to Earth" (*namaḥ pṛthivyai*), but they do not end with those [terms like *svadhā*]. This is because we see it likewise in the modification of the *vāstubali* offering: "Obeisance to Brahman" (*namo brahmaṇe*).

Furthermore, since the distribution of shares in the archetype (*prakṛti*) is observed even through modified injunctions (*vaikṛta-vacana*), such as "they diminish the portions" (*ardhin ṛcayanti*) and so forth, the phrase "reverence to such-and-such" (*amuṣmai namaḥ*) does not intend to prescribe a specific order; rather, having stated both "reverence to such-and-such," it enjoins the offering of the oblation (*balidāna*). Otherwise, it would contradict the injunctions of the *Pariśiṣṭa-sūtra*. Thus says the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. We, however, observe that because the word "offering of the oblation" (*balidānam*) itself expresses the sequence, there is no occasion at all for postulating a sequence based on modified [texts].

For where something is not prescribed in the *prakṛti* (archetype), it is only there that one may postulate what is observed in the *vikṛti* (ectype). But here, since a specific [rule] is taught in the *prakṛti*, the *bhākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) is already satisfied; what occasion, then, is there for a postulation based on what is observed in the *vikṛti*? Nor is there a contradiction with the remaining [texts]. Since the remaining [text] concerns the *prākṛta-bali* (archetypal offering) and the Sūtra concerns the *vaikṛta-bali* (ectypal offering), there is no room for the suspicion of contradiction. Furthermore, the author of the *Pariśiṣṭa* himself [states] regarding those [rules] which are unclear... [text fragment].

Thus, the application of the mantra consisting of the two words "Kammapradīpaḥ" and "Pariśiṣṭaprakāśaḥ" has been stated. Regarding the phrase "namo brahmaṇe" [2.3.182], the commentary says: "iti. Here, "iti" refers back to the previously mentioned pair of words. "Evam" (thus) indicates the sequence. And in this way, the *bali*-mantra is established in the form "pṛthivyai namaḥ," and so forth.

Since the use of words intended for offering, such as *svadhākāra* and others, is generally observed at the very end of the ritual application, it should be understood in this way. For this very reason, [the author] will later state: "One should offer with the *svadhākāra*" and so forth. Furthermore, in this context, the mantra beginning with "Obeisance to the Earth" (*namaḥ pṛthivyai*) is one that begins with an obeisance (*namaskāra*), but it does not end with it; for we see such a form in the modified version (*vikṛti*) of the *vāstūbalī* offering, namely "Obeisance to Brahman" (*namo brahmaṇe*). Moreover, even by the statement regarding the modified version, such as "They satisfy [the deities] with half," we observe that the distribution of portions is established in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*).

The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* states: "The phrase 'namo 'muṣmai' is not intended to prescribe a specific order; rather, having uttered both 'namo 'muṣmai' and 'amuṣmai namaḥ', one performs the offering of the oblation (*balidāna*). Otherwise, there would be the fault of contradicting the injunctions of the *Pariśiṣṭa-sūtra*."

"Let us, however, observe this: since the sequence has been stated by the very term 'balidāna' (the offering of oblations), there is no occasion at all for the assumption of a sequence seen in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). For when something is taught in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is only then that one may postulate what is seen in the modification. But here, because a specific [sequence] is taught in the archetype, the requirement is satisfied right there; so what room is there for the assumption of what is observed in the modification? Nor is there any remaining contradiction."

Because the *Pariśiṣṭa* concerns the *prākṛta* oblation (*balis*), while the *Sūtra* concerns the *vaikṛta* oblation, there is no occasion for [the former] to contradict [the latter]. This second fascicle of the *Karmapradīpa* is a continuation of the first (double) fascicle, which was published in 1909 (as No. 1204) under the editorship and with the commentary of Mahāmahopādhyāya Candrakānta Tarkālaṅkāra. Following the lamented death of this first editor, further progress on the work was suspended for several years; it has now been resumed by the present [editor].

Editor: This second fascicle runs on without a break from the first double page, continuing from p. 192; however, to mark the change in editorship as well as the authorship of the commentary, a new page numbering has been commenced.

This has necessitated the repetition of the title of the work as a heading for this second fascicle, in order to enable possessors of the book to bind the two parts of the commentary—edited by two different editors—either separately or together, as they prefer.

Librarians should note that the new Editor, in accordance with traditional Indian custom, has headed his work with an invocation; this does not form part of the work itself, nor does it indicate that the work is new, but merely serves as an auspicious beginning for the occasion of his undertaking its continuation.

This invocation should have been separated from the following text by a line; furthermore, the first words of both the continued text and the commentary are indented when they should not be, and it so happens that the first letter of the first word of the commentary is a misprint and should be *oṃ* instead of *ā*.

Thus, it is called the "Remaining Portion of the Commentary" (*prabhāśeṣa*).

In the *Bhūmikā* of this work, the refutation of that [opposing] system—which was previously composed as a "blemish" (*kalaṅkāra*) by means of the *Parimilaprakāśavivaraṇa*—is established through the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*, which defends the established tenets (*siddhānta*). Specifically, after first removing the objections shown in the *Prakāśa*, the [author's] own position is determined regarding the sections on *Māyā*; furthermore, the removal of even those objections displayed in the *Prabhā* concerning the earlier section will be elucidated in the *Prakāśa*.

For this very reason, the second half of the verse, "since the salutation has been performed," is appropriately established. In that context, the word *namaḥ* becomes syntactically complete (*nirākāṅkṣa*) only when employed in conjunction with a word ending in the dative case; therefore, the author has included the word "to him" (*amuṣmai*), not for the purpose of indicating that the prior employment of a dative-ending word was necessary.

Thus, the determination of whether the word *namaḥ* (salutation) should be placed before or after [the name] is made precisely according to the modified (*vikṛta*) injunction. This is the underlying idea: the venerable Tarkālaṅkāra also agrees that the statement "for salutation is an act" (*namaskāraḥ kṛtyataḥ*) is intended to mean that since the word *namaḥ* is employed by the author of the Sūtras in the modified rite of offering oblations (*balidāna*), the word *namaḥ* must likewise be employed in the archetypal (*prakṛti*) rite as well.

And thus, since the rule regarding the application of the word *namaḥ* is being established by means of a statement concerning the *vaikṛta* (modified) form, it follows that its prior usage is appropriate there as well; therefore, this provides no room for the arguments of the great scholar Tarkālaṅkāra, who offered both elucidations and refutations. To indicate this, he explains the phrase "namaskāraṃ kṛtvā yataḥ" by completing it with "vāstuvale" and so forth. The word "vāstuvale" [is used] because the word "vikṛtau" (in the modified form) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Regarding the mantra for the *balis* (offerings), it says: "To Earth, to Vāyu, to the Viśvedevas, to Prajāpati. In this context, there arises a doubt: should the mantra be understood according to the principle of supplying missing words (*adhyāhāra*) based on the injunction for cutting the branch—just as one supplies the word *vinadmi* [in the case of the *vinaḍi* offering]—or should the status of being a mantra belong only to that which contains the word *namaḥ*? In this matter, just as in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*) the status of being a mantra belongs to that which contains the word *namaḥ*, so too in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) it is appropriate that the status of being a mantra belongs only to that which contains the word *namaḥ*. Therefore, the mantra in question does not consist of [the word] *svāhā* and so forth; rather, it is as follows: [The mantra is: "To Earth, to Vāyu, to the Viśvedevas, to Prajāpati, *namaḥ*. Thus, by the rule of the model sacrifice, the mantra is established as containing the word *namaḥ*. Just as in the determination [of the mantra] beginning with "namaḥ śaśabdaghaṭitatvam," even in the case of the determination following the *vikṛti* (modification), it is indeed appropriate that it follows the *vikṛti*. This refers to the second method of disposal.

In this regard, although Gṛhyapariśiṣṭakāra Gārgya has mentioned the offerings to the deities of the directions (digbalis) as being constant (nitya), but has not mentioned the three offerings to Indra and the others after the offering to the ancestors (pitṛbali), nevertheless, in the Vāstuyajña, the giving of ten offerings to Indra and the other deities in the ten directions is established by the text: "To the East, to Ūrjā, and to the Waters, [offerings] day after day, constantly. For in that case, the following reasons support the combination (samuccaya): 1. the establishment of the difference [of the ritual] through one's own scripture; 2. the contradiction with the statement in the Prājāpatya section which mentions the priority of the eastern direction in all cases; 3. [and so forth].

1. "Or rather, that which is prescribed for one's own specific [branch] is the rite to be performed"—this is the rule from the *Pariśiṣṭa*; 2. because all [Vedic] branches are subordinate to the primary [sacrifice], there is no reason for a restrictive conclusion; 3. because the unity of the rite is maintained despite the difference in deities; and 4. because the sequence of "first" and "later" is established by the very enumeration in the passage, "The offering to Prajāpati comes first, and that to Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt comes later"—thus six arguments have been stated. Among these, the first argument has already been refuted.

The priority mentioned for the *prājāpatya* offering relative to the *viṣṭakṛt* does not mean that some other *brahmaṇ* rite must be performed before it. By the sūtra beginning with "prayogaḥ," it is stated that those offerings dedicated to Indra, Brahmā, and Vāsuki, which are mentioned among the ten *bali* offerings in the *vāstu-karman*, should be given daily within the sequence of the regular *bali* offerings.

Then, according to the sequence of the domestic rites (*gṛhyāntar-krama*), after the *manyu-bali*, offerings (*bali*) dedicated to Indra, Vāsuki, and Brahmā should be given; these constitute the *rakṣaḥ-pitṛ-bali*. The *homa* and *bali* rituals do not apply to general optional (*kāmya*) rites. First, there are the specific obligatory (*nitya*) *homa* and *bali* rituals. The *bali* ritual is of two kinds: optional, such as the *śrābhāsya* and others, and obligatory, consisting of the fourteen-fold rites beginning with the *pārthiva*. Thus, the *prājāpatya* [bali] and those of the form of the *viṣṭakṛt* and so forth are obligatory, while the optional is [the other].

In the section concerning optional rites (*kāmyādhikāra*), it is heard in the *Āpastamba-Śrautasūtra*: "One should offer the first portion of the cooked food into the fire with the verse 'agne vivasvad uṣasaḥ'; one should present the *bali* offering with the preceding [verse]. Thus one becomes possessed of many cattle, wealth, and grain. Likewise, since this sūtra is capable of preventing [the offering] when specifically prescribed, it ought to be capable of prohibiting the offering to Agni, Dhanañjaya, and others as well. Or, let it be that it is indeed capable of prohibiting them.

Even so, since the aforementioned *Urusūtra* pertains to the ritual application for those who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), and since the *Gautama-kalpa* pertains to those who do not maintain the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), it is not possible for this [latter] to exclude the possibility of combination; thus, there is no occasion for the second reason. By this, the sixth reason is also explained. For, given the principle that all *śākhās* are authoritative, there is no dispute that the description of the non-application of one *Gṛhya-sūtra* in another *Gṛhya-sūtra* is based solely on specific intention (*tātparya*).

In this regard, although there exists for them the statement, "Whether much or little, one's own portion," nevertheless, according to the *Tantraka-rma-pradīpa*, the *bali* rite is restricted to specific branches (*śākhā*) and is of the nature of a general dharma found in the *Saṃhitās* and *Purāṇas*. Thus it is said: "First to Agni, and then to all of them together," and so forth. And the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa* states: "The gods, humans, animals, birds... and so on.

In that regard, when the *hema-bali* rite prescribed for a specific desire (*kāmya*) has been enjoined, it should not be performed before the *hema-bali* rite prescribed as a regular obligatory duty (*nitya*). One may perform it at the end, but never in the middle; for while one ritual action is being extended, another ritual action cannot be undertaken.

1) Since the *Vārtika*, the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*, and other works establish that [the rule] has as its scope those who are incapable, and since for the incapable there is no efficacy in performing specific auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) of obligatory rites (*nitya*), this third argument also does not succeed in its intention to refute the combination [of the two fires]. By this, the fourth argument is also explained. For here, what is intended is the prescription of an alternative performance for one who is not an *āhitāgni* (one who has not maintained the sacred fires), and no prescription of a performance combined with that [fire] is observed.

This is not a fault, because [the performance] of the five [offerings] is prescribed. Since we observe the combination (*samuccaya*) even of distinct principal rites such as the Āgneya, the Agniṣomīya, and the Upāṃśuyāja, it follows that the distinction between rites is not the cause for their non-combination; thus it is said, "it is pure" (*śuddham iti*). For they too have stated: "That which must be performed by one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*)... And Kātyāyana also says: "The Agnyādi [rite], according to Gautama, and the Śākala [rite]. (1) They may optionally occur at the end (kha). This is the exposition of the ritual action (*karmapradaṣaḥ*).

However, when a general optional rite (*sāmānyakāmya*) is to be performed that is distinct from those specifically prescribed for obligatory rites (*nityaviśeṣavihita*), it must never be performed in between them. He states the reason for this: "Not in a single ritual" (*naikasmin karmaṇi*). This is self-evident from the wording itself. For this very reason, the sequence ending with "and the offering to the left of the Kāmya" (*balim cottareṇa*) as stated in the Śruti—"always for one who has eaten and drunk"—is established. By the term "optional" (*kāmya*), it is understood that while there is no necessity here for the general optional rite, there is nevertheless no transgression (*pratyavāya*) in performing it, though there may be merit in doing so.

For this very reason, another *Gṛhyasūtra* states: "One may carry away the offerings for optional rites (*kāmya*) oneself; [the householder] should dwell in a stone-house. In case of illness or while traveling abroad, that house-offering (*tadgṛhabali*) shall not take place. By writing this, [the author] indicates that [the rule] concerning the maintenance of the sacred fires (*agnyādihoma*) pertains to those who have not established the fires (*anāhitāgni*). Thus, it is well known that for those who follow other authorities, there is no possibility of combining [these rites] elsewhere. Keeping all this in mind, he says: "By the word 'optional' (*kāmya*), etc. [and] "of the optional" (*kāmyasya*).

Although in the *Māṭṛkā* the reading appears as "there is no necessity for general optional rites" (*sāmānyakāmyānām anāvaśyakatā*), nevertheless—precisely because another *Gṛhya* text states, "He himself should carry away the optional offerings (*kāmyān balīn*) as long as he dwells in the house"—and because that statement regarding the mere object of desire is intended for the sake of one's own purpose (*svārthapratipādanārthaṃ*), and because there is no indication that the word "optional" (*kāmya*) implies the non-necessity of the general [rites], the reading "of the optional" (*kāmyasya*) alone appears to be appropriate here. [This refers to] what was stated beginning with "the fire-altar and so forth."

And here, according to the *Karmapradīpa*, there are alternative readings: "the *brahman* accompanied by the *maujavali*," "the *brahman* of the *Śākala* school accompanied by the *paurāṇabali*," and "the *brahman* accompanied by all the *balis*. It says: "The *brahman* beginning with the fire-offering and the *śākala* [recitation] are appropriate for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) along with these *balis*."

The *brahma* for the deities beginning with Agni has been stated by the *grantha*: "Agni, Indra, Dhanvantari, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati, and Sviṣṭakṛt. Furthermore, the *bali* offerings for the deities of the directions have been stated as "to each according to their own [deity]. And that which was stated by the author of the Āśvalāyana Sūtra—"They should throw eight wood-chips (*śakala*) into the Āhavanīya fire with the mantras beginning 'This [is for] the sin committed against the gods' (*devakṛtasyainasaḥ')"—refers to the throwing of the eight wood-chips of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) using the mantras beginning with "devakṛtasya," and this applies only to one who has maintained the sacred fires (*sāgnihotrin*).

Thus, in the *Praṇavapariśiṣṭa*, two alternatives appear: "this" (*iyam*). The distinction is that the first alternative is the opinion of Raghunandana and others, while the second is the opinion of Tarkālaṅkāra, Bhūtapīḍita, Ākārādi, and others. Regarding this, since the particle *ca* in the phrase "and thus" (*eva ca*) is well-known to signify conjunction (*samuccaya*), he explains it with the intention that the third alternative alone is logical: "Agni and so forth," [having previously offered food with the *Vyāhṛtis* and with the *Śākala* mantras].

"Having given the *bali* offering to the spirits (*bhūta*), one who maintains no sacred fire (*anagnika*) should eat that [remnant]. And: "But the Brahmin who maintains no sacred fire, having himself offered [the food] with the *vyāhṛti* mantras and the *śakala-homas*, should take the *bhūta-bali* from what remains. Even in these statements found in the *Agnipurāṇa*, the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* of Yājñavalkya, and other sources, the combination of the *brahma-bali* itself with the [other offerings] is explicitly stated. By the phrase "having offered with the *vyāhṛtis*," the inclusion of the primary *brahma-bali* is also effectively established.

As for what the venerable Tarkālaṅkāra has established—that because these Smṛtis refer to another Kalpa, the mention of the Śākala [branch] alone is merely illustrative—where in any Kalpa is such a thing found? For it is stated in the *Kālakarmapradīpa*: "Having offered food with the *Vyāhṛti* mantras and likewise with the Śākala mantras, and having given the *bali* offering to the elements, one who does not maintain a sacred fire should eat that. (46) Similarly, it is said in the *Agni Purāṇa*: "First, having offered food with the *Vyāhṛti*s," and so forth.

Regarding the statement in the *Gṛhyabhāṣya*, "For one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), there is an offering to Prajāpati first and to Sviṣṭakṛt afterwards," this refers merely to these two oblations at the fourteenth *bali* offering; it does not refer to the *bali* offerings for deities such as Gautama and others. Since that [latter] is intended to be expressed elsewhere, it is simply out of place here.

And thus, since the combination of the Kauthumas and all others is indeed intended even for one residing in the heart, it is precisely with this intention that the authors of the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* have rightly explained the term "Kauthuma" and so forth as an option (*vikalpa*). [Regarding the mention of] "Āśvalāyana": by this, the view that "one following the internal differences between Gṛhya and Śrauta texts need not follow [this rule]" is refuted. And as it says here in the *Śākala-grantha*: "With the mantra 'Of the sixfold work of the gods,' etc., according to the sequence..."

In such statements from the Vyāsa-skānda Purāṇas as, "Having worshipped Vaiśvānara with offerings of flowers and unbroken rice (akṣata) accompanied by clarified butter," there is an option (vikalpa) regarding the number [of oblations] being six or twelve; and in that regard, there is an extensive discussion elsewhere concerning the systematic arrangement (vyavasthā), similar to that of Brahmā and others. In this context, the opinion of Sāyaṇa and others is that the *svāhākāra* does not exist in the Śākala recension.

And on this point, the authority is the *Drāhyāyaṇa-sūtra*: "They should offer eight fallen portions of the *gā* [grains] into the *Āhavanīya* fire with mantras beginning with 'devakṛtasya' and ending in the vowel *i*. For here, by the statement "one should offer with those ending in *i*," it is understood that the utterance of *svāhā* is not required for this ritual act. Then, having touched water and looking at the fire with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one should pray to Draviṇodas before the recitation of the *Vāmadevya*.

"One should seek wealth from the consumer of beings," according to the Śruti; thus, one should beg for food from Agni. "And [one should seek] the end of suffering from Nirṛti. The remainder is explained by the words themselves. To the question of what one should beg for and with which mantra, he says: "Longevity, nobility, sovereignty, fortitude, truth, strength, fame, splendor, luster, cattle, seed, the Veda, and indeed Brahminhood."

For where the *svāhākāra* is explicitly mentioned at the end of a mantra, its use is mandatory; however, in this case, there is no such *svāhākāra*, as it is not employed without the recitation of the mantra. The sense is that, just as there is no use of the word *svāhā* when the *prastara* grass-bundle is offered by the *kravāka* priest, so it is here. By this, it is indicated—as established in the *Tarkālaṅkāra* commentary on the *Gṛhyasūtra* and the *Bhāṣya*—that because of the rule regarding the *svāhākāra* at the end of a mantra, the *svāhākāra* is indeed required even in other instances. [The word] "food" (*anna*) [is used].

Regarding this, concerning the description of the *bali* offerings for the *jhaṣka*, *śākala*, *hmadī*, and others, a doubt arises as to whether those *balis* are indeed those prescribed by Jaimini or rather those by Gautama. In the commentary on the *Gṛhyasūtra*, Tarkālaṅkāra Mahābhaya explains: "The *balis* belong to Jaimini even for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*); here, [the rule] of Gautama is not mentioned. Thus, in the *balis* of the *hmadī* and others, the specific mention of "by Gautama" is understood, by which their inclusion alone would follow.

"In company with the *balis*": regarding that which describes the association with the *balis*, there [in verse 2.44] is the *karmapradīpa*. "O Draviṇodās, the witness of all, ordain for us all this: good fortune (*saubhāgya*), success in action (*karmasiddhi*), preeminence in one's lineage (*kulajyaiṣṭhya*), and agency over one's own deeds (*svakartṛtā*). Fame (*yaśas*) is renown; splendor (*tejas*) is firmness; luster (*varcas*) is the radiance of the body; seed (*bīja*) is grain and so forth, or a specific type of sowing; the Veda (*brahma*) is the sacred knowledge; and Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*) is the performance of the duties of a Brahmin, specifically the state of being an unimpeded agent."

Thus ends the section on the Vaiśvadeva. By specifying the particular rule of Gautama, there is an implication—due to proximity—that only those *bali* offerings mentioned by him are to be understood; therefore, the *bali* offerings prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtras* do not pertain to one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). However, the authors of the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* distinguish that those *bali* offerings mentioned in the *Gṛhyasūtras* pertain exclusively to one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), as indicated by the phrase "and of the one who has maintained the fires" (*āhitāgneśca*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves this purpose. "Having touched water and looking at the fire" means: after that, following the optional *baliharaṇa* offerings.

Regarding the question of whether [the Vaiśvadeva] is for the purpose of consecrating the *vaiśvadeva* offerings or for the purpose of producing an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), the great scholar Tarkālaṅkāra has extensively established its status as being for the sake of an unseen merit in his commentary on Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra. Thus, it has already been determined—by means such as the natural force of the words—that this is not a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remnants of the sacrificial oblation (*haviḥ-śeṣa*). Having extracted that point, everything is faultless. Thus ends the section on the Vaiśvadeva. [From] *Karmapradīpa*: Now begins the section on the Brahmayajña.

There is no sacrifice superior to the *brahmayajña*, nor is there a gift greater than its bestowal. All sacrifices and all gifts are finite; the end of this [sacrifice] has never been seen by anyone. (18) There is no sacrifice more excellent than the *brahmayajña* in the form of silent recitation (*japa*). There is no gift more excellent than the "gift of Brahman" (*brahmadāna*) in the form of teaching. He states the reason: "All sacrifices and all gifts are perishable," meaning they possess fruits such as heaven that are subject to destruction.

The meaning is that there is no destruction whatsoever of *dharma* consisting of the gift of the Veda (*brahmadāna*) and recitation (*japa*). Here too, its indestructibility is due to the fact that its fruit is imperishable. And so says Manu: "Attaining equality with [the gods]" (*sārṣṭitām iti*). Likewise: "Brahma—[meaning] from the *brahmayajña*, which consists of recitation. Although the term *brahmayajña* refers specifically to the gift of the Veda based on such statements as "Teaching is the *brahmayajña*," nevertheless, by secondary usage (*gauṇī vṛtti*), the word *brahmayajña* applies even to recitation.

As it has been said: "One should recite the Veda daily, beginning from the very start; that recitation of the Śruti which is performed with focused attention is called the *brahmayajña*. And in the *Bhaṭṭabhāṣya*: "When one performs study and carries out service and so forth while engaged in [Vedic] recitation, all of that constitutes the *brahmayajña*; that is declared to be the supreme austerity. Thus, it is described that even formal study in the presence of a teacher is the *brahmayajña*.

Likewise, the *Pariśiṣṭakamapradīpa* states: "Teaching is the primary *brahmayajña*; the other is secondary. "One should constantly recite the Veda at the proper times without sloth; for they call that his supreme duty (*dharma*), while others are said to be subordinate. By constant study of the Vedas, by giving gifts, by austerity alone, and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth. Remembering one's former birth, a person attains Brahman itself."

He states another result that arises from the constant practice of the *brahma* [the Veda]: "By reciting the *ṛc*s, one should satisfy the gods with streams of honey and milk; by reciting the *yajus* at all times, one satisfies them with streams of ghee. Here, *kulyā* means a small stream, and *nadī* means a river; this verse is indeed a praise. This is the intention of the author of the *Prakāśa*. As he will state in the conclusion: "Therefore, among the great sacrifices consisting of study, the primary one is teaching; in its absence, there is silent recitation (*japa*)."

The sense here is that, because the primary qualified persons (*mukhyādhikārin*) are not available, the injunction for the secondary (*gauṇa*) [qualified person] is performed first. Regarding this, the times for the *brahmayajña* are understood from the statement of Kātyāyana: "It should be performed after the *tarpaṇa* until the sun sets, or after [the *tarpaṇa*] until morning, or at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva*; it is not otherwise except when there is a specific occasion (*nimitta*)."

In this regard, if the performance of the *brahmayajña* were intended to take place prior to the *tarpaṇa*, then the three [prescribed] times would not be established. Furthermore, the use of the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "either after [the *svādhyāya*] or at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva*" would be contradicted. Therefore, for the sake of establishing the second and subsequent times, the following arrangement is made by Kātyāyana: (1) among the *Yajus* mantras, one should recite them; (2) [this constitutes] the *karmayajña*; and (3) the basis for the praise is the attainment of satisfaction resulting from the drinking of honey and milk. The same should be stated for the subsequent [mantras] as well.

The rest is easy to understand. While reciting the *Sāmaveda*, he satisfies [the ancestors] daily with streams of honey and clarified butter; and while reciting the *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ*, he does so even with streams of fat. Here too, as in the case of the sacrifice, the support for the praise consists of abundant streams of various kinds of sacrificial animals. "The *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ*" means the *Atharvaveda*. The plural number is used because it is composed of many sentences. While reciting, he should satisfy them with streams of meat, boiled rice, and honey.

Every day, one should recite the Vākyas, the Purāṇas, and the Itihāsas as approved by the Yoga tradition—for instance, that the Brahmayajña should be performed either before the libations (tarpaṇa), or if it is performed after the libations, then it should be done either before the morning meal or at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite.

And thus, regarding the two views stated by Kātyāyana—"the Brahma-yajña is prior to the libation (tarpaṇa)" and "the Brahma-yajña is after the libation"—it is appropriate to respect only the second view, which is favored [by the author]. Consequently, the statement "and that [Brahma-yajña] is before" (sa ca arvāk) made by the author of the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* cannot be restricted to subjects other than the Vedas (*chandaḥ*). Furthermore, this term "libation" (*tarpaṇa*) refers to libation in general, and not exclusively to the libation for the ancestors (*pitṛ-tarpaṇa*).

For instance, in such cases as "One should give the sacrificial fee to the descendant of Atri" and "One should chant the hymn having placed the fire nearby," there is no restriction to only those [acts] under discussion; rather, in the first case, it may refer to either what is under discussion or what is not, while in the second case, it refers only to what is not under discussion. This is because syntactical connection (*vākya*) is subordinated to context (*prakaraṇa*), and where there is a need for that [context], it prevails. For example: "The *Karmapradīpa*. Syntactical connection (*vākya*) is a specific portion of the Upaniṣads consisting of questions and answers; history (*itihāsa*) includes the *Mahābhārata* and similar works.

And thus Devala says: "Itihāsas are those whose subject matter consists of ancient events concerning sages (ṛṣis), and which have conduct as their fruit. "Reciting daily any one of these, beginning with the Ṛgveda, according to one's ability, one shall satisfy even one's ancestors with streams of honey and clarified butter. This means that not only does one traverse a good path, but by reciting any single one among these works—from the Ṛgveda down to the Itihāsas—as much as one is able, one causes even one's ancestors to be satisfied with streams of honey and clarified butter. The basis for this praise is also to be understood as before.

"Being satisfied themselves, they satisfy him, both while he is living and even after he has died; and he becomes one who moves at will among all the abodes of the gods. [This is seen] in passages such as "he approaches the palace with a mind free from envy. Nor is there here a relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin) elements, so that this [passage] would not depend on the context; therefore, it is appropriate here to understand the statement as referring to the general act of libation (tarpaṇa). And thus, even if the Brahma-yajña is performed before the libation for the names, the libation for the ancestors must still be performed at its own proper time.

In this very same way, the practice of certain learned followers of the Yajurveda also exists; for they perform the *brahmayajña* after the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), and then perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) after the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. Thus, it is established that the statement from the *Karmapradīpa*, "Teaching is the *brahmayajña*, while the libation is the *pitṛyajña*," follows precisely the portion of the injunction beginning with "after the morning oblation."

By this, it is indicated that the statement in the *Gabhilabhāṣya*—namely, that "this libation (*tarpaṇa*) is intended solely for the libation of the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) because of the context, just as in the case of 'the Āgneyī brick' and so forth, which refers to what is under discussion"—is to be considered doubtful. [End of section] 46. [This is from] the *Karmapradīpa*. These gods and ancestors satisfy him; they gratify this living person, or one who is deceased, by accomplishing his welfare in this world and the next. The rest is easy to understand. Even though heavy, he does not touch impurity, and he purifies it.

Whichever ritual (*ṛtu*) one recites, one becomes the partaker of its fruit. It is not merely that there is the attainment of prosperity; even sins such as the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*) do not affect him, for by means of *japa* (recitation), sin is destroyed—this is the meaning. [The text] says he "becomes purifying" (*pāvana*) at the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*); likewise, by reciting the portion of the Veda that prescribes rituals such as the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), one obtains the fruit of that ritual. If it is asked how the fruit of a ritual achievable through great exertion can be stated to come from mere recitation, there is no fault, because there is a distinction in the fruit based on the greater or lesser degree of effort.

Just as in the study of the *Citrā* sacrifice there is a difference regarding cattle—namely, that by performing the *Citrā* one obtains many cattle—so too in the case of heaven, there is a distinction based on whether it is experienced for a long or short duration.

He states another point regarding the result: 23. Concerning the *brahmayajña* enjoined by the sentence "One should study one's own Veda," since no result is mentioned in its own context, there arises a doubt as to whether some result must be imagined, or whether it is more appropriate to imagine a result based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), according to the principle of the *rātrisatra* section.
