Keeping in mind the established logical conclusion of the sūtra "The result [is that of the Veda] because of the mention [in the explanatory passage]"—namely, that when a result is found in an explanatory passage, the *viśvajit* principle does not apply—he says: "A verse..."

Regarding the word *paṭhan* (reciting): he states the distinction between *vākya*, *vākya*, and *itihāsa* with the words *vākya-vākyam*. He mentions another fruit established by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), "They carry the ancestors with the *svadhā*," with the words *ṛgādīnām*. "Whichever season (*ṛtu*) one studies, by that very one his sacrifice becomes performed; this is the supreme fruit of the ritual act. One shall obtain the fruit of giving a cow full of wealth in the land of Vasumatī. Even compared to the *brahmayajña*, the gift of the Veda (*brahmadāna*) alone excels. They obtain the fruit of giving the earth three times over, together with its form as grain."

The gift of the Veda (*brahmadāna*) in the form of teaching excels the *japa* [of the Veda] and the *brahmayajña*, because it yields a greater fruit in terms of wisdom (*medhā*). Therefore, the sacrifice consisting of teaching is primary; in its absence, there is *japa*. Thus ends the section on the *brahmayajña*. The fruit established by the scriptural statement, "He attains union (*sāyujya*) with the Sun," is this [attainment]. [The phrase] "on account of abundance and deficiency" means as follows: it has been said—"For a wise person, even regarding that which is more excellent, there may be a greater degree of hardship."

Furthermore, they say that great good is obtained from your hardship; this was also indicated by Jaimini in the section on *arthavāda*: "Because the fruit is produced from the action, its magnitude is like that [of the action]. He establishes the primacy of teaching over the recitation of scripture (*śruti-japa*) and other acts, which was previously promised, with the words "from the *brahmayajña*. He concludes the section on the *brahmayajña* with the words "therefore," etc. Thus ends the section on the *brahmayajña*. Now, we shall explain the ritual action (*karman*).

Now follows the determination of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the determination of its recipient. Regarding the fee for the Brahman priest which is proclaimed in a particular rite, if no specific fee is mentioned at the conclusion of the ritual, it shall consist of a full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) and so forth. In rites such as the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), and the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), where it is stated in the Sūtras, "The cow is the fee," the question arises: "To whom should it be given?"

Regarding this, he says: If a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed for a ritual action, it should be given to the *brahman* priest at the conclusion of the rite. However, when no fee is specifically prescribed, there should be a fee in the form of a full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) as stated in the Sūtra: "Having filled a bronze cup or a wooden ladle with food—whether prepared or unprepared—or even simply with fruits; this they call a full vessel. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes the passage from the *Maitrāyaṇīya-Pariśiṣṭa*: "In the absence of a fee, one gives roots and fruits as the fee."

Because that statement refers to the case where the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) cannot be obtained. (25) To the extent that the satisfaction of many eaters is produced by a full [vessel], one should not make the *pūrṇapātra* smaller than that; such is the established rule (*sthiti*). By whatever amount of food and so forth, when the vessel—such as a bronze cup (*kaṃsa*) or the like—is full, the satisfaction of many eaters occurs, one should not make that food the *pūrṇapātra*; such is the settled position of the scripture. However, more than that is not prohibited.

66. Regarding the statement "the cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," although there is no doubt as to what constitutes the fee wherever cows and other such items are specified as the fee, nevertheless, the intention is that where such an instruction is not given, a determination of it is indeed required; thus he says, "of the Brahmin. He states the definition of the *pūrṇapātra* (full vessel) with the words "as much as... He explains the word "one" (*ekam*) with the words "as much as... [This refers to] the illustration of the ritual action. It should consist of four handfuls, or even more than four.

Eight *muṣṭis* make one *kuñci*; eight *kuñcis* make one *puṣkala*. Four *puṣkalas* are prescribed as a *pūrṇapātra*. If another person performs the *hautra*, he should receive half of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). If the sacrificer himself performs both [the *hautra* and the *brahmatva*], he should bestow [the full fee] upon another. When someone other than the sacrificer performs the *hautra* rites, then the *brahmā* should take two parts of the great sacrificial fee; however, when the sacrificer himself performs both the *hautra* and the *brahmatva*, then he should give [the fee] to another.

He said to him: 26. “One who desires to give should never bypass a member of a noble family who is studying, nor likewise a nearby preceptor, even when wishing to bestow a gift, if he seeks his own welfare through the non-interruption [of the lineage]. The two terms “one who is nearby” (*sannikṛṣṭam*) and “one who is studying” (*adhīyānam*) are each connected with both [the preceding and following words]. By the word “always” (*sadā*), it is meant that even in a gift other than the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*) which is an integral part of a rite, one who wishes to give should not overstep those two. A gift is bestowed after addressing them thus: “I am giving this to him. For there is no fruit for one who gives without having asked these two, even if the recipient is a worthy vessel (*pātra*).

But when, although he is a twice-born (dvija) living near the teacher's house, no gift is given to him because of his aversion to receiving gifts and so forth, then one should give to another after obtaining permission from him by saying, "I shall give this to him," and not otherwise. The rest is easy to understand. Regarding whether a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to someone else who performs a rite for one's sake, the author says: "One should know... and so on.

Since the *pūrṇapātra* and other such items are taught as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it is understood from this that there is no sacrificial fee for him [the officiant] unless it is given to another. (Karmapradīpa 29) "Even when giving to two who are far away, one should give wealth mentally; one should then give that to others—this is remembered as the rule for giving. Even when those two are far away, one should dedicate the wealth to them by means of their general names and lineages while intending them in the mind, and then give it to others. This is remembered as the rule for giving.

In the reading *dānavidhiḥ paraḥ*, the word *paraḥ* means "most excellent. In the reading *kālavidhiḥ paraḥ*, the meaning is that even the rule for giving at the proper time—such as during the solstices (*ayana*) and so forth—is likewise of this nature, i.e., most excellent. "If one should bypass a Brāhmaṇa who is nearby and studying, and instead give to someone else, having bypassed him, he becomes tainted by the theft of that [gift]. Even when giving to others, if one should neglect one who is present and studying, and gives whatever substance after bypassing him, he becomes tainted by the theft of that [gift].

The meaning is that they incur the sin of stealing that substance. However, "In whose [house] there is a fool nearby and a man endowed with noble qualities is far away, the gift should be given to the one endowed with qualities; there is no transgression regarding the fool. On the other hand, for one who has a fool nearby—whether by virtue of venerable qualities such as study, vows, and so forth—or a person endowed with qualities is situated at a distance, the gift should be given to that qualified person who is far away, and not to the fool standing nearby out of fear of the fault of transgression; for there is no fault of transgression regarding a fool.

Regarding the phrase "it is accomplished": since the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be offered to the one who acts as both the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and the Brahman priest, he says, "When the sacrificer himself [acts as the Brahman]. Even when it is to be given to another, it should not be given to just anyone—whether a stranger or a close acquaintance. "There is no transgression against a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the Veda; for one does not cast [an oblation] into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire. Thus, there is no fault in bypassing a Brāhmaṇa who is destitute of the Veda.

Because it resembles ashes, and because that [fire] is like blazing fire. Thus ends the determination of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the determination of its purpose. Now follows the determination of the nature of the clarified-butter vessel (*ājyasthālī*) and other implements. The clarified-butter vessel should be made from a metallic substance, or it may even be made of clay; this should always be done in all rites involving the sacred fires.

In all rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), for the purpose of placing the clarified butter (*ājya*) to be offered, the vessel for the clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*)—which is made of gold or other materials, or even of clay—should be given to one who is learned or to one who is ignorant; however, it must be given only to one who is physically present (*sannikṛṣṭa*), and not even to an ignorant person who is merely nearby. He explains this meaning clearly with the words beginning "sannikṛṣṭam," while the rest is self-evident. Thus, the determination of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the determination of its recipient are concluded. — [This concludes] the section on the recipient of the fee.

"Or made of earth"—this is an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntaram*). The rest is clear. Thus ends the determination of the nature of the clarified-butter vessel (*ājyasthālī*) and other implements. [From] the *Karmapradīpa*: "In the case of the *caru* and other offerings as well, [the vessel] should always be used; however, when [such vessels] are unavailable, a shallow pan (*bhāra*) or similar item may be used. Because clarified butter is required for the purposes of spreading the *vyāghāra*, the *upastaraṇa*, the *abhighāraṇa*, and so forth, it is stated [in the text]: 'In all fire-rites (*agnikarman')... As for the measurement of the clarified-butter vessel: "One should have it made according to one's desire, taking a very firm, flawless, auspicious, and blessed vessel."

One should take a vessel that is very firm, made of baked clay, auspicious, pleasant to behold, and fashioned by hand—since that which is produced on a potter’s wheel is inauspicious because it belongs to the Asuras. As it will be said: "That which is produced on a potter’s wheel is earthen and belongs to the Asuras. Having taken such a vessel, one should fashion its transformation as desired for the purpose of holding clarified butter (*ājya*). It should be level, of the measure of a sacrificial fuel-stick (*samidh*), firm, and not excessively large-mouthed.

A vessel made of wood or of *audumbara* (fig) is also praised as a pot for the sacrificial oblation (*carusthālī*). A vessel for the oblation that is the size of a span (*pradeśa*) and has a hollowed-out base (*garbhaprastara*) is recommended; it may be made of *audumbara* wood or copper. The rest is self-evident. Furthermore, according to one's own scripture, it should be well-baked, free from burning or hardness, auspicious, neither too loose nor too brittle. This is because the scripture extends to every detail of its constituent parts.

In the sixth [section], in the fourteenth topic (*adhi-karaṇa*), there is a doubt as to whether or not the injunction for substitutes (*pratinidhi*) such as *nīvāra* grains also applies to the sentence "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*). Regarding the ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*), before the performance of the rite: "A lotus-like [object] that is fully blossomed, free from burning, and whose parts are not excessively decayed or hard is known as 'auspicious' (*śubha*). This means that the *maṇḍa* (scum) has not flowed away. There is an alternative reading: *svādukañ caruḥ khinnaḥ*. (Note: The final sentence regarding the lotus appears to be a descriptive gloss on the quality of the sacrificial substance.)

The *mekṣaṇa* (stirring-spoon) should be made of the same wood as the fuel (*idhma*) and be of the same dimensions as the fuel. It should be round, as thick as a thumb at the tip, and capable of performing the act of cutting portions (*avadāna*). Alternatively, it may be made from wood of a different species, such as *khadira*, *palāśa*, or in their absence, any tree except for those mentioned in the Sūtras—namely, the *vibhītaka* and others. It should be the size of one's own span (*prādeśa*), with a rounded handle made from the trunk of a tree rather than from a branch; its tip should be thick and suitable for cutting portions. This very same [implement] serves as the *darvī* (ladle), though I shall state the distinction between them.

The *darvī* (ladle) has its tip as wide as two thumbs; the *mekṣaṇa* (stirring-spoon), however, is like the *darvī*, but I shall state its specific distinction: the *darvī* is circular with a tip as wide as two thumbs, while the *mekṣaṇa* has a tip thickened by one-fourth part. The *musala* (pestle) and *ulūkhalam* (mortar) should be well-proportioned and very firm; they may be of any desired size, or even larger than that.

(1) Having raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there is no common injunction (*samānavidhāna*) because the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) is not understood [to apply to substitutes], [the author replies]: "True; although in the absence of the primary substance, the substitute is indeed implied by the ritual scripture (*karmaśāstra*) itself, nevertheless, at the very time of reflecting upon the meaning of the scriptural injunction regarding rice-grains, the status of being a means of accomplishment is implied for the individual instances delimited by that rice-grain genus (*vrīhitvajāti*), as well as for its constituent parts. Therefore, the reading supported by the Bhaṭṭabhāṣya is: "(1) *śrīpaiṃ vaiṣṇavameva ca*. This is the exposition of the ritual action (*karmaprakāśa*).

Or [the ladle] may be made of *vāraṇa* or *vikaṅkata* wood, according to the scriptural statement: "The sacrificial implement is made of *vāraṇa* or *vikaṅkata*. On account of the force of the Śruti text, "One should not offer with this," which refers to the *juhū* and other implements, the specific material [of *parṇa* wood] prescribed by the rule "The *juhū* is made of *parṇa* wood" excludes other possibilities. Consequently, the general injunction regarding *vāraṇa* wood finds its application only in the case of other implements such as the mortar (*ulūkhala*) and so forth. The *aiṣika* [sacrificial grass] is made of *kāśa* grass; and "it is indeed Vaiṣṇava," as recorded in the Bhaṭṭabhāṣya.

The remainder is easy to understand. By these characteristics of the clarified-butter vessel (*ājyasthālī*) and so forth, the items mentioned in the sūtra—"the *śrāvaṇa*, the *carusthālī*, the *sruva*, the *mekṣaṇa*, the *ulūkhala* and *musala*, the *māñjī*, the winnowing-basket (*śūrpa*), the bronze cup (*kaṃsa*), the *darvī*, and water"—that is, the *ājyasthālī* and others, have been clearly explained. "In the winnowing-basket, one should perform the action with the right hand on the outside and the left hand on the inside, facing toward oneself; however, in the act of pouring, the hands should be turned downward."

In the performance of the *bhūmijapa*, one should perform the *dakṣiṇa* (the southern rite) with the left hand, or with the hand—according to the variant reading *karaṃ karaṃ*—one should turn the right hand downward and, by means of the back of the left hand, make it reversed and directed toward oneself; this is the meaning. Having placed the two hands facing the fire, remaining in their own positions and composed, the performer of the sacrifice should likewise perform the sweeping (*parisamūhana*) in a clockwise direction.

Regarding the means of proof consisting of the genus (*jāti*), the individual parts (*avayava*), and the instrumentality (*sādhanatā*) which were previously understood, even though there is a subsequent cognition upon grasping some parts when all [parts] are unavailable, their status as being subject to the same rule (*samānavidhitva*) is established because they were previously understood in their own form. For they are not taken up by virtue of being *nīvāra* grains in their specific form; rather, they are designated as *nīvāra* because they possess parts of the same genus as the parts that constitute *brīhi*. Thus, the mention of *nīvāra* is for the purpose of indicating the action.

By the sūtra, "One should sweep together [the coals] with the right hand while reciting 'imaṃ stomam'," the sweeping together (*parisamūhana*)—which consists of making the scattered parts into one—is explained. Regarding that, he describes the placement of the hands: to the west of the fire, the two hands are placed facing the fire in all four directions; they are not turned downward (*nyañcau*), but rather spread out, because the unification of the scattered parts is made manifest in that way. They remain in their own positions, not touching the ground, and are moved in a clockwise direction (*dakṣiṇāvartena*).

One should perform the sweeping. The enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) should be as long as an arm, straight, without holes, and without cracks; they should be three in number, with unbroken tips, though according to some authorities, there should be four in each of the four directions. According to the Sūtra, "Some also make the enclosing sticks of *śāma* wood or of leaves," the enclosing sticks are prescribed for the purpose of spreading when there is an absence of *kuśa* grass or its substitutes. "Of *śāma* wood" means made of *jama* wood. By the statement "The enclosing sticks are as long as an arm," their dimensions are clarified. And these are three in number.

According to the opinion of some, however, there are four [enclosures] in the four directions. The rest is easy to understand. He describes the manner of their arrangement: "On both sides of the eastward-pointing [enclosure], one should place another pointing north; then another [enclosure]. If there is yet another enclosure, it should be northward-pointing in the east. One should arrange the enclosures on both sides, south and north. To the west, the next one should be northward-pointing. If one were to place a fourth, then that one should be directed northward in the east.

In the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*, it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that even for substitutes (*pratinidhi*), since the means-status residing in the primary constituent parts must necessarily be brought about for the sake of accomplishing the ritual, and because that status of the constituent parts is already known prior to the injunction of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), they are subject to the same injunction (*samānavidhitva*). Likewise, the *Karmapradīpa* states: "When the actual substance is unavailable, that which resembles it should be taken—just as barley is for wheat, or rice is for *vrīhi*."

When the prescribed substance is unavailable, that which is similar to it should be adopted. He provides an illustration: when the prescribed grains are unavailable, those similar to them are adopted. When autumn-harvested *ṣaṣṭika* rice and the like are unavailable, winter *śāli* rice is adopted. This statement is based on the principle of substitution (*pratinidhi-adhikaraṇa*), for the meaning of the scripture extends to the constituent parts, since the constituent parts are recognized even in the substitute grain.

As for the statement in the *Peṭhna* (or *Śivavacana*) that "one may provide a substitute based on similarity—such as the stalk, root, flower, or fragrance—and in the absence of everything, a part becomes the substitute," the presentation of a substitute there on the basis of similarity in fragrance and so forth is not rooted in logic (*nyāya*), but rather is rooted in the Veda itself. For the principle of substitution applies only where there is the employment of parts of a prescribed substance; however, the stalk, root, or sprout is not employed [as a substitute] in such a manner.

Furthermore, since all injunctions regarding substances and so forth extend only as far as their constituent parts, it follows that even the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as husking (*prakṣaṇa*) enjoined by the sentence "he husks the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), are established [as applying to the parts]. Thus, everything is well-established. Although the parts residing in the rice-grains are first understood as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), their status as a means does not consist in their being located within those grains; for when they are destroyed by acts such as husking, they no longer reside within them. Rather, they are the means by virtue of being parts capable of producing rice-grains. Since this principle applies without distinction even to *nīvāra* grasses used in place of rice, there is no inconsistency.

In this regard, since the very same parts that are fit for [use as] *vrīhi* rice are also present in *nīvāra* millet, one might ask: what is the proof for this? To this he says: "Because the parts of the barley (*yava*) are recognized even in the *gavedhuka* grass. By means of this section (*adhikaraṇa*), it is established—not merely the status of the parts—that things other than those [specific grains], such as the *gavedhuka*, do not possess the capacity to be a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). This is the *Karmapradīpa*.

Thus, this is the meaning of the treatise: when the prescribed substance is unavailable, one should take a similar substance that can be obtained by means of the principle of substitution (*pratinidhi*), based on a greater similarity of constituent parts; if that is unavailable, one takes something similar by means of its stalks and so forth; and if even that is unavailable, one takes a single part. As for the passage in the *Maitrāyaṇī-Pariśiṣṭa*, "If a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is unavailable, one gives roots or fruits as the fee, but one does not sacrifice in this manner," the principle of substitution does not apply there.

For where, as in the case of *brīhi* grains that have been destroyed by threshing and so forth, the means of accomplishment (*sādhanatva*) exists through their constituent parts, there alone is there regard for similarity of parts; but since this is not the case with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), only those roots that are expressly prescribed and are edible are to be taken. Consequently, even this statement is rooted in the Veda itself. However, the meaning of "one should sacrifice" is not "one should not sacrifice without such a sacrificial fee. Just as *kāśa* grass may be used in the spreading of *darbha* grass.

In the absence of that [specific wood], a substitute may be used from the aforementioned plants, with the exception of *śuka*, *tṛṇa*, *śara*, *luṇṭhana*, *balbaja*, and *palāśa*. Furthermore, for this purpose, one should use *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, *khadira*, *rohītaka*, or *udumbara*; in their absence, any forest tree (*vanaspati*) except for *tilaka*, *dhava*, *naupura*, *nimvaka*, *pityaka*, *vidāra*, *vibhītaka*, *āmātaka*, *rājavṛkṣa*, and *raktakaṇṭaka*. *Tilaka* is the white *dhava* tree; *rājavṛkṣa* is the *priyālu*.

*Kvidāra* is well known as *kāñcana* (gold), while *avuvicinvā* is *rakta-śṛṅga* (red horn). This determination of a substitute based on similarity in qualities such as fragrance is rooted in the logic of the *nyāya* (maxim) mentioned above; however, Paiṭhīnasi states that it is rooted in direct scriptural injunction (*vacana*), as in: "If one does not find this [specific substance], one should press *pūtīka* [plants]. He clarifies the preceding point by saying "evam" (thus) and "yattu tataśca" (but as for that...). In the first section of the sixth chapter of the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā*: "There is no substitution for those things whose purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*)."

Likewise, for the sake of the *puroḍāśa* cakes, they prepare the *purīḍabya* cakes using barley-like grains or rice-grains, excluding *caṇaka*, *māṣa*, *masūra*, *kraka*, *kradūṣa*, and *varaka*. Regarding these *purīḍabya* cakes intended for the *puroḍāśa*: *varaka* is *caṇaka*; *kraka* is yellow *kulattha*; *kradūṣa* is *janakradrava*, which is a substitute for *tamālya*; in its absence, one may use curd, milk, or rice-flour for the purpose of the clarified butter (*ājya*).

Where clarified butter (*ājya*) other than *tr̥tā* is prescribed, if that is unavailable, ghee (*ghr̥ta*) should be used. Thus says the Sūtra: "One consecrates as *ājya*: ghee, oil, curd, and gruel. Likewise, the Āśvalāyana [Gṛhyasūtra] states: "Whether it be ghee, or oil, or milk, or curd, or barley-gruel—one should consecrate whatever is designated by the term *ājya*. And in this matter, wherever a substitute is obtained through logical necessity, there the basis is precisely that logical necessity.

It should be understood that for the Maitrāyaṇīya school, the fact that [the text] is rooted in the Veda is equivalent to its being identical to the [Vedic] word itself. Regarding the substitute (pratinidhi): while there is indeed a substitute for those things whose unseen merit (adṛṣṭārtha) depends on specific rules, even if they are very similar, that which is prohibited cannot serve as a substitute. Furthermore, it has been established—and is well known—that in the event a substitute cannot be obtained, one should not take something merely similar to the substitute, but rather something similar to the primary object itself; keeping this point in mind, [the author now considers] the question of which items among the kuśa grass and others function as substitutes.

He explains how this is so with the word *varjam* (excluding). In this regard, the authority is the *Gobhila-sūtra*: "The *kuśa* grass for the *barhis* is cut at the tips," "the *pitṛ* [offerings] have their roots near the base," and "in their absence, [grass] having the color of a parrot's wing, or white, or reddish-white, or the color of a *suṇṭha* flower. This is from the *Karmapradīpa*. Furthermore, even by logical principle (*nyāya*), when only similarity is obtained, a rule (*vidhi*) that prescribes a specific similar item serves as a restrictive injunction (*niyamārtha*), just like the rule: "If one does not find *soma*, one should press *pūtīka* plants."

Therefore, enough with this excessive detail. The exceptions to the substitute and the substitutes themselves are to be understood from the section on substitutes (*pratinidhi*). Thus concludes the determination of substitutes. Now, regarding the word "excluding" (*varjam*): one should refer to the following *sūtra*: "He prepares [the fuel] of non-human [trees], or of *khadira*, or of *palāśa*; in the absence of *khadira* and *palāśa*, [the fuel] of *vibhītaka*, *titvaka*, *bādhaka*, *naupani*, *nimba*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *mālūra*, *khudadhityaka*, *vidāra*, *lebhātaka*, and so forth—of all trees except these, it should be according to the purpose. This *sūtra* is to be kept in mind.

It should be understood that by the word *uddhiti* the wood-apple (*kapittha*) is indicated, and by the word *śālā* the thorn-apple (*kaṣṭaka*) is indicated. Thus ends the determination of substitutes. [From] the *Karmapradīpa*: Now follows the determination of the time for the *śrāddha*. The *piṇḍānvāhāryaka-śrāddha* is recommended when the moon has waned, during the third part of the day, but not too close to the twilight.

37. 3. Regarding the two sūtras: "That day on which the moon is not seen is the amāvāsyā," and "One should perform the amāvāsyā rite on that day when the moon is not seen"—these are to be understood as follows. Of these, the first is intended to enjoin the fast (*upavāsa*), while the second is intended to enjoin the *piṇḍānvāhārya* śrāddha and other rites. In the former case, the non-appearance of the moon is intended to be stated as its essential nature; thus, the term refers to the *kuhū* (the new moon day when the moon is completely invisible), and not to the *sinīvālī* (the new moon day when the moon is slightly visible), for on that [latter] day the moon is indeed visible. In the latter case, however, the waning of the moon is intended.

Therefore, considering that there is no tautology and keeping the meaning of the second sūtra in mind, he says: "The *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* [rite]. Now, one might ask: at which specific moment should the *anvāhārya* and other rites be performed according to this sūtra? How was the determination made by Kātyāyana regarding the time and the manner? To this, he says: "In the third [part]" and "in the afternoon as prescribed in the Smṛtis. The Vedic texts, "He gives in the afternoon" and "He gives when that [day] has passed," should also be kept in mind here.

In response to the doubt as to how the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is [defined as] the time for the ancestors, he says: "Of the day... It is not only by way of traditional recollection (*smṛti*) that the afternoon is the time for the ancestors, but also by way of direct revelation (*śruti*); thus he says: "The forenoon... He explains the portion [of the verse] beginning with "nor the junction of the twilights" (*nāti saṃdhyāsaṃpataḥ*) with the words: "fifteen... And here, that which will be stated later in the *Karmapradīpa*: "The fifteenth *muhūrta* is called *māyā*; one should not perform a *śrāddha* at that time. O Rāma, it should be known as *sā*, and it is censured for all ritual acts. *Karmapradīpa*.

The *darśaśrāddha* refers to the *śrāddha* performed subsequently (*anvāḍā*) following the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. That [rite] is prescribed for when the moon has set—that is, during the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), which consists of the final five *muhūrtas* of the day composed of fifteen *muhūrtas*. For it is said: "The forenoon belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors. Even therein, a threefold division is understood.

This is excluding the period immediately following the *saṃdhyā*, which consists of fifteen *muhūrtas*. The statement from the *Matsya Purāṇa*—"the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* [should be performed]..."—is the authoritative source. Now, an objection: since the aforementioned *smṛtis*, *śrutis*, and other texts indicate that even during the time of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*)—which is divided into three parts—the commencement of the rite is prescribed specifically in the second part, it would be appropriate to perform it then as well. As it is said in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "In the morning, for three *muhūrtas*; and likewise for the same duration [in the afternoon], one should perform auspicious rites."

"The midday consists of three muhūrtas, and the afternoon follows after that. Thus, the restriction [implied by the word] "in that part" would otherwise be untenable; therefore, he says: "by the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. The sense is this: since the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and the Anvāhārya [Śrāddha] follow one after the other, when both are performed starting from the tenth muhūrta—which is the beginning of the afternoon—the performance results in the Anvāhārya being performed precisely at that time, and thus there is no fault.

Now, one might object: "Does not the designation *piṇḍānvāhāryam* itself indicate its immediate succession [to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña], and yet this is not tenable? For that designation can occur otherwise as well, according to the manner about to be explained. Anticipating this doubt, we reply: We do not assert its immediate succession on the basis of the designation alone; rather, it is established by the sequence of the ritual acts (*krama*). Furthermore, the name *anvāhārya* for this Śrāddha is due to its immediate succession [to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña]. For this very reason, the Darśa-Śrāddha occurs immediately after the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.

It should not be argued that otherwise one would fall into the error of postulating a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*); for it will be stated later that [the term] is to be understood through *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability). It is observed that in cases such as *paṅkaja*, it is only a conventional meaning already established (*klṛpta*) that sets aside the etymological derivation (*yoga*), not a merely hypothetical one. Therefore, the status of the *darśa* sacrifice as being subsequent to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* does not follow from the force of the etymology alone, but rather from the statement of Manu himself. For the text says: "A Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires, having performed the *pitṛyajña* at the waning of the moon, should perform the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* Śrāddha every month."

"However, having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires (agnimān) should perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month at the waning of the moon"—it is precisely because of this statement by Manu that [the author] says "otherwise... (anyathā). || 38 ||

46. [Objection: Since the meaning of *yaga* alone is excessively common, as in the case of the word *paṅkaja*, it is more appropriate to assume that the suffix *-ka* denotes a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*). Thus, even by means of the name (*samākhyā*), the sequence can be intended here. To this, he says: "of that which has an established usage. The sense is that, therefore, there is no conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) here. [Objection: Even in the statement of Manu, "But having performed the *pitṛyajña*," the sequence of the *āmnāhārya* is immediately after the *pitṛyajña* alone, and not immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*.

Regarding the *piṭayajña*: because of the statement, "The *pitṛyajña* is indeed the libation (*tarpaṇa*"), the *pitarpaṇa* consists solely of the libation to the ancestors. One might raise the following objection with the intention of questioning how this is consistent: "How can it be reconciled that the *pitarpaṇa* occurs immediately after the *brahmayajña* at midday, or after the morning offering (*prātarāhuti*), given that the *anvāhārya* [rice] is prescribed for the third part of the day? To this, he objects with the word "nanu. As for the phrase "pitṛtarpaṇam": [the opponent asks], "But what is this *pitṛtarpaṇa*? It is a ritual act (*karman*)."

The term *pitṛyajña* does not denote the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, because of the statement in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Having performed the *piṇḍayajña*—which is called *tarpaṇa*—a twice-born man who maintains a sacred fire should always perform the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* śrāddha on the day of the new moon. Nor should it be argued that because the śrāddha is prescribed for one who has already bathed, its sequence following *tarpaṇa* need not be enjoined.

True; however, when the *pārvaṇaśrāddha* is to be performed, since the *pitṛyajña* included within the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) is already accomplished by that very libation (*tarpaṇa*), one might ask: why is the libation to the ancestors alone intended here by the term "ancestral sacrifice" (*pitṛyajña*) in the recitation of Manu? To this it is said: "But having performed the ancestral sacrifice known as the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Thus it has been stated.

Because two statements have the same meaning, the principle applies: "A general rule that is unclear is restricted by a specific one. Just as in the statement "one should divide the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) into four parts," the word *puroḍāśa*—in the concluding sentence "this [cake] one should divide into four"—is understood to refer specifically to the cake used in the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, so too here, the sense is established that Manu’s statement intends only the *pitṛyajña* known as *tarpaṇa*.

Now, an objection is raised: even regarding the aforementioned statement, does the term "libation to the ancestors" (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) refer to the libation that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the bath, or to the libation to the ancestors included within the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*)? It cannot be the latter, because of the prohibition [found] in the *Sāma-Veda*: "Likewise, there is no [other] for the ancestors," which prohibits libations to the ancestors and so forth after the *śrāddha*; furthermore, it will be stated later that the aforementioned statement pertains specifically to those who maintain a sacred fire (*sāgni*). Nor can it be the former, because since the *śrāddha* is prescribed only for one who has already bathed, the immediate sequence [of the libation] following it would not be something to be enjoined. Thus he raises the doubt with the words, "If it is not... (*na ceti*).

In this context, there is an intention to express only the libation (*tarpaṇa*) which is a subsidiary part of the *khāna* (the ritual meal), and not anything else. This is the meaning of the statement in the *Mahāyakṣmapradīpa*: that after the *śrāddha*, the performance of the *piṇḍabali* and the *nityāhuti* follows. Otherwise, since both would be of the nature of a *pitṛyajña* (sacrifice to the ancestors), the performance [of both] would result [simultaneously]. For it has been stated by the author of the *Indogapariśiṣṭa*: "The *pitṛyajña*, however, is the libation (*tarpaṇa*)," and also: "The *śrāddha* may be the *pitṛyajña*, or else the *piṇḍabali*. The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of "and" (*ca*).

Because of the inclusion of the qualification "one who possesses the sacred fire" (*agnimān*), even for one who does not maintain the sacred fire, the daily ancestral rites (*pitrya-nitya*) must be performed immediately following that [Pārvaṇa Śrāddha] on the day of the Pārvaṇa. For this very reason, the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa states, in the section concerning the eligibility for subsequent rites: "Some excellent men desire the daily rite for the ancestors; others do not [desire it] for the ancestors in that same way, but should perform it separately as before. Others say it should be with a separate cooking; some say everything should be as before."

Regarding SC 41: The libations for the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) and other rites such as the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* included within the *jñāna-kāṇḍa* are not to be performed immediately after the *śrāddha*. With the intention that there is no room for doubt—namely, that the restatement of the sequence already established serves to indicate the absence of any other libation in between—he provides the resolution: "True."

And here, because the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is enjoined immediately after the *śrāddha*, he concludes the present subject with the words "those who possess the sacred fire" (*agnimān*), establishing that for those who do not maintain the sacred fire, the libations for the ancestors and the ancestral rites (*pitṛbalī*) must indeed be performed even after the *śrāddha*. By means of this distinction of qualified persons (*adhikāribheda*), he has indicated through an option (*vikalpa*) both the necessity and the non-necessity of performing the libation after the *śrāddha*; regarding this, he states the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*) with the verse beginning "the daily rite" (*nityakriyām*).

By this [it is meant]: "He who performs the Vaiśvadeva rite without having first performed the *pārvaṇa* (or *piṇḍa*) Śrāddha—that Śrāddha becomes as if unperformed; it does not reach the ancestors. (*Karmapradīpa*). This option is established according to the stated principle as being contingent upon whether one possesses the sacred fires (*sāgni*) or is without them (*niragni*). For this very reason, in the *Madhyamapurāṇa*, in the section on rites subsequent to the Śrāddha, it says: "Having completed the daily fire-oblation (*nityāgni*), the knower of mantras should perform the Vaiśvadeva and the regular *bali* offering."

Thus, the daily *śrāddha* is performed in this manner; likewise, following the *ānvāhāryaka-śrāddha* for one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgni*), it is stated: "When a man desires to perform a *śrāddha* for the ancestors, he should then perform the *vaiśvadeva* rite once the ancestral rites have been concluded. Manu also states regarding the rites to be performed by one with sacred fires after the *śrāddha*: "The remnants of the food should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed. One should then perform the domestic *bali* offering; such is the established rule of dharma."

[25] Having returned, prostrated, and circumambulated the fire, the knower of dharma should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite and the *naiṛtyaka* offering. O mighty-armed lord of men, having performed the *śrāddha* and dismissed the Brahmins, one should then perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites. When a man desires to perform the *śrāddha* for the ancestors, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva once the ancestral rite has concluded.

Thus, the statements from the *Gautama*, *Matsya*, and *Bhaviṣya Purāṇas* regarding the absence of fire (*niraniviṣayāṇi*) are [applicable] to those who do not maintain a sacred fire; however, the remaining portion should remain [to be performed] until the directions have been dismissed. "One should perform the domestic offering (*gṛhabali*); thus the law is settled. And from the *Karmapradīpa*: "Having completed the ancestral rite (*pitryaśa*), one who maintains a sacred fire should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*); likewise for others, one should perform the remainder as before. Thus, it is stated that these are merely optional domestic offerings (*kāmyā gṛhabalayah*), and not the ancestral offering (*pitṛbali*) nor the daily ancestral rite (*nityaśrāddha*).

Furthermore, based on the statement of Manu, it is said that one should not perform the *darśa-śrāddha* immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Even in the case of Manu’s statement, if the term *pitṛyajña* refers to the libation (*tarpaṇa*), then because the meaning of "immediately following" is already established by the statement in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, and since there is no contradiction, the statements of Manu and the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*—namely, "the *nitya-śrāddha* and so forth constitute the *pitṛyajña*"—are explained as applying to those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*).

In this sentence, "atrarccheṣaṇam" (here, the remnants of the rice), the necessity of performing the *gṛhabali* (household offering) is expressed, but not the necessity of performing the *pitṛbali* (offering to the ancestors). For it is stated in another Smṛti: "One should personally offer the optional (*kāmya*) oblations as long as one resides at home; however, in the event of illness or while traveling abroad, there may be no *gṛhabali*. Here, by the term *gṛhabali*, only the optional oblations are intended.

Since it has been stated that the state [of the householder] consists in the performance of optional rites (*kāmya*), the description of the *gṛhabali* (house-offering) during the departure [from home] cannot possibly intend to refer to anything other than the optional rite by the term *gṛhabali*. By this, it is indicated that the statement in the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra-bhāṣya* by the great scholar Tarkālaṅkāra—that the *nityabali* (obligatory offering) is also intended by the term *gṛhabali*, and not merely the *kāmyabali*, because there is no authoritative evidence for the latter—is to be considered doubtful.

Regarding this, the statement in the *Tarkālaṅkāra* by the venerable Gāgābhaṭṭa—that because the *Piṇḍayajña* has already been accomplished through the libation with fire (*sāgnitarpaṇa*), the performance of the *Piñcabali* after the *Śrāddha* is not required—contradicts the explanation in the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*. This is because it is argued that the *Piñcabali* is obligatory (*nitya*). However, even though the *Piñcabali* is obligatory, its performance in the case of one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) is precluded by the aforementioned scriptural injunction; thus, its non-performance is logically established, as explained at length [in our work]. Alternatively, it must be stated that [the scriptural injunction] serves the purpose of exclusion (*nivṛttyarthatā*).

Furthermore, there would be the abandonment of what is heard [in the Veda] and the assumption of what is not heard. Since there is no other recourse regarding the statement in the *Matsya Purāṇa*, it must be understood accordingly. Therefore, in order to avoid the abandonment of what is heard and the assumption of what is not heard, it is the immediate succession to the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* that must be enjoined in the statement of Manu. Or, let it be that the statement of Manu, "But the *Pitṛyajña*... has as its purport the *tarpaṇa* (libation).

Nevertheless, because of the statement, "The wise know the monthly *śrāddha* for the *piṇḍas* as the *anyāhārya*," let there be immediate succession to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, but not to the *darśa-śrāddha* known as the *āvika*. Or rather, even according to this verse of Manu: "O Brahmin, therein those ancestors first received the designation of *piṇḍa*; such is its established rule: the ancestors are designated by the term *piṇḍa*. (Karmapradīpa 1.66) Likewise, [there is the authority of] the *sāṅghaiḥ* [text].

By this, it is indicated that the phrase "by this" refers to the subject of one who maintains no sacred fires (*niragni*); thus, in the opinion of the author of the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*, not a single statement [in the text] becomes contradictory. However, for the *Tarkālaṅkāras*, [the following applies]: "Having performed the funeral rites and having prostrated, he who performs the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice after extracting [the portion] from the *pika* [offering], that *śrāddha* becomes as if unperformed; it does not reach the ancestors. Likewise, he should perform the remainder for the ancestors exactly as before."

Statements such as these would otherwise be rendered fruitless from my perspective; however, if one accepts the established alternatives, there is simplicity—just as with injunctions and prohibitions in different Vedic branches—and thus all [scriptural] statements remain consistent. This is the intended meaning. Now, [one might object]: "Even if it is considered a compulsory (*nitya*) part, there would be the consequence of not performing the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice before [the *śrāddha*]. To this, he says: "It is compulsory. The intention is that this follows from the context of the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*. Thus ends the discussion of the ritual action. "They constantly receive worship, just like Vṛṣākapi. (35)

Thus, according to the statements from the *Matsya Purāṇa* and the *Mahābhārata*, the *Piṇḍānām Māsika* is a monthly *śrāddha* that produces satisfaction for one month. Because of the designation, "The *māsika* [śrāddha] should be the *anvāhārya*," the meaning is that the *Piṇḍānvāhāryaka* *śrāddha* is so called because it is a *śrāddha* in which the food (*anna*) produced for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) by means of the *piṇḍas* serves as their *anvāhārya*. It is maintained that this technical name applies even in the case of one who maintains no sacred fires (*niragni*). At that time, another basis for the application of the term is also stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.

"Whatever measure of food the twice-born consume, that is called *anvāhāryaka* at the lunar sacrifice (*candraparicaye*). Thus it is said. Furthermore, the Smṛti is consistent with the statement: "In the daily *śrāddha*, the *gayāśrāddha*, and likewise the *tīrthaśrāddha*, one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* at the beginning of the Veda, and thereafter perform the *śrāddha*."

In every respect, since the term *pitṛyajña-pada* refers to the libation for the ancestors (*piṭatarpaṇa*), the conclusion that it follows immediately after the *piṇḍa-pitṛyajña* is established; thus he concludes the objection with the words "tataśca" (and therefore). Furthermore, while there may be a purposefulness and so forth according to the manner of the statement in the *Madhyapurāṇa*, and while the Manu-smṛti verse might also refer to the libation known as *tarpaṇa*, there is no authority for interpreting the Manu verse as intending that very same *pitṛyajña*.

Indeed, the Śrāddha for the Mantra-Ācārya was not prescribed prior to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña by another statement, such that it would have to be explained in that manner to establish its authority through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By this, the summary [of the opponent's view] is also refuted: "A general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*) that is unclear is to be restricted by a specific one. For this maxim applies only when the general rule is indeed unclear; and here, the statement of Manu is not unclear, since the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is clearly understood by the term *pitṛyajña*, as the ritual action is directly perceived.

The meaning of this is as follows: according to the Bahvṛcas (Ṛgvedins), after the offering of the *piṇḍas*, a small portion of those *piṇḍas* is set aside for the purpose of feeding the Brahmins; this is called *anvāhārya*. Thus, because it is brought (*āharaṇīya*) subsequently (*anu*) after the *piṇḍas* (*piṇḍebhyaḥ*), and is a small portion (*alpa-khaṇḍa*) intended for the feeding of Brahmins (*brāhmaṇa-bhojana-artha*), it is termed *piṇḍānvāhārya*. Furthermore, since the *śrāddha* consisting of the feeding of Brahmins is to be performed subsequently (*anu*) after that offering of *piṇḍas*, the term *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* can also be applied on the basis of its etymological derivation (*pravṛtti-nimitta*).

And thus, although the tenth muhūrta falls within the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), the prescription for performing the *śrāddha* during the third part of that period—the eleventh muhūrta—indicates that the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is to be performed during the tenth muhūrta of the afternoon. Accordingly, the Śruti states: "On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), they perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* in the afternoon. This is also because there is no difference in the underlying purpose (*prayojana*).

For indeed, even for Mādhava, there would be no apprehension of the contingency of performing the *piñcabali* and other rites immediately after the *śrāddha* if the *anupasaṃhāra* (non-extension) were not [intended]; because by Manu’s statement, "But the leavings... (*uccheṣaṇaṃ tu*), which prescribes only the optional (*kāmya*) *bali*, the exclusion of the *piñcabali* is already established. By this, the discrepancy with the statement in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* is also indicated.

For in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, by the single line "Having performed [the *śrāddha*], having prostrated, then... the general obligation to perform the *vaiśvadeva* after the *śrāddha* is enjoined; thus, a specific exclusion of the *piñcabali* and so forth regarding those who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is required.

In this way, since the sequence not observed [in other texts] is possible in Manu’s statement regarding the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, whereas it would be purposeless and unobserved if it were intended to refer to the libation for the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), it is logical that the word "ancestral sacrifice" (*pitṛyajña*) found in Manu’s text refers specifically to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. With the intention of resolving the objection that the *āvāhāryaka* (the monthly śrāddha) must therefore follow immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* based on Manu’s statement alone, he says: "It is replied. — *Karmapradīpa*.

For here, only the technical (pāribhāṣika) afternoon is taken. The purpose of this technical designation is simply its formulation or mention as a name. As it has been said: "Even a name is meaningful insofar as it is intended to establish a relationship between a quality and its result. Furthermore, the definition of the technical afternoon is stated in the *Purāṇa*: "The morning consists of three *muhūrtas*, and the *saṅgava* period is of the same duration. Midday lasts for three *muhūrtas*, and the afternoon follows after that. The evening (*sāyāhna*) consists of three *muhūrtas*."

"One should not perform a *śrāddha* there; it is known as *rājñī*, and is censured in all rites. Even if one were to accept that the term *pitṛyajña* occurring in the *ukta-anuvacana* refers to the *tarpaṇa* (libation), [the author] states that the *darśa* follows immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*: "Or let it be so," etc. Regarding the phrase "of the *piṇḍas*": the meaning is "of the *pitṛyajña* characterized by the *piṇḍas*."

If it is argued that even here the word *piṇḍa* refers exclusively to the ancestors (*pitṛdevatā*) and not to the sacrifice (*yajña*), [the author] says: "In that case, there is another [text]" (*tadānyadapi*). He explains the aforementioned statement with the words "The meaning of this is... (*asyārtha iti*). By this, he states the manner in which the posteriority of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) to the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is established, concluding with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Now, one might ask: how is it that it is not possible for all those aforementioned statements to have some other meaning in some way or another? To this, the teacher Kātyāyana says: "In the third part of the *Śrāddha*," as is understood from the placement of the word. From those aforementioned statements and so forth, it is understood that the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of all of them is precisely the sequence following the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* in the *Anvāhārya Śrāddha*. Thus, the great sage Kātyāyana explains [it] in the *Karmapradīpa*: "The *Anvāhāryaka* rite follows the *Piṇḍas*. And so it is.

This very afternoon is the primary time for the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Thus says Yama: "At the end of the [lunar] fortnight, the knower of Dharma should offer [the oblation] to them in the afternoon, near water, upon *dūrvā* grass, *darbha* grass, or sand. This is because Yama has stated this within the context of that very section: "To those ancestors, O Pitṛs, they give. [The word] "upon *darbha*" means upon things made of *darbha* grass.

The same applies to the *Mikata* [texts], as the *Śruti* also states: "The forenoon belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors. Likewise: "The *Śrāddha* for the maternal ancestors (*mātṛka*) is in the forenoon, that for the paternal ancestors (*paiṭaka*) is in the afternoon; the *Ekoddiṣṭa* is at midday, and that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhi-nimittaka*) is in the morning. Therefore, the tradition (*ācāra*) is what must be respected, not an interpretation fabricated by one's own intellect. Thus it is established that the performance of the *Anvāhārya* [rite] occurs immediately after the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*.

Regarding the statement, "On the new moon day, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña must be performed in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) alone," he shows the scriptural authority for this with the words, "And thus. Now, what is intended by the term *aparāhṇa* in the cited scripture? If it is understood as the latter part—that is, the portion following the twelve and a half *muhūrtas*, taking the literal meaning—then since the Piṇḍapitṛyajña must be performed in the third part [of that], its prescription would apply specifically to the third part even within the *aparāhṇa* consisting of ten *muhūrtas*.

The *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* states that [the text] indicates the procedure for the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) at the tenth muhūrta. Why, then, is only the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) definition [of the afternoon] accepted? To this, he says: "Because of the injunction regarding the [specific] time. For instance, as stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One should perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice on ground sloping toward the east" (*karmapradīpa*). There too, the same afternoon time is prescribed: "The *mātṛka* [śrāddha] is on the eighth day; the *paitṛka pārvaṇa* is on the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*); and the *pārvaṇa* in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) is indeed in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*)."

And so, in the Vāyu Purāṇa (88) and other such passages, there is an injunction for the sake of connecting the technical term *vaiśvadeva* with the eastern region; otherwise, only the *āmikṣā* sacrifice dedicated solely to the Viśvedevas would be connected with that region. Thus, in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva*," the word *vaiśvadeva* and the like are names (*nāmadheya*). Similarly here, the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) was established precisely so that by the word *aparāhṇa* (afternoon), another [time] might not be grasped; therefore, it does not apply to any other meaning.

The meaning is that "grahaṇa" (mention) signifies "asatiḥ" (non-existence). For where a name (*nāmadheya*) has its own primary meaning as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), there it is useful for connecting with a result; but where it has the status of being the thing to be referred to (*uddeśya*), there it is useful for connecting with a quality (*guṇa*). Thus, in that case, it does not have the status of being solely the enjoined, but rather also the status of being the thing to be referred to. In the present context, even though the other [the *apara*] is the thing to be referred to, only the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense is to be understood, not the literal sense. This is what is stated by the words "tad uktam" (this has been said). What then is the technical sense?

Since the term *aparāhṇa* (afternoon) has been defined as a technical designation for a specific portion of time, through this extensive elaboration [the author] has established that the *Anvāhārya* [Śrāddha] must be performed immediately after the *Sāmi* [Śrāddha]. Following that, having first determined that it must be performed even after that [latter Śrāddha], he established the sequence of the *Anvāhārya* as occurring immediately after the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Thus, although there is no specific difference regarding the performance of the *Vaiśvadeva* and other rites in relation to the *Sāmi* [Śrāddha], the sequence for the performance of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is the same in both cases.

Even though the *Piṭhyakṣa-tarpaṇa* is established according to the sound of the word "agnimaccha" in the *Ratilka*, [the author] indicates by way of conclusion that there is no distinction whatsoever because the rule "piṇḍānvāhāryaka" applies generally, using the phrase "evañca. Regarding the primary time for the performance, the *Karmapradīpa* states: "A wise man should perform the Śrāddha in the forenoon during the bright fortnight; however, in the dark fortnight, he should perform it in the afternoon, but he should not eat during the Rauhiṇa period."

The performer of the *śrāddha* should not neglect (*na laiyet*) or bypass (*nātikramet*) the moment connected to the constellation of the *Ṛkṣa* (the Great Bear) from its beginning; the meaning is that he should not perform it after that point. Thus, he cites the statement of Yama as authority for this: "And so says Yama. He explains the word "to them" (*tebhyaḥ*) as "to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ*). Why are only the ancestors mentioned? Because of the context (*prakaraṇāt*); thus he says, "the ancestors" (*pitaraḥ*).

The term *aparāhṇa* (afternoon) is used in its technical sense in the *Śrutis*, the *Brahma-purāṇa*, and other texts; thus [the author] quotes the *Śruti*. He explains the word *mātṛka* and so forth with the term *mātṛkam*. He also cites the statement from the *Vāyu-purāṇa*: "of the bright fortnight. He explains the phrase "one should not pass over the *Rohiṇī*" by connecting it with the first half-verse as well. He demonstrates the non-transgression of the *Rohiṇī* in both cases by extracting it separately with the words "by this."

"But not Rauhiṇa"—this statement from the *Vāyupurāṇa* has no syntactic connection with what is taught in the *Brahmapurāṇa*. As for the objection: "What kind of unprecedented doubt is this—that a word located in one Purāṇa should be construed with another Purāṇa?"—if you ask why the text beginning with "But not" (*na tu*) was composed to resolve such a doubt, the intention is as follows: "A wise man should perform the Śrāddha on the first day of the bright fortnight..."

For in this statement, since the word *śrāddha* must be understood as referring to forms such as the *pārvaṇa* and *anvaṣṭakā* precisely through its syntactic unity with the *Brahmapurāṇa*, it would indeed follow that when determining the meaning of the sentence through that unity, the phrase *rauhiṇaṃ tu* could also be construed with the *ekoddiṣṭa*. However, the intended sense of the rebuttal is this: for the purpose of determination, there is an integration (*upasaṃhāra*) of only those constituent parts located in one Purāṇa with another Purāṇa that possess syntactic unity.

And the phrase "not the *rauhiṇa*" is not an illustration of the ritual action (*karma*). (51) Even one who performs the *śrāddha* in the afternoon should not transgress [the rule]; therefore, the meaning is that one should not perform the *śrāddha* before [the proper time]. By this, the following is stated: the conclusion occurs in the *rauhiṇa* forenoon, while the commencement is in the afternoon; thus, the *rauhiṇa* is the forenoon, but the expression "*rauhiṇam*" does not have the *ekoddiṣṭa* as its scope. This is because the *ekoddiṣṭa* is neither mentioned in this statement nor is it the subject under discussion.

Since the determination of the share [of the day] seeks syntactic unity with the statement in the *Brahmapurāṇa* for the sake of determining its own meaning, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. And thus it is established that, in all cases, by the term "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*), it is specifically the Purāṇic afternoon that is intended.

—(4) As for what was stated by the venerable Tarkālaṅkāra in the Gābhillabhāṣya—that only that which is *parokṣa* (indirect) in the sense of being heard (*śrauta*) should be accepted for determining the meaning of the Veda, and not the inclusion of the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense of *parokṣa* as seen in such passages as "They perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña on the new moon day"—that is refuted by this [present argument].

In the statement, "The *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* śrāddha," the word "third" (*tṛtīya*) is not intended to mean the third part [of the day], but rather is intended to mean that it is to be performed immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Furthermore, according to the statement in another *Gṛhya-sūtra*, "That which is the second [rite] on the new moon day is called *anvāhārya*," it has been established by them as well that this must be performed precisely after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*.

Therefore, if that [time] alone were primary, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, which precedes the third part [of the day], would have no connection whatsoever with the afternoon time; thus, there would be great confusion. For it has been established by the principle, "In a conflict between a subsidiary and a quality, the latter is for the sake of the former," that for time only a connection with the principal act is required, not a connection with the subsidiaries. Consequently, nothing other than the portion of the afternoon belonging to the Purāṇas (the Pitṛs) is to be understood there; this has been explained in detail elsewhere.

[From] the *Karmapradīpa*: "Therefore, the meaning of the noble scripture is established as follows: the entire *pārvaṇa* rite prescribed for the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) must be performed by one without the sacred fire (*niranin*) starting from the *rauhiṇa* [muhūrta] up until five *muhūrtas*. And so it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: 'The period of five *muhūrtas*, beginning with the *muhūrta* after *kutapa*, is desired for the offering of the *svadhā*.'"

In the context of examining the sequence for collecting the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa), while the determination of the term *aparāhṇa* (the afternoon) has been established and the non-transgression of the *Rauhiṇa* time has been described, [the author] extracts and demonstrates the intended meaning with the words "tataśca" (and therefore). Intending to set forth later the rule concerning those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgni*), he first demonstrates here the rule concerning those without such fires (*niragni*) with the words "niragninā" (by one without fire). Regarding the phrase "for five *muhūrtas*," he states the authoritative source with "tathā ca" (and thus). [He explains] "from the *Kutapa*" as follows.

"Fifteen and ten *muhūrtas* are always renowned; that eighth *muhūrta* is known as the time called *kutapa*. This means [the time] from the period whose definition will be stated hereafter. It will be explained immediately below that the *muhūrta* is mentioned only figuratively (*gauṇa*) as the time for the *pārvaṇa* rite, so there is no contradiction. With this very point in mind, he begins to establish it by first analyzing the primary time with the words "so much" (*iyān*). The phrase "only from the technical afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*) means the third part of the day.

He states that the very first muhūrta of the afternoon, or even the muhūrta immediately following it, is indeed a secondary (gauṇa) time—this is what he means by "the fifth. Now, one might ask: why is the Rauhiṇa [muhūrta] considered a secondary alternative (anukalpa) rather than the primary one? To this he says: "Because it does not pervade [the afternoon]. This means that it does not extend throughout the entire afternoon. Furthermore, he says "of the fifth" because there is no scriptural censure (nindā) heard regarding it; thus, the fifth is secondary. Even so, this is the description of the ritual action (karmapradaśa).

53. Regarding the distinction between the two [times]: even for one who has no fire, the primary time is specifically the *aparāhṇa* (afternoon) as defined by the previously cited statement of Yama, namely, "The *aparāhṇa* of the ancestors. Due to some cause—whether through negligence or delay—the *pañcama-muhūrta* (the fifth period) following the *rauhiṇa* may serve as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*), because the *rauhiṇa* is not all-encompassing and because the fifth period is heard of with censure in the *Māyāhala*.

In the absence of an occasion [for a regular Śrāddha], the performance of Śrāddha during a period excluded from the kingdom and so forth is an *āpaddharma* (a rule for times of distress). And thus says Manu: "And because of the hearing of censure"—this is the meaning. This is because there is no hearing of censure even regarding the fifth [period]. Since there is no difference in their pervasiveness, the Śrāddha at night is indeed only an *āpaddharma*; this is what he states with the words "during the kingdom and so forth. Regarding the statement "one should not perform Śrāddha at night," it means that [the night] is excluded (*paryudasta*).

This was stated with the intention of explaining the meaning of the sentence: "One should perform the *śrāddha* at a time other [than the night]. For it has been declared that "she (the night) is indeed called demonic. Now, this statement is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) according to the principle of the section on mantras containing reasons (*hetumantrigadādhikaraṇa*). Just as in the sentence "Others are indeed non-animals compared to horses," the censure of one thing serves as a praise for another, so too here, even though there is a censure of times other than the night, it is actually intended as a praise of the time other than the night; or rather, the prohibition of the *vāna* (bamboo) having the night as its locus must be accepted in accordance with the *arthavāda*. Thus, no doubt remains in this matter.

Now, one might object: this is not a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), but rather a *pratiṣedha* (prohibition); for since the negative particle (*nañ*) is eternal, if it were to denote the mere non-existence of the word-meaning, it would result in the usage "one should perform [the sacrifice] with a jar. By this, the doubt that the word "na" is merely another indeclinable is also refuted; for even there, according to the maxim "and the subordination of qualities [is set aside] because of their being for the sake of that," it is proper that the meaning of the word "na" should connect only with the primary meaning of the verb, as stated in the *Karmapradīpa*.

CC: "One should not perform a *śrāddha* at night, for that is declared to be the time of *Rājasa*; nor during either of the two twilights (*sandhyā*), nor when the sun has not yet risen. (35) And it should not be argued: "This is not a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), but rather a primary prohibitory injunction (*nañ-mukhya-niṣedha-vidhi*)"; for what would be the object of this prohibitory injunction? It cannot be "at night," because in the passage: "At a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) or upon obtaining the requisite materials, one need not observe the [specific] time," there would result the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*).

66. 58. 44. He raises an objection, stating that it is more appropriate for [the negative particle] to have negation as its primary purpose: "Nor [is this so]," etc. The underlying intention is as follows: In those cases where there is an acquisition of the thing being prohibited through natural inclination (*rāga*), the negative particle (*nañ*) results solely in negation, as in "One should not eat *kalañja*," and so forth. By this, the argument to be stated later—that the occurrence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) is the very reason why the negative particle functions as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—is also refuted.

Otherwise, since there would likewise be no occurrence of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the case of "one should not eat *kalaja*," the very status of the word as a non-existent [negation] would result; therefore, in the context of the *śrāddha*, since the praise of Rāma and others is precisely what possesses the status of being the substratum (*adhikaraṇaka*), it is logical that the negative particle (*nañ*) results in a simple prohibition.

If the status of being the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) of wealth (*rāya*) is negated by the word *na rājā*, then there would necessarily result an option (*vikalpa*), since even a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) that is established by the scripture would be negated by the scripture. For this very reason, it is clearly stated in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* that in the case of the rule "one should not cut [the branch] at the first sacrifice," it is not a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) but rather an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

And thus, since the prohibition of having a kingdom as the locus (of the act) would also result in an option (*vikalpa*), it does not have the purpose of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), but rather is indeed a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*); with this intention, he provides the solution [by asking] "Where? Now, one might object: since having a kingdom as the locus is obtained through natural inclination (*rāga*), there can be no option here, just as in the case of the rule "one should not eat kalañja. As it is stated in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*: "For this very reason, when some time is obtained by implication (*ākṣepa*), there is the prohibition of the action of ruling a kingdom."

But surely, by virtue of its primary meaning being already established, let that [negation] also be like the acceptance or non-acceptance of the *ṣoḍaśī* vessel; for in the case of the rule, "One should perform the *ye yajāmahe* at sacrifices, but not at the *anuyāja*s," there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) through exclusion (*paryudāsa*) because of the resulting split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), rather than a split in the sentence occurring due to the negative particle (*nañ*) following its primary sense of prohibition (*niṣedha*).

Since the use of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in cases such as "one should not eat at Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) is well-established on the basis of the perception of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*), otherwise—even there—the taking of the bank (*tīra*) would be a matter of mere whim (*aicchika*), and because there would be no scriptural injunction (*vidhi*), the prohibition would not result in an option (*vikalpa*). Therefore, the claim that this [prohibition] has the purpose of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) contradicts the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā* and other works; hence he says: "In the original sense" (*tāttve*). And thus, by the general statement...

The sense is that since the night-time has already been reached by what has proceeded [from the preceding rule], a prohibition would inevitably result in an option (vikalpa); therefore, an exclusion (paryudāsa) alone is appropriate here. Now, one might object: "In cases such as 'He takes the Ṣoḍaśin cup at the Atirātra' and 'He does not take the Ṣoḍaśin cup at the Atirātra,' even though an option arises, the negative particle (nañ) is treated as an exclusion (paryudāsa) because it connects with the primary injunction rather than being subordinate; likewise, even if an option arises here, let a mere prohibition (pratiṣedha) be accepted. With this intention, he raises the doubt: "But if... (nanu ceti).

"By virtue of the understood primary meaning" means by virtue of the connection with the understood primary meaning. The point is that even when [the particle *nañ*] has the sense of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), there is no loss of its primary meaning. "Even so" (*api*) means "even in the case of an alternative" (*vikalpa*). "Let it be" (*astu*) means "let it be [that an alternative is accepted]. The point is that a complexity resulting in a heavier construction is not a fault when it serves as a result. He resolves [the objection] with the words "No," with the intention that: while an alternative was resorted to here because a connection via *paryudāsa* was impossible across six sentences due to lack of another way, in this case, since *paryudāsa* is possible, it is not proper to accept an alternative.

But surely, even here, although the intent is prohibitive, there is no contingency of an option (*vikalpa*); for by the statement "one should not determine the time," all [actions] are generally prohibited. Alternatively, by supplying a word and resorting to a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), one may maintain the primary sense of the text. Furthermore, the statement "the initiated does not give" has as its purpose the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the injunction "he should give day after day."

If the prohibition were intended for the initiated (*dīkṣita*), then by the phrase "except at the *Hara-hari* [sacrifice]," there would be an optional injunction for giving in the case of the initiated, whereas it would be mandatory in the case of the uninitiated; thus, due to this inequality of injunctions (*vidhi-vaiṣamya*), a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) would result. Furthermore, in the case of an option, since the times are enjoined as alternatives to the injunction being dependent upon that option, and because of the specific prohibition of particular times by the rule "not during the night," a distinction of scope (*viṣaya-viveka*) would arise—similar to the cases of "one offers when the fire is kindled" and "one offers at the footprint"—and therefore he says: "In sacrifices... (*yajatiṣu...*).

For both the general rule (*sāmānyanyāya*) and the specific rule (*viśeṣanyāya*) function only as positive injunctions (*vidhi*), not as prohibitions (*niṣedha*). Otherwise, if the specific statement "one does not [recite] *ye yajāmahe* in the *anuyāja*s," which prohibits what was generally obtained by the rule "one should perform *ye yajāmahe* in sacrifices," were a prohibition, then because a conflict (*vikalpa*) would result even there, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that accepts an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in that case would be untenable.

The intended meaning is as follows: In a prohibition (*niṣedha*), the possibility of the thing to be prohibited (*niṣedhya*) must first be established. In that case, if one were to accept—following the *paribhāṣā* which states, "Having determined that the general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*) has a scope beyond the particular (*viśeṣa*), the exception-rule (*apavādavidhi*) then applies to the general rule"—that the general rule applies to cases other than the particular, then, for the sake of establishing the possibility of the thing to be prohibited, another injunction would have to be assumed (as in the case of rules such as *na tau paṭū kartari*). Consequently, both syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and optionality (*vikalpa*) would result, leading to an excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

The point is this: just as the resort to *paryudāsa* (exclusion) was accepted in the case of "not at the *anuyāja*s," so too here, because it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), the word is not intended as a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), but rather as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Thus, in such instances, it is not proper to favor the primary sense of the negative particle (*nañ*) due to the simplicity of its connection [with the following term]. This refers to the sublation of the ritual action (*karman-pradūṣaḥ*). As for the *ṣoḍaśin*, there is no force of exclusion regarding its taking up (*grahaṇa-paryudāsa-balāt*); for its taking up is already established by another sentence, and in an exclusion, that which is already established cannot be the object of prohibition.

Otherwise, a mere prohibition (*niṣedha*) would result; for what [purpose] would there be the unrestricted application of the injunction regarding the two [types of offerings]? Furthermore, in the case of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the *atirātra* sacrifice, there would be a sublation of the context (*prakaraṇabādha*). Since there is no other possible recourse, it is an injunction of a prohibition (*niṣedhavidhi*). By this, even the result—namely, the prohibition of performing the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* when the sun is not visible—is achieved through exclusion for the sake of the purpose of exclusion. There is no fault [in this], because the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), according to the grammatical tenet: "The instrumental is used for the cause, as in 'he speaks by means of study' (*adhyayanena vartate*)."

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is a connection with the primary meaning. It is not only in prohibitive sentences that one resorts to a connection with a non-primary meaning in order to avoid a split in the sentence; rather, it is also employed in injunctive sentences—as he says, "In the Gaṅgā... The sense is that, compared to a split in the sentence, a connection with a non-primary meaning for a single word is simpler. "By supplying the words 'fish' and 'bank'"—the ellipsis is to be supplied as: "for the sake of establishing the sentence-meaning: 'He who bathes in the Gaṅgā [is one who bathes] in fish and on the bank.'"

[Objection: But surely, in the case of "One should perform the *ye yajāmahe* at sacrifices, but not at the *anuyāja*s," since only one verb is heard, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is not appropriate; thus, it is correct to rely on the individual words.
