However, here, because different verbs are heard in "One should not perform the *śrāddha* at night" and "One should not fix a time," why is a split of the sentence not also accepted? To this, he says: "The initiated... [and so forth].

And thus, just as there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)—despite hearing a difference in verbal suffixes (*ākhyātabheda*)—in the case of sentences functioning as general and specific rules, such as "One should give at night" and "The initiated one does not give," so too here, when a possible interpretation exists, it is not proper to assume a syntactical split. By this extensive argument, the view that [the text] has the purpose of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) on account of the resulting dilemma of alternatives (*vikalpa*) or the resulting dilemma of syntactical splits is also refuted. *Karmapradīpa*. Thus it is said.

Since there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) stating "one should not perform a *śrāddha* at night" with respect to all *śrāddhas*—whether *vaidhṛti*, *ekoddiṣṭa*, *pārvaṇa*, or those performed on special occasions such as at sacred fords (*tīrtha*)—even though this statement of Manu is recited within the section concerning the *darśa-śrāddha*, it nevertheless applies [to all]. For it is said: "One should offer food to the gods and present a single *piṇḍa* in the *śrāddha*; however, once the rite of offering the *piṇḍas* has been performed for him according to the law..."

"The offering of rice-balls (piṇḍanirvapaṇa) should be performed by the sons according to this very procedure," because both the pārvaṇa and the ekoddiṣṭa rites are under discussion. Regarding the established rule that "it is not [performed] on a new-moon day," one might ask: what is the harm in the alternative view? To this, it is replied: "In that case, there would be not only a contradiction of the scripture, but also the fault of contradicting the scripture upon which [the practice] depends."

The sense is that since it is established that a mere sublation of the scripture (*śāstra*) or a mere sublation of livelihood (*jīvana*) is improper, and since both would be sublated in the case of an alternative (*vikalpa*), it is not reasonable to accept that [alternative] when another way is available. Previously, it was stated regarding the sentence concerning the *ṣoḍaśin* that an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is not possible, and therefore the negative particle (*nañ*) is taken to signify a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) due to the lack of any other recourse. Now, he explains the manner in which an exclusion is impossible in that context with the words "regarding the *ṣoḍaśin*. The phrase "by another sentence" means by one that functions in a specific form, and so forth.

And thus, just as in the case of the statement, "One should perform the *ye yajāmahe* in sacrifices, but not in the *anuyāja*s," the meaning of the sentence is that [the *ye yajāmahe* applies] to sacrifices other than the *anuyāja*s; so too here, it is not possible for the sentence-meaning to be "the *ṣoḍaśin* other than the *ṣoḍaśin*" or "the drawing [of the cup] other than the drawing" or "the *atirātra* other than the *atirātra*," because such a meaning is contradicted. For that which is different from something cannot be that very thing itself. Nor is there a self-referential tautology. And thus, the sense is that there is no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in that case.

He also avoids the contingency of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) even in the case of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), stating: "And in the case of a relative negation... [and] "...because it is not something to be negated; thus, there is no conceptual construction."

[Karmapradīpa, 5.8]: "In all cases, one should be equipped with a sacrificial grass ring (parśudāman). Nor should it be argued that because the Ekoddiṣṭa, Pārvaṇa, and other rites are restricted to specific times such as midday, there is no injunction here for merely avoiding the prohibited portions of the day (such as the night), but rather [the injunction applies] to sacred sites (tīrtha) and so forth; for if the prescribed lunar day (tithi) does not coincide with midday or other such times, the Śrāddha would fail to take place. And thus [it is said]: 'The [monthly] rite should be performed on the anniversary of death every month for a year, and likewise every year, while the first [Śrāddha] is performed on the eleventh day. This is the remainder [of the verse].

Even in the case of a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), the formulation of two modes of negation within the alternative (*vikalpa*) would be entirely redundant; thus he says "otherwise" (*anyathā*). Regarding the phrase "of this injunction" (*iyavidheḥ*), the meaning is: "of the two modes of injunction involving the negative particle (*nañ*)."

It was previously stated that it is not possible for the *ṣoḍaśin* sentence to have the purpose of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) because the syntactic connection of the meaning of the term "atirātra" is otherwise untenable; now he states that even the description of the sentence-meaning through an exclusion connected to the term "atirātra" and so forth is not possible: "And in the case of the exclusion of the *atirātra*, there would be a subversion of the context (*prakaraṇabādha*). The meaning of "subversion of the context" is the occurrence of a different subject matter for another sentence.

For if the statement "one does not take the Ṣoḍaśin cup at the Atirātra" were a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), then the sentence "one takes the Ṣoḍaśin at the [other] Atirātras" could not possibly be purposeful, provided that by the phrase "at the [other] Atirātras" the absence of taking the cup at the [specific] Atirātra is intended.

If it were intended that the performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is applicable everywhere—both in the *atirātra* and in the non-*atirātra*—then the purpose of that specific statement would be fulfilled; however, in that case, the statement enjoining the *ṣoḍaśin* cup within the context (*prakaraṇa*) would become redundant. Therefore, there is no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) through the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the word *atirātra*. By this same reasoning, an exclusion through the connection of the negative particle with the word *ṣaṣṭhī* (the sixth day) and so forth is also refuted. Thus, since there is no other alternative, he concludes in the *Karmapradīpa*: "In that case, it is indeed a prohibition. (32)

Thus, according to the statement of Yājñavalkya: "O Lord of Men, on the fifteenth day of both the bright and dark fortnights, as well as during the Aṣṭakās, one should perform [the rites]; now hear from me also regarding the desired objects. And in the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well, there would not be a contradiction of the singular number; for that would result in the sublation of the plural. Therefore, there is a systematic arrangement between the midday and other such times and the portions excluded by the prohibition of night and so forth, in the sense of being the primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*anukalpa*) options. Alternatively, every time except those excluded by the prohibition of night and so forth constitutes the primary option.

The afternoon and so forth, however, are merely recommended. For this very reason, Manu says: "Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight, so the afternoon is superior to the forenoon for the *śrāddha*. Regarding the phrase "another alternative": it means a rule that involves a prohibition (*niṣedha-vidhi*). That is to say, it is a rule connected with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). This implies that the meaning of the negative particle is indeed connected to its primary sense. By this, the second half of the verse—“at both twilights, and when the sun has not yet risen”—is also explained. “The *mātṛka* *śrāddha* is performed in the forenoon, but the *pārvaṇa* in the afternoon.”

"The Ekoddiṣṭa is at midday, but that performed on account of prosperity (vṛddhinimittaka) is in the morning" (25). Regarding this, some hold the view that since the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is prescribed for the morning time itself, the prohibition of the "not-yet-risen sun" (*aciruditasūrya*) must be accepted as an integral part (*aṅga*) of that rite; they argue that an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is not possible there because both [the morning and the non-risen-sun] apply specifically. However, this is not correct; for it is said: "That which is the *ṣoḍaśin*, that which is the *atirātra*, and that which is the *grahaṇa*—all are of one form."

But here, because the phrase "one should not perform [it] at night" connects specifically with the word *aśrāddha* (non-śrāddha), and because in the second half of the verse—"likewise during both twilights"—there is no mention of the *vṛddhi* (prosperity) śrāddha, the sentence containing the negative particle (*nañ*) does not include the *vṛddhiśrāddha*. He states this distinction with the words "by this" (*eteneti*). And the *Matsyapurāṇa* says: "The fifteen muhūrtas are always renowned as the 'time for action' (*karmapradoṣa*). Among them, that which is the eighth muhūrta is remembered as the *kutapa* time."

"Since the sun always becomes dim at midday, therefore it is there that [the rite] yields fruit; thus, the commencement [of the rite] at that time is distinguished. (22) — And thus, the sense is that even at the time when the sun has not yet risen, it is not prohibited for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. Now, one might object: the statement "not at night" occurs within the context of the *darśa-śrāddha*; so how can it include all the aforementioned types of *śrāddhas*? With this intention, he provides the rebuttal: "Even though... and so forth.

Now, one might object: since the *ekoddiṣṭa* and other rites are restricted to specific times such as midday, it is impossible for them to fall within the scope of the time excluded by the word "night. Rather, the status of being a time excluded by "night" applies only to those rites like the *tīrtha-śrāddha* where no specific time is prescribed; thus, in the statement "not at night," only the *tīrtha-śrāddha* is intended, not the *ekoddiṣṭa* and others. Anticipating this objection, the author refutes it with the words "And not... (*na ca*).

He states the resolution—beginning with "vihitā" (prescribed)—that all [the times] are to be included here, based on the reasoning that since the Śrāddha would be rendered null if the midday and other times were not attained on the prescribed lunar day, and since the injunction for the annual Śrāddha would be subverted by the occurrence of a minor transgression [on that day], it is necessary to establish the midday and other times as the primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*anukalpa*) options respectively. Regarding the term "vyavasthā" (establishment): it refers to the systematic arrangement of these times.

Gautama [states] that the primary status belongs to the time beginning with the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) and other such times, while for other times—even for all times except those specifically excluded by the king and so forth—the primary status is merely the excellence of the afternoon and others. He addresses this doubt by citing the statement of Manu, beginning with "Or rather" (*athavā*). Let there be no confusion regarding the ritual action (*karma*).

In the primary ritual procedure (*mukhya-kalpa*), when the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) occurs during the dark fortnight (*asita-pakṣa*), there is no Śrāddha at another time; however, even if that [afternoon] occurs during the bright fortnight (*prāśasya-pakṣa*), there is no fault whatsoever in performing the Śrāddha at another time. The statement regarding the excellence of the afternoon is not contradictory even in the case of the primary ritual procedure. This is because the meaning of the statement is: "The Śrāddha performed in the morning and during the bright fortnight is excellent therein; and the Śrāddha prescribed for the dark fortnight is excellent when performed in the afternoon."

And thus, when that which is performed by one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgni*) is done without the *darśa* [new moon sacrifice], there it is indeed restricted to being without fire (*niragni*). However, the *darśa-śrāddha* performed immediately after that [fireless rite] is specifically praised as excellent; the sense is that this is not the primary time itself. To demonstrate that even the statement from the *Madhyapurāṇa* is an authority for this matter, he says: "of Matsya. He establishes the necessary determination even regarding the secondary alternative (*apacāya*), stating: "in the primary method" (*mukhye kalpe*). This means: in the case where the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) and so forth constitute the primary method.

"It is not [valid] at another time as the primary [time]. The word "primary" (*mukhya*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. It certainly exists as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*). And in that case, the sense is that an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed on account of the transgression of the primary time. In the view that [the secondary time] is praiseworthy, there is no expiation even at another time; nevertheless, the essential point (*niṣkarṣa*) is that it is [still valid] because of the mention of the primary time—this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: if the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) and so forth are the primary times, how can the previous statements which describe them as being "specific" (*viśiṣṭa*) be justified? To this, he says: "The afternoon, etc. (*aparāhlādi*).

In this statement, the superiority of the latter part over the former part—which was established by comparing the latter part to the former—is intended to demonstrate that there is no inferiority even in the former part. The sense is that while the injunction regarding the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) is set aside, it is not a defect [in the rule]; rather, the meaning of the injunction is simply that the rite should be performed in the forenoon during the bright fortnight and in the afternoon (*uttarāhṇa*) during the dark fortnight. He states this very point with the words "yasmāt" (because). 41.4.

*Sūtra 1: The Lamp of Ritual Action.* The Śrāddha should not be performed during the *Rauhiṇa* [muhūrta], nor even during the tenth *muhūrta*, because it is already occupied by the Piṇḍapitṛyajña; rather, it should be performed during the two *muhūrtas* immediately following that, which fall within the technical definition of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). This is the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*). However, due to specific causes (*nimitta*), it may be performed during the two *muhūrtas* immediately following the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, or even after that. Thus, four *muhūrtas* of the day's duration constitute the time for Śrāddha; the fifth *muhūrta* must be avoided because it is characterized by the proximity of the twilight (*saṃdhyā*).

Having established through this extensive elaboration that the time for the *anukalpa* (secondary option) of the *Darśa* sacrifice belongs to the sacrificer and the time for the *anukalpa* of the *Rātri-satra* belongs to the patron (*yajamāna*), and having determined that the *Darśa-śrāddha* is not applicable when the *amāvāsyā* has not been reached within the portion of the day prescribed for the *Darśa*, [the author] now states that it constitutes an *anukalpa* even when the *Darśa-śrāddha* is performed without the *Darśa* sacrifice itself: "If this is so" (*evaṃ ceti*). He states the specific rule regarding the performance of the *Darśa-śrāddha* immediately after the *Darśa*: "After its performance" (*tatkaraṇānantaramiti*). Thus ends the section on the *Sāma*.

Immediately after that, if two *muhūrtas* out of the four *muhūrtas* [of the afternoon] are not to be accepted for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*—due to the tenth *muhūrta* being occupied by the half-day [rite]—then this results: the two *muhūrtas* included within the technical *aparāhṇa*, which constitutes one-third of the day, are its primary time (*mukhya-kāla*); the two *muhūrtas* immediately following that are the secondary time (*gauṇa-kāla*); and the fifteen *muhūrtas* following that are governed by the rule: "not too close to the evening twilight" (*nātimandhyāsamīpataḥ*).

Thus, since it is prohibited by another specific injunction, the sense is that the following statement by Kātyāyana—which concludes that the rule regarding the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* Śrāddha applies specifically to the Sāṃnāyya sacrifice—is established: "The *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* Śrāddha is recommended on the fourth part of the day, before the arrival of the evening twilight (*saṃdhyā*). In this verse, because of the absence of the word "on the new moon day" (*amāvāsyāyām*), [the rule] is understood to apply when the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) extends into the fourth watch (*yāma*). [From the *Karmapradīpa*, 6.23.64: "When the fourteenth day fills the fourth watch..."

The *śrāddha* is prescribed for that very [fourteenth] day when the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is waning. When the fourteenth day extends into the fourth quarter of the next [fifteenth] day, and on the following day the waning moon occupies the third part of the day, then the *śrāddha* is prescribed for the fourteenth day alone. Thus, even though the new moon does not reach the prescribed third part of that day, the *śrāddha* is performed on that very day because the third part is not reached on the subsequent day.

Now, one might object: "In this case, [the statement] 'On that day when the moon is not seen at all, one should perform the Amāvāsyā rite' (Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.1.30) implies the acceptance of a time defined by the waning of the moon; yet, even when the fourteenth day has ended and the new moon (Amāvāsyā) has arrived, there is the injunction for performing the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha. To clarify the underlying intention of Kātyāyana’s statement—which was begun in order to make explicit what was previously obscure—[the author] introduces it with the words "on both days," beginning with: "When [the moon is seen] on the fourteenth day... and so forth.

The meaning is that the determination will be stated later regarding both cases where the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurs during the third part of one day, and where it occurs during the third part of both days. Regarding the phrase "one should perform [the rite] on the fourth part": the meaning is when the new moon occurs during the second part of the fourteenth day. On the fourteenth day, both the waning of the moon and its presence exist during the third part; however, since there is no waning of the moon on the following day even though the third part is pervaded by it, the performance of the rite does not take place on that [latter] day.

By this, it is already explained that even when the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) does not occur on the following day, it refers to the preceding day. All of this is stated by the verse beginning with *caturdaśyāḥ*. However, it is not the view of Gṛhyasūtrakāra Śabara that the term *amāvāsyā* refers exclusively to the time of the moon's conjunction; for he says: "On the day when the moon is not seen at all, one should perform the ritual on that *amāvāsyā*. [Otherwise] there would be a contradiction with the *Śruti*, because the moon is seen on the remainder of that day during the *Minnuvālī* [period].

Nor should it be argued that, on account of the Gābhiila-sūtra stating "even when [the moon] is visible at one time," this time is merely optional; for since Śruti and Smṛti are not of equal authority, no option between them is possible. For this very reason, the objection that [the rule] "only when [the moon] is not seen" contradicts the Sūtra was not raised; because that contradiction is avoided by the option provided in the [Gābhiila] Sūtra, "even when visible at one time. Therefore, he removes that contradiction with the Sūtra "one should perform [it]," considering that the non-appearance of the moon alone constitutes the meaning of the term *amāvāsyā*.

If it is argued that by this [explanation] the Vedic scripture—"on which day the moon is not seen"—is also explained, then here the venerable Tarkālaṅkāra says in his *Ābhilāṣitārthacintāmaṇi*: "The new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is the waning of the moon; the non-appearance of the moon is also the new moon."

"One should give [the gift] when the moon has waned" and "on that very day"—from these two scriptural statements (*śruti*), the first refers to the waning [moon] and the second to the waxing [moon], according to the intended meaning of its rising. Thus, there are two sūtras: "On that very day when the moon is not seen" and "On that very day when the moon is not seen, one should perform the *Amāvāsyā* sacrifice. And in this case, there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the two scriptural statements. For it is not appropriate to interpret the word "not seen" in the scripture as indicating "waning"; otherwise, the two sūtras would be redundant.

Thus, they say that the conventional usage of the term *candracaya* (the waning of the moon) for the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is not untenable. Regarding that new moon day: here, the new moon day can be of three kinds—extending over less time, extending over an equal amount of time, or extending over more time than the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) of the preceding day. The first is called *kṣīṇā* (waned), the second *staṃbhitā* (stilled), and the third *vardhamānā* (increasing). As it has been said: "On whichever day the moon does not appear..."

With regard to its waning, it should be understood that the phrase "when the moon has waned" (*kṣīṇe rājani*) is also intended to mean its disappearance. The meaning of the Vedic statement, "on which day it becomes invisible," is intended to refer to its waning. As for what we have stated previously—that [the Śrāddha] is performed when [the moon is] in the fourth or eighth [lunar mansion]—that too is not intended to mean its invisibility, which would contradict the Sūtra; rather, it is intended to mean its waning. And he will state that this waning occurs during the fourteenth and eighth watches (yāmas) of the night. Therefore, because the Śrāddha is performed on that day when the moon has waned, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "They themselves define [the term] as 'māna' (measurement). Here, if two types of *amāvāsyā* were indicated by the two *sūtras*, then why was it not indicated in any way at all? Thus, even in the two *sūtras*, only the waning (*caya*) is intended. If one asks, 'For what purpose are there two *sūtras*?', it is precisely for the sake of defining that the *amāvāsyā* for the fast (*upavāsa*) is specifically characterized by the waning of the moon, and unlike the *paurṇamāsī*, there is no option between a partial or full [wane]."

And thus, there is no contradiction even when the sentence from the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, "He gives when the moon has waned," is taken as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the sentence from another Vedic text, "When this very moon is not seen. For, once the status of being a single syntactical unit is established, the non-perception [of the moon] will result in the exhaustion [of its digits] by way of logical necessity (*pāṭhika-vidhayā*); therefore, there is no occasion for the fault of having to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as proposed by the Tarkālaṅkāra. In this way, the unity of the two scriptural statements is also established.

Regarding the two sūtras, we do not know what basis there is for determining whether the sūtra "caturdaśyāṃ candra" (on the fourteenth day, the moon) determines the meaning of the scriptural statement, or whether the sūtra "yadaiṣā" (when this [moon]) determines the meaning of the scriptural statement; nor do we see both sūtras. From the very mention of the word "not seeing" (*adarśana*), it is understood that the sūtra proceeds as a single syntactical unit with the scriptural statement regarding non-perception. This is the application of the ritual act (*karmapradarśa*). As for what was said: "Even when [the moon] is visible, [it is so] in relation to the fourteenth day."

The *śrāddha* prescribed for the sight of the moon on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) refers specifically to that day when the moon is visible; it is for the purpose of "seeing" the moon, not for the purpose of its non-decrease. Therefore, there is no contradiction. On that day, is the *śrāddha* to be performed at the time of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)?

Or rather, because the moon's waning is observed at both [the beginning and the end] of the fourteenth watch (yāmaka), there is doubt; otherwise, why did the authors of the Sūtras not employ the word "waning" (*caya*) alone in one instance? You yourselves should deliberate upon this. Thus, it is the opinion of Vācaspatimiśra and others that an explanation based on syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is indeed appropriate here.

Among these two views, the second alone is the opinion of the authors of the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* as well; for the authors of the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*, intending to explain the scriptural sūtra "yadahar eva" in accordance with their own view, raise the objection—"How can it be said that [the rite] is recommended when the moon has waned?"—which contradicts the Śruti, and then dispel this doubt by demonstrating that the Śruti has the sense of "cayana" (the act of piling), beginning with the words "nanu" and so forth. This is what is meant by "tāvaddarśanam."

The meaning is that it does not refer merely to the word "non-perception" found in the *Sūtra*. And thus, it is indicated that it is logical for the statements regarding the waning [of the moon] and the non-perception [of the moon] to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). Now, an objection is raised: "If the time for the *śrāddha* is indeed the waning of the moon, then how is the description of the *śrāddha* even when it is not waning justified by the *Sūtra* which says, 'Even when [the moon] is visible on one occasion'? To this, he replies: "On the fourteenth day. He states this because, in this context, the word "visible" (*dṛśyamāna*) is not intended to imply the absence of waning.

Now, if the *śrāddha* is indeed to be performed on the fourteenth day as well, then should it be performed on that day only at the time of the new moon (*amāvāsya*), or is it proper to perform the *śrāddha* even without that [specific] time? This is the sense: "If one should wait for the new moon, one may offer [the oblation] even when the sun has set. (Karmapradīpa).

If the new moon (amāvāsyā) occurs during the third watch or the fourth watch of the day, then one should wait for it for the sake of the *śrāddha*. However, if the new moon falls during the final muhūrta of the fourth watch, then one should perform the *śrāddha* precisely at the end of the last watch of the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*). This is because the Vedic injunction, "One should offer to the ancestors on the new moon," would otherwise be contradicted.

[The author] states, "On that day," in order to dispel the doubt and objection that the subsequent portion of the text—namely, the statement that "the term *amāvāsyā* refers to the waning of the moon"—would be contradicted by the argument: "If the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is indeed the waning of the moon, then it would be appropriate to perform the *Śrāddha* even without waiting for the final watch of the fourteenth day; and if it must be performed on the [fifteenth], then it is not logical that the term *amāvāsyā* refers to the waning of the moon. **Sanskrit Text:** *candra- 60 (6 " candracaya evā'māvāsyā, tarhi vinā'pi pratīkṣāṃ caturdaśyantimayāme śrāddhaṃ kartuṃ yujyate, yadi ca pratīkṣā kartavyā, tarhi candracaya evā- māvāsyeti na yuktamiti "candracayaparatvādamāvāsyāpadasye"tyuttara- granthavirodhāpattirityāśayaśaṅkānirāsārthaṃ " amāvāsyāṃ pratīkṣeta " iti ślokāṃśasya pravṛttirityāha- taddine iti ||* **English Translation:** [The author] states, "On that day," in order to dispel the doubt and objection that the subsequent portion of the text—namely, the statement that "the term *amāvāsyā* refers to the waning of the moon"—would be contradicted by the argument: "If the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is indeed the waning of the moon, then it would be appropriate to perform the *Śrāddha* even without waiting for the final watch of the fourteenth day; and if it must be performed on the [fifteenth], then it is not logical that the term *amāvāsyā* refers to the waning of the moon. Although the waning of the moon (*candra-caya*) alone is what is denoted by the term *amāvāsyā*, nevertheless, because the waning of the moon during the first watch of the new moon day is primary—being more significant than the waning occurring during the fourth or eighth watches—it is proper to understand [the rite] as being performed at that time; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, in the passage, "On the *amāvāsyā* they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña," the term *amāvāsyā* likewise intends the waning of the moon itself; thus, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña must also be performed on the fourteenth day itself.

In this way, designations such as "piṇḍānvāhāryaka" and scriptural statements such as "the second śrāddha on the new moon day is the anvāhāryaka" become logically consistent. Regarding the term "aparāhṇe" (in the afternoon), since there is no specific definition provided here as was done previously, it is understood that the *paurāṇika* (mythological) definition alone is intended here. Furthermore, it has already been established previously that the *paurāṇika* definition of "afternoon" alone is authoritative, and not the "third part of the day" (tṛtīyāṃśa) definition.

In the passage, "On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), by means of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña," the word *amāvāsyā* refers to the time of the waning of the moon (*cayaparatva*). For this very reason, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is also performed on that same day, because at the time of the fourteenth lunar day (*caturdaśī*), the waning of the moon is obtained during the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). Therefore, Manu says: "Having completed the Pitṛyajña, one who maintains the sacred fires [should offer it] when the moon has waned. He states the time of the moon's waning: "In the eighth part of the fourteenth day, the moon becomes exhausted."

It is fivefold: as the first digit (ekanakalatva), the second digit (dvitīyakalatva), the third digit (tṛtīyakalatva), the fourth digit (turīyakalatva), and as the total waning (sarvacaya). If it is argued that since all these constitute the meaning of the term "waning of the moon" (candracaya), there would follow the performance of *śrāddha* even on other lunar days—just as on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*)—the following is intended: the state of the fourth digit and the state of total waning constitute the meaning of the new-moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Therefore, the time for *śrāddha* extends as far as the state of the fourth digit.

Since that period of four *nāḍikās* occurs during the eighth watch of the fourteenth day and the ninth watch of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the time for the *śrāddha* rite extends from the eighth watch of the fourteenth day until the end of the ninth watch of the new moon.

In this regard, just as in the statement "one should not overstep the *ṛhiṇa*," the *ṛhiṇa* (the fifth muhūrta) serves as a secondary option (*anukalpa*), so too here, the fourth part of the day serves as a secondary option, while the waning of the moon (*caya*) is the primary [time]. This distinction must be understood; thus, even the mention of the afternoon (*pratīc*) and so forth becomes meaningful. [From] the *Karmapradīpa*: the meaning is that the time for the waning (*caya*) begins from the remainder of the fourteenth lunar day until the eighth watch (*yāma*) of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Now, is "waning" (*caya*) destruction or subtlety? It cannot be the first; [because...]

It cannot be the first [alternative], because that [decrease] is absent in the waxing moon; nor can it be the second, because if it occurred in the new moon alone, there would be no decrease, which would result in the impossibility of the *cayā* (the waning phase). It is said in reply: both the state of having the fourth digit remaining and the total destruction are denoted by the term *caya*. For decrease (*caya*) is of two kinds: partial decrease and total decrease. Partial decrease is the state of having the fourth digit remaining, and that occurs during the final watch of the fourteenth lunar day.

The complete waning [of the moon] occurs on the seventh new moon day, and on the eighth, there remains only the fourth digit (kalā); thus, there is no occasion for the performance of śrāddha on another lunar day. He establishes this very point by citing the statement of Kātyāyana: "On the eighth part of the fourteenth day... and so forth.

For when the state of the fourth digit (*turīyanakalatva*) occurs by way of increase (*caya*), it is designated by the term "increase" (*caya*); and when it occurs by way of decrease immediately following total destruction (*sarvakṣaya*), it is designated by the term "minute" (*aṇu*). Thus, it is entirely logical that on the fourteenth day, during the eighth watch, it is conventionally referred to by the term "increase," and on the ninth watch of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), by the term "minute."

The venerable Nārāyaṇa Pāṭhaka maintains that the word *punaḥ* (again) serves as the indicator for the natural consistency [of the text] in the sense that the state which exists during the eighth watch of the fourteenth day is exactly the same immediately following the eighth watch of the new moon day; however, the great scholar Tarkālaṅkāra explains the passage from the Gṛhyabhāṣya—"in the eighth part of the fourteenth day"—differently.

Their intention is as follows: the reading "maṃtritaṃ bhavedaṇuḥ" is not authoritative, because the reading "tataḥ kila bhavedaṇuḥ," which includes the particle *kila*, is seen in all the treatises; furthermore, it has been read in that very way by Śūlapāṇi and other highly authoritative scholars. Those who know the movement of the moon declare a distinction between these two: "It remains for a day and a night; with one-quarter of a *kalā* remaining, at that very end it undergoes complete waning—thus say those who know the circle of luminaries (*jyotiścakra*). In short—even while following the opinion of Nārāyaṇa Pañcānana, Vācaspati Miśra reads here simply as "tataḥ" (from there), and neither does he read "na vā punaḥ" (nor again), nor is such a reading appropriate.

For if the same kind of waning (*kṣaya*) that occurs during the final watch of the fourteenth day were intended to apply to the portion of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) as well, then it would be improper to designate it by the term *āgu* instead of the word *caya*, because that would result in a mere figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Because of this statement, [the time for the conjunction] is the first watch of the new moon (amāvāsyā), or at its end, that is, the final watch of the new moon. Likewise, because it is appropriate, the first watch of the first day of the month of Bhādrapada is also a time for the conjunction. Thus, the specific designation is that the conjunction of all [planets] is understood to occur only in the seventh watch of the new moon, and not in the first watch of the new moon.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "it would again become an atom" (*punaḥ kila bhavedaṇuḥ*): the application of the word "atom" (*aṇu*) here is possible only through the further reduction of constituent parts (*avayava-apacaya*). Since such a reduction is impossible on the new moon day (*amāvāsya*) or the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*), the term does not apply in its primary sense. Rather, it refers to the state of being merely another minute particle (*aṇumātra-avasthāna*), and moreover, to the state of having only a fourth part remaining. Thus, the sentence "it would again become an atom" must be accepted as intending the absence of accumulation (*caya-abhāva*) by way of describing the meaning of the statement that [the moon] arises on the new moon day or the eighth day. It is understood as "it becomes minute," "an atom is produced," or "it is reduced to a minute state."
