To the question, "In what case, then, is there no conceptualization? he says: this is clearly understood from the preceding and following passages regarding the "object" (*viṣaya*). Thus, even when the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurs during the third part of the day prescribed for the observance, if one performs the rite on the previous day, it is nevertheless proper to perform it on the following day—specifically during the period characterized by the waning of the moon—even if the new moon occurs at twilight or during the night, just as in the case where the new moon occurs [at a time] other than the third part of the day.

For it has been stated by the authors of the *Tarkālaṃkāra* themselves: "On the fourteenth and eighth lunar days of the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Jyeṣṭha, no *śrāddha* is performed because there is no waning of the moon (*candracyuti*) at that time; rather, it is performed only on the new-moon day (*amāvāsyā*). If the new-moon day is not obtained on the preceding day, the *śrāddha* may be performed on the following day as well, since the waning of the moon is attained then. Thus, one must investigate how they could have stated that "on the preceding day alone no *śrāddha* is performed" when the new-moon day falls at night.

If it is argued that because it is prohibited, the lunar day (tithi) is not applicable there, then in that case as well, since the time of the conjunction with the twilight (*sandhyā-sampāta*) is prohibited by the rule "not until the twilight has fully set in," it is equally appropriate to perform that rite on the following day alone.

Regarding the statement, "One should complete the fourteenth lunar day at the end of the watch," although—according to the method of Tarkālaṅkāra—the use of the word *su* (well/at the end) does not intend to imply a connection with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) for the entirety of the fourteenth day's watch, nevertheless, a connection with even a single portion of that watch is certainly required; for it is said "the remaining watch of the fourteenth day," rather than "the fourth part."

(1) The use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in *upedhvam* is because it is derived from the root *i* with the suffix *āṣet*. There is an alternative reading: *gatādhyām*. [This refers to] the description of the time for the *pitṛyajña*: "One should observe the increasing new moon (*vardhamānāmāvāsyā*) on the following day; the *pitṛyajña* should take place when [the moon] covers three or even more *yāmas*. 'Increasing' (*vardhamānā*) means extending over the third part of the day in comparison to the waning [moon]. Even in the absence of obtaining the [lunar] wane at the end of that [day], the *śrāddha* should take place on that very same [day]. Thus, there is an option regarding the limit."

And so says the *Laghuhārīta*: "Indeed, there is no possibility of performing the *śrāddha* during the remaining watches beginning with the fifth, because it is prohibited. Since this prohibition applies without distinction, the term "fourth watch" (*turīya-yāma*) refers exclusively to the portion of time other than the *saṃdhyā*. Thus, the conclusion of Tarkālaṅkāra is not in accord with that of Kātyāyana; enough of this excessive detail.

Having determined the subject matter—namely, when the *śrāddha* should be performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) that has been exhausted by the preceding elaboration—he points to the section beginning with "mixed" (*saṃmiśrā*) in order to explain it; for that section was undertaken to resolve the doubt as to when the *śrāddha* should be performed on a mixed new moon day. Thus he indicates it: "mixed."

If the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) lasts until the preceding day and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) persists until the following day, that too is a mixed new moon; if the new moon on the following day exceeds the duration of the fourteenth day on the preceding day, that is a mixed new moon. Regarding this, some consider the fourteenth day to be censurable, while others consider it fit for ritual performance; such is the meaning of the statement, "that which is the fourteenth day... and so forth.

And here, there is no option regarding the *vardhamānā* [meter], because its commencement occurs in the subsequent [section]; rather, it is only for the *staṃbhitā* [meter] that there is an option—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Where, then, is there no option? To this, he introduces the verse beginning with "SE karmapravacaḥ": "The *pūrvā* and *darśā* [days] should be performed as even *vimuhūrta* by the Bahvṛcas; the *kuhū* [day] should be performed by the Adhvaryus; and by the Sāma-gāyins as they desire."

By the *adhvaryus*, who are followers of the *Yajurveda*; for the followers of the *Sāmaveda*, there is freedom of action as they desire. One should always perform the *caru* offering on the day following the [lunar] fortnight (*pakṣādau*). Other wise men maintain that one should perform it only in the forenoon; by the phrase "others," even the view of non-performance is indicated. Thus ends the determination of the time for the *śrāddha*. Regarding the question "In which [time]?"—it says, "The *pitṛyajña* occurs then. This means that the *pitṛyajña* and other rites should be performed on the very next day.

He states that there is no harm even in the absence of the moon’s rising during the *vardhamānā* [period], saying: "The moon... (2.24). Regarding the statement, "When [the breath] is arrested, there is conceptualization," he also cites the words of Hārīta as authoritative, saying: "And likewise... The phrase "as one desires, with the songs of the Sāman" refers to the subject at hand. According to others, just as there are distinctions between the branches (*śākhā*) of the Veda, there is also a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) according to the different Vedas; thus, for others as well, there is indeed an option.

The statement, "Alternatively, [one may study] one's own branch," is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); for this very reason, the conclusion reached in the *Ācārādhikaraṇa*—that the *smṛtis* of Gautama and others are to be studied by all—is logically established. Indeed, dharma and adharma are not determined by difference of region or difference of person. "Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda in due order, the study of all the Vedas is mandatory for everyone."

The sense is this: although the study of a specific branch (*śākhā*) other than one’s own Veda is prohibited, nevertheless, the study of another Veda is not prohibited; thus, for all [these cases], there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*). Thus ends the determination of the time for *śrāddha*. [Now begins] the *Karmapradīpa*, the section on *Śrāddha* (80). Now, regarding those *śrāddhas* for which one whose father is living is eligible, it is stated that even this *smārta* *śrāddha* must be performed in exactly the same manner as the *vaidika* [rite].

As it has been said: "When there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, Śruti alone is more authoritative; when there is no conflict, the Smārta [practice] should always be performed, just like that which is Vedic. Now, if the performance of the Śrāddha is indeed based solely on Smṛti, how can its performance be enjoined? For a human-authored Smṛti is not an authority regarding Dharma. Furthermore, the authority of the Smṛtis—composed by Manu and others who were knowers of the Vedas—is established only through the inference of a Vedic basis, provided that those [Smṛtis] have no perceptible worldly motives that could be suspected.

For indeed, many Smṛtis are found to be rooted in worldly gain (*lābha*) and the like. It is for this very reason that Jaimini’s Sūtra, "And because of the observation of a motive" (*hetudarśanācca*), is appropriate. The Smṛti rule, "The entire Audumbarī post is to be wrapped," is likewise explained by this [Sūtra]; for even there, there is no authority based on being rooted in Śruti. Thus, there would be no settled rule as to which Smṛti is authoritative and which is not; therefore, he says: "Śruti... and so forth.

This is the established rule: a Smṛti that is not contradicted by Śruti is authoritative; a Smṛti that is contradicted by it and has a perceptible motive is not authoritative. Thus, since the Smṛti regarding the performance of Śrāddha is not contradicted by the Veda and has no other [perceptible] motive, its status as authoritative remains intact. The sense is that, like a rite based on Śruti, a rite based on Smṛti must also be performed. Furthermore, this Śrāddha is not to be performed for one who has sacrificed for three ancestors (pitrāditrayayājī), but rather for one who performs the rites for one or two ancestors.

Among the three groups beginning with the father (*śrāva-pitr-ādi*), even if only one is deceased, the *pārvaṇa* rite is performed for all three persons; however, if the father and the others are living, only the *āgrahāyaṇī* (or *āgrahāyaṇī-śrāddha*) is performed. Thus says Viṣṇu: "He who performs the *śrāddha* while his father is living should perform it for those for whom his father would have performed it; while his father and grandfather are living, he should perform it for those for whom his grandfather would have performed it; while his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are living, he should not perform it at all. This is what is meant by the phrase "the father and so forth" (*pitr-ādi*).

And he cites the statement of Viṣṇu as authoritative: "And likewise" (*tathā ca*). For here, seven daughters are intended. They are as follows: the first alternative is that [the daughter inherits] while her father is still living, provided the others have died; in this case, the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is made to the grandfather, the great-grandfather, the paternal grandfather, and the paternal great-grandfather. The second alternative is that [she inherits] when both the father and the grandfather are living, provided the great-grandfather has died; in this case, however, the offering of rice-balls is made to the great-grandfather, the grandfather, the paternal grandfather, and the paternal great-grandfather.

The third case, however, concerns one who lives by cremation (citayajñajīvana), wherein no one offers the *piṇḍa* [funeral cake]. This means that for one who lives by cremation, there is no entitlement even to the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* (prosperity rite). When only the father has died while the grandfather and great-grandfather are still living, then this is the fourth alternative. The conclusion here is that one *piṇḍa* is offered to the father, another to the grandfather, and two are offered to the deities beyond the great-grandfather.

The fifth position, however, belongs to the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) when he is deceased while the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) is still living; in that case, immediately after the offering of the two *piṇḍas* to the father and grandfather, another must be given to the great-grandfather’s grandfather (*pitāmahapitāmaha*). This is the *Karmapradīpa*. Here, by the phrase "one who should perform the *śrāddha*," even the alternative of non-performance is indicated. He whose father is deceased should, having placed the *piṇḍa* for his father, give [the other two] to those beyond the great-grandfather.

And the particle *eva* (only) should be understood as follows: [the rule applies] that the father is the deceased, but not the grandfather or great-grandfather. He whose father and grandfather are both deceased should, after offering two rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to those two, offer to the great-grandfather’s grandfather. Here too, by the force of the particle *eva*, the survival of the great-grandfather is implied. He whose grandfather is deceased should, after placing a rice-ball for him, offer to the two ancestors beyond the great-grandfather. Here too, the particle *eva* is to be supplied.

This is the sixth auspicious occasion (*kalya*): when one obtains the opportunity [to perform the rite] upon the death of the grandfather (*pitāmaha*), while the father and great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) are still living. In this alternative (*vikalpa*), having offered the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to the grandfather, two rice-balls must be offered beyond the great-grandfather.

Regarding the seventh alternative, where the father’s grandfather is deceased while the great-grandfather is still living, the conclusion is that after offering two *piṇḍas* to the father and the father’s grandfather, one should offer [the third] to the great-grandfather’s father. Keeping this purport of Viṣṇu’s statement in mind, he says: "And in this case... The intention is as follows: the offering of *piṇḍas* must be performed in sequence for three ancestors, whether they are deceased or not yet deceased. This should be understood from the *Vārāhapradīpa*.

A wise person should perform the *śrāddha* for his mother in this very manner; [he should offer] with mantras according to the rule, and for the remaining [ancestors], it is without mantras. Thus is the method of *śrāddha* when the father and others are living: just as there is no offering to the father while he is alive, so too when three [ancestors] are living, there is no offering—according to that principle. "According to the rule" (*yathānyāyam*) means in accordance with the rule. He explains "with mantras according to the rule" by saying "according to the rule."

The meaning is as follows: *ūha* (adaptation) is the modification of either a mantra or a ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*) that has been extended by analogy (*atideśika*). Thus, since even in the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* (the ancestral rite for maternal grandfathers), the mantras occur precisely through that extension, it must necessarily be understood that the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *pitṛ-pārvaṇa* (the ancestral rite for paternal ancestors). To this effect, he says "in this way" (*evam*) in the *Malamāsa-tattva*; the phrase "while the father and others are living" (*pitrādi-jīvane*) is its explanation.

In the *Śrāddhamayūkha*, the extension (*atideśa*) is described according to the statement: "For the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*s) as well, the *vaiśvadeva* ritual is indeed performed in the same manner. However, in the *Hemādri*, it is stated: "The restatement [of the rule] regarding the modification (*ūha*) that is established by logic is for the sake of a single performance; otherwise, there would be a doubt that it does not apply. In any case, the modification (*ūha*) is indeed accepted by all. Here, by the phrase "in the mantra," it is understood that for all mantras containing the word "father" (*pitṛ*), the term "maternal grandfather" (*mātāmaha*) is substituted.

Even so, the word *pitṛ* (father) is used here [in the mantra] in its primary sense as referring to the progenitor (*janaka*), and not in the sense of the state of being a father (*pitṛtva*) produced by the *śrāddha* rites ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. This has been stated in the *Mayūkha*: "The word *pitṛ* is employed in two ways: in some cases it denotes the quality of being a progenitor, as in the verse beginning 'He whose father has passed away' (*pitā yasya tu vṛttaḥ syāt*); in other cases it denotes the status resulting from the *sapiṇḍana* rite.

For example, having realized that the meaning [of the word *pitṛ*] is not applicable [to the maternal grandfather], one should substitute the word *mātāmaha* for the word *pitṛ* in the mantras; however, when the meaning is applicable, this is not done. (68)

For instance, in such passages as "svadhā va tarpayata me pitṝn" (Svadhā! Satisfy my ancestors), "āyantu naḥ pitaraḥ" (May our ancestors come), "eta pitaraḥ" (Come, O ancestors), "atra pitaraḥ" (O ancestors, here), and "devatābhyaḥ pitṛbhyaśca" (To the deities and to the ancestors), the word *pitṛ* (ancestor) does not refer solely to one's biological father because of its plural form; rather, it is primarily applied to all [ancestors], including the maternal grandfather and others, by virtue of being the cause for attaining the status of an ancestor (*piṭatva*). This is seen in such statements as: "When the deceased has attained the status of an ancestor through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite," and so forth. This [status] is conditioned by the *piṇḍa* (rice-ball) produced by the *śrāddha* performed at the end of the ritual procedures. Thus it is said.

For this very reason, the word *pitṛ* (father/ancestor) is applied to the *sapiṇḍas*, as in such passages as: "Thereafter, one should commence the *śrāddha* with devotion for the six ancestors," and "One should pour the vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors. Thus, since it is necessary to determine in which mantra the word *pitṛ* occurs by virtue of the primary condition of being a progenitor (*janakatva*) and in which it occurs by virtue of another condition, he begins [the discussion] with the words "tathā hi" (for instance). Regarding the phrase "svadhā astu": [an objection is raised] "But how can there be reference to the progenitor here? To this he replies: "Because of the plural number (*bahuvacanāt*)."

In this context, the mere use of the plural number does not preclude reference to the progenitor; rather, it refers only to those instances where the word is not accompanied by other mantra-texts containing distinct terms such as *pitāmaha* (grandfather) and so forth. Therefore, bearing in mind the distinction that even when the plural ending occurs—as in “May the fathers be purified, may the grandfathers be purified” (*śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ śundhantām̐ pitāmahāḥ*)—the word *pitṛ* does not refer to the progenitor, he says: “But where... (*yatra tu*). Thus, this is established: where there is reference to the progenitor, there [the plural refers to him]; but where there is no such reference, there it does not.

Now, one might object: even in the verse beginning with "O Pitṛs," although the word *pitṛ* refers to progenitors, because of its association with a specific gender and its plural ending, it denotes the ancestors—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. For this very reason, it is stated: "Thereafter, the offering of the Śrāddha is for the six Pitṛs. Consequently, since the meaning is already fully encompassed, there is no need for separate words for the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) and so forth. [The mantras are: "O Father, this is for you"; "O Grandfather, this is for you"; and likewise, "To the Pitṛs..."

In expressions such as "svadhāstu pitāmahebhyaḥ svadhāstu," the application of words like *pitṛ* (father) and so forth is based on the relationship to the one offering the *śrāddha*. In that context, because the meaning is not inherent (*asamaveta*) in the maternal grandfathers and others, there are mantras such as "mātāmahedaṃ te 'rghyam. Furthermore, even when referring to a single individual, the plural form is used—as in "svadhāstu pitṛbhyaḥ"—just as in the usage of the plural in the mantra "aditiḥ pāśān pramumoktu."

Since it is appropriate to proceed with the *mudāya* (the modified sacrifice) itself, how could the word "father" (*pitṛ*) not also apply to the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and others in the modification (*vikṛti*)? To this, he says: "from six" (*ṣaḍbhyaḥ*). Thus, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the word "father" does not refer to the grandfather and so forth through a direct connection (*liṅgasamavāya*), but rather solely by virtue of the attainment of the class-property "fatherhood" (*pitrkatva*). The sense is that, because that basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—namely, fatherhood—is common to the maternal grandfather and others, its meaning is not inherently restricted to the specific individuals in the archetype; therefore, it applies in the modification as well.

An objection is raised: "Surely, where the word 'father' (pitṛ) is applied by virtue of the condition of being a progenitor, let the plural number there have a non-inherent meaning; but where [the application] is by virtue of the condition of being a progenitor, how can it have an inherent meaning? And thus, how is the validity of such expressions as 'svadhā to the fathers' (pitṛbhyaḥ svadhāstu) to be established? In response to this doubt, he says: "Even in the case of one," and "Aditi."

The two mantras, "aditiḥ pāśaṃ pramumoktu" and "aditiḥ pāśān pramumoktu," are recited in the section concerning the immolation of a single animal (*ekapaśu-kathāga*) according to different Vedic branches (*śākhābheda*). In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the mantra containing the word *pāśa* in the plural form should be displaced (*utkarṣa*) to a rite involving many animals. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the plural number is subordinate to the meaning of the base noun (*prakṛtyarthopasarjana*) and serves as an indicator of the action (*karmapradīpa*). Thus, it remains applicable here.

Likewise, the sense is that excellence is not intended [as a primary meaning], according to the principle from the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* stating, "When a quality is mentioned, it is improper to assume [an unintended] implication. By that principle, the use of the plural number here is also justified. The phrase "O Father, this is for you (*pitara idam te 'rghyam*)" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the entire series beginning with "May the ancestors sip it (*unvantāṃ pitaraḥ*). By this, the *Mayūkha* states: "In this matter, the venerable grandfather [holds that] there is no occasion for considering whether or not to perform *ūha* (modification) in the formula 'O Father, this is for you.'"

This is not contradictory to what was stated: "Because these [mantras] lack the status of being mantras by virtue of being mere utterances (*abhilāpamātra*), otherwise, by the statement 'for the rest, excluding mantras,' it would follow that Śūdras could utter them. Since the word 'mantra' is used in its primary sense for Vedic mantras—which are not of human origin—and in a secondary sense elsewhere, it is for this very reason that the conclusion in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* (Pāda 1) regarding the non-mantric status of *ūha* and the like is logically established. Thus, what was said is also not inconsistent. 6.

In reality, however, the mantra "O Father, this is for you, the *arghya*" is indeed a mantra; for in the *Śūdrakaṭaka-śrāddha* and other rites, the application of the mantra "O Father, this is for you, the *arghya*" is actually observed. Indeed, the opinion of the authors of the *Prakāśa* is that one cannot conclude that the sentence "O Father, this is for you, the *arghya*" used by them is not a mantra simply because of that, and thereby assert that even the version used by members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) lacks the status of a mantra.

Therefore, it is appropriate that the subsequent description of phrases such as "O brother, this is for you" is understood to originate from human intellect. Likewise, it appears more reasonable to hold that the phrase "O father, this is for you" is not merely an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) [of the specific deceased], but rather a general indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) applicable to both oneself and others. By this same principle, the plural form is also used in the *śrāddha* for one's maternal grandfather and others, because its meaning is not inherently connected to the specific subject at hand.

Therefore it has been said: "Therefore, one should not [use] the plural. Thus the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) has also been explained. As stated in the *Mayūkha*: "And it should not be argued that because the plural number in the archetype (*prakṛti*) does not refer to the actual object when there is only one father, therefore in the modified rite (*vikṛti*) only the form ending in the singular should be employed; for it is settled in the ninth section concerning the *pāśa* (the 'noose' discussion) that even if the plural in the archetype does not refer to the actual object, in the modified rite the very same form—unaltered in its constituent parts—is to be employed."

Now, if in passages such as "nanveta pitaraḥ," the word *pitṛ* ending in the plural does not refer to biological fathers, then in cases such as "piḍhbhyaḥ svadhā'stu pitaraḥ," it would likewise not refer to biological fathers; consequently, the grandfather (*mātāmaha*) would become the recipient of the *svadhā* offering there. To this, he says: "to the *pitṛs*. This must be investigated: in the *śrāddha*, is the status of being a deity (the object of worship) restricted to the deceased biological fathers and so forth, or rather to the deities presiding over them, such as the Niṣvāttas and others?

On this point, the *Nirnayamindu* states: "In this context, by the words *pitṛ* (father) and so forth, the status of deity is attributed only to the progenitor and others, not to [deities such as] the Vasus and others. This is because of the *Śatapatha Śruti*: 'O [Name], this for your father, the sacrificer'; 'O [Name], this for your grandfather, the sacrificer,' and so on; and because of the *Viṣṇu Smṛti*: 'He whose father is deceased should, having offered the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to his father... As for that which Manu and Devala say: "The Vasus are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras are to be known as the grandfathers... [this refers to the *Karmapradīpa*.]

Yājñavalkya said: "The Prapitāmahas are likewise the Ādityas; this is the eternal Śruti. [66] "The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the Pitṛs, the deities of the Śrāddha"—this is for the purpose of knowing their non-difference. And this knowledge of non-difference is established by such scriptural statements as: "Viṣṇu is his father, O Janaka, for he is indeed the sacrifice itself; Brahmā is to be known as the Pitāmaha, and I am the Prapitāmaha. Thus ends the section on action.

It has been established that there is no contradiction in meaning through either a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*), but rather a systematic arrangement according to practice (*yathācāra*), and so forth. Śūlapāṇi also clearly elucidates this very point. The distinction regarding compassion is as follows: since the statements of Manu and others are *smṛti* (tradition), whereas [the injunctions] such as "Asāv etat te" are *śruti* (revelation), Kātyāyana’s statement—"In the case of a conflict between *śruti* and *smṛti*, the *śruti* alone is more authoritative"—shows that the statements of Manu and others must be interpreted otherwise, for the purpose of removing obstacles. This has been explained therein.

In the Hemādri, it is stated: First of all, in the case of the deities of the Śrāddha, the injunction does not prescribe that the sacrificer should view his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather as being identical with the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs and so forth; for there is an absence of Vedic texts, indicative marks (liṅga), and other such evidence to support that. Indeed, it is not taught that one should perform the visualization of the Smara Pitṛs and others upon one's own father and ancestors, in the manner of the injunction, "One should meditate upon the sun as Brahman."

As for the injunctions in the words of Manu, Devala, and others regarding the non-difference (*abheda*) of Vashtha and the other ancestors from the Pitṛs and so forth—that too does not mean that one should perform the visualization (*dṛṣṭi*) of Vashtha and the others as being the Pitṛs. This is because such an interpretation is possible through a figurative intent (*prāśastya*), just as in the case of the statement, "The sun is the sacrificial butter" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*). Thus, the injunction of the vision of non-difference is refuted. Nor are there injunctions for Agni, Yama, and the others to serve as the deities of the *śrāddha*, since: "He is a true son who follows his father while he is still living. (68.4)

"One should satisfy those who are established [in their respective realms] with various kinds of *śrāddha* offerings. Passages such as these indicate that the deceased humans themselves attain the status of deities. For this very reason, the use of dative-case forms such as "to the father" (*pitre*) and "to the grandfather" (*pitāmahāya*) is also highly appropriate; thus, logically, the ritual action is directed toward the father and others themselves. However, if—on the basis of the plural form in the expression "Svadhā to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ svadhā*)—the word "ancestors" (*pitṛ*) were understood to refer to the class of Pitṛ-deities...

If [the mantra] were applicable to all [ancestors], then expressions such as "to the grandfathers" (*pitāmahebhyaḥ*) would be unnecessary, as this would result in redundancy. Furthermore, if mantras such as "Come here, O fathers" (*eta pitaraḥ*) were intended for the *agnivāttas* and others, then their status as deities (*devatātva*) would be even more clearly established. Having thus demonstrated through the three means of *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya*—in accordance with the views of Hari, Hara, and others—that the *agnivāttas* and others alone possess the status of deities, [it is concluded that they are to be worshipped] "through the vision of non-difference. However, this position is the one that ought to be accepted as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

For this very [practice] is seen in the *Ācāra*; this alone is approved by all those who possess universal vision; and this alone is indeed faultless. For it has already been stated previously [in verse 64] that the purpose of such [descriptive] statements lies in their being injunctions (*vidhi*). Even if, in the sentence "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*), it were to be so [that the post is actually the sun], what would be lost for the ritual action? At most, there would simply be the presence of qualities (*saguṇatva*); thus it has been described.

And thus, the view accepted by Nirṇayasindhu, Śūlapāṇi, Viśvarūpa, Hemādri, and others is that the deities are indeed Janaka and so forth; according to their system, in the formula "O Father, this is for you" (*pitara idaṃ te 'si*), and so on, the status of the deities as Vasu and others—accepted by Kriyāsamuccaya and other authorities—is established even in cases such as "O Father, this is for your benefit" (*pitara idaṃ te 'rtham asi*) and so forth. He explains this with the words "these [deities]" (*ete*). Regarding the phrase "in the Agniṣṭhātta and so forth," [he says] "O Fathers, this is your garment" (*etad vaḥ pitaro vāsaḥ*).

Furthermore, just as the plural number in the word *pitṛ* (father/ancestors) is not intended to be significant even when it refers to Vāsava and the other [Vedic ancestors], so too is the word *pitṛ* [in the context of the Śrāddha]; the sense is that since the words *pitṛ*, *mātāmaha*, and so forth are synonyms for Vāsava and the others, the Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather and others is not necessarily required here. By this, it is indicated that although there is a difference in the fruit depending on whether Vāsava and the others are the deities or Janaka and the others are the deities, [the rite remains the same]. This is from the *Karmapradīpa*. Regarding this, the authors of the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* state:

Even though [the identification] is not seen in the *Ācāra* [section], the position that [the sacrificial post] has Vāsudeva and other deities as its presiding deities (*devatā*) is indeed logical; however, they indicate that in the case of [the view] regarding the *Agniṣvātta* ancestors and so forth, this is understood through the word "but" (*iti tu*). This is their intention: it is well known that Hemādri stated that whatever was established in the *Hemādri* regarding the purpose of the non-difference knowledge (*abheda-jñāna*) from the words of the mantras and so on—even in cases such as "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*), if the intended meaning is simply the knowledge of non-difference between the sacrificial post and the sun, there is no loss [of validity].

Furthermore, in that case, the futility of the section on the *Tattvasiddhipetika* remains unavoidable. As for what was stated in the *Hemādri*—namely, that there is no scriptural text (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), or the like regarding the vision of non-difference (*abheda*)—no refutation of that has been made therein either. For in the *Hemādri*, no alternative interpretation whatsoever was offered for those scriptural texts and indicative marks that were established in favor of Agniṣvātta and the other deities; thus, the position that Agniṣvātta and the others are indeed the deities is the more sound one.

This has been stated in the *Mitākṣarā*: "For in this context, it is not Devadatta and others alone who are designated by the words 'father' and so forth as the recipients (*sampradāna*) in the rite of *śrāddha*; rather, they are [designated] only when accompanied by the presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-devatā*). Just as by the words 'Devadatta' and so forth neither the body alone nor the self alone is expressed, but rather selves qualified by the body, even so Devadatta and others are expressed by the words 'father' and so forth only when accompanied by their presiding deities."

Furthermore, the presiding deities such as Vāsava and others, being pleased by [the offerings of] food, drink, and so forth from the sons and other [relatives], satisfy those [deities] within Devadatta and others, and subsequently endow the sons and others with the fruit [of their actions].

Just as a mother, being herself satisfied by consuming food, drink, and other sustenance not given to her, yet nourishes even the child within her own womb, so too do those who bestow gifts and the like [reap results]; she binds them with the fruit of counter-action. In that same way, the sons of Aditi—those very ancestors who are the Ādityas—are designated by the terms *pitṛ*, *pitāmaha*, and *prapitāmaha*. 44. That is the teaching on karma. 61. Those who are the Pitṛs are indeed the Ādityas themselves; they are what is expressed by the words *pitṛ*, *pitāmaha*, and *prapitāmaha*.

"It is not only Devadatta and others who are deities of the *śrāddha* and serve as the recipients (*sampradāna*) in the *śrāddha* rite; rather, humans satisfy their own ancestors—such as Devadatta and others—who have themselves been gratified by the *śrāddha*, through the excellence of their knowledge and devotion. That Hari, Hara, and others also hold this very view is described in the *Hemādri* itself.

As for the fact that Śūlapāṇi has accepted even the statement of Kātyāyana—"But when there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti"—as his own support, this contradicts the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *Tantravārttika*, which states: "But where the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is perceptible and the Śruti is inferential, how is it then? Śruti alone is more powerful.

By the statement of Kātyāyana, it is established that Śruti is more powerful than Smṛtis devoted to injunctions; however, it does not apply to a conflict even when the Smṛti is devoted to an injunction regarding a mantra whose indicative mark is based on Śruti.

By stating, "This is the eternal Śruti," the venerable Manu indeed demonstrates that even the status of the Vasus and others as deities is established by the eternal Veda; how, then, can his statement be interpreted otherwise in contradiction to another Śruti? For the venerable Manu establishes that the words "father" and so forth found in the Śatapatha Śruti—such as in the passage "O [Agni], this is for your father, the sacrificer"—refer specifically to the Vasus and other such deities.

And thus, since the authority of the authors of the Smṛtis is stronger than that of the authors of the Nibandhas (digests), we observe that the authors of the Nibandhas have been forced to interpret the words of Manu and others otherwise. For the statements of the Smṛtis are of the nature of direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and were not conceived by Manu and others through their own intellect; whereas the statements of the Nibandhas are of the nature of analytical investigation (*parīkṣā*). Therefore, we too consider the view that Vāsuki and others are indeed the presiding deities (*devatā*) to be appropriate. Thus, regarding the rites for the father and mother, Manu says: [text follows]

In the verse "etad vaḥ pitaro vāsaḥ," the mantra should also be applied to each individual *piṇḍa* (funeral cake). Even though the attainment of the *pitṛs* (ancestors) is the occasion [for the rite], because there is a single intended referent (*eka-paratva*), the use of the plural number and the collective application (*samasta-prayoga*) are grammatically correct. Thus, it is established that the conclusion of the authors of the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa*—that in the view where words such as "mahān" refer to the Vasus and so forth, no modification (*anūha*) is required, and this is established by logic—is not untenable. This is proven.

In this view, following the statement "the same applies to the maternal grandfathers," the modification (*ūha*)—though not established by logic—is not improper in the *śrāddha* for maternal grandfathers and others because it is based on scriptural authority. However, there is no intended meaning for the phrase "according to rule" (*yathānyāyam*). This was stated with the reading *mantraheneti* accepted in the aforementioned *Viṣṇu-smṛti* passage; but if the reading is *saṅkhyeheneti*, the meaning is that one should reflect upon the fact that the plural number in the word "according to rule" lacks a corresponding referent.

And thus, in accordance with the aforementioned statement, in the *śrāddha* for maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) and others, in formulas such as "Svadhā to the Pitṛs," one must apply the word "maternal grandfather" (*mātāmaha*) and so forth precisely in the singular form. Even in cases such as "Let there be *svadhā* to the Pitṛs," since the plural number is used only in reference to the Agniṣvātta ancestors and others, how could the plural number therein be considered to have a meaning not inherent to the context? Furthermore, [if that were so], the formula "Let there be *svadhā* to the paternal grandfathers" (*pitāmaha*) and so forth would also result in being redundant. To address this, [the author] says: "etad... [and so on].

This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for [mantras] such as "siṭabhdhaḥ khadhā'stu. Regarding the phrase "pitṛloke": the meaning is that even though [the word *pitṛ*] refers to Agnivāttas and others, it has a singular referent. He states the reason for its having a singular referent: "because of the application of the mantra to each individual *piṇḍa*. The point is that, because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than the direct statement (*śruti*), the plural number is understood to have a singular referent in accordance with the application of the mantra—just as, for example, the word *indra* in the mantra "kadācana" refers to *agni*. Thus, the *Brahmapurāṇa* says: "Reciting 'etadaḥ pitar vāmasu,' [one offers] separately, separately..."

"Then Vāma should recite: 'O such-and-such [name], this [is for you]'"; thus ends the *Karmapradīpa*. Regarding the formula "O Pitṛs," this very same application is used even in the annual *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. However, in the *preta-śrāddha*, because the word *pitṛ* (father/ancestor) lacks collective meaning, the term *preta* (departed) is used; yet the plural number remains as in the original model (*prakṛti*). To support the fact that the plural in the aforementioned mantra refers to a single individual, he cites the testimony of the *Brahmapurāṇa*, beginning with the words "And likewise."

If, however, in the *śrāddha* for maternal grandfathers and others, the modification (*ūha*) of the mantra "mantrahana yathānyāyam" is accepted for the sake of logical consistency—even though Agni-vāttā and the other deities remain the same—the distinction of the vessels and so forth is indeed observed based on their being the substratum for the paternal ancestors (*pitṛs*) and the substratum for the maternal ancestors (*mātāmahas*). In that case, since the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would not be inherent (*asamaveta*), the modification of the sacrificial vessel (*havirdhāna*) is perfectly justified. Now, an objection is raised: in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite performed annually (*māṃvatsarika*), in the phrase "etadaḥ pitaraḥ," the singular number is indeed required.

Therefore, the statement of Viṣṇu—"One should modify the mantras in the singular in the *ekoddiṣṭa*"—is justified. The meaning is as follows: in the *ekoddiṣṭa*—that is, in the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha performed on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) or during the *cayana* rites—one should modify the mantras so that they are in the singular; this is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), as explained in the *Mayūkha*. Hence he says, "Thus," referring to the *sāṃvatsarika-ekoddiṣṭa*. [As stated: "The *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed for the ancestors on the day of death; if a person abandons the *ekoddiṣṭa* and performs the *pārvaṇa* [instead]..."

The meaning is that this is established by the statement of Vyāsa: "One should know that to be unperformed, as indeed is the case for the slayer of a father. (Karmapradīpa). In the Nirṇayasindhu, it is stated: "In this regard, one view is that for the legitimate son (*aurasa*) there is the *pārvaṇa* rite, while for the adopted son (*dattaka*) and others there is the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; another view is that for those with a living father there is the *pārvaṇa*, and for those whose father is deceased there is the *ekoddiṣṭa*," and so forth—all of which should also be considered here. "Ityeva" means "only in the plural form."

The meaning is this: according to the *Purāṇas*, that which is prescribed as a single offering (*ekoddiṣṭa*) should be performed in the same manner as the *pārvaṇa* rite; however, in the case of the single offering for the deceased (*pretakoddiṣṭa*), because the rule for modification (*ūha*) is established by the specific mention of the "deceased" (*preta*) in the singular, the status of being an ancestor (*pitṛtva*) cannot arise through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. For this very reason, the word "father" (*pitṛ*) is excluded by Āśvalāyana.

As for what was stated in the *Mayūkha*—namely, that since there is no evidence for this statement having the *preta-ekoddiṣṭa* (the single offering for the deceased) as its subject matter, and because the word *preta* is not perceived [therein], and because enjoining both [the word *pitṛ* and the plural suffix] would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), the use of the plural form of the word *pitṛ* is established even for the *purāṇa-ekoddiṣṭa* by the logic of the ninth *pāda* section—[we reply: in that case, since the plural suffix specifically pertains to the *preta-ekoddiṣṭa*, and because there is no syntactical split due to the enjoining of a qualified whole (*viśiṣṭa-vidhāna*), that [objection] is untenable. 19.

— This is the intention of the authors of the *Prakāśa*. They hold that this rule for modification (*ūha*) is intended by the logic [of the text] specifically regarding the statement of Viṣṇu; however, since the singular number is not established by logic, and because in reality even at the *pretaśrāddha* the singular number is not appropriate, they say "but at the *pretaśrāddha*" with this intent. [The reason given is] "because the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has a meaning that is not inherent to the context."

The point is that even in the view where the deities are Agniṣvātta and others, because they lack identity with Devadatta and the rest after the *piṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, they are not denoted by the word "father" (*pitṛ*). As for the plural number: in the *Nirṇayasindhu*, it is explained that although Viṣṇu’s injunction states, "In the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, the mantra is modified to the singular," the plural form may also be used here according to the scriptural statement. Regarding the phrase "for the remaining [relatives], excluding Manu," the portion concerning the "remaining ones" refers to brothers and so forth, as stated in the *Hemādri*: "The ancestral rite is prescribed for the fathers; for the remaining ones, i.e., for brothers and others."

The *śrāddha* should be performed excluding [mantras such as] "O Pitṛs, rejoice," "Svadhā to the Pitṛs," and so forth. The meaning is that even for the mantra "O Pitṛs, this is for you," there is a mantra containing the word "Pitṛ" (father) but excluding the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*), and it applies only to those [ancestors] other than the maternal grandfather. And in this context, the mention of the number [of ancestors] is indicative; it does not, however, constitute a prohibition of mantras in the *śrāddha* for the father and others. Thus it has been explained.
Śūlapāṇi, however, explains: "Even when the paternal uncle and others are mentioned, the purpose of the exclusion of mantras is that they are not joined with the words [of the mantra]."

"The *Kālataru* states: 'The purpose of [specifying] the *ekoddiṣṭa* for paternal uncles (*piṭavya*) and others is to exclude the mantras for the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth. However, in the *Śrāddhamayūkha*, it is established by the venerable grandfather (Gadādhara) that: 'For those born of Brahmin women and for the son of a Śūdra woman, the purpose is to exclude the mantras; thus, the *śrāddha* for them and for the son of a Śūdra woman is performed without mantras. Furthermore, prior to the instruction of the vows (*vrata*), they should perform the *śrāddha* with the deities according to the eastern direction, as per the tradition of Marīci.'"

In that regard, keeping precisely the reading "mantrahina" (devoid of mantras) from the statement of Viṣṇu in mind, the meaning is that the scriptural prohibition of all mantras for the *pitṛ* (ancestors) is intended; it does not mean, according to the view of Hemādri, that only those mantras containing the word *pitṛ* are prohibited. Nor is there any evidence for the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of mantras concerning the *bhagāpukṭi* (the offering to the wives of ancestors) as suggested by the view of Ācārya Madhusūdana, because there is no authority for such a restriction on the remaining ritual elements (*śeṣapadārtha*) in the manner of Mayūkha. With this intention, he says "of the remaining ones. The meaning is "of these [remaining ones]. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the paternal uncles (*pitṛvya*) and others are included.

[This concerns] the *karmapradaśa*. In the case of [the substitution of] a brother or others, there is indeed a sublation (*bādha*); however, it is not that the mantra "O brother, this is for you" is merely modified, but rather that this is a completely different expression arising from the desire born of the intention to perform the *śrāddha*. And thus says Hārīta: "One intends with the mind, expresses with speech, and accomplishes through action. Thus, even recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is sublated, as in the *Kalpasūtra*, by the statement of sublation: "devoid of the mantra."

It has been stated that when both the father and the grandfather have passed away, one should perform the *nava-śrāddha* for two [deceased] according to the procedure for a single vessel (*pātra-vidhi*). Regarding this, the *Kalpataru* explains: "The rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) are devoid of mantras. Śulapāṇi maintains that the mantra mentioned in the *Pitr-paddhati* is not to be employed at all, nor is the mantra containing the word *pitṛ* (father) to be used. However, with the intention that both of these views are untenable because there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for such a restriction regarding specific mantras, he says: "Ita pitaraḥ" (Come, O fathers).

Now, if [it is argued that] phrases such as "O brother, this is for you" lack the status of being mantras, how then can they be employed? To this he says: "Others. He states "And likewise" to show that this usage is also approved by Hārīta according to his own statement. Now, since there is recognition of the mantra-status in cases such as "I offer this to you," how can it be said that these are not mantras? To this he says: "Recognition also... [as in] "O brother," just as in the case of the *Kalpasūtras*.

For just as it was established in the *Kalpasūtra-adhikaraṇa* (the section on the Kalpasūtras) under the *Satapāda* that the status of being the Veda—which is recognized in the case of the Kalpasūtras and others accepted through the rule of study (*adhyayana-niyama*) and which concern subjects such as the *brahmayajña*—does not exist [as an independent Veda], so too is the sense of the term *ajā*. This is the direction [of the argument]. It is even more so [in the case of the *Ajā* mantra].
